talks.title: Practitioners' Perception of ML-Based Security Tools and Explanations
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Practitioners' Perception of ML-Based Security Tools and Explanations.
talks.summary:
Study Design

Jaron Mink (UIUC) presents interview findings on SOC practitioners’ views of ML-based security tools and explanations. Eighteen professionals with at least one year using classification tools participated in hour-long interviews covering backgrounds, ML usage, and three explanation types.

ML Plus Rules in Practice

Most SOCs combine ML with rule-based detection rather than using either alone. Rules anchor detection for known behaviors with lower false positives; ML supplements detection of novel activity but alone draws skepticism due to false-positive load.

Benefits and Pain Points

Practitioners weigh usability, effectiveness, adaptability, efficiency, and security. ML’s black-box outputs hinder trust, yet complex third-party rules are also opaque—“find who wrote the signal.” Hybrid approaches balance coverage and alert volume.

Explanations and Needs

Added ML explanations are evaluated against whether they resolve operational challenges. Correct classification under non-adversarial conditions remains the paramount unmet need; practitioners doubt ML alone meets SOC requirements despite industry AI hype.

talks.title: DVFS Frequently Leaks Secrets: Hertzbleed Attacks Beyond SIKE, Cryptography, and CPU-Only Data
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning DVFS Frequently Leaks Secrets: Hertzbleed Attacks Beyond SIKE, Cryptography, and CPU-Only Data.
talks.summary:
Hertzbleed Beyond SIKE

Researchers show DVFS-based Hertzbleed side channels extend past the broken SIKE protocol to patched cryptographic implementations and non-CPU components when power differences affect CPU frequency.

Amplification Requirement

Single-instruction Hamming-weight leaks are too small at millisecond DVFS granularity; attackers need gadgets that cumulatively change power draw, as in the original SIKE analysis.

Revived Crypto Targets

BearSSL ECDSA and classic McEliece implementations thought mitigated against prior side channels leak leading-zero nonce bits through timing when combined with existing lattice attacks.

GPU Cross-Component Leaks

Pixel-stealing SVG filter attacks thought fixed by constant-time GPU rendering can return because GPU power draw influences CPU frequency, letting JavaScript infer cross-origin iframe pixel colors.

talks.title: Bitcoin-Enhanced Proof-of-Stake Security: Possibilities and Impossibilities
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Bitcoin-Enhanced Proof-of-Stake Security: Possibilities and Impossibilities.
talks.summary:
Context

Anusratas presents joint work on Bitcoin-enhanced proof-of-stake security, motivated by Ethereum's merge and PoS goals: lower energy, faster confirmation, and validator accountability.

Accountability limits

Accountable safety identifies at least one-third double-signing validators after conflicting finalizations, but evolving stake and posterior-corruption attacks—publish attack chains only after unbonding—block slashable economic penalties for late-joining clients.

Babylon architecture

Pair a PoS chain with Bitcoin as a data-limited timestamping server; periodic succinct commitments (block hash + aggregated BLS signatures) anchor unbonding order so late clients can reject post-unbond attack chains.

Properties and costs

Babylon claims slashable safety, optimal resilience bounds, and improved liveness (one-third to one-half); experiments used hourly OP_RETURN timestamps (~$10K/year at $0.90 fees), but fee spikes could push costs toward ~$360K, driving aggregation across chains.

talks.title: Beyond Phish: Toward Detecting Fraudulent e-Commerce Websites at Scale
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Beyond Phish: Toward Detecting Fraudulent e-Commerce Websites at Scale.
talks.summary:
## Beyond Traditional Phishing Detection

Researchers at IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy present work on fraudulent e-commerce sites that steal payments without delivering goods. Unlike credential-phishing pages, these scams mimic legitimate storefronts—FTC-reported losses are substantial—and extend to fake pet-adoption and donation schemes.

## Building a Ground-Truth Dataset

The team collected roughly 29,000 online shopping sites, labeling about 23,100 legitimate and 6,100 fraudulent through manual verification. Category analysis of page source revealed scam typologies beyond simple brand impersonation, requiring features beyond URL similarity, logo presence, or login forms used in classic phishing detectors.

## Novel Detection Signals

Fraudulent sites often add social-media links to feign legitimacy, but behavioral patterns differ: inconsistent contact information, suspicious payment flows, and template reuse across unrelated "brands." Machine-learning models trained on these features outperform phishing-oriented classifiers on this domain.

## Scale and Responsible Disclosure

The system operates at web scale, surfacing persistent scams still online months later. Researchers reported findings to hosting providers and e-commerce platforms; Safe Browsing uptake varied. Code and data are released publicly to help hosting companies and security vendors protect consumers from payment fraud, not just credential theft.

talks.title: Silph: A Framework for Scalable and Accurate Generation of Hybrid MPC Protocols
talks.teaser: Silph scales hybrid MPC compilation via partitioned ILPs and cross-boundary mutations for accurate primitive assignment.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with privacy-sensitive workloads—such as chat history in hosted AI—and asks whether parties can compute jointly without revealing inputs. Secure multi-party computation (MPC) enables that across trust domains, but communication and computation costs slow adoption. Researchers therefore hand-tune hybrid protocols that mix primitives like garbled circuits and arithmetic secret sharing, balancing layer costs against expensive conversions between representations.

Recent hybrid MPC compilers automate primitive assignment, yet coarse block-level heuristics miss fine-grained wins, while linear-program approaches can support only two primitives or blow up compile time as constraint counts grow. Silph targets the hybrid protocol assignment problem with an ILP formulation that supports arbitrarily many primitives, then scales solving by partitioning the program graph, running local ILPs, and applying mutations so neighboring partitions inform cross-boundary conversion costs. A final combination ILP merges mutation choices into a global assignment.

Evaluated on Cersei atop the ABY two-party framework across nine benchmarks on AWS, Silph reports dramatically faster compiles than prior tools—sometimes hours versus under two minutes—and up to roughly 3.6× faster execution when finer assignments beat garbled-circuit-only choices. Practitioners should treat hybrid MPC as a compile-time optimization problem where partitioning and boundary-aware refinement matter as much as the cryptography itself.

talks.title: SQUIP: Exploiting the Scheduler Queue Contention Side Channel
talks.teaser: Shows how AMD Zen's split schedulers leak multiplication timing between SMT threads, enabling covert channels and RSA key recovery.
talks.summary:
This talk looks at the difference between the CPU back ends of AMD Zen and Intel Skylake processors. Skylake uses one unified scheduler, while Zen splits the scheduler queues, and the speaker asks whether that split design can be exploited. The threat model has an attacker and a victim on the same core, running on two SMT threads. The attacker has no architectural access to the victim, so it relies on a timing side channel to tell when the victim performs multiplications, which only one arithmetic unit can execute.

The method fills the multiplication queue to a chosen level, using dependent long-latency operations to hold multiplications back, and then times reads with rdtsc or rdpru. Instead of adding serializing fences to counter out-of-order execution, the attack relies on whether those timing reads get reordered. Queue limits were visible on the AMD parts tested, with 16 micro-ops on Zen 2 and 22 on Zen 3, and no comparable limit on the Intel design. The effect works as a covert channel across hyperthreads, reaching up to 2.7 megabits per second on Zen 2, with Zen 3 noisier. It also works across processes, in virtual machines with more noise, and with SMT enabled.

As a demonstration, the speaker recovers an RSA key from square-and-multiply, where set exponent bits appear as extra multiplication peaks. Key recovery took about 40 minutes at a low rate. The speaker notes that countermeasures are described in the paper. The practical takeaway is that sharing SMT siblings across security domains leaks information. Disabling SMT is the blunt fix, while core scheduling offers a more selective way to keep trusted processes apart.

talks.title: No Privacy in the Electronics Repair Industry
talks.teaser: Covert tests at repair shops reveal technicians viewing customer files while owners get no privacy policies.
talks.summary:
The study measured how electronics repair shops handle customers' personal data, combining covert visits with surveys and interviews. In a battery-replacement test, no provider stated a privacy policy even when asked. National chains refused devices without a passcode, while some regional and local shops accepted them without credentials. National and regional providers stored passcodes alongside addresses and emails.

In the covert part, six devices running hidden recording software, with a disabled audio driver as a pretext, were dropped off at 16 shops with browsing history and private photos. Technicians opened photo folders, and at some shops copied files to USB drives or viewed browser history. Local shops produced the most violations. Some chain staff left no trace in recent-files lists, while two local shops' logs could not be recovered.

A survey of 100 participants and 30 interviews found that 50% were reluctant to repair for privacy reasons, and 33% of broken devices went unrepaired for that reason. About 70% noticed no safeguards, and 20% used no protection before drop-off. The researchers call for a three-part response. Manufacturers and OS developers should build tamper-resistant logging and better BIOS diagnostics. Providers should move away from all-access PIN requirements, explain what access they need, and use video recording with random audits. Regulators should enforce consistent policies, perhaps with inspection certificates like restaurants. Customers cannot reasonably encrypt data or remove soldered storage themselves.

talks.title: Space Odyssey: An Experimental Software Security Analysis of Satellites
talks.teaser: Presents a firmware-based security analysis of three satellites, an ESA case study, and a developer survey on satellite threats.
talks.summary:
Satellites underpin telecommunications, navigation and Earth observation, yet most published security work has focused on the links between users and satellites rather than on the satellites themselves. The team analysed firmware from three satellites, obtained from partners and reverse engineered, to learn how they work and which weaknesses they contain. From these case studies they built a threat taxonomy that starts from attacker goals such as denial of service, malicious data manipulation and seizure of control, then maps the bus and payload systems and the possible lateral movement between them.

The talk detailed one case: ESA's OPS-SAT open research satellite. The team found missing access control on the communication system, which let them reach the command and data handling system. A buffer overflow in a telecommand handler then gave arbitrary code execution, since neither address space layout randomisation nor stack cookies was present. From there they ran arbitrary actions and took full control. A developer survey of 19 professionals across space agencies, universities and companies, covering 17 satellites, found that many respondents did not know or would not say whether third parties could control their satellite, and few named access control as a defence.

The takeaway is that retrofitting security onto satellites is hard: bare-bone operating systems make modern mitigations difficult to add, and updates crawl over links offering only minutes of contact at low bit rates. Authentication and access control should be treated as baseline requirements from the design stage.

talks.title: SPHINCS+C: Compressing SPHINCS+ With (Almost) No Cost
talks.teaser: Presents SPHINCS+C, a compressed variant of the post-quantum signature scheme that trades a little signing work for smaller signatures.
talks.summary:
SPHINCS+ is a hash-based post-quantum digital signature scheme chosen by NIST for standardization, but its signatures are large and its operations are slow compared with classical schemes. The talk presents SPHINCS+C, which keeps the original structure and instead replaces two of its building blocks: the WOTS one-time signature and the FORS few-time signature. The core idea is to add a counter to the message digest and search over counter values until the digest falls into a subdomain where the checksum is already fixed. Because the signer publishes the counter, the verifier only checks that the value lies in that subdomain and then runs the rest of the scheme. In FORS, a similar step forces one leaf to zero, which removes work for both signer and verifier.

The speaker addressed the obvious concern that a variable-length search is not constant time. The argument is that the search depends only on the public message and public parameters, not on secret key material, so its running time reveals nothing secret. The team also bounded the chance of an unusually slow signature: for the parameter sets they examined, taking nine times the expected time has a probability below 2^-64. Benchmarks on ordinary servers showed that the timing variance from normal system noise was similar to the variance from the search itself.

For the same signing time, the compressed scheme can reduce signatures by up to about 20 percent. One example moves a parameter set from roughly 7,800 bytes to around 6,300 bytes, which is still large but a clear improvement. Applied to the original parameters, the compression is strictly better in size and speed. The authors also released a Sage script so practitioners can search for parameter sets that suit their own priorities of size or speed, along with the paper and code. More complex optimizations were left as future work.

talks.title: Leaking Arbitrarily Many Secrets: Any-out-of-Many Proofs and Applications to RingCT Protocols
talks.teaser: Presents an any-out-of-many proof that hides how many ring members are real, aimed at anonymous cryptocurrency transactions.
talks.summary:
Public blockchains record transaction details in plain text, so privacy-focused cryptocurrencies use confidential transaction schemes and ring signatures to hide who paid whom. Monero-style systems use a one-out-of-many proof, which allows only one real signer in the ring. That becomes inefficient when a user spends from several accounts in one payment, because each account must be signed separately, lowering efficiency and weakening anonymity in practice.

The speaker introduces an any-out-of-many proof that lets a prover show knowledge of the secrets behind a binary vector, where each one marks a real key in the ring, without revealing which positions are real. The construction uses an amortization technique together with a challenge chosen by the verifier, so a prover cannot combine keys to forge a proof without knowing each individual secret. Because the number of real signers stays hidden, a ring with one real signer looks the same as one with several. Balance and range proofs stop a prover from spending money with an all-zero vector, so the optimization does not weaken security.

The talk also outlines a generic framework for quadratic relations that compresses these proofs to logarithmic size, and a trapdoor accumulator that reduces blockchain state size. A prototype RingCT protocol was evaluated against existing schemes. The proof was the smallest among those compared and its proving time was the fastest, while verification was slightly slower than one comparison scheme. The takeaway is a RingCT design with higher anonymity, smaller proofs and lower burden on network nodes, which could also suit multi-party ring signatures and anonymous voting.

talks.title: MagBackdoor: Beware of Your Loudspeaker as A Backdoor For Magnetic Injection Attacks
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning MagBackdoor: Beware of Your Loudspeaker as A Backdoor For Magnetic Injection Attacks.
talks.summary: Titillio presents MagBackdoor, shifting voice-command injection from microphones to loudspeakers driven by nearby magnetic fields. Simulations show static fields can silence speakers while alternating fields induce audible output without normal coil current; experiments on iPhones with and without speaker hardware show only loudspeakers relay injected waveforms into microphones. A compact electromagnet hidden in a power socket uses PWM amplification and Bluetooth control to trigger wake words at distance.

talks.title: Discovering Java Deserialization Vulnerabilities via Structure-Aware Directed Greybox Fuzzing
talks.teaser: Presents a directed fuzzer for finding Java deserialization gadget chains, with six new flaws found in real applications.
talks.summary:
Java deserialization rebuilds objects from byte streams, which is handy for remoting and storage, but it lets an attacker inject objects across a trust boundary. Magic methods run during reconstruction, so attacker-controlled fields can be chained into security-sensitive methods, forming what are called gadget chains. The speaker reviewed earlier approaches. Gadget Inspector combines static analysis and symbolic execution but suffers from precision problems, high false positives and manual triage. A 2022 hybrid approach relies on points-to analysis, which is heavyweight for large applications.

The proposed method is a structure-aware directed greybox fuzzer. It first runs a lightweight, summary-based analysis to find candidate chains, and it runs class hierarchy analysis only when a call is polymorphic. Reflection is used to build property trees that describe the fields each class needs, so generated injection objects keep valid structure. Seeds are scheduled with a feedback metric that combines gadget coverage with distance to the target sink. Mutation works on a parametric sequence, with identifier bytes marking which properties to change while preserving structural validity.

In the evaluation, the approach statically identified 20 of 34 known gadget chains across 22 common Java libraries and generated working injection objects for 16 of them, with no false positives. Each chain was fuzzed for about 120 seconds and the experiments were repeated 10 times. Applied to four popular Java applications without deserialization entry points, it found six new vulnerabilities, five of which have CVE IDs. The speaker noted limitations: the static analysis is imprecise and depends on expert-supplied source and sink definitions, and turning findings into practical exploits still needs manual work. The takeaway is that lightweight static analysis paired with directed fuzzing can surface deserialization flaws that purely static tools miss.

talks.title: Low-Cost Privilege Separation with Compile Time Compartmentalization for Embedded Systems
talks.teaser: Presents a compiler that splits embedded firmware into isolated compartments at compile time with low overhead.
talks.summary:
Embedded devices such as smartwatches and washing machines run firmware on low-power processors, so developers often run every component in one privilege mode to avoid the cost of context switching. A flaw in one part can then reach every other part. The talk proposes compartmentalization, which divides firmware into isolated pieces, and presents CRTC, a privilege-aware language and compiler that enforces this at compile time.

The approach has two phases. Identification uses a program dependency graph and privilege as the guide: thread discovery finds threads, MMIO discovery finds devices, and everything left over becomes the kernel compartment. Enforcement gives each compartment its own language dialect. The kernel dialect has the most freedom but cannot touch MMIO directly. The driver dialect uses system view description files and points-to and value range analysis to map each device's registers. The thread dialect is the most restricted: it requires memory safety through Checked C and 3C conversion and limits each thread to its own resources. Cross-compartment communication goes through a compatibility layer that checks requests and moves resources. The prototype modifies LLVM, Checked C and a tool, and was evaluated on FreeRTOS and Zephyr on an STM32F4.

Reported runtime overhead averaged 2.63 percent and memory overhead averaged 1.75 percent. Most runtime cost came from safety instrumentation and object tracking, which becomes noticeable when dynamic objects are shared between compartments. In the Q&A, the speaker said kernel code written in assembly is currently trusted rather than checked, and deferred how to handle it. The takeaway is that compile-time checks can provide practical isolation on low-power embedded devices.

talks.title: UTOPIA: Automatic Generation of Fuzz Driver using Unit Tests
talks.teaser: Converts existing unit tests into library fuzz drivers, using root definition analysis to keep inputs semantically valid.
talks.summary:
Library fuzzing relies on fuzz drivers written by hand, which becomes costly as APIs multiply and projects evolve. Earlier automated methods synthesize API sequences from client code, but they can reach invalid states or produce incomplete sequences. This talk proposes Utopia, which reuses the API call sequences already in a project's unit tests and converts those tests into fuzz drivers, since unit tests capture the correct usage developers intend.

The harder problem is supplying valid arguments. Utopia analyzes each parameter's attributes, such as output parameters, loop counts, allocation sizes and file paths, and constrains fuzzed values to match, for example capping a value used for allocation. Its root definition analysis traces data flow backwards from the final API call to find where a test assigns constants to variables, and injects fuzz input there so relationships between arguments across calls stay consistent. Assertions were also studied; keeping them generally performed better, though results varied by library.

On 55 popular open-source projects, Utopia generated 5K working drivers without human intervention and found 123 bugs. Compared with manually written fuzzers, it achieved roughly twice the coverage in the reported results, and on six libraries it explored up to 37 times more library code than the corresponding unit test in one hour. Limitations include unit tests aimed at internal functions, which applications cannot reach, missing error checks, and unconventional API designs. The takeaway is that existing unit tests offer a practical base for library fuzzing.

talks.title: SoK: Anti-Facial Recognition Technology
talks.teaser: A synthesis maps anti-face recognition defenses across five stages and scores them on robustness, coverage, and usability.
talks.summary:
Unwanted facial recognition has spread through free lookup services, commercial platforms, and scraped training data, while legal protections remain patchy and slow. The presenters introduce a fictional privacy-conscious user searching academic advice and finding a chaotic list of cosmetics, eyewear, and data-poisoning ideas, then explain why their system-of-knowledge paper tries to organize that landscape.

They distill modern face recognition into five attack surfaces: image collection, preprocessing, feature-extractor training, reference-database enrollment, and live query matching. Prior anti–face recognition proposals are sorted into those buckets. They then evaluate stage-specific approaches against five desired properties: long-term robustness, broad coverage for people already online, need for third-party help, and burden on the user or bystanders, marking where literature already meets each goal versus where success is uncertain.

Image-collection and preprocessing defenses score well on low disruption but struggle with coverage and solo use; training-time poisoning demands unrealistic effort; database and query-time tricks show mixed promise and may harm others or age poorly as models evolve. The talk closes on open problems: static faces, adversarial arms races, thin usability studies, and ethical tension between blocking misuse and preserving legitimate recognition.

talks.title: SoK: History is a Vast Early Warning System: Auditing the Provenance of System Intrusions
talks.teaser: Surveying audit provenance, three practical advances, and trade-offs between log shrinkage and breach-detection utility.
talks.summary:
Operating system auditing underpins reactive security when preventive controls fail, yet the literature long treated it as a minor theme compared with flashier topics. The speakers frame a systematization of knowledge on auditing the provenance of system intrusions: parsing audit logs into dependency graphs that explain execution history, amid a post-2015 surge of work driven by breach dwell times and investigation cost.

Rather than walking through every taxonomy table, the talk stresses three practical advances from recent research. Execution partitioning splits process activity into autonomous units so investigators can follow suspicious chains without drowning in noisy graphs, as illustrated by simplifying a complex ransomware-style trace. Provenance around alerts is argued to predict whether an alarm is genuine versus benign background behavior. A third thread is long-retention telemetry: algorithms such as log garbage collection, causality-preserving reduction, and dependence-preserving reduction remove dead-end or redundant events while aiming to keep actionable causal structure.

The empirical core compares eight reduction techniques on DARPA Transparent Computing engagement data using an in-house induction toolchain. Individual methods vary widely by workload; stacking them yields roughly elevenfold shrinkage versus about eightfold for one strong baseline alone, not multiplicative combinations of order-of-magnitude wins. Pairing reduction with gzip compression reaches far larger savings in the reported table. Re-running three contemporary anomaly detectors on progressively reduced logs shows precision, recall, and attack-path retention falling as compression grows more aggressive—arguing future schemes must quantify forensic utility, not only anecdotal case studies. The session closes with industry engagement, labeled datasets, and open measurement artifacts as next steps.

talks.title: Clockwork Finance: Automated Analysis of Economic Security in Smart Contracts
talks.teaser: Presents a formal verification method that bounds MEV in smart contracts by checking transaction reorderings.
talks.summary:
Decentralized finance now handles very large sums, and its smart contracts execute deterministically and atomically, so they compose easily. That composability creates maximal extractable value (MEV), where block producers profit by reordering, censoring or inserting transactions, as in sandwich attacks. The speaker argues that audits, functional testing and static analysis focus on bugs and data leakage and miss this economic side, so the work reasons directly about economic properties using formal verification.

The authors give a formal definition of MEV, which did not previously exist, and use it to judge whether a new contract composes securely with an existing state. In practice, contracts are simplified into over-approximating models and run in the K framework, which includes EVM semantics. Transactions with symbolic parameters are reordered, and the tool either proves a bound on MEV or returns a concrete counterexample ordering. Counterexamples are replayed on a client to remove false positives. Optimizations skip reorderings of a single user's transactions, randomize the exploration order, and exploit path independence in Uniswap.

Evaluation on automated market makers found an average of 0.5 MEV per block, and composed analyses covered MakerDAO using Uniswap as an oracle. The paper also covers governance attacks, flash loans and airdrops. In questions, the speaker explained the limits: the analysis covers one block and a few dozen transactions, and miner insertions are given as manually specified templates. Developers can bound MEV before deployment, while users and researchers can analyse historical transactions.

talks.title: When and Why Do People Want Ad Targeting Explanations? Evidence from a Mixed-Methods Field Study
talks.teaser: A four-week field study shows when people want ad targeting explanations and why creepy or unexpected ads trigger that demand.
talks.summary:
Behavioral advertising relies on opaque profiling, and platforms have added optional explanations for why a user sees a given ad. The presentation motivates research on two gaps in those designs: which ad encounters should trigger an explanation, and what information people actually want when they ask.

The team ran a four-week experience-sampling study with 60 participants using a browser extension. When sampled ads appeared, notifications led to questionnaires about whether users wanted more detail, plus context and perceptions such as creepiness or unexpectedness. Across more than 4,000 responses, participants sought explanations for roughly 30% of ads that caught their attention. Regression models showed perceptual factors predicted demand better than context or pre-study personality and privacy attitude measures alone, though combining all factor types fit best.

Follow-up interviews highlighted why explanations mattered: people used them to test mental models of targeting, from browsing history and purchases to data sharing or even physical-world listening, and to gain agency over metadata use. Others declined when they already understood the link or felt resigned that explanations would not change collection. The talk closes with design directions—proactive, user-defined rules when fine-grained data raises concern, and pairing explanations with actionable privacy controls rather than one-size-fits-all disclosure.

talks.summary: Carolin presents a systematization of decentralized finance attacks drawn from cross-validated incident feeds, using the bZx flash-loan price-manipulation case to illustrate sub-dollar fees versus six-figure profits. She maps modern Ethereum execution through public mempools, Flashbots private relays, sandwich accelerations, and imitation front-runners, reports many attacks are non-atomic with multi-day windows, and sketches bytecode n-gram similarity between victim and attacker contracts as an early warning signal before mempool exploitation.

talks.title: Towards a Rigorous Statistical Analysis of Empirical Password Datasets
talks.teaser: Derives provable bounds on password guessing curves from leaked samples, without knowing the true password distribution.
talks.summary:
Data breaches have exposed billions of passwords to offline guessing attacks. Defenders want to know how an attacker's chance of success grows with the number of guesses, the guessing curve, but the true password distribution is unknown. Using frequencies from a leaked sample tends to overestimate this curve at large guess counts, while assuming one fixed cracking model may underestimate it.

The work introduces four techniques that bound the guessing curve with high confidence, about 99 percent in the evaluation. A frequency upper bound relies on concentration inequalities. A sampling lower bound splits a sample in two and uses one half as a cracking dictionary against the other. An extended lower bound adds a cracking model once the dictionary is exhausted, keeping it useful for very large guess counts. A linear programming approach searches for distributions consistent with the sample. On leaked datasets, the bounds are tight for small guess numbers, the linear programming bound is tighter for moderate ones, and the empirical distribution overestimates at large guess numbers.

Two applications follow. For hash cost, the bounds give a provable lower bound on the security gained by increasing hashing cost, which an organization can weigh against extra computing expense. For composition rules, comparing password sets before and after a six-character minimum shows only a slight gain in resistance to offline attacks. Overall, the talk argues that rigorous bounds, not raw frequencies, should guide estimates of offline cracking risk.

talks.title: Practical Program Modularization with Type-Based Dependence Analysis
talks.teaser: Type-based dependence analysis delivers modular partitioning of C and C++ programs and Linux kernel hardening via typed flows.
talks.summary:
Large monolithic programs in unsafe languages bundle thousands of compilation units with little internal trust boundaries, so one memory vulnerability can compromise an entire system. Attackers routinely leverage cross-module access after an initial bug, which motivates partitioning code so modules that should not interact cannot reach each other's data or code.

The presentation introduces type-based dependence analysis, which tracks which modules may pass which data types through the only two inter-module channels the work identifies: function arguments and global variables. Because those channels carry type information, the approach avoids classic pointer-analysis pitfalls such as alias explosion while still supporting transitive dependency queries for a chosen type and module. The speaker describes handling C type casts, nested structure fields, flow direction, and a type-elevation refinement, plus LLVM implementation choices when opaque pointers obscure types.

Two evaluations anchor the method. Refining indirect-call target sets using dependencies within related modules removes more than thirty percent of spurious targets compared with prior typing, with roughly eight minutes of analysis on a large Linux kernel tree. Separately, labeling capability-related kernel structures shows that about 99.9 percent of modules never write to them, suggesting strong isolation opportunities. The closing message is that modularization based on typed cross-module flows can underpin compartmentalization and related defenses, with caveats where false negatives matter for enforcement rather than analysis.

talks.title: Analyzing Leakage of Personally Identifiable Information in Language Models

talks.title: Deep perceptual hashing algorithms with hidden dual purpose: client-side scanning facial recognition
talks.teaser: Shows how perceptual hashing built for image copy detection can hide a facial recognition purpose.
talks.summary:
Client-side scanning proposals use perceptual hashing to compare images on a device against fingerprints of known illegal content, flagging matches before end-to-end encrypted messages are sent. The speaker, from Imperial College London, argues that these systems are presented as having one narrow capability, and presents research challenging that claim.

The work shows that a state-of-the-art neural perceptual hashing model can be trained with a modified objective so it also performs facial recognition of a chosen target person. Training mixes a primary copy-detection dataset with a secondary face dataset. On copy detection, the dual-purpose model performs similarly to a single-purpose baseline, and on the target face task its recall rises sharply, while general face recognition on non-target individuals stays poor. To get the target's hashes into the database without an auditor noticing, the authors use collision attacks: a benign-looking image is perturbed so its hash matches a template hash of the target while still looking like ordinary content.

The takeaway is that an auditor checking the algorithm's behaviour and the database may not detect the hidden purpose, so the real capabilities of such tools are not fully understood. The speaker suggests that reproducible, fully auditable training pipelines would help, though they doubt that is realistic, and hopes the findings inform legislators and policy makers.

talks.title: Attitudes towards Client-Side Scanning for CSAM, Terrorism, Drug Trafficking, Drug Use, Tax Evasion
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Attitudes towards Client-Side Scanning for CSAM, Terrorism, Drug Trafficking, Drug Use, Tax Evasion.

talks.title: A Security RISC: Microarchitectural Attacks on Hardware RISC-V CPUs
talks.teaser: Shows new side channels on RISC-V CPUs that leak secrets via instruction cache timing and retired-instruction counters.
talks.summary: Lucas outlines how RISC-V’s sparse documentation of unprivileged cache flush and timer behavior complicates microarchitectural attack research, then introduces three primitives: cache-and-time instruction-cache disclosure without shared memory, flush-and-fault I-cache probing via deliberate faults, and cycle-drift using mandated cycle and retired-instruction counters that leak across privilege modes. Case studies break KASLR, bypass branch-predictor mitigations, detect interrupts, and attack AES tables on Allwinner and SiFive cores tested under Linux.

talks.title: RoFL: Robustness of Secure Federated Learning
talks.teaser: Shows how zero-knowledge range proofs can let clients prove norm-bounded updates in encrypted federated learning aggregation.
talks.summary:
Federated learning trains a shared model across many devices without centralizing their data, yet client updates can still leak information, which is why secure aggregation is used to hide them. The gap is that the server cannot tell whether a hidden update is well formed, and malicious clients can scale their updates to overpower honest ones. The talk examines whether bounding update norms is a defense. The answer depends on the attack goal: norm bounds stop attacks aimed at typical samples, but targeted attacks on long-tail samples still get injected over time, behaving much like data poisoning.

To enforce such bounds without exposing updates, the work extends an existing additive-masking secure aggregation protocol with verifiable correctness. The server checks that the masking values sum to the unmasking key, using an additively homomorphic commitment encoding. Clients attach bulletproof range proofs showing each parameter respects an infinity-norm bound, or a proof over summed squares for an L2 bound. Bulletproofs were chosen because they work directly over homomorphic commitments and batch efficiently.

A prototype was compared against a secure aggregation baseline on a model with about 270,000 parameters, where client-side range proof generation was the main bottleneck. Optimizations cut that timing considerably, and L2 norm-preserving compression helped bandwidth, while infinity-norm optimizations had little effect there. For an 800,000-parameter language model, overhead was only about a factor of 1.2. The takeaway is that norm bounds are a practical defense against many poisoning attacks, and efficient proofs make them viable in secure federated learning.

talks.title: Improving Developers' Understanding of Regex Denial of Service Tools
talks.teaser: Pairs ReDoS tools with anti-patterns and fix strategies that improve how developers read detection and repair reports.
talks.summary:
Regular expression denial of service turns ambiguous backtracking matchers into a CPU drain: crafted input can saturate servers, with past outages measured in tens of minutes. Prior work automated vulnerable-regex detection and repair, yet tooling often fails adoption when developers cannot interpret what tools report.

The presentation targets usability by pairing detectors and fixers with anti-patterns that name vulnerable structure and fix strategies grounded in choices developers already make. A formal ambiguity model singles out concatenation and Kleene star as the sources of unbounded ambiguity, yielding six anti-patterns and five mitigation strategies. Worked examples cover overlapping quantifiers and alternation inside star, plus fixes that narrow character classes or cap repetition so overlap disappears.

On roughly two hundred nine thousand regexes, the anti-pattern set matches automatic detection on about ninety-nine percent of vulnerable cases with strong precision and recall versus earlier pattern catalogs. A nine-developer study on project regexes found bare tools left participants with weak self-reported understanding; the augmented workflow raised detection understanding to strong and fixing to very strong. Practitioners can layer these explanations atop existing ReDoS tools after a short training session rather than replacing current scanners.

talks.title: WeRLman: To Tackle Whale (Transactions), Go Deep (RL)
talks.teaser: Deep reinforcement learning analyzes whale transactions and shows fee volatility erodes selfish-mining security thresholds.
talks.summary:
Classic arguments treat blockchain safety as an honest-majority problem near fifty percent hashing power, while selfish mining showed rational miners near twenty-five percent can beat honest behavior when rewards are modeled as fixed per block. Later work that looks only at transaction fees or only at block subsidies reaches different extremes and does not match present Bitcoin, where both reward types coexist and some transfers pay far more than others.

WeRLman treats those outsized payments as whale transactions, enlarging the mining state beyond two chain lengths to track where high-value fees sit. Prior dynamic programming does not scale, so the approach trains a neural policy with deep reinforcement learning, long Monte Carlo look-ahead, known transition probabilities, and scaling tricks tuned to mining symmetry. On constrained models where optimal policies are known, the learned strategy matches the optimum; on the full model it estimates the smallest miner share that beats honest mining for many whale-premium settings.

Raising the premium parameter steadily lowers the security threshold. Heuristic on-chain estimates suggest that as halvings shrink fixed subsidies, fee volatility dominates and the threshold could fall under thirteen percent within roughly thirty years—well below many miners today—while open tooling is offered to study these incentives further.

talks.title: No One Drinks From the Firehose: How Organizations Filter and Prioritize Vulnerability Information

talks.title: On the Evolution of (Hateful) Memes by Means of Multimodal Contrastive Learning
talks.teaser: Researchers apply CLIP contrastive learning to map hateful meme variants and score clusters for platform moderation.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames online memes as multimodal carriers of ideology, noting that hateful variants evolve new image–text combinations to evade moderation. To address that, the work fine-tunes OpenAI’s CLIP on the Fortune dataset of roughly 12.5 million image–text pairs so image and text embeddings align in a shared space.

Building on analogies to word-vector regularities, the authors describe visual and visual–linguistic semantic regularities in CLIP space. One pipeline starts from a known hateful meme image, finds cosine-similar visual variants, then infers imagery influencers; a case study around a widely known antisemitic template yields more than 3,000 variant–influencer pairs, with manual checks on 100 samples reporting 78% variant and 53% influencer accuracy. A second pipeline fuses a base meme with named entities drawn from posts to target precise textual swaps, with strong hit rates for geopolitical and nationality entities. Community detection on a variant graph summarizes major families.

Fused embeddings also support retrieval, key-phrase and toxicity scoring via tools such as Google’s Perspective API, and large-scale clustering to surface highly hateful groups and their targets. The speakers position the framework as a practical aid for moderators tracking evolving hate, including coordinated campaigns.

talks.title: Practical Timing Side-Channel Attacks on Memory Compression
talks.teaser: Shows how decompression timing differences in memory compression can leak secrets across a network, found by a fuzzer.
talks.summary:
Shared hosting and cloud services can let a side channel in one tenant's data path leak secrets. This talk shows that the time needed to decompress memory-compressed data, used in databases, file systems and virtual memory, can reveal whether a guess sits next to a secret. The attack relies only on timing measured over a network, not on output size.

The authors built compressor, an evolutionary fuzzer that generates memory layouts with a secret, a known prefix, guesses, incompressible padding and repeated data. It keeps the layouts that produce the largest timing gap between correct and incorrect guesses. The search surfaced two edge cases in LZ77 and Huffman decoding. Fully incompressible data decodes almost instantly, while nearly incompressible data that still passes through Huffman decoding is slow, a gap of up to 50 microseconds in one library. Case studies covered memcached behind a PHP application across 14 network hops, PostgreSQL behind a web API, and Chrome's virtual memory compression driven from JavaScript, which recovered a 64-bit heap pointer and broke ASLR. At that gap, about 100 requests per guess were estimated to be enough.

Suggested mitigations include keeping secrets out of compression alongside attacker-controlled data, randomising secret placement, adding padding, dropping sequence compression, and rate limiting network attackers. The main takeaway is that compression edge cases can create remotely exploitable timing differences, and the source code has been published.

talks.title: Security and Privacy Challenges, Advice, and Opportunities at Cybercafes in Kenya
talks.teaser: Examines password habits, account recovery and privacy risks at Kenyan cyber cafes, where staff often choose logins for customers.
talks.summary:
Collins presents a study of the security and privacy advice given to customers at cyber cafes in Kenya. The work started with his mother's experience renewing a driving licence on a public computer after the government moved services online. The operator had told her to use her national ID number as both her username and password. Cyber cafes matter because many Kenyans have no personal computer or printer, and most customers are new to computers.

The team ran 36 semi-structured interviews in Nairobi, with 14 managers and 22 customers, recruited by visiting commercial and residential cafes. Printing and government services were the most common uses, followed by job applications, email and photography. Customers struggled with basic computer use, setting up online accounts, and recovering locked accounts after losing a phone number or email address. Managers often chose passwords for customers, favouring memorable options such as ID or phone numbers, or patterns built from names and birth years. Some wrote passwords down or saved them on shared machines, and their advice differed from cafe to cafe. Concerns centred on account hijacking, impersonation and sessions left logged in, as well as scams that used documents such as CVs. Managers responded by logging customers out, deleting data and clearing downloads.

The authors conclude that cyber cafes play a key role in access to services, and that customers would benefit from training and security awareness, which they urge the government to lead as its services go digital. Because ID numbers are also required for mobile money and other services, reused passwords carry real risk. The authors suggest phone-based password managers and alternative authentication methods, while noting that shared devices need further study. Collins also points out that the findings reflect Nairobi only and rely on what participants reported.

talks.title: Always Contribute Back: A Qualitative Study on Security Challenges of the Open Source Supply Chain

talks.title: Jigsaw Puzzle: Selective Backdoor Attack to Subvert Malware Classifiers
talks.teaser: Shows a clean-label backdoor that poisons malware classifiers against one chosen family while evading common defenses.
talks.summary:
Malware classifiers are often retrained on samples gathered from the wild, such as from VirusTotal, which gives attackers a way to poison training data. Prior backdoors usually use one trigger for all families, leaving a footprint defenders can detect. This talk presents Jigsaw Puzzle, a selective clean-label backdoor that protects only an attacker-chosen family while others are classified normally.

The attacker adds benign-labelled samples carrying a trigger to the training set, without controlling labels or the training process. The trigger, found through alternating optimization over binary features, completes only for the target family, so its triggered samples are predicted benign while other families stay detected. Injected code gadgets keep the APK's original functionality intact. Across about 150k samples from 400 families, attack success on the target was mostly high, success on other families was mostly low, and F1 stayed close to a clean model.

Against defenses such as MNTD, STRIP, activation clustering and Neural Cleanse, the attack largely evaded detection; MNTD's AUC stayed mostly near 0.5, versus 0.96 for a conventional backdoor. The speaker argued that these defenses assume triggered inputs all go to one label, and a trigger spread across the feature space enlarges the search space. Possible mitigations include scanning each family, using more homogeneous representations, and collecting benign samples only from reliable sources, though a robust defense remains an open problem.

talks.title: CSI:Rowhammer - Cryptographic Security and Integrity against Rowhammer
talks.teaser: Shows a memory-controller design that checks every DRAM access with a MAC to stop Rowhammer bit flips.
talks.summary:
The talk examines why many Rowhammer countermeasures fall short. Several rest on assumptions, such as a blast radius of one or detection through performance counters, that later research showed to be incomplete. The speaker proposes a generic data integrity approach, CSI:Rowhammer, which detects any bit flip regardless of its source, whether Rowhammer, cosmic rays or something not yet known.

The design has the memory controller compute a cryptographic MAC on every DRAM read and write, stored in the extra chip of ECC memory. A mismatch lets a single bit flip be corrected in hardware. Larger corruptions are passed to a new operating system exception handler, which can brute-force the correction or reload disk-backed data and recompute corrupted page tables. The handler and the key sit in a small four-page secure memory on the CPU, so an attacker cannot hammer them. Approximate MAC comparison tolerates flips in the MAC itself, at some cost to its strength.

In the evaluation, a prototype with a modified Linux kernel showed a geometric-mean performance overhead below one percent on PARSEC and SPLASH-2x. The highest overhead was just over four percent on DDR4, and about five percent on the memory-bound ocean CP benchmark. The security analysis found that five data bit flips need 2^26 brute-force attempts, and ignoring three MAC bits still leaves 41.2 bits of strength. In the worst case an attack leads to denial of service rather than privilege escalation. Questions covered timing side channels and adding memory encryption, which would add security at a performance cost.

talks.title: ShadowNet: A Secure and Efficient On-device Model Inference System for Convolutional Neural Networks
talks.teaser: Presents a TrustZone-based system that hides CNN model weights while offloading linear layers to untrusted on-device GPUs.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses a privacy gap in on-device machine learning, where attackers can extract deployed models from phones even when the model files are encrypted. Cryptographic protections such as multi-party computation and homomorphic encryption are considered too computationally heavy, while trusted-execution designs keep models private but cannot use the AI accelerators that phone vendors are now adding. The speakers present ShadowNet, a system for convolutional neural network inference that tries to use those accelerators without exposing the model.

The central observation is that most computation in these networks sits in linear layers, which the speakers say account for about 95 percent of MobileNet's weights and 99 percent of its inference time. Weights are transformed offline, and fresh random masks are applied to inputs for every inference. The linear operations run on the untrusted GPU, and results are restored inside the secure world, while non-linear layers stay there. The prototype ran on a HiKey 960 board with a Mali GPU, with Android in the normal world, OP-TEE in the secure world and TensorFlow Lite, and with the OP-TEE kernel modified to avoid remapping weight memory on each world switch.

Evaluation covered six CNN models, from MobileNet-style classifiers to a YOLO-based object detector. Accuracy and consistency matched the baseline, and inference time rose by 0.6 to 1.6 times, with GPU acceleration cutting overhead by up to 30 milliseconds per inference. A formal argument suggested an observer of the normal world gains nothing beyond black-box querying, and two model-stealing attacks performed identically on original and transformed models. In questions, the speakers distinguished their threat model from Slalom, which protects only inputs, and suggested lightweight verification of GPU results could be added. Code release was planned.

talks.title: On the Importance and Challenges of Reproducible Builds for Software Supply Chain Security
talks.teaser: Shows why reproducible builds matter for supply chain security, using interviews with contributors who build them.
talks.summary:
The talk starts with Ken Thompson's 1984 Turing Award lecture on the trusting trust attack, in which a compiler is modified to insert a backdoor that survives inspection of the clean source code. The proposed defense, diverse double compiling, needs several compilers to produce bit-for-bit identical binaries, which only works if builds are reproducible. The speaker lists common sources of nondeterminism, including build timestamps, build paths, file system ordering, archive metadata, randomness and uninitialized memory.

The research team ran a qualitative interview study. They contacted 110 people from the reproducible-builds.org mailing list and interviewed 24, six of them in person at the 2022 Summit in Venice. Motivations included wanting software that behaves deterministically, developer security against coercion or mistakes, and cost savings from caching identical artifacts. Obstacles included slow responses from upstream projects, sparse documentation, build directory names being embedded, and cryptographic signatures stored in files. Helpful factors were self-driven contributors, good interaction with upstream and downstream projects, and patience. Current CI results show Debian Bookworm AMD64 at 96.2 percent reproducible and Arch Linux core at 90.2 percent.

The speaker recommended secure-by-default reproducible builds in open-source projects, organizational buy-in from industry, and liability rules that target commercial entities rather than open-source projects. In the questions, the speaker argued that software bills of materials help but can be wrong or forged, so rebuilding and comparing outputs is still needed.

talks.title: SCAPHY: Detecting Modern ICS Attacks by Correlating Behaviors in SCADA and PHYsical
talks.teaser: Correlates SCADA execution-phase violations with physical anomalies to catch modern ICS attacks that abuse legitimate tools.
talks.summary:
Industrial control attacks such as the Ukrainian power grid malware and Stuxnet enter through the IT side, reach the SCADA layer, and then act on physical processes. The talk explains why existing detection falls short. Physical anomaly models react to effects after the fact and raise false alarms from benign faults, while host and network anomaly detectors are evaded by modern attacks that use legitimate SCADA tools. These checks also run in isolation, with no correlation across the cyber and physical domains.

The proposed approach, called SCAPHY, splits SCADA operation into distinct execution phases, such as initialization and process control with its monitoring and authoring stages, rather than treating it as one continuous thread. An attack is flagged either as an injection, where extra system operations run in the wrong phase, or as a bypass, where traffic reaches the PLC without going through the expected phases. To connect these host-side violations to physical impact, the method maps which actuator states each OPC event depends on, toggles them in a running system, and assigns each actuator an impact score. Actuators that move against the process trajectory or drive it outside its calibrated set point are treated as physical anomalies.

In the evaluation, replaying the Ukrainian grid malware showed anomalous system operations during process monitoring. Hardware-in-the-loop testbeds at Sandia National Labs covered several physical processes and were tested with attacks based on an industry-standard ICS framework, reporting 95 percent accuracy and an average detection time of about 9 to 10 seconds. Real-world exploits from a separate ICS attack framework were also observed interacting with the SCADA software stack. The practical takeaway is that correlating host-level phase behavior with physical impact gives an ICS intrusion detector context that either domain alone cannot provide.

talks.title: LAMBRETTA: Learning to Rank for Twitter Soft Moderation
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of LAMBRETTA: Learning to Rank for Twitter Soft Moderation.
talks.summary: The LAMBRETTA system targets claim-driven Twitter soft moderation: it extracts proposition spans from labeled misleading tweets with Open Information Extractor and ClaimSpotter, then learns to rank n-gram keywords with a LambdaMART random forest using semantic similarity to related tweets rather than body-only keyword extractors. On 2020 election data it surfaces 100k+ candidate tweets while cutting moderator false-positive load 5.33× versus the next method, though manual review still finds debunking tweets flagged and only 4.3% later received official labels.

talks.title: IPvSeeYou: Exploiting Leaked Identifiers in IPv6 for Street-Level Geolocation
talks.teaser: Shows how leaked MAC-derived IPv6 identifiers on home routers let remote attackers locate devices to street-level precision.
talks.summary:
The talk presents IPvSeeYou, a location privacy attack against home routers that use legacy EUI-64 IPv6 addressing. That scheme embeds a device's MAC address in the lower 64 bits of its address. Many customer premises routers combine a router, switch, cable modem and Wi-Fi access point in one unit, and their wired and wireless MAC addresses often sit at predictable offsets from each other.

The attack draws on two data sets. The first comes from probing random addresses inside residential ISP networks so that customer routers return ICMP error messages revealing their WAN address; this gathered more than 60 million unique WAN MAC addresses over about a year. The second is a collection of geolocated Wi-Fi BSSIDs from open war-driving databases. Per-manufacturer offsets, derived for each OUI, link about 12 million WAN MAC addresses to geolocated BSSIDs. Early checks against friends, family and colleagues worked, and a large US residential ISP confirmed over 80% accuracy at zip code level. A traceroute-based extension geolocates non-EUI-64 devices by placing them near EUI-64 neighbors on the same last-hop router.

Disabling EUI-64 addressing would prevent the attack in principle, and one manufacturer released a patch to do so. Many devices are hard or impossible to update, so the speaker expects the attack to remain practical for several more years.

talks.title: Private Access Control for Function Secret Sharing
talks.teaser: Private access control packles let evaluators gate FSS use without learning which function a user's access key unlocks.
talks.summary:
Function secret sharing lets cloud servers evaluate a user's function on data without learning what function they run, but multi-user deployments still need different evaluation rights. Evaluators cannot tell one secret-shared function from another, which clashes with ordinary access control. The talk defines private access control packles: an access key grants use of a function while authentication reveals nothing about that function, backed by verification keys in an access control list.

The construction centers on distributed point functions as a building block for broader FSS schemes. A dealer proves knowledge of the correct access key; evaluators expand the point function into a secret-shared one-hot form, derive multiplicative shares of the verification key, exchange audit tokens, and accept only when those tokens collapse to the group identity. The protocol is argued complete, a proof of knowledge, and zero-knowledge under standard assumptions.

The paper also models secret and public-key access control lists, gives more efficient packles, and generic packles for arbitrary FSS. On private information retrieval, packles add roughly 1.5× to 3× overhead versus plain FSS-based PIR, with cost amortizing on larger records. In anonymous communication systems such as Express and Spectrum, packles can cut server overhead by up to 70× when mailbox counts grow large. Practitioners gain a way to gate FSS evaluation without breaking its privacy guarantees.

talks.title: Blue Is the New Black (Market): Privacy Leaks and Re-Victimization from Police-Auctioned Cellphones
talks.teaser: Shows how phones resold at police auctions expose personal data, weak locks and criminal evidence to whoever buys them.
talks.summary:
Richard Roberts and collaborators asked whether phones sold at police auctions still hold sensitive data. Police can auction nearly any item with monetary value, and owners may not know police hold their phone. The team bought 228 phones in 40 bulk lots from a major online police auction house for 4,245 dollars.

Sixty phones were broken, leaving 168 working devices. Forty-nine opened straight to the home screen, and 11 more fell to common PINs or patterns. One had its PIN written on a sticky note. In all, 61 phones were open to anyone without tools. The data included nude images on 18 phones, browsing histories on 51, 194 saved username and password pairs, five passports and 14 driver's licenses. Some phones had not been used in over a decade.

Some phones belonged to criminals and still held evidence of their crimes, including a screenshot from a site selling stolen credit cards and 24 stolen credit histories, 23 with full Social Security numbers. The researchers argue that reselling such phones re-victimizes the people whose data they hold. After disclosure in October 2022, the auction house added a notice that personal information had been removed, but later purchases showed some SD cards still held data. They advise locking phones, wiping them remotely, and destroying rather than reselling them.

talks.title: Threshold BBS+ Signatures for Distributed Anonymous Credential Issuance
talks.teaser: Shows how several servers can jointly issue BBS+ signatures for anonymous credentials, removing the single issuer point of failure.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces the BBS+ signature scheme, an elliptic-curve signature whose structure makes it efficient to prove statements about signed messages in zero knowledge. That property is why it is used for anonymous credentials. The speaker points out that a single issuer is a single point of failure: if it is compromised, credentials can be forged. The problem addressed is how to split the signing task across several servers, where the main obstacle is inverting a secret that sits in the exponent.

The proposed protocol is a two-round, low-latency multi-party scheme that draws on earlier threshold ECDSA work and an old inversion technique based on padding with random nonces. Most steps are symmetric operations, and the group operations are confined to the final step, where the client assembles the signature and checks that it verifies. The main contribution is malicious security without zero-knowledge proofs or cut-and-choose. The analysis reduces adversarial cheating to additive offsets on four protocol values. The best achievable guarantee is security with abort, not identifiable abort.

Benchmarks on LAN and WAN setups show that signing time stays within seconds as the party count grows from 2 to 32. A single BBS+ signer takes about 1.5 milliseconds, so the MPC overhead is roughly 3x on a LAN and about 40x on a WAN, mostly due to latency. The speaker compares the approach with RP-Coconut, noting that the client needs fewer pairing operations. The talk closes by placing BBS+ among threshold signature schemes, where it needs one multiplication against two for ECDSA.

talks.title: TeSec: Accurate Server-side Attack Investigation for Web Applications
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning TeSec: Accurate Server-side Attack Investigation for Web Applications.

talks.title: TEEzz: Fuzzing Trusted Applications on COTS Android Devices
talks.teaser: Presents a black-box fuzzer that tests Android trusted applications on commercial phones, using type and state awareness.
talks.summary:
Smartphones keep their most sensitive data, such as biometric templates, PINs and cryptographic keys, inside a trusted execution environment. On Arm devices this runs in TrustZone's secure world, where vendor trusted applications serve normal-world client apps that can reach them only through the secure monitor. Fuzzing these components is hard: the isolation gives little introspection and no coverage feedback, the shared memory carries complex structured data, and the components keep state across calls.

The fuzzer presented, TEEzz, works as a black box. It first finds the Android components that talk to a trusted application and extracts their interface descriptions, parses those into an abstract syntax tree, and generates type-aware mutators from them. Rather than going through high-level libraries that sanitize inputs, it hooks the lower-level interface with dynamic binary instrumentation, records parameters by their types, and correlates them with raw bytes to build a seed corpus. Recording output parameters also captures value dependencies between calls, which helps model the target's state machine.

Across four devices with two proprietary TEEs, the work found 40 unique bugs. In the open-source OP-TEE reference implementation it found 13 previously unknown bugs. A ground-truth experiment on a modified OP-TEE showed that the state-aware seed corpus reached higher coverage than a coverage-guided AFL run in some scenarios. In the Q&A, the speaker said porting to another vendor's TEE depends on the vendor, and that the hook generation follows automatically from function definitions. The takeaway is that trusted applications are a real attack surface, and black-box, type- and state-aware fuzzing is a workable way to test them.

talks.title: SoK: Cryptographic Neural-Network Computation
talks.teaser: Surveys cryptographic frameworks for private neural network inference and training, comparing their accuracy and speed trade-offs.
talks.summary:
This systematization of knowledge surveys privacy-preserving neural network frameworks, grouped by the privacy service they offer: oblivious inference, where a client queries a model without revealing its input and without learning the model; outsourced inference and training, where an untrusted server computes on encrypted data and models; and multi-party training, where several data owners build a shared model without exposing their data. Trusted-hardware designs and several attack-defense topics were excluded from the scope.

Linear layers such as matrix multiplication are handled differently from nonlinear ones. Homomorphic encryption schemes struggle with activations and pooling, often using polynomial approximations that lower accuracy, and fixed-point arithmetic forces large parameters that slow things down. Hybrid designs using secret sharing and garbled circuits handle comparisons more efficiently, and three-party schemes that assume non-colluding servers usually reach higher throughput. Training is harder still, since functions such as batch normalization and softmax are costly to approximate. In the evaluation, the authors tested frameworks over wide-area networks; mixed-protocol frameworks still performed best but needed at least 100 megabytes per second of bandwidth.

The talk closes with open problems: better accuracy and speed, helping non-experts choose parameters for changing models, and a universal compiler for rapid prototyping and fair comparison. The full work is planned as an interactive website with a genealogy of the papers.

talks.title: Skilled or Gullible? Gender Stereotypes Related to Computer Security and Privacy
talks.teaser: Maps US survey respondents' gender stereotypes about security and privacy behaviors, and the reasons they give for them.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether people in the United States hold gender stereotypes about routine security and privacy behavior, and what reasons they offer to justify those beliefs. The presenter argues that stereotypes work at the group level and matter because they can shape how people are advised. Those who think bias is absent tend to repeat it. Earlier work mostly found correlations, such as women reporting weaker password habits, so stereotypes are proposed as a possible underlying cause.

The study used a mixed-methods design. A pre-study survey of 202 US crowd workers on Prolific surfaced nine candidate stereotypes, and affinity diagramming of security advice and user behavior papers added more. A main survey then tested 19 stereotypes by asking who is more likely to act in a given way, followed by open questions about why and a sexism scale. Stereotypes about women were mostly negative, including sharing sensitive information on social media, being emotional, falling for shopping scams, and being gullible. Stereotypes about men were largely positive, with nine of ten tied to protective actions. Men participants held four beliefs favoring men that women did not. Higher sexism scores tracked stereotype belief, and rationales often drew on other stereotypes and societal expectations.

For practitioners, the takeaways are to avoid gendered personas, recognize that there is no average user, and remember that crowd-worker samples carry their own biases. The authors point to future work on whether stereotypes lead to weaker security advice for women and on stereotype threat during account setup, such as whether a reminder of gender lowers 2FA use.

talks.title: SecureCells: A Secure Compartmentalized Architecture
talks.teaser: Presents a hardware design for fine-grained compartmentalization, with user-space switch instructions and an FPGA prototype.
talks.summary:
SecureCells, a compartmentalized architecture from EPFL, aims to stop a single bug from compromising a whole program. The speaker points out that modern software mixes third-party libraries and modules, and browsers run JavaScript from unknown sources. Compartmentalization adds a layer above defenses such as memory safety by isolating parts of a program behind defined interfaces. Existing mechanisms often weaken the attacker model, cost too much to isolate at fine granularity, or suit only narrow domains; Intel MPK, for instance, does not check code accesses.

The design has three pillars. Cell-granularity access control uses a permissions table in place of page tables, with separate read, write and execute rights per compartment, enforced by the MMU. User-space instructions switch between compartments, mark valid entry points, transfer or drop permissions instead of copying buffers, and check exclusive access to guard against data races. Implementing it requires changes to the register file, pipeline and MMU, plus a range-based TLB tagged with compartment identifiers so it need not be flushed on switches.

An FPGA prototype on an in-order RISC-V core achieved eight-cycle compartment switches, about three orders of magnitude faster than microsecond-scale system calls. Permission transfers in firmware took around 200 cycles, and microcode cut that by up to 70 percent. Questions covered pipeline flushes and comparisons with Intel MPK and ASID/PCID-style tagging. The takeaway is that hardware-enforced, fast compartmentalization is practical and flexible, with the full stack released as open source.
