talks.title: IEEE S&P 2023 Short Talks
talks.teaser: A session strings software-security talks on side channels, identity, MPC trust, mobile SDKs, and cloud attestation gaps.
talks.summary:
An IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy software session strings together brief presentations from academic and industry researchers rather than one continuous narrative. It opens with a live demonstration that amplifies CPU cache timing differences until an audience can tell hits from misses, arguing that disabling high-resolution timers may not end practical side-channel leakage when humans participate in the measurement loop.

Mid-session speakers shift to organizational and protocol angles. One advocates data-centric identity, access control, and threat detection anchored on what organizations store in the cloud. Another explores asymmetric trust in three-party secure computation between semi-honest and fully malicious models. A vendor-led segment compares TikTok and ByteDance SDK permissions across Android apps, noting wide SDK reuse beyond a single brand. Researchers also sketch secret-shared email delivery with multi-party computation for server-side search, critique adapter-signature definitions with counterexamples for coin mixing and payment designs, and relate long-lived medical credentials to PDF parsing datasets and crypto agility.

The block closes with confidential-computing attestation reviews for Intel TDX and SCONE, including specification gaps around certificate chains, withheld hash inputs, and MAC verification, plus a brief announcement of a free graduate summer school on software testing and automated vulnerability discovery in Germany. Practitioners hear a sampler of active software-security research and product-facing problems rather than a single deep dive.

talks.title: mmEcho: A mmWave-based Acoustic Eavesdropping Method
talks.teaser: Shows how a millimeter-wave radar can recover speech from the vibrations of nearby everyday objects without machine learning.
talks.summary:
The talk tackles eavesdropping in rooms where soundproofing, background noise or hidden microphones make conventional spying hard. The speaker, a professor at Shandong University, reviewed earlier options: sensors that must be pre-installed on a device, optical methods that a closed curtain can block, and Wi-Fi sensing that recognizes only a small vocabulary.

The proposed mmEcho system points an off-the-shelf millimeter-wave radar at everyday objects such as curtains, paper, tin foil and chip bags, which vibrate when someone speaks nearby. It finds the strongest reflecting surface from measured velocity, then refines phase values, including correcting phase wrapping, so tiny vibrations can be captured at a sampling rate that covers the speech spectrum. Pure signal processing turns these measurements into audio, with noise reduction at the end, and no trained model is needed.

The radar sat about one meter from the object with drywall between them, and tests varied distance and angle. Quality was judged with MCD, word error rate and MOS scores. Paper performed worst because much of the signal passes through it, while tin foil and chip bags did best. Five languages showed little difference, and the speaker compared the method with earlier radar eavesdropping on phone calls. In questions, the speaker said machine learning could still be added for noise reduction. The takeaway is that contactless radar can recover speech from nearby objects without prior installation or training data.

talks.title: It’s (DOM) Clobbering Time: Attack Techniques, Prevalence, and Defenses
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding It’s (DOM) Clobbering Time: Attack Techniques, Prevalence, and Defenses.
talks.summary: Sohail presents CISPA research on DOM clobbering, where attacker-controlled element names shadow security-sensitive JavaScript variables to redirect script loads. The team generates more than 31,000 novel clobbering markups across browsers and ships DomClobber at domclob.xyz. A Puppeteer pipeline models property graphs from live pages, finds taint paths into sinks, and dynamically confirms roughly 9,400 flows on top sites with dozens of working exploits on GitHub, Vimeo, and Fandom-class properties. Sanitizer tests show sixteen popular HTML cleaners still pass clobbering payloads even in strict mode, motivating namespace isolation patches in DOMPurify and OWASP cheat-sheet patterns.

talks.title: Inducing Wireless Chargers to Voice Out for Inaudible Command Attacks
talks.teaser: Shows wireless chargers' magnetic fields can inject inaudible voice commands into phone microphones, hijacking voice assistants.
talks.summary:
Voice assistants on smartphones can often be triggered even when the screen is locked, and earlier injection methods relied on ultrasound, lasers or electromagnetic waves, which need active transceivers, precise alignment or costly gear. This talk proposes using the magnetic field of a wireless charger as the carrier. The speaker explained that microphone components sit exposed in the strong charging field, so a modulated signal can induce a voice current inside the microphone.

Two attack variants were presented. In the hardware attack, a charger whose microcontroller can be controlled drives its coil with pulse-width modulation to emulate audio, and the microphone's nonlinear behaviour down-converts the high-frequency charging signal into the audible band. In the parasite attack, a small battery-free label placed on a public charger harvests power and carries a flower-petal-shaped coil array, so a coil sits beneath the microphone whatever the phone's orientation. Feasibility tests showed recognition improving with charging power, and the attack held up in most environments but not on a bus, where noise exceeded 70 dBA.

The closing section covered countermeasures: upgrading microphone hardware, detecting abnormal wireless charging signals in software, disabling microphones while charging, and capping charging power at the manufacturer level. In questions, the speaker said the attack worked at distances under five centimeters and that the parasite takes about one percent of the charging power. The takeaway is that charging pads in public spaces can become a voice-injection channel.

talks.title: FLUTE: Fast and Secure Lookup Table Evaluations
talks.teaser: Presents FLUTE, a two-party protocol that evaluates lookup tables securely with a faster online phase than prior methods.
talks.summary:
The talk presents FLUTE, a protocol for evaluating lookup tables in secure two-party computation under the semi-honest model, where both parties follow the steps but try to learn as much as they can from what they see. The motivating case is a patient keeping symptoms private while a provider keeps its machine learning model private. Lookup tables replace chunks of a circuit with fewer, wider gates, which reduces the number of communication rounds. Each table is rewritten as a Boolean sum-of-products formula and viewed as a generalized dot product built from ABY2's existing gates.

The benchmarks on floating-point circuits were the core evidence. Online communication was about 100 times lower than SP-LOOT and three to four times lower than an OT-based truth-table approach, while total communication was about 20 times lower than the truth-table approach and roughly comparable to SP-LOOT. Against garbled circuits, total communication was about two times better. In a LAN setting the online phase ran 1.3 to 2.3 times faster than the ABY2 baseline, with total runtime worse by 10 up to 50. In a WAN setting, online runtime improved by 3.4 to 3.8 times, and the protocol could beat the baseline on total runtime.

In the discussion, the speaker noted that setup can be partly amortized across lookup tables that share input wires, and that the function inside a table is freely programmable. Homomorphic encryption approaches were not compared. The takeaway is that lookup tables trade some setup cost for a faster online phase, which matters most when online performance dominates. The implementation is open source.

talks.title: Breaking Security-Critical Voice Authentication
talks.teaser: Shows how spoofed voice audio can be reshaped to evade speaker verification and anti-spoofing countermeasures.
talks.summary:
Voice authentication is now used by banks and other service providers, where a caller repeats a random phrase that is compared with a stored voiceprint. The speaker notes that these systems depend on anti-spoofing countermeasures, which run alongside speaker verification and speech recognition to separate synthetic audio from genuine speech. Earlier black-box attacks, such as transferring adversarial examples or issuing many queries, were described as impractical against deployed systems with attempt limits.

The attack starts from high-quality fake speech and applies transformations that remove the cues countermeasures rely on. Leading and trailing silence is replaced with natural silence, and an echo is added to mimic a real recording environment. The central part of the spectrum, where consonants carry intelligibility, is boosted, and spectral gating removes steady artifacts that persist over time. A final adversarial optimization is run against a speaker verification model, targeting the victim's enrolled voiceprint rather than a transferred surrogate.

Evaluation used 474 hand-picked samples from 48 users, created with 13 spoofing algorithms, and tested against several representative systems over apps and phone calls. The attack required no interactive queries, typically up to three or six attempts of under four seconds each, and reached success rates as high as 100 percent, compared with zero percent without the optimization. The speaker argued that these voice checks are not as secure as they are commonly claimed to be.

talks.title: Sound Verification of Security Protocols: From Design to Interoperable Implementations
talks.teaser: Links symbolic protocol proofs in Tamarin to verified Go implementations of WireGuard using separation-logic program verifiers.
talks.summary:
Protocol security is often proven on abstract models, but deployed software runs real code, leaving a gap between a verified model and its implementation. This talk presents an approach that closes that gap. Protocol roles are first modelled and checked in the Tamarin prover for the security properties of interest. A tool then derives input/output specifications for each role from that model, written in an input/output separation logic.

These specifications serve as preconditions for an existing implementation, which is checked with off-the-shelf program verifiers such as Gobra for Go. The verifier must show that the code is memory safe, free of undefined behaviour, and performs only the I/O the specification allows. The refinement argument means every trace the implementation can produce under a symbolic attacker is contained in the specified traces, so properties proven in the model carry over to the code. A simple Alice-and-Bob protocol illustrated how the role-level reasoning works.

The approach was evaluated on WireGuard. The protocol model was about 400 lines of Tamarin code, and a simplified Go implementation of about 600 lines was verified. The effort produced roughly 1,200 lines of generated specification and about 2,800 lines of proof annotations for memory safety and for connecting the specification to the code. In the Q&A, the speaker noted that the work covers trace properties only, not observational equivalence, and that key handling and information flow are not yet addressed. The takeaway is that a verified model can be tied to existing code, though the proof annotations must be maintained as the code changes.

talks.title: SNAP: Efficient Extraction of Private Properties with Poisoning
talks.teaser: Shows how a small amount of poisoned training data lets attackers infer private dataset properties from a model.
talks.summary:
The talk presents SNAP, a property inference attack that uses data poisoning against machine learning models. The concern is that organizations training on user data can leak aggregate facts, such as what share of people in the dataset have a given condition. The threat model assumes an adversary who slips a small poisoned portion into the training set, then queries the deployed model as a black box and receives either confidence scores or only predicted labels.

Poisoning pushes the confidence distributions of models trained on different property fractions apart, creating a separation the attacker can exploit. Earlier meta-classifier attacks needed hundreds or thousands of shadow models and high poisoning rates; SNAP instead fits Gaussians to shadow-model confidences, sets a threshold, and uses no more than eight shadow models. Across four datasets and 18 properties, accuracy exceeded 90 percent at about five percent poisoning for most properties, and under 0.6 percent for medium-sized ones. Extensions cover label-only attacks, property existence, and size estimation via binary search with up to 14 models. Against prior work, the talk reported 34 percent higher accuracy, 56 times faster execution, and four to six times less poisoning.

The takeaway is that differential privacy did not stop these attacks, and defending against property inference remains an open problem. In questions, the speaker said the poisoning uses label flipping rather than clean-label poisoning, and that detection of poisoned data was not tested directly. An optimized variant was described as lowering the poisoning rate to around one percent even for larger properties.

talks.title: DepthFake: Spoofing 3D Face Authentication with a 2D Photo
talks.teaser: Shows how a single 2D photo and a projected infrared pattern can spoof a commercial 3D face login.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether a commercial 3D face authentication system, which pairs a structured light depth camera with RGB liveness checks, can be fooled using one 2D photo of a victim. Existing depth estimation methods did not produce the absolute depth values these systems need, so the team trained a CNN that predicts depth from a single photo, weighting the nose and eye regions in its loss. The reported normalized mean error is under 2%.

Getting that depth into a physical device was the harder part. Projecting infrared straight into the camera failed, since the sensor only receives dots and cannot form depth from them. The attacker instead blocks the victim's own projector and uses an external one to bounce a modulated infrared pattern off the photo back into the sensor. The template pattern is read with an external infrared camera and reshaped using similar-triangle geometry. For the RGB check, the team used a black-box, query-based evolutionary attack, corrected color shift from reprinting, and mapped five keypoints to align RGB and depth inputs.

Tests covered 50 victims against one commercial depth camera and three commercial systems, and the vendors were notified. The projector could sit within 5 cm of the device, and face angles under 30 degrees with resolution above 480p worked best. A live access-control demo showed a plain photo replay failing while the spoof opened the door. Suggested defenses include stronger liveness models, detecting depth regions beyond the projector's limited projection size, and randomizing the structured light pattern, though the speaker noted that hardware makes per-authentication randomization difficult.

talks.title: A Real-World Hardware Trojan Detection Case Study Across Four Modern CMOS Technology Generations
talks.teaser: Shows how SEM imaging and image comparison can reveal tiny hardware Trojan edits across four modern chip generations.
talks.summary:
The talk tackles a supply chain risk: a contract manufacturer could alter a chip's design before fabrication, so a trusted lab must confirm the silicon matches the design files. To test detection fairly, a red team secretly edited the design files for four previously fabricated research chips at 65, 40 and 28 nanometers, introducing four cell insertions and six cell replacements. A blue team, acting as the analysis lab, then examined the chips without knowing where the changes were.

The blue team milled and etched the back side of each chip, then imaged the bottom layer with a scanning electron microscope, a slow process taking one to two days per chip. The resulting mosaics reached hundreds of gigabytes. The design layout was aligned to the images, each standard cell was cropped and labeled, and scripts flagged added cells through visible via contacts and replaced cells through template matching against a reference cell. Across chips with up to about 1.5 million cells, only 367 candidates remained for manual review. Debris on some sample areas and lookalike cells in the 28 nanometer chip caused misses.

Image comparison can therefore catch small, late modifications in full-size chips, though smaller nodes with similar-looking cells need better imaging or machine learning. The team released its anonymized images, design files and OpenCV code for further research.

talks.title: Not Yet Another Digital ID: Privacy-preserving Humanitarian Aid Distribution
talks.teaser: Shows a card-based aid distribution design that blocks double dipping while hiding recipients' identities from auditors.
talks.summary:
Humanitarian groups hand out aid in person, and paper name lists are slow to search once distributions grow. A plain central database with biometric checks would scale, but it would expose sensitive recipient data to anyone with access, including auditors and local authorities. The team worked with the International Committee of the Red Cross, first mapping the registration, distribution and auditing phases to learn which functions a digital replacement must keep.

The design moves eligibility checks onto a tamper-resistant card issued per household. The card holds a household key, the entitlement record and a period counter. At each distribution, the station sends a period number and the card returns a tag computed from that key and the period. A repeated tag reveals double dipping, while the tags look random, so a station cannot link one household's behavior across periods. For auditing, the card signs its tags and entitlement commitments with a global key, and stations forward only aggregated totals using a homomorphic commitment, letting auditors check signatures, tag uniqueness and sums without seeing individual records.

The authors describe smart card and smartphone versions, the latter using zero-knowledge proofs instead of trusting hardware, and report formal proofs and scalability evaluations for hundreds of thousands of households. In discussion, a stolen card fails authentication, and the design must tolerate unstable connectivity. The takeaway is that limiting disclosure, especially to auditors, protects recipients even though attendance at a station stays visible.

talks.title: SoK: Certified Robustness for Deep Neural Networks
talks.teaser: Surveys certified robustness for neural networks, comparing relaxation and randomized smoothing on scalability and benchmarks.
talks.summary:
Adversarial examples are tiny, deliberately crafted input changes that can make deep neural networks give confident wrong predictions, which is a safety concern for systems such as autonomous driving. Defenses keep being broken by later attacks, so the talk turns to certified robustness, which tries to prove that no adversarial input exists within a set radius around a test point. The focus is on p-norm bounded perturbations, which are seen as generalizable to other threat types.

Two main families were covered. Linear relaxation combined with branch and bound replaces each nonlinear activation with linear bounds and splits unstable neurons into subproblems to tighten the result; it is presented as the tightest and most scalable option for generic networks, handling models with up to about one million neurons. Randomized smoothing trains a base classifier under Gaussian noise and predicts the most likely label over noisy copies of an input. It requires changing inference but scales to ImageNet-sized data, and its certified radius follows from top-class probabilities and the noise variance.

The systematization contributes a taxonomy, a discussion of open challenges, a benchmark of existing approaches, a leaderboard and an open-source toolkit. Certified accuracy is high on small datasets but falls sharply on larger ones such as ImageNet. In the Q&A, the presenter advised that randomized smoothing is the strongest choice when enough runtime is available, while relaxation with branch and bound fits cases where inference must stay unchanged or runtime is limited. Scaling verification to large language models was named as future work.

talks.title: mmSpoof: Resilient Spoofing of Automotive Millimeter-wave Radars using Reflect Array
talks.teaser: Shows how a reflective array can spoof automotive radar distance and speed without active transmission.
talks.summary:
Automotive millimeter-wave radars support features such as adaptive cruise control and emergency braking by estimating the distance and speed of the vehicle ahead. The talk asks whether these radars are safe enough. Earlier spoofing attacks needed custom waveforms actively transmitted by the attacker and tight synchronization with the victim, sometimes over wired links, which is impractical on a road.

The proposed mmSpoof attack uses a reflect array that captures the incoming radar wave, adds a frequency shift and reflects it back, so it needs no active transmission and no synchronization. In FMCW ranging, the shift appears as a time difference: a positive shift makes the target seem closer and a negative shift makes it seem farther, avoiding the limit of delay-based spoofing, which can only lengthen apparent distance. The same shift also changes the Doppler frequency and therefore the reported velocity. The authors decouple the two by applying shifts at multiples of a specific value to change only distance, and small shifts to change mainly velocity. A prototype was built from two phased arrays and a software-defined radio, which estimates the radar's start frequency, chirp time and slope in real time.

In static tests with the reflector placed between 30 and 100 meters from the radar, the reported distance fell exponentially toward zero while velocity dropped and recovered, mimicking a braking pattern that could disable emergency braking. In a moving test, the radar's estimate shifted from about 80 to 130 meters as the ground truth changed from 50 to 100 meters, with an extra 3 meters per second of velocity error. The speaker suggested high-resolution radar, multi-sensor fusion and per-sensor parameter changes as countermeasures, and stressed that current radars are not foolproof.

talks.title: Investigating Package Related Security Threats in Software Registries
talks.teaser: Maps novel attack vectors across package registries and mirrors, measuring how many packages and maintainers are exposed.
talks.summary:
Developers rely on open-source packages hosted on registries such as PyPI and npm, and on mirrors that copy those packages to speed up downloads. The talk follows the life cycle of a package, from publishing and updating to unlisting, mirror syncing and download, and shows where each stage creates weak points. The speaker cites more than 2.2 trillion downloads across the top four registries in 2021, alongside a 615 percent rise in software supply chain attacks.

The speaker walks through several attack vectors. Reusing the name of a deleted package lets an attacker republish it under the same name. Maintainer account hijacking becomes possible when an email domain used for registration expires and is bought again. Redirection hijacking exploits the redirects GitHub creates after a project is renamed or transferred: an attacker re-registers the old username and publishes a malicious copy. Mirrors that fail to sync unpublished packages leave ghost packages that can be overwritten, and some mirrors answer requests inconsistently. Case-sensitive name confusion, scope-name issues and cross-registry confusion complete the list.

To measure impact, the researchers monitored several registries and 17 mirrors over one year. They found vulnerable packages and accounts across all major registries, with Cargo the exception because it ties users to a GitHub ID rather than a username. Delayed mirror syncing and internal packages were key causes of exposure. The team reported the issues to the affected stakeholders, received positive responses, and was told the problems had been fixed. The takeaway is that registries and mirrors need stronger rules for deleted names, account ownership and redirects.

talks.title: PublicCheck: Public Integrity Verification for Services of Run-time Deep Models
talks.teaser: PublicCheck shows how API-only users verify cloud ML model integrity using decision-boundary samples with low query cost.
talks.summary:
Machine learning models increasingly ship as paid cloud APIs, with developers, agents, hosts, and end users each touching deployment. Integrity checks that only bind a model owner to a single cloud operator fall short in that commercial chain: verifiers often see only black-box predictions, white-box weights may be encrypted or unavailable, verification keys can leak to malicious clients, and the hosting party can answer probes with a substituted or trimmed model.

The presentation introduces PublicCheck, aimed at public verification of a runtime deep model in service. The core idea is to treat stable predictions on inputs clustered near the classifier decision boundary as a fingerprint, on the premise that unauthorized model changes shift boundary behavior. To keep API cost down and resist abuse, perturbations are searched in a low-dimensional latent space from a pretrained autoencoder, with disentangled latent dimensions tied to semantic attributes, bounded ranges where predictions become unstable, and smoothing so verification traffic is hard to separate from ordinary business queries.

Evaluation is described across four datasets and several integrity attacks, including opposing-vector and compression-style tampering. The speaker reports unchanged normal task performance, black-box-only fingerprinting, high detection accuracy with on the order of five to ten API queries in their examples, and faster verification-sample generation than pixel-space perturbation baselines. Five adaptive attacker models—sample collection, bypass, fingerprint recovery, and related goals—are said to be defeated via randomness, smoothness, and uncertainty baked into sample generation, with fuller detail deferred to the paper.

talks.title: AEM: Facilitating Cross-Version Exploitability Assessment of Linux Kernel Vulnerabilities
talks.teaser: Shows how a Linux kernel exploit working on one version can be migrated to other kernel versions by aligning memory operations.
talks.summary:
Linux kernel exploits often work on only one version, because code changes between releases shift the memory layouts and behaviour that exploitation depends on. Rewriting an exploit for each release is slow and needs deep kernel knowledge. The talk presents AEM, an approach that migrates an existing working exploit to another kernel version instead of building a new one from scratch.

The method records the critical memory operations of the successful exploit as a dependency graph, then runs the failing exploit on the target kernel and aligns its memory operations against that graph. When an operation is missing or touches the wrong data, the tool adjusts system call arguments and tries again. Migration counts as successful only when all critical operations are reproduced on the target. The speaker walked through an example where a missing check blocked a read of a control flow hijacking address, and the fix was to bypass that check.

The prototype is built on symbolic execution and was evaluated on 78 real-world exploits drawn from public databases, technical articles and an existing automatic exploit generation project. The authors reproduced 28 of them and migrated 56 of 90 version pairs that could not be reused as-is. Failures were attributed to missing symmetric multiprocessing support in the engine and to kernel functionality and data structures that changed too much. The takeaway is that exploit reuse across kernel versions can be automated by aligning memory behaviour, not just code.

talks.title: Practically-Exploitable Cryptographic Vulnerabilities in Matrix
talks.teaser: Covers six attacks on Matrix's end-to-end encryption, five practically exploitable, mostly where its sub-protocols interact.
talks.summary:
Matrix is a federated platform for secure communication, used through apps such as Element by about 80 million users, including European government organisations and militaries. Its end-to-end encryption combines sub-protocols for cross-signing identities, out-of-band verification, pairwise channels, group messaging, key requests, key backups and secure secret storage. Before this work, its cryptography had received little study.

Of six attacks found, five were practically exploitable, and proofs of concept were built for attacks two to five against Element and the reference libraries. The first lets a home server forge group membership messages, which are neither encrypted nor authenticated; it was still unfixed at the time of the talk. The second abuses user-to-user verification: a server-controlled device identifier shares a namespace with cross-signing keys, so a crafted string makes a client attach a device key to an attacker's hierarchy, enabling an active man-in-the-middle. The later attacks chain impersonation, first via forwarded keys, then a crafted ciphertext that removes the forwarded flag, and finally a forced backup key that exposes backed-up sessions.

Asked about specification versus code, the speaker said the work began with the specification and used the implementation to fill its gaps, since gaps often appeared in both. Most attacks have since been fixed. The main takeaway is that the attacks mostly occur where sub-protocols interact rather than in their internals, and the design had little formal analysis.

talks.title: MPCAuth: Multi-factor Authentication for Distributed-trust Systems
talks.teaser: Presents a way for users to authenticate once to many servers holding split secrets, without exposing their authentication profile.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses how a user should authenticate to a distributed-trust system, where a secret is split across several servers so that no single server holds it. Two simple designs are weak. Routing login through one master server creates a central point of attack, while having the user authenticate separately to every server multiplies the work, such as checking and typing several email passcodes. The speaker presents MPCAuth, in which the servers act together as one logical server so the user authenticates just once, and the scheme covers factors including email, SMS, U2F, passcodes and biometrics.

The core technique pairs TLS with MPC. The servers run the TLS handshake and encryption inside MPC, so they assemble one email containing a single passcode and send it to the email provider without any individual server seeing plaintext. For email login, each server computes a PRF of a jointly generated password, the user enters that password once, and each server checks its own value. Email addresses and other authentication profile details stay secret-shared, so they remain hidden from every server. The prototype was built on MP-SPDZ, EMP and WolfSSL, and the reported run time was 12.2 seconds for a fresh TLS connection, with 0.4 seconds of online latency when a persistent connection is reused. The speakers also demonstrated sending such an email to Gmail.

The security model tolerates corruption of up to n minus one of n servers, and an attacker succeeds only if every server or every factor is compromised. In the Q&A, the speaker said a failed server would at most cause denial of service. The takeaway for practitioners is that distributed trust can be combined with a single user login, provided the login data stays hidden inside MPC.

talks.title: Continuous Intrusion: Characterizing the Security of Continuous Integration Services
talks.teaser: Shows how weak runner isolation and long-lived tokens in CI platforms let attackers steal secrets and alter artifacts.
talks.summary:
Continuous integration services take code from a hosting platform, schedule builds and tests on runners that launch executors, and upload resulting artifacts to third-party storage. Recent token theft and customer-data incidents prompted a closer look at this workflow, where test code is untrusted and components authenticate to each other with tokens.

The research examined isolation and token handling across seven popular platforms. Runners may use plain processes, containers or virtual machines, and some reuse a runner for later jobs from other repositories without cleaning up. Several platforms also issue long-lived tokens beyond the one-time task and artifact tokens. In a TeamCity case, a collaborator with access to one repository obtained a reused personal token from a shared job and reached another repository. A custom tool, Inspector, extracted tokens from jobs and tested what they could reach; among the platforms, only Bitbucket's Docker mode leaked no tokens. Two vectors stood out: re-registering a rogue runner after stealing its registration token, and injecting code into artifacts using a long-lived artifact token.

Vendors were notified and responded positively. Practitioners should avoid sharing self-hosted runners between public and private repositories, and platforms should adopt stronger isolation, with Docker-based separation of authentication presented as the better model. The speaker noted that Inspector was not yet open source.

talks.title: WarpAttack: Bypassing CFI through Compiler-Introduced Double-Fetches
talks.teaser: Shows how compiler-introduced double fetches in switch jump tables can be raced to hijack indirect jumps and bypass CFI.
talks.summary:
WarpAttack targets the gap between what compilers assume and what control-flow integrity (CFI) relies on. The speaker shows that a switch statement can be compiled so a shared value is read twice: once for the bounds check and again to compute the indirect jump target. If another thread changes that value between the reads, the jump can land on an attacker-chosen address that CFI does not check.

The threat model matches CFI's: an attacker with arbitrary read and write who also needs a triggerable gadget with this double fetch and a concurrent thread to win the race. Losing the race may simply crash the program. The speaker described three obstacles: separating compiler-made double fetches from ordinary ones with a new binary model, filtering false positives with a fixed instruction window, and handling a race window as short as two instructions by running victim and attacker loops at different speeds. Stack contents are checked before overwriting to avoid crashes.

The team found more than 1,600 victim gadgets across six programs, including Firefox and Chromium, and saw the issue with both GCC and Clang. A proof of concept against the latest Firefox succeeded at a rate of 0.45 in 20 seconds. Similar gadgets appeared on ARM, RISC-V and MIPS, though only stack-based variants there. The takeaway is that compiler optimizations can silently break security assumptions, and avoiding switch jump tables was raised as a possible but unmeasured mitigation.

talks.title: Precise Detection of Kernel Data Races with Probabilistic Lockset Analysis
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Precise Detection of Kernel Data Races with Probabilistic Lockset Analysis.
talks.summary: Gabriel Ryan presents probabilistic lockset analysis (PLA), sampling syscall traces to learn stable memory accesses and predict unguarded races far faster than exhaustive schedule fuzzing. On a recent Linux kernel the tool reports 183 races in 24 hours—including a decade-old network crypto leak missed by prior fuzzers—and validates each prediction with forced concurrent schedules and stack traces.

talks.summary: Ka Wang introduces Volttack, showing how injected high-frequency ripple on IoT power rails bypasses expected PSR filtering and EMC bands to falsify sensor readings or actuator commands on automotive pedals, environmental monitors, servos, and valves. Attackers with brief physical access can swap batteries, tap sockets, or clamp cables; demos double braking distance and over-open coolant valves, motivating supply monitoring and stronger rejection above legacy test limits.

talks.title: Effective ReDoS Detection by Principled Vulnerability Modeling and Exploit Generation
talks.teaser: Shows how modeling regex vulnerabilities and generating attack strings finds more exploitable ReDoS bugs in real-world projects.
talks.summary:
ReDoS is a denial-of-service problem in which a crafted input forces a regular expression engine's matching to consume CPU for an extremely long time. The talk explains that rejecting a string requires the engine to explore every possible path through the expression's automaton, so the cost grows sharply as the input gets longer. The speaker described two weaknesses in existing static, dynamic and hybrid detectors: their vulnerability patterns are mostly drawn from the structure of an expression rather than its semantics, and the attack strings they generate can fail because neighbouring sub-expressions also accept the same characters.

To address these, the work models vulnerabilities by unfolding loop sub-expressions and summarizing global features of the unfolded form, which yields three patterns that also account for severity. For attack generation, the authors identify five categories of interference between sub-expressions and derive conditions that steer generation so the vulnerable part really is the only part that matches. In the evaluation, using four existing datasets and three self-collected sets with more than 300 thousand regular expressions from real projects, the tool identified more vulnerable expressions than the compared tools, and an ablation study showed that both the modeling and the generation strategy contribute significantly.

Applied to more than 300 real-world projects, the approach yielded 69 exploitable ReDoS vulnerabilities after manual validation of projects that also accept user-controllable input. These were reported to vendors, resulting in 21 CVEs. The speaker noted that the flagged expressions were only candidates, and that only a small share proved exploitable. The practical takeaway is that exploitability depends on whether attacker-controlled input actually reaches the expression.

talks.title: TELEPATH: A Minecraft-based Covert Communication System
talks.teaser: Modded Minecraft tunnels blocked web traffic by swapping only packets that keep encrypted game-state causality intact against censors.
talks.summary:
Nation-state censorship often combines blacklists, deep packet inspection, and traffic fingerprinting, so circumvention channels must resemble permitted applications rather than standalone protocols classifiers can spot. The presentation argues that tunneling through a real cover app beats mimicking one, then shows why naive traffic substitution still fails for stateful games: encrypted Minecraft traffic still exposes partial state through packet sizes, and a template-following strawman can produce impossible traces such as map updates reaching a dead player before respawn.

The proposed Telepath system uses non-disruptive content substitution, replacing only state-independent traffic while leaving state-dependent messages intact so server and client stay consistent. Game-specific analysis labels visual effects and synchronization traffic as substitutable; in Minecraft, map updates dominate downstream bandwidth and position sync dominates upstream, with covert throughput reported around 1300 kilobits per second client-bound and about one to two kilobits per second server-bound. Evaluations loaded eight point nine of nine blocked popular sites, six in under one minute, with one timeout from heavy requesting; audio streaming up to 256 kilobits per second is also described.

Practitioners should treat statistical indistinguishability as insufficient when the cover application is stateful: invariant violations enable one-shot detection without classifiers. The takeaway is to subsume circumvention inside normal encrypted gameplay and respect application logic, not only packet timing and size distributions.

talks.title: Finding Specification Blind Spots via Fuzz Testing
talks.teaser: Cross-checking specifications, mutants, and unit tests exposes mistaken specification blind spots in verified codebases.
talks.summary:
Formal verification can prove that an implementation matches its specification, yet the program is only as correct as that specification. The presentation argues that specification completeness often receives less attention than proof tooling, and shows how gaps can hide bugs: a verified add-one function could pop an element from the list while the original spec still passed until length constraints were added.

The proposed approach treats the specification, implementation, and unit test suite as three independent views of the same requirements. When a mutant passes verification, outcomes are classified by whether tests cover the behavioral gap—intentional design, inconclusive need for manual review, or a mistaken spec hole when tests fail. Enumerative mutation does not scale to thousands of sites, so the work adopts evolutionary mutant generation guided by verification feedback, rewarding mutants that reduce verification errors without introducing new ones.

Case studies on a blockchain payment network and an AWS TLS protocol implementation reportedly yielded multiple confirmed mistaken gaps, including a missing sequence-number increment spec tied to replay protection. Practitioners should treat verified code as dependent on spec quality and can use test-backed mutant fuzzing to find fixable blind spots before assurance claims harden.

talks.title: ELSA: Secure Aggregation for Federated Learning with Malicious Actors
talks.teaser: Introduces Elsa, a two-server secure aggregation protocol for federated learning that stays private against a malicious server.
talks.summary:
Federated learning trains models while data stays on client devices, but gradients can leak sensitive information, and malicious clients can send malformed updates that degrade accuracy. Earlier secure aggregation schemes that split trust across two servers address these problems, but they impose high client communication and high latency. This talk presents Elsa, a distributed-trust protocol aimed at privacy when one server is malicious, resilience to malicious clients, and concrete efficiency.

The speaker starts from a fully malicious-secure two-party design, which becomes impractical because clients must stay online and the computation is very slow. Relaxing the goal to malicious privacy allows the many-client setting to reduce to a single client. The central idea is that a client who knows the servers' random tapes can replay their interaction and spot any deviation, so an honest server can detect a cheating peer. The added client cost is only two lambda bits per client, where lambda is the security parameter. A further trade-off lets clients supply correlated randomness to lower latency at the cost of more communication.

In the evaluation, both Elsa variants beat a prior two-server baseline on client communication and latency, and one variant cuts client communication by more than two orders of magnitude for a modest latency increase. Against a single-server baseline the gains are also large, though the speaker notes that baseline needs only one server while Elsa relies on the two servers not colluding. In the Q&A, a hash mismatch leads to removing the affected client rather than aborting the protocol, and extending beyond two parties would erode the protocol's advantage.

talks.title: Vulnerability Discovery for All: Experiences of Marginalization in Vulnerability Discovery
talks.teaser: Interviews with 16 participants reveal how marginalized people enter vulnerability discovery and what blocks them.
talks.summary:
The security industry faces a worker shortage and a lack of diversity in senior roles. The speaker argues that diversity matters for equity and for technical results, since varied perspectives reduce blind spots. The study conducted 16 semi-structured interviews with people from historically underrepresented groups in vulnerability discovery. Each participant walked through their career from first interest in security to the present, and the interviews were analyzed with open coding.

Participants entered the field through friends or family, through tinkering or a general interest in programming, or through a draw toward a specific aspect such as the subject matter, the pay, or the community. Learning resources were either structured, like challenges, certifications and courses, or unstructured, like on-the-job learning, videos and hacking sites. A first good mentor marked a turning point for participants, who had reported limited growth before and rapid growth after. Mentors offered hands-on help, connections to programs and a filtered set of resources, and seeing people like themselves succeed also made participants feel welcome.

Challenges included learning materials that assume a technical background, a competitive field with few entry positions where only the first finder is paid, and a community that often did not take them seriously. Some mentors were unhelpful, sometimes because they mentored only out of financial or workplace obligation. Every participant described facing explicit discrimination. Affinity groups helped some people but were hard to navigate for those with intersecting identities. Suggestions include mentee-mentor matching, open office hours, anonymous mentoring, and clearer minimum requirements with ways to assess soft skills.

talks.title: FIDO2, CTAP 2.1, and WebAuthn 2: Provable Security and Post-Quantum Instantiation
talks.teaser: Presents formal security proofs for the FIDO2 WebAuthn and CTAP protocols, plus a post-quantum variant of each.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the problem of password reuse, which weakens online accounts. FIDO2 is a passwordless approach built from two sub-protocols, WebAuthn 2 and CTAP 2.1. It adds a hardware authenticator, such as a security key, next to the client and the relying party, and the goal is for the relying party to authenticate the authenticator through the client.

For WebAuthn 2, the speaker showed that if the registration phase is authenticated and the authenticator's state stays secret, the relying party can always authenticate the authenticator, even when the authentication phase is unauthenticated. A fully unauthenticated version is open to man-in-the-middle attacks, and a forged registration challenge can compromise the authenticator state without either side noticing. The proposed WebAuthn 2 Plus fixes this by having both sides store a hash of the registration challenge and comparing it during authentication. CTAP 2.1 addresses the problem of malicious software flooding the user with confirmation prompts. It runs reboot, setup, binding and validation phases tied to a PIN, and the proof shows that the authenticator only processes trusted messages from bonded clients.

The full FIDO2 flow runs CTAP 2.1 first and then WebAuthn 2, and the authors prove the resulting protocol under stated channel and secrecy assumptions. Hybrid and post-quantum instantiations of both sub-protocols keep the same security guarantees against quantum attackers. The main takeaway is a formal statement of which channels must be authenticated and which secrets must stay private for FIDO2 to hold.

talks.title: Locally Differentially Private Frequency Estimation Based on Convolution Framework
talks.teaser: A convolution view of LDP encoding yields Wiener-filter deconvolution that sharpens private frequency estimates.
talks.summary:
The presentation introduces locally differentially private frequency estimation, where many users hold private values from a finite domain and a server must learn how often each value appears without collecting cleartext. Users perturb encodings locally; the collector aggregates reports and inverts the randomization to recover approximate frequencies. The speaker positions this task as a building block for richer private analytics and cites telemetry, settings, and emoji-usage style deployments.

Standard pure-LDP estimators rely on fixed correction using flip probabilities, but noise amplification limits accuracy. The work models encoding and perturbation as circular convolution via a transition matrix, casts aggregation as a noisy convolution, and moves to the frequency domain with an FFT. A Wiener deconvolution filter, built from estimated power spectra of the true frequencies and additive noise, adapts to signal-to-noise ratio. Practical variants (DW and IRW) refine spectrum estimates; an AMR-style ensemble helps on less smooth frequency vectors.

Benchmarks on several protocols report strong gains when data are smooth; KR and OUE remain competitive at extreme domain sizes. Wiener filtering favors smooth spectra, so gains shrink on harsh distributions and FFT limits carry over for non-stationary signals. Q&A covers infinite domains, unbiasedness, and poisoning robustness without extra defenses beyond prior estimators.

talks.title: Threshold Signatures in the Multiverse
talks.teaser: A multiverse threshold signature design delivers succinct keys and reusable partial signatures across many overlapping signing universes.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with standard threshold signatures: many parties hold secret shares, partial signatures aggregate once enough parties participate, and security holds if fewer than the threshold are corrupt. That model fits blockchains but assumes one distributed key generation per fixed participant set and threshold, which breaks down when the same people must participate in several overlapping groups, each with its own members and quorum rules. Re-running full DKG for every such universe makes each party’s secret state and signing work grow with how many universes they join.

The speakers introduce multiverse threshold signatures, where many universes can coexist with universe-specific parties and thresholds while each party keeps a succinct secret key and can reuse the same partial signature across every universe they belong to. They build on threshold BLS using pairing-friendly groups, let parties choose compact individual secrets instead of one correlated DKG, and combine partial signatures with public curve points so aggregation still reaches the desired threshold. A custom SNARK enforces well-formed public aggregates because the raw pairing trick alone is forgeable; each universe needs a minimal one-round setup for its verification key. They also note fully adaptive security and malicious robustness, plus a follow-on ePrint scheme that trades slightly larger signatures for avoiding per-universe setup after a one-time message.

Practitioners designing multiparty signing for blockchains or federated trust should weigh when separate quorums can share one key and one partial sign step versus when SNARK-backed setup per universe is acceptable, and when the newer silent-setup variant is worth the efficiency trade-off.

talks.title: Mew: Enabling Large-Scale and Dynamic Link-Flooding Defenses on Programmable Switches
talks.teaser: Presents Mew, a P4 switch defense that shares flow state across switches to counter adaptive link-flooding attacks at scale.
talks.summary:
Link-flooding attacks saturate a network link with high-volume traffic, often sent by bots outside the network, slowing transmission for everyone who relies on it. Traditional defenses depend on a central server that collects state from devices, which can take hours on large networks and sits far from the attacks. The speaker argues that internet service provider networks are better placed to respond, and that programmable P4 switches are fast, but they have limited memory, hold only a partial view of the network, and need downtime to update.

The proposed system, Mew, addresses these limits in three parts. Distributed storage spreads flow state across switches: when a new flow arrives, the first switch caches it briefly, nearby switches vote on which one should record it, and a switch ID is attached to packets so the right switch can find the state. Cooperative defense APIs let a network manager set when switches synchronize, for example when a link becomes congested, so a group can combine events and detect rolling attack patterns. Dynamic memory allocation, using a memory access proxy, lets functions share memory and be relocated while the network keeps running.

The prototype was tested on a testbed of five servers and five P4 switches. Under the distributed storage strategy, Mew used memory more efficiently than the compared approaches. It kept mitigating crossfire and rolling attacks that the baseline systems missed, and lowering a baseline's threshold to catch them caused false positives on benign users. When attackers switched vectors every 60, 15, or 5 seconds, Mew mitigated attacks within seconds, while the baseline suffered downtime longer than 15 seconds. In questions, the speaker noted attackers could still congest several ingress switches, and the authors plan to release source code on GitHub.

talks.title: BlindHub: Bitcoin-Compatible Privacy-Preserving Payment Channel Hubs Supporting Variable Amounts
talks.teaser: Proposes a Bitcoin-compatible payment hub that hides amounts and payer-payee links while supporting variable payment sizes.
talks.summary:
Payment channels let parties transact off-chain, and a hub in a star topology routes payments through one intermediary. This talk asks how such a hub can stay secure and private while remaining Bitcoin-compatible. It defines three goals: atomicity, where either both sides complete a payment or neither does; relationship anonymity, so the hub cannot learn who pays whom; and interoperability. Prior schemes such as A2L and TumbleBit reach the anonymity and compatibility goals but only for fixed payment amounts.

The proposed blind channel hides the amount itself. The sender commits to the amount and proves the commitment matches the value used in the channel, and the hub signs over the commitment, so only the sender sees the updated balance. Atomicity comes from a blind adaptor signature that reveals the witness only once the other leg completes. Randomizable puzzles and signatures let each party re-randomize commitments before passing them on, which breaks links through the hub. Registration beforehand addresses griefing, where a receiver opens many payments and never releases them. A time lock lets the channel close eventually, and the hub cannot force an early close.

The prototype takes about 17 seconds per payment using an older serial proof technique, and the speaker estimated under 10 seconds with a newer one. In questions, compliance concerns about mixer-like use came up, and the speaker said future work would address them. The takeaway is that amounts, sender-receiver links and variable payment sizes can be combined in a Bitcoin-compatible hub.

talks.title: Rethinking Searchable Symmetric Encryption
talks.teaser: Examines why searchable encryption schemes that return only document identifiers fall short when full documents must be fetched.
talks.summary:
Encrypting documents before upload protects them from breaches, but the client still needs a way to search them. The talk frames the options: deterministic and order-preserving encryption are efficient yet leak information, while ORAM, fully homomorphic and functional encryption are strong but slow. Searchable symmetric encryption aims for the middle ground. The speaker covers the single-client, single-server model with an honest-but-curious server and shows how an encrypted inverted index is built, including the duplicate entries added for security.

The core problem is that most SSE research returns only document identifiers, not the documents themselves. Three ways of adding retrieval were assessed. Storing full documents inside an index-only scheme causes unacceptable storage overhead because of duplication. Using ORAM or private information retrieval keeps storage low but makes computation very expensive, since these tools are not built to fetch many documents per query. Storing documents separately and relying on the scheme's identifiers avoids both costs but exposes the system to statistical attacks, which the authors devised and say improve on earlier work.

The takeaways are that index-only schemes do not generalize to document retrieval, and that no known method retrieves documents in bulk both securely and efficiently. In questions, the speaker argued that co-occurrence leakage also affects relational databases, and said that retrieving only metadata has no supporting scheme in the literature. Practitioners should treat secure system-wide SSE as an open problem.

talks.title: One Key to Rule Them All: Secure Group Pairing for Heterogeneous IoT Devices
talks.teaser: Pairs heterogeneous IoT devices into shared group keys using physical events they sense, even when sensors differ.
talks.summary:
Context-based pairing lets nearby devices create cryptographic keys by observing the same physical events, such as a door closing, rather than asking a user for a PIN. Existing approaches usually need identical sensors, and the prior PerCept work pairs only two devices and struggles with continuous measurements and overlapping events. The speaker presents IoT Cupid, a group pairing system for devices with mixed sensing modalities.

Events are detected by applying thresholds to the rate of change in each sensor reading, which covers both instantaneous and delayed sensors. Fuzzy clustering then sorts events into types so simultaneous events still land in the right groups. The time intervals between occurrences of an event become shared evidence that feeds a group key exchange, with the timings used as a password. An outside attacker cannot reproduce them, and the design needs only 32-bit entropy, which is said to give four times faster pairing than fuzzy commitment approaches requiring 128-bit entropy. In two real-world studies, a 20-device group with four event sources derived a key in 39 milliseconds on average.

Adding or removing devices re-triggers pairing, and periodic liveness checks revoke keys of failed devices. Devices sharing no events can communicate through an intermediary device that belongs to both groups. The talk closes with the point that physical context can replace user-driven pairing for heterogeneous IoT hardware.

talks.title: QueryX: Symbolic Query on Decompiled Code for Finding Bugs in COTS Binaries
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of QueryX: Symbolic Query on Decompiled Code for Finding Bugs in COTS Binaries.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this presentation, Iyoung Sang Kang from Georgia Tech introduces QueryX, an extensible static checking tool that supports symbolic queries directly on decompiled code to discover vulnerabilities in commercial off-the-shelf (COTS) binaries. The research, conducted during Kang's PhD alongside colleagues Insu Yun and Taesoo Kim, tackles the scalability and accuracy trade-offs inherent in binary static analysis.

While extensible static analysis tools like CodeQL and Joern allow human analysts to write source-level queries, feeding decompiled code into them results in high false positive rates and missed bugs because source analyzers are unaware of underlying binary specifics (e.g., memory layout and data sections). Conversely, binary tools like angr and BAP rely on low-level binary intermediate representations (IR), which lack high-level abstractions like types and control flow, making queries complex and tedious to write. QueryX bridges this gap by enabling analysts to write high-level, analyst-friendly symbolic queries on decompiled code while remaining binary-aware.

### Key Topics
- **Limitations of Source and Binary Checkers**: Source-code query engines fed with decompiled code fail due to binary-unaware semantics like memory layouts and missing data sections. Binary IR tools (like angr) force analysts to deal with low-level details, resulting in verbose query code.
- **Decompiler Neutral Representation (DNR)**: QueryX introduces a new intermediate representation, DNR, to retain high-level decompiled code structures while injecting critical binary details, such as stack memory layouts and binary-embedded data sections.
- **Analyst-Friendly Symbolic Queries**: QueryX allows queries to be written using JavaScript syntax against decompiled code ASTs. Analysts can register execution callbacks on specific function calls (e.g., `malloc`, `memcpy`) to inspect symbolic states.
- **Real-World Bug Hunting in Windows Kernel**: Applying QueryX to the Windows kernel uncovered multiple zero-day vulnerabilities, including integer overflows that lead to heap buffer overflows.

### Technical Details
QueryX operates across four primary modules:
1. **Decompiler Module**: Takes target binaries and generates decompiled code (using Hex-Rays).
2. **Lifter Module**: Translates the decompiled code into DNR by calculating stack memory layouts, lifting stack variable accesses, and resolving global variable reads using a dedicated program data section that holds initial binary values and permissions.
3. **Query Interpreter**: Executes analyst queries written in JavaScript syntax, mapping query logic to decompiled AST nodes without forcing analysts to write queries against DNR directly.
4. **Analyzer Module**: Runs symbolic execution from function entry points, traversing AST nodes and firing registered callbacks (such as `collect_alloc` and `check_memcpy`). Callbacks read AST node values from the symbolic state and query the Z3 solver under current path constraints to detect issues like heap overflows.

In an evaluation comparing query complexity for a Windows kernel heap overflow caused by a 2-byte integer overflow, angr required 267 lines of code, whereas QueryX required only 33 lines due to its access to high-level decompiled type information. QueryX also outperformed Joern and CodeQL on a benchmark dataset by achieving higher true positives with fewer false positives.

### Takeaways
QueryX demonstrates that combining the high-level readability of decompiled code with binary-aware memory modeling yields practical, concise, and highly effective bug-finding queries. Applied to the Windows kernel across four query types, QueryX uncovered 15 new vulnerabilities (including 10 CVEs and 7 heap overflows), earning $180,000 in bug bounties. Future work noted during the Q&A includes further evaluating semantic equivalence between decompiled code and native binary code.

talks.title: User Perceptions and Experiences with Smart Home Updates
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding User Perceptions and Experiences with Smart Home Updates.
talks.summary:
### Overview
This presentation details an empirical research study conducted in collaboration with Julie Haney at the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) examining how consumers perceive and experience software and firmware updates for smart home IoT devices. With approximately half of U.S. households owning at least one IoT device, updates serve as a primary mechanism for manufacturers to patch security flaws and deliver functionality. However, consumer hesitation, disruption, and lack of technical savvy often impede timely patching. To address the lack of large-scale empirical studies in this area, the researchers surveyed 412 demographically diverse adult participants who were active users and administrators of smart home devices across five key categories: virtual voice assistants/smart speakers, smart thermostats, smart security devices, smart sensors, and smart lighting.

### Key Topics
- **Device Ownership and Category Differences**: Participants owned an average of nine smart devices, with 35% owning 10 or more. The study examined how perceptions varied across device types with varying levels of sophistication and perceived privacy/security exposure.
- **Perceptions of Update Importance and Urgency**: Assessing whether consumers view IoT device updates as critical and time-sensitive.
- **Current vs. Preferred Update Modes and Notifications**: How updates are handled (automatic vs. manual), how users are informed of new updates, and how they would prefer these mechanisms to work.
- **Security and Privacy Concerns**: Consumer trust in device security and privacy, and how concern levels correlate with update behaviors.

### Technical Details & Survey Findings
- **Importance and Urgency**: Overall, 86% of participants agreed that smart home updates are important, and 83% agreed they should be urgent. However, pairwise comparisons revealed significant differences: lighting updates were viewed as significantly less important and less urgent than other categories, while security devices were rated significantly more urgent and important than voice assistants.
- **Update Delivery Modes**: Automatic updates were the most commonly implemented method across all categories and were preferred for voice assistants and thermostats. In contrast, users preferred manual updates for security devices and sensors. Between 13% and 21% of respondents did not know how updates were currently handled on their devices.
- **User Agency and Preferences**: Over 50% of participants expressed a desire to choose between automatic and manual updates and to select their notification methods. Additionally, 40% wanted the capability to uninstall an update if it caused issues or disruptions. Companion apps were the most common and preferred notification channel, though roughly 25% reported having to learn about updates independently via social media, websites, or friends.
- **Security and Privacy Perceptions**: Only about one-third of participants were moderately or extremely concerned about security across all device categories. Voice assistants (perceived as always listening) and security devices elicited higher security and privacy concerns than thermostats, sensors, or lighting. Crucially, 77% of respondents believed their devices were secure, and 77% believed their devices actively protected their privacy—assumptions the speaker noted as surprisingly optimistic given typical IoT vulnerability profiles.

### Takeaways & Manufacturer Guidance
- **Transparency and Communication**: Manufacturers should clearly communicate the purpose of updates, when they are applied, and what changes they make, potentially leveraging cybersecurity labels to help non-technical consumers evaluate device security.
- **Configurable Control and Agency**: Rather than imposing a rigid, one-size-fits-all automatic update model, manufacturers should offer configurable options, such as choices between manual and automatic updates, scheduling installations for convenient times, and providing fallback/uninstall options when updates introduce compatibility or functionality defects.
- **Centralized Management**: To alleviate the burden of managing updates across dozens of devices, centralized apps or smart home hubs should consolidate notifications and coordinate update processes across multiple vendors.

talks.title: Private Eye: On the Limits of Textual Screen Peeking via Eyeglass Reflections in Video Conferencing
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Private Eye: On the Limits of Textual Screen Peeking via Eyeglass Reflections in Video Conferencing.
talks.summary:
### Overview
With the widespread adoption of video conferencing during and after the COVID-19 pandemic, eyeglass reflections pose an unintended side-channel vulnerability. The presentation introduces "Private Eye," a project that characterizes and quantifies the limits of information leakage from eyeglass reflections captured by participants' webcams. Termed a "webcam peeking attack," this threat involves a remote conference participant eavesdropping on the screen contents of another attendee without controlling the victim's hardware.

### Key Topics
- **Hardware & Computational Evolution:** Video cameras have transitioned from standard 720p laptop webcams and 1080p external cameras toward 4K streaming sensors. In parallel, adversaries can employ multi-frame super-resolution and image registration over consecutive frames to enhance reflection quality.
- **Environmental & Optical Factors:** Information leakage is influenced by reflection pixel size (governed by screen-to-glass distance, camera resolution, glass curvature) and signal-to-noise ratio (affected by ambient room lighting). Notably, auto-exposure controls cause lighting intensity to impact reflection clarity non-monotonically, and stronger prescription glasses with flatter surfaces leak more detail.
- **Text vs. Website Layout Recognition:** While reading small body text is difficult with existing hardware, identifying large texts or entire website layouts presents an immediate risk.

### Technical Details
- **Evaluation Methodology:** The study combined controlled laboratory experiments (single-letter tests) with user studies involving 20 participants viewing HTML text of varied sizes. Amazon Mechanical Turk workers were used as a baseline to humanly recognize reflected text, complemented by multi-frame super-resolution.
- **Text Leakage Limits:** With current webcams (720p/1080p), adversaries can read large fonts (roughly 56 pt or 10 mm physical height on screen, found on sites like Twitch). Predictive mathematical models indicate that future 4K webcams will allow peeking at most HTML header text, though body text remains challenging.
- **Website Identification:** Attackers can identify website layouts and shapes rather than specific text. On the Alexa Top 100 dataset, the researchers achieved over 90% accuracy in identifying the visited website (such as Bing) using present-day webcams.

### Mitigations & Takeaways
- **Individual Reflection Testing:** Platforms like Zoom could implement a per-session calibration test displaying known patterns to quantify current reflection risks and alert users.
- **Software Filtering:** The authors developed a Python prototype that detects the eyeglass area in the camera feed and applies an adjustable blur filter before streaming.
- **Principle of Least Pixels:** Treating this as an "over-sensing" issue where sensors capture more data than necessary, video conferencing systems should adopt a "principle of least pixels"—defaulting to lower resolutions and requiring deliberate user authorization for higher-capability video streams.

talks.title: PyFET: Forensically Equivalent Transformation for Python Binary Decompilation
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in PyFET: Forensically Equivalent Transformation for Python Binary Decompilation.
talks.summary:
### Overview
PyFET presents a novel technique for improving Python binary decompilation through Forensically Equivalent Transformations (FET). Developed via a joint collaboration between the University of Virginia, Georgia Tech, and the University of Tennessee Knoxville, PyFET addresses the problem of decompilation failures in Python malware binaries compiled to bytecode. Decompilers often fail or produce incorrect output when processing complex Python binaries. Instead of modifying or patching complex decompiler codebases, PyFET directly modifies and transforms the binary bytecode beforehand to make it compatible with existing decompilers.

### Key Topics
Decompilers encounter two primary categories of failures when processing Python binaries:
- **Explicit Errors:** Failures where the decompiler raises an error message, often providing hints such as approximate bytecode offsets or function names.
- **Implicit Errors:** Silent failures where decompilation finishes without warning but introduces semantic or structural corruptions. In a controlled study of 3,000 source files from PyPI and other repositories, researchers observed severe implicit bugs, including code coupled into incorrect scopes, unexpected `else` blocks injected into `try-except` statements, and while-loops inadvertently replaced with if-conditions.

To identify implicit errors, the authors developed a pattern-matching and mutation-based validation method. When a suspected pattern matches, the code is mutated with a corrected snippet, recompiled, and checked against the original binary at the target offset. This technique uncovered more than 22,000 previously undetected implicit errors across five decompilers.

### Technical Details
To fix binaries without triggering side effects in decompilers, PyFET introduces Forensically Equivalent Transformations (FETs), extending semantically equivalent transformations (SETs). When strict semantic equivalence fails to prevent decompiler crashes, FET relaxes semantics while preserving critical forensic context:
- **Transformation Rules:** PyFET utilizes 30 transformation rules targeting problem areas such as shortening lengthy conditional statements, dividing logical expressions, converting lambdas into standard functions, simplifying consecutive control flow, and moving statements (e.g., relocating a `return` statement outside a `with` block while capturing the result in a dedicated `fet_return` variable).
- **Iterative CFG Optimization:** Rather than transforming entire binaries indiscriminately, PyFET inspects the control flow graph (CFG). It starts at the failure node, applies applicable transformation rules, and progressively expands to adjacent nodes along connecting edges until decompilation succeeds or all paths are explored. This strategy limits auditing to approximately 33% of nodes.
- **Evaluation:** In an evaluation involving over 35,000 malware samples provided by ReversingLabs, 44.6% failed baseline decompilation, with failure rates rising on later Python versions. PyFET resolved more than 17,000 errors across five decompilers and successfully addressed binaries protected by obfuscators such as PyArmor/PJ Orion and opcode remapping.

### Takeaways
Attempting to build a single "perfect" Python decompiler or patch disparate decompiler engines creates significant maintenance overhead and regression risks. Transforming Python bytecode directly via forensically equivalent rules provides an effective, scalable pre-processing pipeline that dramatically boosts decompilation success across diverse decompilers and heavily obfuscated real-world malware.

talks.title: Characterizing Everyday Misuse of Smart Home Devices
talks.teaser: A two-survey study maps how unauthorized smart-home use becomes interpersonal misuse and what makes owners comfortable or upset.
talks.summary:
The presentation contrasts familiar worries about skilled external attackers and vague manufacturer data practices with a less studied risk: people in the home or social circle who use connected devices without clear permission. Unauthorized use is defined as operating a device without explicit owner consent; misuse is the subset that causes harm or discomfort, and the speaker argues that severity alone does not predict how upset someone will feel.

Two Prolific surveys in the United States anchor the work. An open-ended characterization study with 100 participants fed thematic coding, which shaped a closed prevalence survey of 483 demographically representative respondents. Reported events span mild entertainment access through surveillance, environment changes, broken hardware, and unwanted purchases. Five factors—intent, relationship, sensitivity of exposed information, how lasting effects are, and mental models of what the device stores or exposes—help explain divergent reactions to similar incidents.

Prevalence results suggest unauthorized use is widespread: 43% of respondents experienced it on their own devices and 20% reported using someone else’s device without explicit permission, with smart TVs, speakers, and media players most often involved. Among those with unauthorized-use experience, follow-up questioning surfaced 110 misuse incidents, predominantly from friends or family rather than strangers. Ordinal logistic regression linked greater discomfort to monitoring, damage, deleted data, changed settings, and purchases, and to lacking permission or uncertain frequency; child or sibling relationships correlated with more tolerance. The closing argument is that IoT security research should weigh these everyday interpersonal misuses alongside external technical threats.

talks.title: Limits of I/O Based Ransomware Detection: An Imitation Based Attack
talks.teaser: Shows how mimicking benign file I/O patterns helps ransomware evade detectors, including commercial and academic tools.
talks.summary:
Many ransomware detectors judge programs by their I/O behavior, learning patterns from observed samples. This talk asks whether those detectors hold up against an attacker who deliberately copies normal activity. The proposed imitation attack has two phases. Offline, it records how a benign program, such as a browser, an archiver or a compiler, accesses files, including open behavior, read counts, bytes written and access order, and condenses this into a behavioral template. Online, the attack program follows that template and, in place of ordinary writes, writes encrypted file contents to the target files.

The prototype was tested against six ransomware detectors: three industrial products, including Windows Defender, and three academic systems. The imitation still evaded these tools. Its encryption time was not much longer than that of traditional ransomware samples across imitations of browsers, office editors, file compressors and compilers. Simple defenses, such as detectors keyed on file types or on directory scanning, either missed the attack or produced a considerable false positive rate.

The takeaway is that a practical detector for this kind of attack is non-trivial and may need substantial manual feature engineering. The prototype has been released publicly so detector developers can use it to improve their methods. The speaker also suggests combining I/O monitoring with other signals, such as detecting communication with a remote server during the infection phase.
