talks.title: Multi-Round Single-Server Secure Aggregation with Applications to Private Federated Learning
talks.teaser: Presents a secure aggregation protocol that cuts round trips so federated learning can train models privately.
talks.summary:
Federated learning lets phones and other client devices train a shared model by sending locally computed weight vectors to a server, which adds them up in each iteration. Those individual updates can still leak information about a client's data, so secure aggregation is used to let the server learn only the sum. Existing protocols were built for one sum, so repeating them every iteration means many costly server round trips, and clients often drop offline partway through.

The talk presents Flamingo, a system that reduces the number of round trips so an entire training session can run privately. It starts from a dropout-tolerant protocol in which clients mask their vectors with pairwise secrets that cancel out in the sum. A small set of decryptors, holding secret-shared keys, can recover the masks of clients who went offline, and only about a third of them need to respond. A one-time setup phase is reused across iterations by deriving per-iteration seeds from the pairwise secrets, so the costly setup never repeats. Against a malicious server that lies about iteration numbers, an extra round with the decryptors cross-checks the rounds.

The speaker argues that round trips, rather than server computation, dominate the cost in practice. Reported results show about a five to six times improvement over prior work, with almost no accuracy loss compared with a non-private baseline. The takeaway for practitioners is that federated learning protocols should minimize interaction rounds, since each extra round lets more devices drop out. Poisoning attacks and cross-round inference attacks are left out because they fall outside the threat model.

talks.title: How IoT Re-using Threatens Your Sensitive Data: Exploring the User-Data Disposal in Used IoT Devices
talks.teaser: Examines whether factory resets and other disposal methods really erase personal data from IoT devices before resale.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at what happens to personal data left on Internet of Things devices when owners sell, give away or discard them. The speaker argues that this disposal problem has not been studied systematically. The work starts with an online questionnaire of diverse participants, which found that reusing devices is common, that password habits are weak, and that about 41 percent of respondents do not erase their data before passing a device on. Of those, about 42 percent did not know how to do it.

To measure the risk at scale, the researchers built a device-free analysis system that examines firmware images rather than physical hardware. It looks for code that collects user input and stores it, pairing source and sink APIs, and it infers vendor-specific functions from the library calls they wrap. Across more than 4,000 firmware images from 11 vendors, the system found over 120,000 user data collections, and more than 43 percent of the analysed firmware gathered at least one sensitive item. Over 60 percent of those items were stored in plain text.

The team then tested disposal methods on real devices by enabling features, planting marker strings, and running forensic analysis before and after each reset. Many methods left markers behind, because flash storage often keeps old data after a rewrite. A sample of 500 firmware images suggested that about 13 percent carry a risk of ineffective disposal. The takeaway is that disposal is part of IoT security, and that users and vendors both need clearer erasure guidance.

talks.title: LangSec Keynote: Trojan Source and Bad Characters: Invisible Hacks and Reluctant Patching
talks.teaser: Shows how Unicode bidirectional controls hide source code logic and fool language models, and what vendors did in response.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how Unicode bidirectional control characters can make source code look different to a human reviewer than to a compiler. Placed inside comments and string literals, these characters can visually reorder tokens so a line appears harmless while its real logic does something else. A short C example shows an admin check that reads as false yet prints an admin message. The speakers argue that such an edit could be merged into a popular open-source XML parser and then spread to downstream projects through package managers.

The second half applies the same trick to machine learning. Changing the logical order of characters while keeping the display fixed, inserting invisible characters, swapping in homoglyphs, or adding backspaces can make text look normal to people while confusing NLP systems. Examples include evading toxic-content detection and a translation case where an account number in an invoice is changed in the output. Disclosure went to about nineteen maintainers and vendors, with responses ranging from rapid fixes to dismissal. Editors and code hosting sites such as GitHub and GitLab added warnings, while only one large NLP provider was reported to have mitigated the issue.

The closing discussion asks why machine learning teams have not sanitized inputs as code teams have, pointing to blame between ML and security groups, the cost of retraining models, and market concentration. The takeaways are that Unicode makes invisible source vulnerabilities easy to hide, breaks text-based machine learning, and that defenses exist for both, such as rejecting unterminated bidirectional sequences and flagging hidden characters in editors and linters. Audience questions covered legitimate nested bidirectional text and words that mix scripts.

talks.title: ZeeStar: Private Smart Contracts by Homomorphic Encryption and Zero-knowledge Proofs
talks.teaser: A compiler-backed framework hides smart contract state with homomorphic encryption and automatically generated zero-knowledge proofs.
talks.summary:
Public blockchains store smart contract data in cleartext, which makes sensitive on-chain applications hard to justify. Earlier privacy designs often stop at payments, depend on trusted hardware or operators, or leave developers to stitch cryptography into contracts by hand. ZeeStar extends prior CK work toward more general contracts: expressive application logic, no trusted manager, and a path where authors reason about privacy types rather than proof circuits.

The core pattern encrypts each balance under its owner’s key. Self-owned fields update by decrypting locally, applying the intended operation, re-encrypting, and attaching a non-interactive proof that the change is valid. Foreign fields update via additive homomorphism, again with proofs that tie the new ciphertext to the old one. A Solidity-like source language marks privacy with @owner-style annotations and explicit reveal points so illegal cross-key arithmetic fails at compile time. The compiler lowers programs to Ethereum Solidity that accepts ciphertexts, collects constraints, and verifies a Groth16 zk-SNARK on chain.

The implementation leans on efficient elliptic-curve tools and embeds decryption limits (roughly 32-bit plaintexts) into the type system. Twelve compiled examples include an automated take on a prior private wallet; desktop proof generation stays at most about one minute, while execution gas is on the order of 3,004,000. Formal guarantees target correctness and annotation-respecting privacy, though observers still see which storage slots are touched. Deploying a contract implies a per-function trusted setup for its generated circuit.

talks.title: TROLLMAGNIFIER: Detecting State-Sponsored Troll Accounts on Reddit?
talks.teaser: Shows how coordinated reply and repost patterns on Reddit can flag suspected state-sponsored troll accounts.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at state-sponsored troll accounts that push narratives and false information on social media, including Russian state-linked accounts active around recent US elections. These accounts are run manually, so they do not show the strict synchronization that bot detection usually relies on. The speaker argues the signal lies in interaction: accounts from one campaign reply to each other, follow up on each other's threads and repost identical titles. A seed set of 335 Russian state-sponsored Reddit accounts active from 2015 to 2018 showed these habits more often than random users on the same subreddits.

The tool, TROLLMAGNIFIER, pre-filters a Reddit archive from 2005 to 2020 down to about 53,000 candidate accounts, rebuilds thread structure from raw records, and builds features covering account age, activity and interaction with known trolls. A random forest classifier, checked with 10-fold cross validation, flagged 1248 potential trolls. With no ground truth and no reply from Reddit, validation relied on proxies: 298 accounts were later suspended or deleted, 66 were created on the same day as a known troll, and 824 met at least one of four conditions. Word graphs built from crypto-related language and synchronized activity bursts also resembled the known trolls. Case studies showed small teams stirring controversy and accounts posting dog pictures to look legitimate.

The main takeaway is that loose coordination is a usable detection signal, and the authors see the system as a blueprint for production tools. Limits include the need for a known seed set and the absence of definitive proof that flagged accounts are trolls. Future work would look at campaign-independent behavioral features and at the narratives the accounts push.

talks.title: Security Analysis of the MLS Key Derivation
talks.teaser: Proves that MLS key derivation keeps keys secure under standard cryptographic assumptions, mapping which keys stay honest.
talks.summary:
The talk analyzes the key derivation step of Message Layer Security (MLS), an upcoming IETF standard for secure group communication. It first defines the properties a key exchange should offer, including forward secrecy, post-compromise security, asynchronous operation, and handling members who join or leave a group. It then explains how MLS uses a ratchet-tree structure, where members derive and encrypt path secrets so the whole group agrees on a root value, and a key schedule that mixes that value with an internal secret and an external secret.

The central result is an honesty graph, which marks each derived key as honest when an attacker cannot know it. Tree derivations keep honesty from their inputs, while a key schedule step is honest if either of its two inputs is. The security proof rests on assumptions about pseudorandom functions, dual pseudorandom functions and public key encryption, and proceeds in three steps: an argument over the tree, a hybrid argument over the continuous key schedule, and a combination of both.

The speaker motivated post-compromise security by noting that messaging sessions now last far longer, so regular key updates limit how much history a stolen key exposes. An audience question on whether a stolen key could enable impersonation went unanswered. Standardization was expected this year or early next year.

talks.title: Practical Asynchronous Distributed Key Generation
talks.teaser: Presents an asynchronous distributed key generation protocol that tolerates one-third malicious nodes without timing assumptions.
talks.summary:
This talk covers asynchronous distributed key generation, a protocol that lets a set of nodes jointly produce a common public key while each node holds a secret share. The setting allows up to one third of nodes to be malicious and makes no timing assumptions about message delivery. Such keys bootstrap threshold signatures, threshold wallets, threshold encryption and randomness beacons. Earlier asynchronous constructions either had heavy communication costs or produced keys that were group elements rather than scalars, which blocks use with standard schemes such as BLS threshold signatures.

The protocol runs in four phases: each node shares a random secret, nodes broadcast which sharings they completed, and then they run parallel binary agreements. The circular dependency between agreement and common coins is broken by using the completed sharings as entropy for those coins. An agreement where all honest nodes start with the same input can finish without a coin, which covers nodes that contributed nothing. The final key is the sum of secrets from the agreed set. The prototype took about 45 seconds for 128 nodes at low threshold, but high thresholds were much slower because of the costlier sharing step.

The talk concludes that communication scales as kappa times n cubed, with expected logarithmic rounds. The authors also built a homomorphic high-threshold sharing scheme based on the decisional composite residuosity assumption. That high-threshold sharing is the bottleneck, so faster versions, constant-round designs and lower bounds remain open problems.

talks.title: Security Foundations for Application-Based Covert Communication Channels
talks.teaser: Introduces formal security definitions and a provable framework for covert channels hiding data in real application traffic.
talks.summary:
Application-based covert communication channels wrap a cryptographic layer around a network application, altering its inputs or outputs so hidden data rides on ordinary-looking traffic. Such tunnels appear in censorship circumvention tools, yet undetectability has usually been judged only by empirical testing against sampled traffic. This paper sets out formal definitions for the application, the covert channel, and a security game for a passive eavesdropper.

The adversary must tell covert traffic from reference traffic, and the advantage splits into an embedding term and a user term, so a user model can be assessed separately. The authors observe that surveyed systems embed only on the user side or only on the wire side. Protozoa, which hides data in WebRTC video, and Balboa, which works on Icecast audio, are treated as replace-and-restore schemes: they overwrite payloads, then put valid data back so the receiver does not misbehave. The proof bounds their insecurity with three terms covering sync indistinguishability, the security of the encrypted channel, and user indistinguishability.

The Q&A touched on why the classic computational steganography model was not adopted: it treats the channel as a black box and embeds messages atomically, which does not fit real systems whose structure is known. Future work includes modelling uncertainty about the application and an active probing notion. For practitioners, the framework offers a provable baseline for judging whether a covert channel stays undetectable.

talks.title: DeepCoFFEA: Improved Flow Correlation Attacks on Tor via Metric Learning and Amplification
talks.teaser: Shows how embedding networks and windowed majority voting make Tor flow correlation cheaper and more accurate.
talks.summary:
The talk examines flow correlation attacks against Tor, the anonymity network. A network-level observer such as an internet service provider or government can record traffic entering and leaving Tor and try to match the two ends using packet sizes and timing. Prior correlators compare every inflow with every outflow, which scales quadratically and leaves very few true matches among many candidates.

DeepCoFFEA trains an embedding network with anchor, positive and negative sub-networks that share weights, using a triplet loss so correlated inflow and outflow traces land close together. Negatives are selected with a margin, so training needs only n triplets and cost grows linearly. At decision time, each flow is split into overlapping windows, each window is embedded and compared by cosine similarity against a threshold, and a majority vote over the windows sets the final result. The speaker reported the false positive rate falling from 12 percent to 0.13 percent, better ROC performance than DeepCorr, and evaluation about two orders of magnitude faster.

The authors also tested the approach against website fingerprinting defenses WTF-PAD and Front and against testing data collected at widely separated times, and correlation still held. Future work includes more realistic data, newer deep learning traffic analysis, removing the remaining pairwise cosine step, and designing defenses against this attack style. In questions, the speaker said cosine similarity was picked empirically and that a proposed defense performed slightly better than others.

talks.title: Sphinx: Enabling Privacy-Preserving Online Learning over the Cloud
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Sphinx: Enabling Privacy-Preserving Online Learning over the Cloud.

talks.title: Hark: A Deep Learning System for Navigating Privacy Feedback at Scale
talks.teaser: Shows how a deep learning pipeline mines Play Store reviews to surface and rank privacy concerns for app developers.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses a gap in developer-user communication. The Play Store data safety section tells users how their data is handled, but the reverse channel, where users tell developers about privacy concerns, has received less study. The presenter, Hamza, introduces Hark, a system that takes Play Store reviews, identifies privacy-related feedback, tags each review with fine-grained issues, groups those issues into themes, and quantifies them.

The pipeline combines several models. The privacy classifier is trained on a near-balanced dataset: rather than relying on keywords, natural language inference matches reviews against privacy hypotheses drawn from existing taxonomies, and crowdworkers label the candidates. A T5 generator writes concise issue labels, which are clustered by embeddings and summarized into theme titles. Two more models assign one of 28 emotions and score feedback quality. In the evaluation, fine-tuning T5 on the sampled data raised AUC by 0.17 over a regex-sampled dataset, while a bag-of-words SVM lagged behind. Run across 626 million reviews, about 6 million were classified as privacy, producing over 300 themes with more than 1,000 reviews each. Unneeded access was the largest theme, with over half a million reviews.

The system was built around topical diversity, broad privacy concept coverage, glanceability, and navigability, so developers can grasp the main concerns and drill into specific issues or emotions on demand. In the Q&A, the speaker explained that three levels balance detail against readability, and that an app might have 30 or 40 themes. A practical takeaway is that off-the-shelf models produced noisy results on reviews, so tuning to the domain mattered, and overlapping issue wording can split counts across categories.

talks.title: Waldo: A Private Time-Series Database from Function Secret-Sharing
talks.teaser: Shows a time-series database that answers multi-predicate aggregate queries while hiding data, filters and access patterns.
talks.summary:
Cloud databases increasingly store time-series data from smart homes, industrial IoT and remote patient monitoring, but a server compromise can expose both the records and the filter values used in queries. The talk presents Waldo, a time-series database meant to hide stored contents, query filter values and search access patterns, such as how many records match a predicate. It assumes three non-colluding servers in an honest-majority setting, where at most one may be malicious, and lets the schema and query structure remain visible.

The construction relies on function secret sharing, where a function is split into two keys that each hide it yet together yield shares of its output. The talk starts with aggregate queries over public data using two servers, then moves to private data by storing each feature as a one-hot table with one column per record, so filters become evaluations the keys can run. Because that table must also stay hidden, the contents are split with replicated secret sharing across three servers, and the same protocol runs on each share before the results are summed.

Against an ORAM-based multi-dimensional tree and a generic MPC baseline, the speaker reported an 8x latency difference from the MPC baseline and a 37x difference from the ORAM baseline for around a thousand records, with a much larger throughput gap to ORAM because appends are costly there. Q&A covered the limit that filtered feature domains must be small, and whether the design extends beyond three servers, which the speaker had not yet examined. The takeaway is that append-heavy time-series workloads can get private filtering with low latency and bandwidth, at the cost of relying on three independent servers and bounded domains.

talks.title: Publicly Accountable Robust Multi-Party Computation

talks.title: Formal Model-Driven Discovery of Bluetooth Protocol Design Vulnerabilities
talks.teaser: Presents formal models of Bluetooth pairing and mesh provisioning that uncover new design flaws exposing secret keys.
talks.summary:
Some Bluetooth weaknesses come from the specification itself rather than from implementations. This talk presents formal models of Bluetooth key sharing and data transmission, built to find such design flaws. Earlier formal studies looked at only one pairing mode, treated the two phases separately, ignored compromised devices, and skipped Bluetooth mesh. This model covers BR/EDR and mesh pairing and provisioning, plus authentication and encryption during data transfer. Protocol modes and stacks are modular pieces that can be recombined, and a semi-compromised device is modeled with an application layer that cannot reach the keys.

Verified properties include authenticity for pairing and provisioning, secrecy and strong secrecy of the key sent during mesh provisioning, and secrecy of transmitted data. The model flagged violations matching five known weaknesses and two new issues. In the first, a man-in-the-middle records and replays commitment and random values to bypass authentication, then derives the session key and decrypts the secret key sent to the device. In the second, a dual-stack pairing over BLE also generates a BR/EDR key, so a malicious app on one device can reach BR/EDR services on the other. The mesh flaw was reported to the Bluetooth SIG and received a CVE. Testing found the mesh attack affected 20 of 25 implementations, and the cross-transport attack affected five of six devices.

The presenter noted limits: unlimited parallel sessions in key sharing are not modeled, and some Bluetooth protocols are left out. For practitioners, the takeaway is that formal analysis of the specification can expose flaws regardless of implementation, and that key derivation across transports deserves close review.

talks.title: HAMRAZ: Resilient Partitioning and Replication
talks.teaser: Turns sequential programs with security policies into Byzantine-resilient distributed systems.
talks.summary:
Distributed services that span several organizations and cloud providers may include servers that behave arbitrarily. The talk uses a healthcare billing service as an example, where a patient's record must stay hidden from an insurer while the service keeps integrity and availability despite failed or attacked servers. Existing work covers confidentiality and integrity with information flow control, or availability with Byzantine quorum replication, but the quorums must be supplied by hand.

The presenter introduces HAMRAZ, which takes a sequential program and security policies written as type annotations, then outputs a distributed system that meets them. Trustworthiness types combine confidentiality, integrity and availability lattices, with resiliency sets describing which groups of principals may be Byzantine. The program is first restructured so each partition makes at most one object call. An information flow type inference system then decides where methods and objects are placed and how many replicas are needed, using communication and storage quorum systems. The resulting constraints are solved through linear arithmetic.

Six small use cases were run on a cluster. Synthesis finished in minutes, stayed responsive as Byzantine faults grew up to the policy bound, and scaled replication with the resiliency specification. The main takeaway is that availability can be reasoned about with a type system instead of being configured by hand. Future work targets declassification and endorsement to relax the conservative control, and extending the approach to object-based languages such as Java and C++.

talks.title: CirC: Compiler infrastructure for proof systems, software verification, and more
talks.teaser: A shared compiler stack turns high-level programs into circuits for zero-knowledge proofs, SMT, and constrained optimization targets.
talks.summary:
User-programmable cryptosystems such as multi-party computation, fully homomorphic encryption, and zero-knowledge proofs all need compilers from high-level languages into circuit-like representations. Existing compilers are often incomplete in academia or narrowly limited in industry, partly because each project repeats the same hard lowering steps on its own.

CirC is proposed as LLVM-style shared infrastructure built around existentially quantified circuits: mutation-free, control-flow-free, fixed-size computations with domain-specific knowledge constraints. A rich circuit IR (CIR) feeds optimizers and backends for zero-knowledge proofs, SMT formulas, and integer linear programming, while a Circify library helps front ends embed stateful semantics. A case study rebuilding a ZoKrates-class blockchain compiler reportedly took about a week and seven hundred lines versus tens of thousands in the reference optimizer, with slightly better average output on the standard library. Cross-target workflows use the SMT backend to choose minimal loop unrolling before lowering to a proof backend.

The talk also outlines C and Datalog front ends, linting via SMT, and demonstrating old OpenSSL vulnerability behavior inside a zero-knowledge proof, plus ongoing MPC and FHE backends and a Z Sharp language extension. Practitioners should see CirC as a platform to reuse circuit optimizations and pair proof generation with solver-backed compilation tricks rather than building monolithic compilers alone.

talks.title: BadEncoder: Backdoor Attacks to Pre-trained Encoders in Self-Supervised Learning
talks.teaser: Shows how a poisoned self-supervised image encoder can backdoor many downstream classifiers while keeping clean accuracy.
talks.summary:
Self-supervised learning trains an image encoder without labels, and downstream classifiers are then built on top of its feature vectors. The talk raises the risk that a shared pretrained encoder carrying a backdoor can affect every classifier built from it. It introduces BadEncoder, a backdoor attack on pre-trained encoders, in which an attacker, either a malicious encoder provider or a third party distributing a model, embeds a trigger such as a small white patch.

The attack crafts a backdoored encoder by minimizing two losses together. The effectiveness loss pushes trigger-stamped images toward the feature vector of a reference image from the target class, while the utility loss keeps the encoder's outputs on clean inputs close to those of a clean encoder. In experiments with SimCLR, the backdoored encoder gave high attack success rates on downstream tasks such as traffic sign recognition, while clean and backdoor accuracy stayed similar. A real-world case study using an encoder collected from the internet showed comparable results. Neural Cleanse and MNTD did not detect the backdoor, and PatchGuard offered insufficient robustness guarantees against it.

The main takeaway is that an insecure encoder becomes a single point of failure across a whole ecosystem of downstream models. The speaker concludes that existing defenses are insufficient and that secure self-supervised learning algorithms are needed.

talks.title: Bad Characters: Imperceptible NLP Attacks
talks.teaser: Shows how invisible Unicode tricks silently evade text-based NLP models, including deployed toxicity filters and translators.
talks.summary:
The talk argues that text-based machine learning models can be fooled by adversarial examples that a human reader cannot notice. Earlier text attacks relied on visible edits such as misspellings, paraphrases or reordered words, while this work changes only the underlying Unicode encoding, leaving the rendered text identical.

Four techniques are covered: invisible zero-width characters, homoglyphs borrowed from scripts such as Cyrillic and Greek, bidirectional control characters that reorder display, and injected characters removed by deletion controls. A genetic algorithm searches combinations of these to push a model toward a wrong output. In one machine translation example, a single reordering produced garbled French. In a toxicity case, five random characters followed by deletions lowered a toxic score from 96.8 to 8.2 percent. Across tested models, including deployed systems from large technology companies, performance fell as the number of perturbations rose, dropping to near zero for most models by five perturbations.

Defenses fall into two groups. One is deterministic preprocessing, such as resolving control characters or mapping homoglyphs to a common character before inference. The other is running text through optical character recognition so the model consumes rendered glyphs instead of raw bytes. The takeaway is that pipelines should sanitize text inputs much as databases sanitize user input, and that defenses should be retrofitted now.

talks.title: Membership inference attacks from first principles
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Membership inference attacks from first principles.
talks.summary:
### Overview
This presentation explores membership inference attacks against machine learning models from first principles, aiming to determine whether a specific example was included in a target model's training set. The speaker explains that while directly computing the probability distribution of high-dimensional neural network weights is intractable, attackers can instead evaluate model loss on a specific input as a scalar value. By re-evaluating membership inference through per-example parametric distributions rather than single global thresholds, the authors present an attack that is both conceptually grounded and significantly more effective in high-precision regimes.

### Key Topics
- **Foundations of Membership Inference**: Framing membership inference as a statistical test comparing the probability that a model was trained on an example versus not trained on it.
- **Limitations of Weight-Space Modeling**: The computational impossibility of modeling distributions over million- or billion-dimensional neural network parameter spaces directly, motivating loss-based scalar metrics.
- **Per-Sample Distributions vs. Global Thresholds**: Demonstrating that different training examples (e.g., an image of a cat versus an airplane) have vastly different baseline loss distributions, making fixed, global decision thresholds inadequate.
- **Evaluation Flaws in Prior Work**: Critiquing the reliance on average-case accuracy across an entire dataset, which obscures whether an attack can reliably identify vulnerable individuals at low false positive rates (FPR).

### Technical Details
To estimate the loss distributions, the methodology trains multiple "shadow" models by masking subsets of the training data (typically 50% randomly masked per model). The models are partitioned into two sets for a target image: models that saw the example during training (IN) and models that did not (OUT). Computing the loss on the target image for each set yields two distinct empirical distributions.

While a non-parametric histogram would require training thousands of models (e.g., 10,000 models), the authors fit parametric Gaussian distributions to each set, reducing the requirement to approximately 16–32 models (or as few as 8). The crossing point of these fitted Gaussians provides a calibrated, per-example decision threshold. Furthermore, the likelihood ratio between the distributions provides a calibrated confidence estimate for any given prediction.

Evaluating across ROC curves in log-log scale reveals that prior attacks boasting high average accuracy (e.g., around 59%) perform essentially at random guessing at low false positive rates (<10% FPR). In contrast, the proposed method outperforms prior work both on average accuracy and dramatically at low FPR regimes. The paper also supports both an "online" variant (training models specifically with/without the query point) and an "offline" variant that performs almost as well without retraining per query point.

### Takeaways
The speaker highlights a critical conclusion: many existing beliefs in the membership inference literature may need to be re-evaluated. Prior claims that certain defenses (such as weight decay) are ineffective were established only against weak, average-case global threshold attacks, leaving open whether they protect against strong attacks operating at low false positive rates. The primary trade-off of the proposed approach is the computational cost of training multiple models, though its principles also extend downstream to attribute inference and data extraction.

talks.title: Committed to Trust: A Qualitative Study on Security & Trust in Open Source Software Projects

talks.title: SoK: Social Cybersecurity
talks.teaser: Maps research on how people share accounts, devices and advice, and where today's privacy tools fall short socially.
talks.summary:
Uc Woo presents a systematization paper on social cybersecurity, which looks at how people protect privacy and accounts alongside family, partners and peers. The team began with about a thousand keyword-search results and narrowed them to roughly 100 papers involving social coordination, then coded them into themes.

The review sorts the work into four domains. Sharing access covers streaming accounts, devices, finances and workspaces, where couples and coworkers often share passwords informally. Shared authentication covers relying on family to log in and Nextdoor's neighbor vouching. Self-presentation covers survivors of intimate partner violence creating false profiles and teens using coded language instead of audience tools. Influence covers seeking advice and copying peers' habits. Each domain is compared across levels of social distance.

Through a social-technical gap lens, the team found that systems are often worked around rather than built for social needs, so users either change their social habits or accept weaker privacy. Collective tools like Tor see little adoption. The speaker urges designs with more social observability, cooperation and stewardship, plus collective action for public privacy. Ending account sharing after a breakup is highlighted as an actionable gap.

talks.title: The Experts' Insights on the Peer Review Process of Evaluating Security Papers
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for The Experts' Insights on the Peer Review Process of Evaluating Security Papers.

talks.title: Understanding and Mitigating Illicit Cryptomining on Continuous Integration Service Platforms
talks.teaser: Findings cover CI cryptomining abuse, large-scale measurements, and jitter mitigation that cuts hash rates with modest job overhead.
talks.summary:
Commercial continuous integration platforms tie into public code hosts and run containerized or virtualized build jobs, often including free tiers that offer substantial compute. Attackers abuse those resources for cryptomining, sometimes as obvious workflow jobs and sometimes by hiding miners inside Docker builds, test images, or jobs that look benign. The work names these repository-to-platform mining setups and shows adversaries scaling profit by opening many hosting accounts, wiring one repository to several CI providers, and reappearing after platforms block accounts.

Detection combines repository-side signals—parsing CI configuration commands with regular expressions for wallet and pool parameters—with platform-side job logs and runtime statistics where hash-rate or pool feedback may appear. A study of roughly five hundred thousand GitHub repositories flagged hundreds of suspects; manual review judged almost all as malicious, linked to about two hundred instances across twenty-three commercial CI services, and estimated Monero-focused revenue near eight hundred thousand dollars between March 2017 and May 2020, with activity rising and falling alongside coin prices.

Mitigation targets mining pools’ strict completion windows: injected delays must crush miner returns yet stay tolerable for ordinary CI work. The approach profiles memory access, uses permission tricks and brief sleeps on suspicious pages to add jitter tuned to hash workloads, and evaluation reports average hash-rate drops above ninety-five percent with most real CI jobs seeing only about ten percent relative runtime overhead.

talks.title: Privacy-from-Birth: Protecting Sensed Data from Malicious Sensors with VERSA
talks.teaser: Presents VERSA, a hybrid hardware-software design that keeps sensor data private on tiny microcontrollers.
talks.summary:
Shashi, a PhD candidate, presents privacy from birth, which aims to protect sensed data from the moment an analog stimulus becomes digital until it leaves the device. The focus is the lowest tier of IoT hardware: microcontrollers with tiny memory, no MMU or MPU, no trusted execution, and code running straight from flash. Software integrity checks can reveal a compromise on such chips only after the fact, and they cannot stop compromised code from leaking readings.

The proposed design, VERSA, pairs a hardware monitor beside the CPU with a software routine stored in ROM. A controller authorizes a specific software module with an HMAC-based token, and the hardware keeps the sensor memory locked to everything except that module while it runs. During its run, interrupts and DMA are blocked and entry and exit points are fixed; any violation resets the device. The module wipes its own stack, and the ROM routine clears leftovers at boot after a reset. The hardware was written in Verilog, formally verified, and implemented on openMSP on an FPGA.

The reported hardware overhead was about 13 percent on the openMSP core, placing the design alongside other hybrid architectures, while a purely hardware design was faster. Verification time grew linearly with binary size because the HMAC work scales with the code. The speaker noted that the work is a research prototype and that TrustZone-capable chips are the existing alternative, though costlier. The takeaway is that hardware-enforced sensor privacy on very low-end microcontrollers can be achieved at modest cost.

talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Exposed Infrastructures—Discovery, Attacks and Remediation of Insecure ICS Remote Management Devices.

talks.title: Exploit the Last Straw That Breaks Android Systems
talks.teaser: Shows how feeding data to Android system services can exhaust server memory and cause denial of service.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how Android system services store data that apps send them over IPC. Apps can free their own memory right away, yet the server may keep the same data for a long time, and developers are often unsure when it should be released. Memory limits per process can also trigger Android's recovery mechanism when exhausted, and many size checks are incomplete. The speakers call this a straw attack: repeatedly injecting data until a service's memory runs out.

To find such cases, the team built StrawFather, which combines static and dynamic analysis. Static analysis locates long-lived containers that grow with each operation and traces which service interfaces can feed them. A grey-box fuzzer then runs those interfaces, scoring inputs by how close they get to the target or how much memory they consume, and it adaptively shifts between exploration and exploitation. On three patched Android systems it found 35 vulnerabilities and 474 vulnerable interfaces.

Over 90 percent of the exploitable interfaces were caused by flaws in the deserialization process, and 158 required system permissions. Almost all vulnerabilities also worked on three vendor devices from Huawei, Samsung and vivo, which block rooting, and ninety percent could be triggered within 78 seconds on average. One case involved an account manager interface that accepted unlimited accounts and reloaded them at boot, causing a permanent denial of service through a reboot loop. The team also found similar issues in 76 of 100 top free Google Play apps and argued that stronger checks on app-supplied data are needed.

talks.title: Analyzing Ground-Truth Data of Mobile Gambling Scam
talks.teaser: A ground-truth study maps mobile gambling scams through social engineering, sideloaded apps, and concealed payment channels.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with how mobile gambling fraud lures victims through instant messaging and installable apps that block withdrawals, noting large reported losses and gaps in prior web-only measurement of the scam lifecycle.

The core contribution is analysis of more than one thousand incident reports and associated scam apps from 2020, modeled in four stages: gaining contact, delivering apps, pressuring deposits, and blocking payouts. Qualitative coding of reports quantifies role-play personas, recruitment channels beyond phone and email, scammer-driven versus victim-initiated app installs, and incentive versus pressure deposit tactics. Technical sections compare sideloaded Android and iOS packages to legitimate gambling apps, abuse of online app generators, permissive SDK targets, CDN-backed backends with young domain registrations, and payment flows including cryptocurrency and peer-pay abuse through marketplace money mules.

Practitioners gain a structured kill-chain view for detection and disruption, plus concrete infrastructure and payment signals that differ from reputable app-store gambling offerings.

talks.title: Scraping Sticky Leftovers: App User Information Left on Servers After Account Deletion
talks.teaser: Shows how apps and websites keep personal data after account deletion or uninstall, and a toolchain to detect it.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at personal information that stays on app and website servers after a user deletes an account or uninstalls an app. The speaker notes that many services collect sensitive details such as email addresses, phone numbers, and in some cases government ID or banking data, yet few offer a real way to delete them. Leftover records can be exposed or altered, and they conflict with what users reasonably expect when they remove an account. The work sorts the problem into four cases: no deletion feature, data kept after deletion, data kept after uninstall, and no stated retention period.

To study this, the researchers built a four-part toolchain for Android apps and websites. A deletion analyzer uses static analysis to find deletion wording, map it to screens, and trace it to click handlers, while a retention analyzer looks for stated time windows. A leftover account analyzer automates sign-up, deletion and re-registration on a device, watching for warnings that an account still exists, and it reverse engineers decompiled APK files to find the server calls for account creation, update and deletion. A cleaner reinstalls uninstalled apps to remove their accounts. Across 1,435 Google Play apps with email sign-in, 254 retained data after install or uninstall, 17 retained data after deletion, and 437 had no deletion button. The reported F-measure was 88.4 percent.

Some steps still needed manual help, such as captchas and verification prompts. When the team contacted one company, customer service said some information was kept for research, and a later check of another app found data still present months after deletion. The takeaway for practitioners is that users cannot assume deletion works, and developers should offer real deletion and publish accurate retention periods.

talks.title: Domains Do Change Their Spots: Quantifying Potential Abuse of Residual Trust
talks.teaser: The work measures lingering DNS trust after domain turnover and shows how cheap re-registrations attract millions of client connections.
talks.summary:
Expired domain names can pass to new registrars without any signal to phones, browsers, or background updaters that still resolve and contact those names. The speaker frames this gap as residual trust: clients keep behaving as if the old operator still controls the hostname, which may leak data or pull stale resources to a stranger.

The team built an experiment around roughly two hundred re-registered drop domains, each pointed at honeypot web, SSH, Telnet, and FTP services on dedicated address space. They ranked candidates using passive DNS popularity, filtered scanning and bot noise with placebo hosts and blocklists, and matched requests to archived site patterns from the Wayback Machine and third-party references. Over four months they logged hundreds of millions of requests from millions of unique source addresses, finding that most names saw little abusive trust traffic but a thin tail of outliers drew sustained volume. Residual-trust traffic did not reliably fade; some series stayed flat while others decayed. Case studies span trackers, embedded scripts on third-party blogs, API and nameserver roles, and high-volume torrent-related naming.

Practitioners should treat domain lifecycles as asset-management problems: monitor resolutions before public release, retire dependencies aggressively, and where possible verify content integrity rather than trusting DNS labels alone. The work argues the abuse surface is large yet inexpensive to probe.

talks.title: PGPATCH: Policy-Guided Logic Bug Patching for Robotic Vehicles
talks.teaser: See how policy formulas guide candidate repairs for logic bugs in robotic vehicle software.
talks.summary: The talk presents PG Patch, a tool that uses temporal logic policies to repair logic bugs in robotic vehicle software. It maps policy terms to code, generates candidate patches, and checks them against developer tests; an evaluation across three vehicle control software projects reports that it fixed about 86% of the collected bugs. A user study found participants created more correct policy formulas than source code patches and spent less time writing formulas.

talks.title: SwarmFlawFinder: Discovering and Exploiting Logic Flaws of Swarm Algorithms
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of SwarmFlawFinder: Discovering and Exploiting Logic Flaws of Swarm Algorithms.

talks.title: HardLog: Practical Tamper-Proof System Auditing Using a Novel Audit Device
talks.teaser: An external append-only audit device and event-selective flushing defend enterprise logs against in-memory tampering with low overhead.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens on a longstanding weakness in enterprise system auditing: for performance, audit records must be buffered on the host that may already be compromised, and studies cited in the talk suggest log tampering appears in a large majority of attack investigations. Synchronous forwarding of every event is ruled out because machines emit vast event rates and network latency cannot keep pace.

HardLog is described as pairing host-side Linux kernel auditing with an external audit device on a fast local interface such as USB or PCIe. The device accepts only append operations from the OS while administrators retrieve or discard logs over an authenticated, encrypted channel. Because full synchronous protection on every entry remains too costly, logs flush entirely before critical events such as code-execution syscalls, while non-critical traffic receives bounded-delay background protection through scheduling and resource isolation so protection speed depends mainly on the device link. A prototype built around kernel audit, USB 3.0, and a commodity ARM board reportedly protects non-critical entries within about fifteen milliseconds under stress tests and matches or beats auditd overhead on most benchmarks.

Practitioners should treat the design as a way to recover log availability—not merely tamper detection—when the OS is untrusted after compromise, while accepting a software-only threat model and rare paths that might escalate privilege without critical syscalls.

talks.title: AccEar: Accelerometer Acoustic Eavesdropping with Unconstrained Vocabulary
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning AccEar: Accelerometer Acoustic Eavesdropping with Unconstrained Vocabulary.

talks.title: Practical EMV Relay Protection
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Practical EMV Relay Protection.

talks.title: Anti-Tamper Radio: System-Level Tamper Detection for Computing Systems
talks.teaser: Shows how radio waves between antennas can detect physical tampering such as needle probing of a server's enclosure.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from physical attackers who access a device to extract secrets such as cryptographic keys or implant malicious functionality. System-level tamper detection is presented as an unsolved problem. The speaker introduces Anti-Tamper Radio, which places antennas in the monitored environment, sends a signal between them, and flags changes in the reflected response. Needle probing served as the test attack, on the reasoning that catching a small metallic needle should also catch more invasive tampering. Test enclosures had holes drilled in their lids, and a Cartesian robot positioned the needles repeatably.

Measurements used a vector network analyzer and a mean normalized deviation score. In an empty aluminum box, needle insertion was detectable, and detectability grew with needle diameter and depth. In a running 19-inch server, metal walls limited useful coverage to the area near the antennas, so sensitive and insensitive regions were defined. Powering the server on added airflow, vibration and temperature swings, and with a threshold that avoided false positives, only about half of the sensitive region was detected. A setup phase that measured the untampered system and excluded high-variation spectral regions raised detection to 114 of 117 positions.

A low-cost version built from single-chip ultra-wideband transceivers, costing about ten US dollars in total, gave a preliminary detection result. Non-metallic probes remain untested, and blind spots would need modeling, perhaps with full-field simulation. The takeaway: radio-based tamper detection can hold up in a running server with realistic noise, provided the tamper circuitry sits within the sensitive region.

talks.title: IRShield: A Countermeasure Against Adversarial Physical-Layer Wireless Sensing
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for IRShield: A Countermeasure Against Adversarial Physical-Layer Wireless Sensing.

talks.title: Evaluating Physical-Layer BLE Location Tracking Attacks on Mobile Devices
talks.teaser: Shows how radio hardware imperfections in BLE beacons can fingerprint smartphones and track their owners in the field.
talks.summary:
Bluetooth Low Energy devices broadcast beacons constantly, and although MAC address randomisation limits identifier-based tracking, the physical radio signal still carries manufacturing imperfections such as carrier frequency offset and IQ imbalance. An attacker with a software-defined radio can measure these and use them as a fingerprint. The speaker explains that short BLE preambles make precise estimates hard, so the approach reconstructs the whole decoded packet as a reference and fits a model of the radio's impairments to it, which yields much tighter estimates.

Field tests examined whether this works outside the lab. Fingerprints were taken in an office and matched later at a food court, a coffee shop and a busy walkway. Across 17 target devices, including smartphones, smartwatches and laptops, false positive and false negative rates averaged around three percent. Across roughly 650 devices collected over two days at a room exit, most had fingerprints that did not overlap with others. Challenges noted include chipsets with near-identical or absent IQ offset, temperature drift of the crystal, and receiver placement given differing transmit power.

In a home-tracking scenario, the receiver was placed at a residence and checks ran every 10 seconds over about an hour, detecting entries and exits with high accuracy despite 30 to 40 other devices nearby. The speaker proposed defenses such as time-varying offsets added in hardware or firmware, and noted that a software-only approach would drain batteries. The takeaway is that physical-layer imperfections can undermine address randomisation, so hardware-level mitigations deserve attention.

talks.title: Universal Atomic Swaps: Secure Exchange of Coins Across All Blockchains
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Universal Atomic Swaps: Secure Exchange of Coins Across All Blockchains.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Arvind, a postdoctoral researcher at Carnegie Mellon University, presents joint research with Giulio (MPI) and Pedro (IMDEA) on universal atomic swaps across blockchains. Cross-currency token exchange is a fundamental economic activity, yet existing trustless solutions struggle with atomicity—ensuring that either both parties receive their swapped coins or neither does. Traditional solutions rely on centralized exchange services (which require high availability and risk coin theft), third-party smart contract blockchains (which can be complex and expensive), or Hashed Time-Locked Contracts (HTLCs) within payment channels. However, HTLCs rely on specialized scripting, limiting interoperability with simpler blockchains, incurring high on-chain fees, and degrading token fungibility. The authors introduce a universal, multi-asset atomic swap protocol that eliminates the need for HTLCs and special scripts, requiring only standard signature verification scripts.

### Key Topics
- **Limitations of HTLCs**: HTLCs require specialized script support, increase on-chain transaction costs, and harm token fungibility because transactions stand out on-chain.
- **Multi-Asset Atomicity Notion**: In multi-asset exchanges, traditional definitions can allow a malicious party to claim a subset of coins and refund their own assets. The proposed model enforces that if Alice claims even a single coin on her side, Bob is guaranteed the ability to claim all coins on his side.
- **Adaptor Signatures**: A cryptographic primitive defined over an NP relation and signature scheme that links signature validity to the revelation of a witness, allowing off-chain atomic linkage.
- **Verifiable Timed Discrete Logarithms (VTD Log)**: A cryptographic commitment tool used to replace on-chain lock-time/timeout scripts for handling refunds privately and off-chain.

### Technical Details
The core construction focuses on Schnorr and ECDSA signatures and operates across four main phases:
1. **Setup Phase**: Alice and Bob establish payment channels where channel addresses are shared public keys with distributed secret key shares. To handle timeouts without on-chain lock-time scripts, parties exchange Verifiable Timed Discrete Logarithm (VTD log) commitments to their secret key shares (set to duration $T$ for Alice and $T + \Delta$ for Bob), which both parties begin brute-forcing immediately.
2. **Lock Phase**: Alice selects a statement-witness pair for an NP relation. Using a two-party computation protocol, Bob obtains pre-signatures for his outgoing transactions under Alice's statement. Similarly, pre-signatures are generated for Alice's incoming transactions using the identical statement instance.
3. **Swap Complete Phase**: Alice uses her witness to adapt the pre-signatures into valid signatures, publishing them on-chain to claim her coins. Bob observes the published signature on any blockchain, extracts the underlying witness using the adaptor signature extraction algorithm, adapts his own pre-signatures, and posts them to claim all corresponding coins on his side.
4. **Timeout Phase**: If the swap does not complete, users finish brute-forcing the VTD log commitments after time $T$ (or $T + \Delta$). Recovering the counterparty's key share gives the party the full channel private key, enabling immediate unilateral refund of unswapped coins via standard transactions without revealing lock-time scripts or channel expiry logic on-chain.

### Takeaways
The proposed universal atomic swap construction makes cross-chain swap transactions look like ordinary payment transactions, lowering on-chain gas costs (demonstrated on Ethereum) and protecting token fungibility and privacy across any cryptocurrency supporting basic digital signatures. Open problems include mitigating denial-of-service risks where participants go offline to trigger refunds, and achieving scriptless atomic swaps that allow unconditional redemption regardless of timeouts.

talks.title: Using Throughput-Centric Byzantine Broadcast to Tolerate Malicious Majority in Blockchains
talks.teaser: Shows a blockchain that stays usable with a malicious majority, using a new high-throughput Byzantine broadcast protocol.
talks.summary:
Many blockchains assume an honest majority, because classic Byzantine agreement cannot tolerate a malicious fraction above one half. The speaker argues this limit does not carry over to blockchains, since a chain is a sequence of blocks and some adversarial blocks are acceptable. The talk introduces BQ, which is built on Byzantine broadcast: a randomly chosen proposer sends each block, and honest nodes agree on it even when the malicious share exceeds half.

The central obstacle is throughput. Running a well-known Byzantine broadcast protocol directly gave only 0.072 kbps in the experimental setting, and running parallel instances fails because an adversary can align idle rounds. The proposed overlay BB protocol staggers forwarding across rounds, has nodes compensate for the resulting delays, and uses relay filtering against injection attacks and limits on beacon bias.

Experiments with 10,000 nodes, each capped at 20 Mbps and 20 outgoing overlay connections, reached about 163 kbps at f equal to 0.7. That is more than 2000 times the baseline and above the roughly 14 kbps cited for Bitcoin. Proofs cover overlay BB correctness when at least one committee member is honest, and BQ safety and liveness under majority failure. Q&A noted that light clients still rely on full nodes. The takeaway is that broadcast-based design can offer usable throughput beyond the usual majority threshold.

talks.title: mmSpy: Spying Phone Calls using mmWave Radars
talks.teaser: Shows how mmWave radars can recover phone call audio from vibrations at a distance, using signal processing and neural networks.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the risk of phone calls in which people share sensitive details such as card numbers, and asks what happens if someone can listen in from across the room. It presents mmSpy, a system that uses millimeter-wave radars, the same class of sensors used in automotive ranging and health monitoring, to pick up the tiny vibrations a phone's earpiece speaker produces. The radar's frequency-modulated chirps reveal the distance to each reflecting object, and the strongest reflection is assumed to be the phone. Tracking that reflection's phase changes over time yields an audio signal.

The recovered audio is very noisy, so the pipeline applies band-pass and spectral subtraction filtering, then a neural enhancement network and a convolutional classifier for spoken digits and keywords. Because large radar datasets do not exist, the authors turn existing audio datasets into synthetic radar-like data and then adapt the models to a small set of real captures with transfer learning. Experiments varied phone models, radars, datasets and distances up to six feet. Digit classification reached about 80 percent accuracy at best and dropped with distance, and the synthetic-data approach outperformed training directly on radar recordings. Body movements and breathing added spikes, but some audio stayed recoverable.

The speaker closed with limitations, including training on more phones, handling motion, and recognizing accents, and with possible defenses such as vibration-absorbing materials and beamforming speakers that direct sound away from the phone's back. In the Q&A, the speaker explained that a radar isolates one point while a microphone captures everything nearby, and that a protective case reduces the effect less than expected, based on a small unpublished test. The main takeaway is that such eavesdropping is feasible and should be recognized as a threat.

talks.title: How Not to Protect Your IP - An Industry-Wide Break of IEEE 1735 Implementations
talks.teaser: Exposes systemic flaws in IEEE 1735 and breaks six major FPGA tool vendors' IP encryption schemes.
talks.summary:
Modern system-on-chip design relies on third-party intellectual property cores, and IEEE 1735 was meant to let vendors ship encrypted IP that design tools decrypt only in memory. The presentation argues the standard’s trust model is structurally weak: RSA private keys for entire product lines sit inside tools that run on customers’ machines, the standard does not mandate strong secret handling, and legal bans on reverse engineering are poor defenses against motivated attackers.

The speakers report examining six widely used flows from Intel, Xilinx, Cadence, Siemens, Lattice, and Microchip. Three implementations left keys essentially unprotected, enabling recovery in about an hour. The others layered white-box cryptography, obfuscation, and anti-debugging, stretching attacks to days or roughly two weeks for Xilinx Vivado. Because IP is often encrypted for multiple tools at once, compromising one weaker toolchain can void protection elsewhere. The Xilinx walkthrough uses library signature matching to locate crypto, defeats anti-debugging, analyzes an obfuscated dispatcher, and treats peculiar RSA routines as white-box implementations. Reimplementing the white box in Python achieves code lifting; collaborating with a cryptographer then yields five embedded RSA keys, including factorization of 2,048-bit moduli in about two hours, enough to decrypt Vivado-protected cores.

Practitioners should treat IEEE 1735 confidentiality as limited rather than absolute, prioritize integrity and authenticity where vendors care most, and assume proprietary RSA white-box schemes need independent scrutiny. Vendors can still raise attack cost with software protections, but the talk concludes the standard requires revision with explicit key-protection requirements.

talks.title: Mind the Gap: Studying the Insecurity of Provably Secure Embedded Trusted Execution Architectures
talks.teaser: Examines how proven embedded enclave designs still leak through implementation mismatches and a DMA side channel.
talks.summary:
The talk asks how evidence for the security of computer systems can be produced, using an ATM withdrawal example to contrast testing with formal proof. Testing can reveal violations but cannot guarantee that a property holds, while proofs rest on axioms that must still be checked against the physical implementation. The speaker's group examined two embedded research prototypes that come with published formal proofs: a trusted execution environment whose enclaves were extended with interrupt support, and a remote attestation architecture with a hardware access-control module.

The team listed around 20 assumptions, found them unsatisfied in the two implementations, and built 17 attacks grouped into implementation-model mismatches, missing attacker capabilities and deductive errors. One example was an access-control module wired to a DMA address signal shifted by one bit, which let an attacker read the attestation key with a single DMA request. The first system had many more mismatches, which the speaker linked to automatic model extraction from the code. The team also found a novel cycle-accurate side channel arising from contention on a shared memory bus between the CPU and DMA peripherals. Combining it with interrupt measurements let an attacker tell apart enclaves that should be indistinguishable.

The speaker closed with guidelines: keep implementation and model tightly connected through extraction, derivation, or simultaneous differential testing combined with fuzzing. Developers should study the embedded enclave literature for known timing and interrupt latency attacks, model attacker capabilities as composable primitives, and audit interfaces at trust boundaries. Formal verification should not replace empirical testing. The attacks are available in a public repository where they run in continuous integration.

talks.summary: Xen Hahu presents IRQDebloat to automatically strip unused interrupt handlers from vendor firmware, shrinking driver attack surface on routers that ship dormant Bluetooth stacks and other peripherals. The pipeline reverse-engineers IRQ dispatch tables and patches binaries when vendors refuse feature toggles.

talks.title: "Adversarial Examples" for Proof-of-Learning
talks.teaser: Adversarial optimization forges shortened weight sequences that spoof proof-of-learning while beating honest provers on gradient cost.
talks.summary:
The presentation targets two machine-learning assurance problems: proving who trained a model when extraction attacks loom, and checking that distributed workers actually ran collaborative training. Prior watermarking, fingerprinting, and verifiable-computation defenses trade off proof strength against model utility or require awkward training or inference changes.

Proof-of-learning records sparse checkpoints and metadata so a verifier can replay key optimization steps. The speakers assume an attacker knows architecture, loss, and hyperparameters and can alter the training set but not honest randomness or batching. They spoof proofs by treating desired weight transitions like adversarial-example problems: perturb inputs so gradient steps land on chosen weights with tiny, hard-to-spot changes. A basic attack optimizes step by step; an advanced one batches key checkpoints and interpolates intermediate weights so convergence needs roughly ten optimization rounds. Analysis and CIFAR-100-style experiments show spoofing can need fewer gradient evaluations than generating a legitimate proof when the forged chain length sits in analyzed bands; split non-overlapping datasets stress a verifier who cannot tell which corpus was perturbed.

Practitioners should treat PoL as sensitive to data integrity, checkpoint spacing, and reproduction thresholds that stay loose early in training. Stricter checkpoint rules, stage-dependent verification limits, or heavy verifiable-computation overlays raise cost but narrow the attack window. Question time highlights unsettled variants such as hashed training data, dependence on GPU numerics, and whether perturbations must stay visually plausible under human review.

talks.title: Model Orthogonalization: Class Distance Hardening in Neural Networks for Better Security
talks.teaser: Shows how enlarging distances between class pairs in neural networks hardens them against natural and injected backdoor triggers.
talks.summary:
Backdoor attacks plant small triggers in deep learning models so that inputs carrying the trigger get pushed to an attacker's chosen label. Most defenses target backdoors that were deliberately injected, yet the speaker argues that benign models can contain natural backdoors too. In one example, a model downloaded from the Keras model zoo had a small trigger that made turtle images be predicted as birds with high confidence. Robustness is measured by class distance, the smallest change in norm needed to move inputs from one class to another. This distance is directional, so the two directions between a pair of classes can differ.

Standard adversarial training leaves decision boundaries close to many samples, so the proposed approach aims to enlarge pairwise class distances while keeping normal accuracy. Hardening every class pair is costly, so the method first runs a universal backdoor generation warm-up to probe how promising each source class is. A scheduler then uses accumulated distance changes to choose which pairs to harden. The speaker also shows that hardening both directions of a pair at once, using two-sided backdoor generation, keeps the boundary perpendicular to the line between class centres instead of cancelling out.

Experiments covered standard datasets and 89 pretrained models, on both naturally and adversarially trained models. Reported results include large average distance gains with limited accuracy loss. For injected backdoors, the attack success rate fell from almost 100 percent to 1 percent across 15 backdoored models, while baselines reached 27 at most. A practitioner can take away that distance-based hardening can focus on the class directions that matter most, such as preventing malware from being turned benign.

talks.title: Model Stealing Attacks Against Inductive Graph Neural Networks
talks.teaser: Shows how black-box queries let an attacker clone inductive graph neural networks with little data.
talks.summary:
The talk examines model stealing attacks against inductive graph neural networks, which classify nodes in graphs unseen during training. The adversary has only black-box API access to a deployed target model. By submitting a query graph and collecting the returned predictions, embeddings or two-dimensional projections, the attacker trains a surrogate model. A stealing adversary aims to match the target's accuracy, while a reconnaissance adversary aims for close agreement on any input, so the surrogate can be used to craft adversarial examples without querying the target.

Six attacks are defined: type 1 assumes the adjacency matrix is available, type 2 reconstructs it first, and each has three response types. Across three popular GNN architectures and six datasets, surrogates stay close to their targets. On PubMed, the target scores above 0.9 accuracy and the surrogate around 87% or more, a drop of roughly 4 points. Embedding plots show target and surrogate separating classes in similar regions. Type 2 often matches type 1, and the graph reconstruction method strongly affects results. A query graph covering only about 3% of nodes remains effective. Adding Gaussian noise to the responses only slightly reduces surrogate performance.

The takeaway is that inductive GNN APIs can be cloned even from small query budgets, and simple noise is not enough of a defense. The speaker plans to study differential privacy and watermarking as future defenses. In the Q&A, differential privacy was discussed as a way to hide edge information, with the trade-off that it can lower the target model's utility.

talks.title: DeepSteal: Advanced Model Extractions Leveraging Efficient Weight Stealing in Memories
talks.teaser: HammerLeak and mean clustering turn Rowhammer-leaked DNN weights into substitute models with near white-box adversarial transfer.
talks.summary:
Machine learning delivered as a cloud service puts high-value model weights on hardware that untrusted tenants may share. The presenters frame model extraction as building a substitute network with accuracy and decision-boundary fidelity close to the victim’s, which strengthens follow-on adversarial attacks beyond what architecture-only leakage allows.

They assume co-resident inference on CPU, known architecture but unknown parameters, and no direct querying. DeepSteal combines HammerLeak, a generic Rowhammer data-stealing pipeline, with mean clustering training on partially leaked weights. HammerLeak evicts anonymous victim pages via swapping, fills a page set to steer reallocation, uses cache anchors to release pages in batches during PyTorch layer execution, then steals weight bits page by page. Recovered most significant bits define per-weight ranges; clustering pulls unknown bits toward projected means while fully known weights skip the penalty.

On vision benchmarks they report about 95% HammerLeak success, rising substitute accuracy and fidelity toward roughly 90% with more hammer rounds on ResNet-18, and adversarial transfer nearer white-box than prior remote side channels that recover structure alone—about an 18-point accuracy gain in their comparison. Discussion clarifies CPU-focused anchoring, diminished applicability when enclave memory encrypts weights, flips confined to attacker-controlled rows, and one-time memory templating per boot.

talks.title: How to Attack and Generate Honeywords
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in How to Attack and Generate Honeywords.
talks.summary: The talk compares honeywords, slow hashes, and threshold cryptography for surviving password-database leaks, arguing decoy passwords best balance usability and detection. Honeywords sit beside real hashes so offline crackers trigger alerts when they guess a decoy online, but generation must make fakes statistically indistinguishable. The team proves optimal attacker strategies for untargeted and targeted guessing over sweetword lists, then derives design principles: tweak-tail and model-syntax hybrids should yield flat success curves, while independent honeywords need probabilities mirroring real password models. They implement four generators using list, PCFG, and Markov components on roughly one hundred million passwords, reporting under eight percent success within ten thousand guesses in both attack modes. A student study still beats automation slightly, motivating hybrid models. Future work covers model blending weights and stronger generative networks that stay unrelated to each user password to avoid side channels.

talks.title: SNARKBlock: Federated Anonymous Blocklisting from Hidden Common Input Aggregate Proofs
talks.teaser: A scalable anonymous blocklisting design uses succinct aggregated zero-knowledge proofs to enforce bans without linking users.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with a familiar tension: online communities need to block repeat abusers, yet strong identity checks undermine pseudonymous participation. Prior anonymous blocklisting work lets users post with unlinkable tags while proving they are not already banned, but proofs grow linearly with the ban list. At millions of entries, verification and upload costs become impractical, and users cannot reuse prior work when posting again.

The speaker walks through why naive SNARK wrapping and fixed-size chunking fail on cost, circuit growth, and ban evasion, then introduces SNARKBlock built on a zero-knowledge aggregation primitive with update unlinkability and succinct proofs. Chunked non-membership checks share a hidden common identity across aggregated proofs without revealing it across sessions. For very large blocklists, aggregate proofs stay on the order of hundreds of kilobytes with sub-second server verification, with offline chunk work amortized across updates.

Practitioners should view this as evidence that accountability for moderation can be decoupled from persistent deanonymization when cryptography is used carefully. Identity issuance remains an operational question—phone numbers, passports, or other Sybil-resistant hooks—but the scheme aims to separate the identity provider from day-to-day service behavior while preserving blocklist soundness, non-frameability, and anonymity.

talks.title: Spiral: Fast, High-Rate Single-Server PIR via FHE Composition
talks.teaser: Shows how the Spiral scheme combines homomorphic encryption schemes to make single-server private retrieval faster and smaller.
talks.summary:
The talk covers single-server private information retrieval, in which a client fetches a record without the database learning which one it wants, even when the server behaves maliciously. The speaker defines four measures for comparing such schemes: query size, server throughput, rate (record size relative to response size), and public parameter size. Earlier constructions had drawbacks. One combined two encryption schemes but was never implemented and had very large queries, while another kept queries small but returned scalar ciphertexts that lowered the rate.

The proposed scheme, Spiral, aims to keep the small queries of the second approach and the high rate of the first. It adds simple key switching to convert between scalar and matrix ciphertexts, and it uses three further techniques: automatic parameter selection driven by a cost model, a carefully chosen ciphertext modulus that allows mostly 32-bit multiplication, and coarser encoding of a less important part of matrix ciphertexts. On a database of about 250,000 records of 30 kilobytes, Spiral improves on prior work in query size, rate and throughput, but its public parameters are larger.

A streaming variant reuses one query across changing databases, such as video chunks or a polled mailbox, so a large query can be amortized over the stream. In that setting the speaker reported throughput above 1.5 gigabytes per second and a packing step that raises rate further at some cost to throughput. The main takeaway is that private retrieval is approaching practical speeds. All benchmarks were single-threaded, and the speaker noted that the work is naively parallel.

talks.title: Private Approximate Nearest Neighbor Search
talks.teaser: A two-server protocol delivers private approximate nearest neighbor search with sublinear communication and lighter cost than FHE or 2PC.
talks.summary:
Nearest and approximate nearest neighbor search drives recommendation and similarity workloads, but queries expose user profiles while full database access exposes proprietary catalogs. Prior private approaches trade badly: two-party computation needs gigabytes of traffic at million-item scale and lacks default malicious security, while fully homomorphic encryption keeps the client light but leaves the database with hours of work even on tiny sets.

The presentation outlines a two-server design where the client privately probes locality-sensitive hash tables via private information retrieval built from distributed point functions. A strawman that returns colliding candidates leaks neighbor identities and features; the protocol instead sorts candidates by tightening collision radii across tables, returns only identifiers, and applies oblivious masking so only the first matching neighbor id stays visible while later entries become random. Guarantees target user privacy against a malicious server and database privacy against colluding malicious clients, with malicious security interpreted as privacy under deviation rather than full correctness.

Reported benchmarks on standard ANN datasets show sub-megabyte to low-megabyte communication, hundreds of milliseconds to a few seconds of server time at tens of thousands to ten million items, and orders-of-magnitude gains over FHE compute and two-party communication. Practitioners should weigh the residual leakage from how many empty buckets precede the answer, the non-collusion or single-server generalization assumptions, and whether privacy-without-correctness-under-attack matches their threat model.
