talks.title: Surakav: Generating Realistic Traces for a Strong Website Fingerprinting Defense
talks.teaser: Generates realistic GAN-learned sending patterns to hide Tor page loads from website fingerprinting attacks with lower overhead.
talks.summary:
A local eavesdropper can still run website fingerprinting against Tor users, inferring which page is loaded from packet timing and sizes. Lightweight defenses like WTF-PAD and Front add little overhead but resist deep learning attacks poorly, while Walkie-Talkie and Tamaraw are stronger but rigid. Surakav trains a GAN on burst sequences from real page loads, using a generator, a discriminator, and a pre-trained fingerprinting model as an observer.

Training on 100 randomly chosen classes of 1,000 instances each cut the Wasserstein distance from 0.9 to 0.02, and about 90% of generated traces were classified into their expected classes. At runtime, client and proxy send bursts shaped by a generated trace, with timing gaps sampled from a kernel density estimate. Burst size adjustment, tuned by a delta window, and random response on the proxy side reshape traffic in real time.

Tested over the real Tor network as a pluggable transport, with a user in Hong Kong and an entry node in the US, against 100 monitored pages among about 60,000 others. Against the strongest attack, the true positive rate fell from 97% to 6% at the heavier setting. Versus Front, it saved 42% data overhead at similar protection; versus Tamaraw, 40% less data overhead and 10% less time overhead. Latency rose 16 to 18% on average. Learned sending patterns can thus give strong protection with less overhead than fixed-pattern defenses.

talks.title: Timing-Based Browsing Privacy Vulnerabilities Via Site Isolation
talks.teaser: Shows how process reuse under site isolation leaks which sites a user has open, and when they are in focus.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how Chromium's site isolation, which places different websites in separate renderer processes, opens a timing side channel that reveals browsing behaviour. Processes are scarce, so browsers reuse them aggressively, even across tabs. A page can load a target site inside an iframe and time the load: a newly created process takes measurably longer than a reused one, so the attacker learns whether that sensitive site is open somewhere in the browser.

The attacker can also tell foreground from background tabs. To remove network noise, the probe uses an unsafe port, which the browser refuses immediately, or a cached static resource such as a favicon. Under CPU stress, background processes slow more than foreground ones, and HTML parsing speed distinguishes newly created processes. Testing the Alexa top 3000 sites on a desktop and a laptop with extra tabs showed high pairwise differentiation. Chromium versions from the release that enabled site isolation, and Edge, were vulnerable. Firefox's experimental site isolation separated the absent and background cases easily, but the other distinction needed deeper study.

The main lesson is the tension between process scarcity and separating cross-site frames, which makes this a reliable leak. The authors reported discussions with the Edge and Chrome teams, including a Chrome-proposed mitigation that prohibits process reuse between a top-level frame and an iframe. Whether that policy reaches Chromium remains open.

talks.title: MeshUp: Stateless Cache Side-channel Attack on CPU Mesh
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of MeshUp: Stateless Cache Side-channel Attack on CPU Mesh.

talks.title: Augury: Using Data Memory-Dependent Prefetchers to Leak Data at Rest
talks.teaser: Shows how an Apple M1 data memory-dependent prefetcher can leak pointers that were never read into the core.
talks.summary:
Most microarchitectural attacks so far leak data that a program has already read into the core, either speculatively or not. This talk presents a different class of leak: a data memory-dependent prefetcher, or DMP, which reads the contents of memory and starts cache fills based on what it finds, including pointers. A conventional prefetcher overshoots the end of an array because it does not know the array's bounds, and a DMP can then dereference a secret pointer sitting past that end, bringing it into the cache without the secret ever entering the core.

The speaker reported finding such a DMP in the Apple M1 by comparing a pointer-dereferencing access pattern against a baseline with identical addresses, generated by a pseudorandom generator, where the pointer version ran significantly faster. A proof of concept used the prefetcher to check whether an arbitrary pointer maps to valid memory, which can help break address space layout randomization with less noise than cache side channels. The team also showed that code protected by speculative load hardening leaks the same way, because that defense only protects the core. Keeping secrets out of the attacker's address space was discussed as a mitigation, but future DMPs may reach further than Spectre.

The DMP was also triggered accidentally by storing pointers on the stack, so latent gadgets in privileged code may need to be found and removed. The speaker offered questions for analysing any DMP: what activates it, which values it transmits, how an adversary receives them, and which memory informs prefetching. In the Q&A, the team said Apple had been notified with no known way to disable the prefetcher, and that reach past a loop can extend up to 64 kilobytes on the M1.

talks.title: Graphics Peeping Unit: Exploiting EM Side-Channel Information of GPUs to Eavesdrop on Your Neighbors
talks.teaser: Shows how GPU power-state switching leaks electromagnetic signals that reveal browsed websites and typed keystrokes nearby.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether someone with no physical or logical access to a discrete GPU can still steal sensitive information from it, and answers yes. The starting point is dynamic voltage and frequency scaling (DVFS), which moves a GPU between performance levels as its workload changes. Each level switching on and off produces electromagnetic emissions tied to the GPU memory clock, and watching a single level, usually the second lowest, is enough to tell activities apart.

Spread spectrum clocking weakens these emissions, so the researchers folded periodic spectral components to recover workload patterns from weak signals and filtered out strong periodic noise. Using only a software-defined radio and an antenna, they tested six GPUs from low-end and high-end lines released over six years. Signals reached several meters in most directions and passed through apartment walls with varying loss. Two case studies followed. Website fingerprinting across 50 sites in Chrome, classified with a deep learning model, succeeded on every tested GPU, though accuracy varied by card. Keystroke timing inference recovered intervals between keys typed by volunteers on a Facebook login page, with AMD cards generally less exposed than the other GPUs tested.

Disabling DVFS was also examined. It costs performance and energy efficiency, and it did not remove the problem: new signals appeared at a different data rate that still followed activity, and website fingerprinting became even more accurate. Possible countermeasures include better electromagnetic shielding, strong jamming noise, lower DVFS sensitivity, and random background workloads, each with drawbacks. The main takeaway is that DVFS itself leaks activity information, and eliminating that leakage is challenging.

talks.title: SoK: Demystifying Binary Lifters Through the Lens of Downstream Applications
talks.teaser: An empirical study benchmarks popular binary lifters on pointer analysis, similarity, decompilation, and sanitization tasks.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames binary lifters as producers of intermediate representation whose usefulness must be judged by what later analyses can do with that IR, not by informal notions of expressiveness alone. Because lifted IR can look very different from compiler-generated LLVM depending on the lifter, the work evaluates expressiveness empirically through four downstream applications: pointer analysis with SVF, discriminability analysis via neural code comprehension-style vectorization, decompilation through a RetDec-based pipeline, and AddressSanitizer-style checking on lifted code.

Four widely used lifters are compared in a cross-compiler, cross-platform setting, with compiler IR treated as an upper bound and MaxSM configured without imposed optimizations for one baseline. The study separates emulation-style IR, which expands each machine instruction into many low-level operations without reliable variables or prototypes, from higher-level IR that summarizes behavior more readably but sacrifices precise executability. Pointer analysis largely fails across lifters because accurate variables and types from stripped binaries remain hard; RetDec can improve when debug information or predicted debug metadata is available. For similarity tasks, higher-level lifted IR tends to beat emulation IR and benefits from optimization. Decompilation quality is measured via structural metrics such as goto counts and average line length, where compiled IR usually wins though RetDec comes close. Functionality tests show emulation lifters often pass more cases while higher-level lifters decompile with lower success rates. AddressSanitizer experiments find MaxSM surprisingly competitive despite missing stack variables.

Practitioners should treat LLVM optimization as essential for concise, discriminable lifted IR, assume type and variable recovery will bottleneck pointer analyses unless augmented by reverse-engineering research, and choose lifters by whether they need runnable emulation IR or readable high-level IR for a given pipeline.

talks.title: Heapster: Analyzing the Security of Dynamic Allocators for Monolithic Firmware Images
talks.teaser: Locates heap allocators in raw monolithic IoT firmware binaries and tests them for exploitable heap states.
talks.summary:
Dynamic allocators such as malloc and free manage heap memory and often serve as building blocks in exploit chains, but most prior work covers desktop-style libraries. This talk turns to monolithic firmware images, where the operating system, libraries and application share one binary, usually without symbols, which is common in IoT devices. The research asks whether such firmware uses a dynamic allocator at all, and whether that allocator resists known heap attacks.

The Heapster pipeline recovers functions from a raw Cortex-M image and identifies basic memory routines such as memcpy by running candidates on known inputs. A static taint analysis then links pointer sources to those routines, and candidate allocators are kept when they return addresses inside the heap region that differ between calls. Each candidate pair is checked for last-in, first-out reuse. Across 799 images, 340 used a dynamic allocator, spanning about 10 families and 32 variants. For security testing, hundreds of heap action sequences were generated and symbolic execution was used to inject exploitation primitives into 32 representative allocators. All of them were vulnerable to at least one primitive: heap overflows triggered overlapping chunks 100 percent of the time, while double free did so in less than 75 percent of images.

A real STM32 board running an application with an unidentified allocator confirmed the findings, as board logs showed chunks allocated outside the heap or overlapping. The takeaways are that firmware allocators are varied and sometimes unusual, that every tested one could reach a vulnerable heap state, and that the framework is open source. Asked about bias, the speaker agreed the last-in, first-out assumption could favour some allocators, though it follows from the chosen research scope.

talks.title: Investigating Influencer VPN Ads on YouTube
talks.teaser: Investigates YouTube creators' VPN sponsorships, measuring their reach and the security claims they make to viewers.
talks.summary:
The speakers examine a form of sponsorship in which YouTube creators place VPN advertisements inside their own videos. They open with a gaming video whose sponsor segment presents the product as educational, and they explain why this matters: earlier usable security work on how people understand tools such as secure messengers now extends to VPNs.

To measure the phenomenon, the team drew a random sample covering about 1.4 percent of YouTube's videos by the end of 2020, searched English subtitles for VPN mentions, and watched about 1,700 candidates by hand. That yielded 243 VPN ads with roughly 63 million views, which scales to an estimated 16,000 videos across the platform. Each ad was coded by adversary, action and asset. The ISP was usually described as surveilling browsing activity, the government as watching everything, and hackers as stealing passwords and card details. Overclaims such as complete anonymity and military-grade encryption appeared often. Surfshark ads stressed credentials, while Virtual Shield ads stressed government threats, reflecting the content of their host channels.

Affiliate links appeared in nearly every case, and the few accurate ads came mostly from tech channels. The speakers recommend that VPN companies set and enforce clear guidelines that acknowledge limits, that creators understand products before promoting them, and that government agencies pursue misleading endorsements. They also call for research on how these ads shape viewers' understanding of privacy and security.

talks.title: "They're not that hard to mitigate"—What Cryptographic Library Developers Think About Timing Attacks
talks.teaser: Surveys cryptographic library developers on timing attack mitigations, the checking tools they know, and why they rarely use them.
talks.summary:
The talk asks why timing attacks, first described in 1996, are still found in cryptographic code even though constant-time coding practices and checking tools exist. The speaker team surveyed developers of open-source cryptographic libraries. They invited more than 200 developers from 36 libraries and received 44 valid responses from 27 libraries. Every respondent knew about timing attacks, though opinions on how pressing they are varied.

The survey covered threat models, protections and testing. 23 libraries included timing attacks in their threat model, with 20 covering remote attacks and 16 covering local ones. Thirteen libraries claimed full protection, ten claimed partial protection, and three claimed none. The most common defence was constant-time coding practice, used by 21 libraries, followed by algorithm choices, blinding, secret slicing and specialised assembly. Random delays were described as masking the signal rather than removing it. Of the 44 respondents, 33 had heard of at least one checking tool, but only 19 had tried one, most often citing lack of time. Respondents were most willing to use dynamic instrumentation tools, less willing to use statistical runtime tests, and least willing to use formal analysis, which they saw as too much effort.

The speakers closed with recommendations for four groups. Tool builders should make their tools installable, documented and current, with worked examples. Library developers should run checks automatically in continuous integration and fix leaks fully. Secrets should be marked in code so that users and compilers can respect them, and standardisation bodies could require constant-time reference implementations.

talks.title: Why Crypto-detectors Fail: A Systematic Evaluation of Cryptographic Misuse Detection Techniques
talks.teaser: Shows how mutated crypto misuse cases exposed 19 unknown flaws in nine detectors, and why trivial code still evades them.
talks.summary:
Cryptographic API misuse detectors are widely used to flag insecure cryptography, but benchmark results can be misleading. The talk gives examples: one benchmark accepted DES in ECB mode as secure until an independent developer reported it, and Java silently falls back to ECB when only AES is specified. The speaker models three developer types: a benign developer who misuses APIs by accident, a developer whose fix only removes the warning, and an evasive developer who deliberately hides misuse.

The researchers built a taxonomy of 105 misuse cases from about 20 years of academic and industry sources, then wrote usage-based mutation operators and placed the mutants in open-source applications at different code locations. Running nine detectors on these mutated applications revealed 19 previously unknown flaws, grouped into five flaw classes plus one about incorrect input analysis. Some detectors ignored classes whose names contained "android", and others did not scan every DEX file. Introducing a variable or extracting a method evaded seven of nine detectors, and statically computable conditions were left unanalysed by five.

The main takeaway is that detectors are often built around analysis techniques rather than security outcomes, and vendors disagree on what they promise, such as whether a flaw must appear in real code to be in scope. The speaker argues for security-focused design, a shared understanding of detector guarantees, and combining static and dynamic analysis, since dynamic analysis has reachability limits.

talks.title: DEPCOMM: Graph Summarization on System Audit Logs for Attack Investigation
talks.teaser: Shows how dependency graphs from system audit logs get condensed into process communities and ranked attack paths.
talks.summary:
Causality analysis of system audit logs can produce dependency graphs so large that analysts struggle to review them during an attack investigation. This talk presents DEPCOMM, a method that condenses such a graph. It groups processes that work closely together, along with the resources they touch, into process-centric communities, and it compresses repetitive edges that come from routine activity such as backups and file updates.

To find the communities, the method runs random walks from each process node and learns behavior representations from those walks using skip-gram, a technique borrowed from word embeddings. A soft fuzzy clustering step lets a process belong to several communities. Information flows between communities are scored on four weighted features, and the top-ranked paths serve as each community's summary. The evaluation covered six attacks in a test environment and eight attacks from a second dataset, with data sets ranging from about 15 million to about 100 million events. On average the graphs split into 18.4 communities, 70.7 times smaller than the originals, with 15.7 nodes per community.

Manual inspection showed that the top two paths were enough to represent the main system activity and attack behavior, so analysts would need to examine only 12.7 percent of extracted paths. Against nine community detection algorithms, the method's F1 score averaged 2.29 times higher, and it beat DeepWalk by 1.65 times. Node and edge counts fell by 38.4 and 44.7 percent on average. Ground truth was built through keyword searches and manual labeling, then checked by outside researchers. The speaker also described pairing the communities with rule-based detection to explain which parts of a graph relate to an attack.

talks.title: SIRAJ: A Unified Framework for Aggregation of Malicious Entity Detectors
talks.teaser: Presents a self-supervised method that aggregates conflicting malicious-entity detector reports into high-quality ground truth labels.
talks.summary:
Security services such as URL scanners, antivirus engines and IP blocklists often disagree on whether an entity is malicious. Common fixes use a fixed vote threshold, which trades precision against coverage and assumes the sources are independent. Scanners specialise by threat type, flip verdicts over time, are unreliable when new, and often correlate, while supervised learning needs costly labels that must be refreshed as threats change.

The proposed framework, SIRAJ, is self-supervised and learns from historical reports without labels. Three pretext tasks drive it: recovering masked or corrupted scanner entries to capture dependencies between scanners; predicting future verdicts from current ones to handle flipping and early unreliability; and a regulariser that aligns representations of original and corrupted views and of current and future views. The resulting encoder yields embeddings that carry over across threat types and time.

Evaluation covers phishing URLs, malware URLs, malware files and IP blacklist data, using reports aged from six hours to one week. A semi-supervised variant needs only about 100 labels, while an unsupervised variant clusters embeddings and treats small clusters as malicious. The method keeps a high, steady F1 score across report ages and label budgets, whereas baselines fall off with early reports and small training sets. The main takeaway is that learned aggregation of multiple feeds can produce better ground truth earlier, without relying on hand-picked thresholds.

talks.title: SoK: Authentication in Augmented and Virtual Reality
talks.teaser: Maps authentication in AR and VR apps and academic research against 20 criteria covering usability, security and deployability.
talks.summary:
AR and VR headsets are used in sensitive settings such as medicine and the military, and are expected to become personal devices, so they need authentication that works well. Passwords are the usual default, but entering them on a floating virtual keyboard is slow, awkward and open to shoulder surfing. The talk presents a systematization of knowledge that pairs a survey of users and developers with an evaluation of real apps and prior research.

The survey drew 139 user and 49 developer responses, producing 20 criteria in four groups: deployability, usability, accessibility and security. Examining 178 apps on the HoloLens 2 and HTC Vive, the researchers found seven authentication methods, and knowledge-based options such as passwords, PINs and paired accounts dominated. Token-based QR codes and short codes improved usability but needed a second device. Iris scanning and automatic paired accounts looked most promising, though iris scanning is not on every device and automatic paired accounts could let a manufacturer see a user's accounts.

Across 38 papers describing 43 proposed mechanisms, knowledge-based schemes were again most common, and obfuscated or gaze-based PIN entry helped resist shoulder surfing. Physical biometrics required almost no effort, behavioral ones needed active movement, and three multi-factor schemes offered the strongest security. The closing message calls for deployable methods, more accurate and privacy-aware biometrics, wider federated login and better password manager support in the meantime.

talks.title: A Logic and an Interactive Prover for the Computational Post-Quantum Security of Protocols
talks.teaser: Shows why classical proofs fail against quantum attackers and extends an interactive prover to verify post-quantum protocols.
talks.summary:
Charlie presents work on proving that cryptographic protocols stay secure once quantum computers exist. Classical protocol proofs assume a probabilistic attacker running on a Turing machine, and the standard reduction technique rewinds that attacker by replaying it with a fixed source of randomness. The talk explains that the no-cloning theorem makes this replay impossible for a quantum attacker, so many pen-and-paper proofs may be wrong in the quantum setting. The speaker also notes that the Squirrel prover, an interactive theorem prover for a high-level protocol logic with computational guarantees, had a soundness argument that covered only one-shot attackers sharing randomness.

To fix this, the team proved a variant of the soundness result that works for interactive black-box attackers. That change required three syntactic restrictions on the logic, which were enough to make the prover sound in the post-quantum setting. They then used the extended prover to check several recently proposed key exchanges built from key encapsulation mechanisms. Some case studies rely on Diffie-Hellman assumptions and were shown not to be post-quantum secure.

The main takeaway is a post-quantum sound interactive prover and the first computer-verified proofs of some post-quantum key exchanges. Future directions include scaling to larger protocols and studying more complex properties such as compromise security. The speaker said full automation of such proofs is unlikely, though parts of the process can be simplified.

talks.title: Noise: A Library of Verified High-Performance Secure Channel Protocol Implementations
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Noise: A Library of Verified High-Performance Secure Channel Protocol Implementations.
talks.summary:
## Overview
Nostar is a verified implementation framework for the Noise protocol family, a collection of approximately 59 protocols (expandable with new features) used for key exchange and contract establishment. Noise protocols are already deployed in real-world applications like WhatsApp and WireGuard VPN. The core problem Nostar addresses is that while many Noise implementations exist across programming languages, none are formally verified, leaving them vulnerable to bugs commonly discovered in protocol implementations (such as TLS and Signal).

## Technical Architecture
Nostar comprises three integrated components:

1. **Protocol Compiler**: Transforms Noise protocol patterns into specialized, verified C implementations
2. **Verified Library Stack**: Provides a high-level defensive API exposing memory-safe, type-safe, and functionally correct code
3. **Formal Security Analysis**: Uses symbolic methods to prove authentication and confidentiality guarantees

The verification toolchain builds on F* (a theorem prover with dependent types and program verification) and Low* (an effectful subset for writing verified C-like code), with compilation to C via the Karamel framework. This approach has been successfully applied in the Everest project for providing verified HTTPS components.

## Key Innovation: Partial Evaluation
The central technical contribution is using partial evaluation to transform a generic interpreter-based specification into specialized compiled code. Rather than writing separate implementations for each protocol, the speaker describes a technique where:
- A single High* interpreter processes protocol token lists
- Low* rewrites this interpreter with preconditions, postconditions, and functional correctness properties linked to the high-level spec
- At compile-time, F* specializes the code by inlining the interpreter, evaluating matches, and eliminating recursive calls

F*'s dependent type system enables extremely precise control flow with no runtime token processing or list manipulation. The speaker compares this to C++ template metaprogramming applied at the protocol definition level, using partial reduction techniques previously employed in cryptographic primitives like Hacl* and vectorization code.

## API Design and Security Properties
The high-level API (accounting for over 75% of generated code) implements:
- Verified state machines abstracting handshake and transport phases
- Misuse-resistant patterns that prevent sending data before security guarantees are established
- Dynamic checks and verified key management utilities for validation, loading, and secure storage

Security analysis is formalized in Dollar* (a photosymbolic analysis framework), with one generic symbolic proof operating at the interpreter specification level. This enables analysis of all 59 protocols simultaneously, in contrast to tools like ProVerif that typically require per-protocol proofs.

## Implementation Results
The framework generated code for all 59 Noise patterns with 8 cipher suite variants each, totaling 472 instantiations. Benchmarks show competitive performance against existing implementations, with execution speed superior to all tested alternatives except WireGuard (which is hand-optimized for a single pattern).

## Limitations and Q&A Clarifications
Formal proofs cover functional correctness and some constant-time properties (by avoiding operations like division), but do not extend to C compiler behavior or memory-zeroing guarantees (which are implemented manually). Adding new protocols at the pattern layer is straightforward, but extending the API or updating security proofs requires more substantial work due to subtle symbolic analysis constraints.

talks.title: Transcending TRANSCEND: Revisiting Malware Classification in the Presence of Concept Drift
talks.teaser: Revisits the TRANSCEND malware classifier and adds conformal evaluators that reject unreliable predictions as data drifts.
talks.summary:
Malware classifiers struggle when attackers react to a deployed detector and the data distribution shifts over time, a problem usually grouped under concept drift. The talk revisits TRANSCEND, a 2017 approach that adds a conformal evaluator and a calibration step so a classifier can reject predictions it should not trust. The speaker explains how non-conformity measures produce per-class p-values, and how the same tools can evaluate a classifier's predictions instead of predicting labels.

The work contributes a theoretical link between conformal evaluation and conformal prediction, and proposes evaluators that are both sound and scalable. Three variants are compared: a transductive evaluator that is statistically sound but infeasible on large datasets, an approximate batched version that is faster but relies on an unsound assumption, and an inductive evaluator that trains one classifier and calibrates on a held-out set. A cross-conformal ensemble recovers statistical support from the full training data while remaining easy to parallelise. Per-class thresholds are tuned for a target rejection rate and F1 score.

Experiments cover Android malware over a five-year span with a linear SVM, a Windows dataset with gradient-boosted trees, and PDF malware using a drift-robust feature space. On Android, the inductive evaluator performed similarly to the approximate transductive one at a fraction of the compute, about 11 CPU hours versus 46. Relying on the classifier's built-in probabilities degraded as drift grew, while conformal evaluation kept more statistical support. The practical takeaway is that rejecting uncertain predictions under drift is feasible, and the evaluator can be decoupled from rejection to guide uncertainty sampling.

talks.title: Asleep at the Keyboard? Assessing the Security of GitHub Copilot's Code Contributions
talks.teaser: Measures how often GitHub Copilot's suggested code contains security vulnerabilities across weakness types, languages and prompts.
talks.summary:
Hammond Pierce of NYU presents an assessment of GitHub Copilot's code suggestions from a security standpoint. Functional benchmarks reward code that works but say nothing about whether it is safe, so the study asked how often Copilot proposes vulnerable code. The team built 89 scenarios covering 18 of the MITRE top 25 weakness types, written in Python and C, plus Verilog scenarios for hardware weaknesses. Most results were checked with CodeQL, while Verilog output was marked manually because no suitable scanner exists for it.

Across about 1,689 generated programs, roughly 40 percent contained security vulnerabilities. The scenarios were deliberately chosen to be security-relevant, so this is not a rate for all Copilot output. C results were slightly worse than Python. Examples included a buffer overflow when converting floats to strings, a use-after-free, and a command injection built from a URL parameter. For password hashing, Copilot often chose MD5, likely reflecting outdated patterns in its training data. Small prompt edits mostly changed little, but including a vulnerable SQL function pushed the output toward SQL injection. Verilog output was often poor, with C syntax leaking into hardware files.

The takeaway is that Copilot should be treated as an assistant whose output needs automated scanning and peer review. Some problems, such as banning specific functions, can be filtered, but bugs like use-after-free require reasoning about execution order that the model does not perform. The snippets were only tens of lines long, so the effect on large codebases remains untested.

talks.title: Are We There Yet? Timing and Floating-Point Attacks on Differential Privacy Systems
talks.teaser: Shows how floating-point gaps and sampler timing leaks break differential privacy guarantees in real libraries.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how differential privacy systems can leak information in practice, even when the theory behind them holds. The presenters tested two open-source libraries, one of them Google's differential privacy library, using two attack families: floating-point attacks on continuous Gaussian noise samplers and timing attacks on discrete distribution samplers.

For continuous Gaussian samplers, the speaker explains that the uneven spacing of floating-point numbers makes some outputs impossible for a given sampling function. An output that the function could never produce reveals which neighbouring dataset was used. The team built a feasibility check that tests candidate noise values against three commonly used Gaussian implementations. Against a counting query protected by Gaussian noise, the attack reached about 90 percent success, well above the 50 percent random baseline. The speaker says the same idea applies to training deep networks with DP-SGD, where it could reveal whether a particular record was in the training data.

For discrete samplers built on geometric draws, the number of retries grows with the noise magnitude, so runtime leaks the noise size. Measured runtimes showed a clear positive linear relationship with noise magnitude, and trials reached up to 99 percent success for a relatively large epsilon. Batch sampling makes the timing channel harder to exploit. For mitigations, the speaker suggests dropping the second value from paired Gaussian generators or aggregating several samples, switching to discrete distributions with constant-time implementations, and buffering samples offline. The takeaway is that both attack classes can invalidate the privacy guarantees of the systems tested.

talks.title: De-Identification's Impact on Minority Representation and Privacy Preservation in the US Census
talks.teaser: Compares swapping and differential privacy in the US Census, measuring accuracy for minority groups and re-identification risk.
talks.summary:
This talk examines how the decennial U.S. Census balances data accuracy against privacy when it releases demographic tables. Those tables feed redistricting and funding decisions, so errors matter, and the data must also resist re-identification. The presenters compare swapping, the method used in 2010, with differential privacy, which the Census Bureau adopted for 2020. Swapping exchanges attribute values between similar records, while differential privacy adds calibrated noise controlled by an epsilon parameter.

Because the Bureau's swapping implementation and its differentially private algorithm were not available to them, the researchers combined a theoretical analysis with experiments on synthetic census-like data. They found that swapping adds more error for subpopulations that differ from their surrounding state, and that diverse counties saw markedly worse accuracy under swapping, while low-diversity counties did not. In a linkage attack on a diverse and a non-diverse county, individuals became identifiable at low swap rates, with privacy becoming acceptable only around swap rates of roughly 0.2 and 0.05 respectively. Minority groups made up most of the population at risk, and differential privacy's error decreased predictably across diversity levels.

The takeaway is that, for minority groups, swapping could not match differential privacy on accuracy and privacy at the same time. The closing discussion touched on how epsilon is chosen in practice, with the Bureau raising it after community feedback on sample data, and on how little guidance exists for setting it.

talks.title: Locally Differentially Private Sparse Vector Aggregation
talks.teaser: Covers locally differentially private schemes that sum k-sparse vectors with improved error and compact encodings.
talks.summary:
Clients often report high-dimensional vectors that are sparse—such as a few movie ratings among thousands of titles or masked gradients in federated learning—while a server must estimate the coordinate-wise sum without learning individual inputs. Standard private mechanisms like adding Gaussian noise to every coordinate erase sparsity and inflate communication, and prior dense or central sparse releases do not match the aggregation setting cleanly.

The presentation develops encodings from a one-hot sparse case through randomized response and a strawman scheme that treats each nonzero entry as a separate virtual client, then a bucket-and-hash design with Laplace noise that cuts error by about a factor of √k. A central idea is that hash collisions can shrink L1 sensitivity between neighboring inputs, allowing less noise on buckets without weakening privacy guarantees under a unified local LDP formulation that subsumes event-level and user-level variants.

Reported theory matches prior communication while improving error optimality, including new user-level lower bounds skipped in the live walkthrough. On synthetic data with 10⁵ clients, the method tracks best among baselines; at sparsity 64 it cuts L∞ error roughly sevenfold with about 68 bytes per client, and movie-rating experiments show multi-fold error drops at the lowest communication cost. Practitioners gain a primitive suitable for frequency estimation, hypothesis tests, and clustering pipelines at companies collecting browser or ad telemetry under strict local privacy.

talks.title: Statistical Quantification of Differential Privacy: A Local Approach
talks.teaser: Estimates differential privacy lower bounds for black-box algorithms via kernel density estimates, using fewer samples.
talks.summary:
Differential privacy quantifies how much an algorithm can reveal about any single individual through one parameter, epsilon. When an algorithm is a black box, because its code is unavailable or too complicated to audit, its privacy level cannot be read off from a proof, so its outputs must be tested instead. The usual approach draws samples from the algorithm run on two neighbouring databases, estimates probabilities for a chosen set of outcomes, and reports the largest resulting loss as a lower bound. Choosing suitable outcome sets is difficult, and the sampling cost is high.

The approach presented skips the choice of outcome events. It estimates the probability densities of the two output distributions with kernel density estimators, which are smoothed histograms available in common Python libraries, and then maximises the resulting real-valued privacy loss directly. In the reported comparisons, this needed about 2.3 to 3 percent of the sample sizes used by earlier methods while still giving fairly tight lower bounds, and it runs on an ordinary desktop. The authors also derive theoretical guarantees that the estimated bounds converge at a stated rate, which earlier work often could not prove.

In the question session, one point was that if the algorithm is known to come from a parametric family, the estimate could likely converge faster, possibly at a square-root-of-n rate. Another was that a covert channel hidden in the last digits of an output may not be seen by a density estimator, so a bound from this method does not confirm privacy. The takeaway is that a simpler estimation strategy can outperform more elaborate ones when auditing black-box mechanisms.

talks.title: TASHAROK—Using Mechanism Design for Enhancing Security Resource Allocation in Interdependent Systems
talks.teaser: Tax-based mechanisms steer behaviorally biased defenders toward better security investment across interdependent networks.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses how defenders should spend limited security budgets when attacks can spread across interdependent systems. The speaker models the system as a directed acyclic graph of assets, where several defenders each protect a subset of nodes and can jointly invest in edges to lower the chance that an attack propagates. Defenders are treated as behaviorally biased, misperceiving risk in line with prospect theory rather than acting as fully rational optimizers.

The speaker reports that this misperception leads to suboptimal investment and a much higher expected loss, with a 2x increase in one example. Selfish investment by each defender makes the problem worse, so the work adapts two tax-based mechanisms, externality and VCG, that charge each defender according to how its investments affect others. The authors prove that taxes decrease as behavioral bias grows, and that there is no guarantee of budget balance in this game. Evaluation on four attack graphs drawn from real failure scenarios, including distributed energy resources, SCADA control, e-commerce and voice over IP, showed lower social cost than selfish investment and several baseline approaches.

In the question session, the speaker explained that initial attack probabilities were estimated from CVE data, and that cyber insurance is a possible extension rather than part of the current model. The takeaway is that a central authority can use incentive-based taxes to steer behavioral defenders toward socially better security spending, while rare, high-impact events remain an open extension.

talks.title: Cats vs. Spectre: An Axiomatic Approach to Modeling Speculative Execution Attacks
talks.teaser: Models Spectre-style speculative execution with axioms borrowed from weak memory consistency, then checks programs against them.
talks.summary:
Spectre vulnerabilities, disclosed in 2018, exploit microarchitectural optimizations, so programmers need precise formal guarantees about what a processor may do. Operational semantics model microarchitectural state explicitly, which makes them hard to extend when a new attack appears. The talk proposes an axiomatic style instead, drawing on the programming languages community's decades of work on weak memory consistency. In that approach, every possible behavior is generated first and then filtered by a set of axioms.

The recipe has three steps: choose which instructions execute, define the data flow between them (data, control and read-from relations), and decide with axioms whether the microarchitecture allows the resulting behavior. A bounds-checked array access with an attacker-controlled index illustrates this. A branch misprediction can transiently execute an out-of-bounds load that architectural semantics would forbid. For store-to-load forwarding, relaxing program order for write-read pairs permits a speculative reordering, and a fence restores the ordering. A tool built on these semantics was compared with two existing tools across four vulnerability families, and the axiomatic model could express behaviors from all four. The analysis works on assembly using bounded model checking, which requires unrolling loops, and scalability remains limited.

The main takeaway is that axiomatic models are modular and easy to adapt to new speculation behaviors. They can state hardware and software contracts that specify guarantees without encoding every implementation detail.

talks.title: ProVerif with Lemmas, Induction, Fast Subsumption, and Much More
talks.teaser: Explains new lemma, axiom and subsumption improvements that make the ProVerif protocol verifier faster and more precise.
talks.summary:
Designing a security protocol is hard, and automated checking can catch logical flaws before deployment. This talk focuses on ProVerif, a long-standing verifier that works in the symbolic model, where the attacker controls the network but cannot break cryptography. Its known weak points are false attacks, which arise when the protocol is translated into logical clauses, and non-termination, which mostly comes from saturating those clauses on stateful protocols.

The authors add lemmas, axioms and restrictions to the tool. Lemmas are proved first and then reused when proving later queries, while axioms are assumed true and become the user's responsibility, restoring precision lost in translation. They also add natural numbers with addition and subtraction for counters, and temporal queries to cut false attacks. For speed, subsumption checks now use feature-vector indexing, filtering candidate clauses with cheap measures such as symbol counts and term depth before the costly matching step. Subsumption had consumed about 80 percent of runtime. The noise framework case dropped from a week to 20 minutes, and another protocol sped up about 900 times. Across literature and unpublished files, 40 to 50 queries that previously failed or did not terminate now gave answers.

Open limits include missing primitives such as xor under abelian groups, and memory growth: a TLS with encrypted client hello case exhausted 200 to 300 gigabytes. Usability is also a target, since users must choose which features to activate. Practitioners modelling stateful protocols can use these features to make hard cases tractable.

talks.title: Blacksmith: Compromising Target Row Refresh by Rowhammering in the Frequency Domain
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Blacksmith: Compromising Target Row Refresh by Rowhammering in the Frequency Domain.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Patrick presents Blacksmith, a scalable Rowhammer testing tool and fuzzer operating in the frequency domain. As DRAM scaling has significantly reduced the activation threshold required to trigger bit flips—dropping from roughly 139,000 activations in DDR3 (2012) to around 10,000 activations in newer DDR4 devices (mid-2019)—DRAM manufacturers like Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron deployed in-DRAM mitigations called Target Row Refresh (TRR). TRR mechanisms attempt to estimate frequently hammered rows and inject preventive refreshes before data loss occurs. However, Blacksmith demonstrates that existing TRR mitigations across major DDR4 and LPDDR4X devices are fundamentally flawed.

### Key Topics
- **Target Row Refresh (TRR) Limitations**: TRR mitigations rely on frequent item count algorithms implemented under strict silicon area and timing constraints, often without formal security analysis. They typically comprise a sampler (which tracks activation frequencies) and an inhibitor (which issues preventive refreshes).
- **Limitations of Uniform Hammering**: Prior attacks primarily used uniform n-sided patterns where all aggressors were accessed at identical frequencies, allowing sampler heuristics to track them easily.
- **Frequency-Domain Rowhammering**: By systematically exploring non-uniform access patterns, the authors mapped critical attack parameters into frequency-domain properties: phase (timing/offset relative to refresh commands), amplitude (hammering intensity or peak access count), and frequency (hammering across multiple refresh intervals).
- **Blacksmith Fuzzer**: A generic, extensible fuzzing framework that crafts complex patterns combining varied frequencies, phases, and amplitudes to systematically trigger bit flips.

### Technical Details
- **Timing Window Constraints**: DRAM relies on JEDEC standard DDR timing, requiring cell retention for at least 64 ms with periodic refresh commands sent approximately every 7.8 µs on DDR4. In an interval between consecutive refreshes, an attacker can issue roughly 166 activations, summing to around 1.3 million activations across a full 64 ms refresh window.
- **Parametric Observations**:
  - *Phase/Timing*: Testing on Samsung DIMM A10 showed bit flips only occurred when aggressor pairs were hammered immediately before a refresh command, suggesting sampler inactivity prior to refresh.
  - *Amplitude/Intensity*: Increasing hammering intensity boosted bit flips only up to a sweet spot; exceeding it caused flips to drop because the sampler detected the aggressor and triggered TRR.
  - *Frequency/Pattern Length*: Extending patterns over multiple refresh intervals (e.g., hammering heavily only every second interval) was necessary to induce flips on specific hardware, such as SK Hynix DIMM B2.
- **Evaluation Results**: Evaluated against 40 test devices from Samsung, SK Hynix, and Micron, Blacksmith triggered bit flips on 100% (40/40) of the devices, outperforming Trespass (which triggered flips on 15/40). On a Samsung device (A17), Blacksmith produced roughly 138,000 bit flips. Additionally, all tested LPDDR4X devices were vulnerable.
- **Exploitation**: Using established attack patterns, page table entry (PTE) exploits succeeded on 30 of 40 devices, yielding exploitable bit flips within three seconds to two hours and eight minutes.
- **Generalization**: When approached by an unstudied vendor with an unanalyzed proprietary DDR4 device, Blacksmith discovered bit flips in less than four hours.

### Takeaways
Current proprietary, obscure TRR implementations deployed by DRAM manufacturers fail to prevent Rowhammer bit flips under non-uniform, frequency-domain access patterns. The speaker concludes that hardware vendors must transition away from ad-hoc mitigations toward principled defenses with provable security guarantees, citing research such as ProTRR.

talks.title: SoK: Practical Foundations for Software Spectre Defenses
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding SoK: Practical Foundations for Software Spectre Defenses.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Sanjay presents a systematization of knowledge regarding software-based defenses against Spectre attacks. Spectre fundamentally breaks standard processor execution assumptions by exploiting speculative execution mechanisms—such as branch predictors, return target predictors, indirect jump predictors, and memory disambiguation/data flow prediction. Because early mitigation efforts relied on ad hoc, reactive patches that failed to cover slightly altered attack patterns or cross-process mistraining, the speaker advocates for formal methods, principled attacker models, and domain-appropriate abstractions to systematically eliminate speculative leaks.

### Key Topics
- **Mechanisms of Spectre**: Out-of-order execution, branch misprediction bypassing memory bounds checks, indirect jump prediction, function return prediction, and data-flow store-to-load forwarding.
- **Limitations of Early Defenses**: Flaws in ad hoc solutions such as pattern matching in compilers (e.g., Microsoft's QSpecter flag), recurring manual kernel patches (Linux eBPF), and browser mitigations (Google Chrome's strict site isolation undermined by Spook.js).
- **Attacker Modeling and Abstraction Sweet Spots**: Why models that are too narrow (e.g., step-counter leakage models or influence-only models like 007) miss critical attacks like port contention or cross-process training, whereas overly expressive models (Constantine, Foundations, Inspector) introduce excessive false positives.
- **Domain-Specific Approaches**: Translating sequential security definitions into speculative semantics for cryptographic code (constant-time models) and sandboxed environments (e.g., WebAssembly, Linux eBPF).
- **Multi-Layer Verification and Compilation**: Establishing secure translation from high-level languages (C, Rust, Haskell) down through intermediate representations to structured assembly and machine code.

### Technical Details
The speaker highlights two primary application domains where formal software defenses have shown success:
1. **Cryptographic Software**: Building on sequential constant-time security (where execution traces and memory access patterns do not depend on secret data), tools like those in High-Assurance Cryptography and Hunting the Haunter extend constant-time semantics to speculative execution paths. Because cryptographic code tends to feature regular control flow and structured data, tracking speculative misprediction paths is mathematically tractable.
2. **Sandboxed Systems**: In environments like Linux eBPF and browser WebAssembly/JavaScript, sandboxes treat any out-of-bounds read as an immediate leak. Tools like FaCT/FEniCS-style systems, FaSym, or Swivel leverage sandbox host control to rewrite code and eliminate dangerous speculative paths.

More generalized tools such as Spectector and FaST adopt relative non-interference: programs running speculatively must not leak any more information than they would under normal sequential execution. To restore broader properties destroyed by Spectre (memory safety, type safety, and control flow integrity), research spans several abstraction layers:
- **Binary/Assembly Level**: Verified by tools such as Binsec and Spectector.
- **Structured Assembly & IR**: Tools like Jasmin, Blade, and FaCT work at structured assembly or LLVM IR, inserting barriers or transformations.
- **Sandboxed IR / High-Level Languages**: Swivel validates WebAssembly transformations. Blade establishes formal semantics between LLVM IR and assembly to prove that the resulting machine code remains Spectre-free, while hardware-software contracts bridge the gap between software semantics and hardware guarantees.

### Takeaways
To achieve sound, long-term software defenses against speculative execution vulnerabilities, security must be rebuilt from the ground up using formal methods rather than reactive patching. Developers and security architects must select attacker models tailored to their domain (e.g., constant-time for crypto, strict isolation for sandboxing) to avoid false positives and missed attacks. The ultimate goal is end-to-end, compiler-verified preservation of sequential security properties from high-level source languages down to hardware.

talks.title: Quantifying Blockchain Extractable Value: How dark is the forest?
talks.teaser: Measures blockchain extractable value on Ethereum and introduces a copycat transaction replay attack.
talks.summary:
The talk examines blockchain extractable value (BEV), the profit traders and miners capture on decentralized finance platforms by reordering, copying or inserting transactions. Unlike traditional markets, where regulators police manipulation, these practices are largely unregulated. The speaker explains that a miner can order transactions freely, giving it a large edge over other players.

Over a 32-month window on Ethereum, the team measured about 540 million USD in extracted profit, described as a lower bound since only three activity types were captured. The data covered roughly 11,000 extracting addresses, 50,000 cryptocurrencies and 60,000 markets, with smaller markets contributing a surprising share. Sandwich attacks and arbitrage profits rose from a few hundred or a thousand dollars to around 100 million, while liquidations spiked during market crashes, with about 90 million in liquidation events. The speaker then introduced transaction replay, a copycat attack that copies a victim's transaction, swaps in its own sender address and replaces the victim's address in the input data. Across 188,000 profitable transactions, roughly 0.02 percent of the total, it could have extracted about 35 million USD, processing each transaction in about 0.2 seconds on average.

The speaker also linked extraction to consensus risk: an analysis suggests a miner holding 10 percent of hashing power could rationally fork the chain when extraction reaches four times the block reward, and the largest opportunity observed was 874 times the block reward. Such forks would threaten stability and make double-spending easier. The speaker argued that replay attacks cannot generally be prevented, since blockchain data is transparent, and suggested the technique could also serve as a defensive tool by front-running an attacker.

talks.title: SAILFISH: Vetting Smart Contract State-Inconsistency Bugs in Seconds
talks.teaser: Combines static analysis and symbolic execution to detect reentrancy and transaction-order bugs in large Solidity contracts within seconds.
talks.summary:
Decentralized protocols rely on smart contracts that hold enormous value, yet reentrancy and transaction order dependence still drain funds when existing analyzers trade scalability for precision or lean on narrow bug signatures. The presentation motivates a broader notion called state inconsistency: two schedules that invoke the same public functions in different orders can end in different storage states when hazardous read-write pairs on shared variables flip their relative ordering.

The SAILFISH pipeline first runs Explorer static analysis over an intraprocedural control-flow graph to build a storage dependency graph and enumerate hazardous access pairs, then Refiner applies value summary analysis to precondition symbolic execution on program slices so path constraints can confirm or discard reachability. A bank-style withdraw walkthrough illustrates single-function reentrancy, and evaluation on roughly 90,000 open-source Solidity contracts reports about 31 seconds per contract, near-complete recall on a manually checked sample with about 1.5% false positives, and 47 bugs missed by other tools.

Practitioners should view SAILFISH as a fast vetting pass for reentrancy and ether-flow TOD rather than full protocol assurance. Question time notes prototype limits on multi-contract composition without available source, room to sacrifice precision for block-time monitoring, and no coverage yet for sandwich or oracle manipulation attacks.

talks.title: Jigsaw: Efficient and Scalable Path Constraints Fuzzing
talks.teaser: Shows how compiled path-constraint functions and gradient descent speed up branch flipping for concolic fuzzing.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from coverage-guided fuzzing, which stalls when it needs an input that flips a specific branch. The speaker treats branch-flipping speed as the product of two factors: how many attempts a method needs to find a satisfying input, and how many attempts it can make per second. Black-box fuzzers, grey-box fuzzers such as Angora and AFL++, and solver-based white-box tools are placed along that trade-off, with SMT solvers doing local search or bit-blasting to a SAT problem.

The Jigsaw approach compiles the functions that encode path constraints and runs a gradient-descent search over these small, pure functions, which allows linear scaling across cores. Repeated constraint checks are cached in memory to avoid redundant just-in-time compilation, and constraints that perform the same check reuse one compiled function, giving a cache hit rate close to 100 percent on the speaker's dataset. In a test of about 10 million constraints from 14 programs, Jigsaw solved branches faster than several SMT solvers, and its throughput beat Angora in a like-for-like no-code-search comparison. Plugged into a concolic executor, it finished symbolic execution faster than SymCC, and paired with AFL++ in a hybrid setup it performed well on a Google fuzzing benchmark.

The main limitation is solving power. The local search approach solved 94 percent of the constraints that Z3 handled, and it cannot identify unsatisfiable queries, so it runs until timeout. Bitwise operations and division are hard for gradient descent. The speaker stresses that these limits come from the chosen algorithm rather than the design, and the tool is open source. The takeaway is that compiling small constraint functions can make solver-backed fuzzing much faster.

talks.title: [WOOT2021] Sensor Security
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding [WOOT2021] Sensor Security.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this WOOT 2021 keynote presentation, Dr. Sara Rampazzi, an assistant professor at the University of Florida and member of the Florida Institute for Cybersecurity, examines sensor security within the growing ecosystem of the Internet of Everything (IoE). As autonomous cyber-physical systems and artificial intelligence increasingly make critical decisions without direct human supervision, they fundamentally rely on sensors to perceive their surroundings. However, physical sensors and electronic components possess vulnerabilities stemming from physical phenomena that allow external analog signals—such as light, sound, and electromagnetic interference—to alter device behavior and manipulate higher-level software and machine learning models without requiring conventional software compromise or malware.

### Key Topics
- **The Internet of Everything and Autonomous Decisions**: How connected devices, smart homes, healthcare devices, and autonomous vehicles rely on sensors to gather environmental data for automated actions.
- **Sensor Exploitation Mechanisms**: Five core physical factors exploited by attackers: coupling (e.g., resonant frequency EMI), non-linearities in hardware components, intermodulation/frequency generation, predictable periodic behavior/timing, and over-sensing/accidental transduction.
- **Signal Injection via Light (MEMS Microphones)**: Demonstrating how voice-controllable systems (Google Home, Amazon Echo, Facebook Portal, smartphones, tablets) can be commanded using amplitude-modulated lasers.
- **Downstream System Compromise**: Leveraging compromised voice assistants to execute actions across connected IoT ecosystems, such as unlocking smart locks, opening garage doors, and starting cars.
- **Autonomous Vehicle Perception Spoofing**: Attacking LiDAR systems using precise timing and relay attacks to feed fake echo signals into obstacle-detection systems, fooling machine learning perception frameworks (like Baidu Apollo).
- **Hardware-Software Co-Design for Defense**: Moving past isolated software patches and appreciating the physical reality of hardware to engineer resilient defenses.

### Technical Details
- **MEMS Microphone Light Vulnerability**: MEMS microphones contain a movable diaphragm and a stationary back plate forming a parallel-plate capacitor, coupled to an onboard ASIC. Due to photoacoustic and photoelectric effects across the membrane and ASIC, incoming light irradiance induces measurable voltage changes. Modulating the current driving a laser diode with an amplified audio signal creates an amplitude-modulated light beam that translates into clear voltage signals mimicking acoustic voice commands.
- **Attack Range and Penetration**: Using optics and a low-power 5 milliwatt laser pointer setup (achievable with setups as cheap as ~$300), commands were successfully delivered through windows and between buildings up to 110 meters away across more than 17 tested devices.
- **Compounding IoT Flaws**: Light injection attacks succeeded in manipulating downstream infrastructure due to weak default configurations, lack of authentication on multi-user speakers, bypassable voice personalization (via text-to-speech spoofing), routine automations bypassing PIN entry, and lack of brute-force rate limiting on spoken PINs.
- **LiDAR Spoofing and Adversarial Injection**: LiDAR determines distance by timing reflected laser pulses. By exploiting sensor periodicity, synchronized relay attacks injected false reflections, projecting an adversarial horizontal line that tricked the Apollo autonomous driving perception model into detecting nonexistent obstacles, stopping simulated and moving vehicles.

### Takeaways
- Sensors serve as both the primary target and an entry medium to compromise all layers of a system, from silicon to machine learning models.
- Traditional security countermeasures (cryptography, memory safety, software patching) cannot remediate physical over-sensing vulnerabilities once hardware is deployed.
- Mitigations require a layered defense combining hardware modifications (e.g., non-exposed acoustic ports, shielded boards), multi-sensor input validation, and anomaly detection algorithms.
- Security researchers, hardware manufacturers, and software engineers must break down domain silos and treat hardware and software as a single unified system to anticipate emerging attacks.

talks.title: [WOOT2021] The Remote on the Local: Exacerbating Web Attacks Via Service Workers Caches
talks.teaser: Explains how cross-site scripting lets attackers read and poison service worker caches for persistent same-origin compromise.
talks.summary:
Progressive web applications depend on service workers to intercept requests and on the Cache API to store responses for offline use. The presentation argues that because page scripts in the same origin can access that cache—not only the service worker—a single cross-site scripting flaw becomes far more damaging than usual.

An adversary can read leftover authenticated resources, rewrite cached HTML and JavaScript so injections survive across visits, or staple a small reflected XSS into broader compromise such as stealing credentials from a sensitive page that normal DOM-bound XSS could not reach. Tampering extends to cached HTTP metadata, weakening content security policy, framing restrictions, sandboxing, and permission policies, which enables clickjacking, leak-style attacks, and access to camera or microphone where headers once blocked it. A recorded demo on a client-only notes application illustrates password theft after cache corruption. A June 2020 crawl of roughly 150,000 sites and four million pages found low service worker adoption but frequent Cache API use alongside workers, weak content security policy on most such sites, and blind execution of a test payload on about 65 percent of probed targets.

Developers are urged to treat cache contents as security-sensitive. Restricting Cache API access to service worker contexts by default—with an explicit opt-in for legacy patterns—and hardening workers by matching cached response URLs to request URLs are offered as mitigations browser vendors had not yet adopted at the time of the talk.
