talks.title: [WOOT2021] Adventures in Video Conferencing
talks.teaser: Covers exploit-market incentives, WebRTC fuzzing, remote SCTP exploitation, and consent-breaking call logic across major messengers.
talks.summary:
The speaker opens from Project Zero’s mission and notes how quickly video calling spread through browsers and messaging apps, while public guidance emphasized encryption more than memory-safety flaws in protocol parsers. She ties high Zerodium payouts for mobile conferencing targets to a multi-year hunt centered on WebRTC’s signaling, ICE/STUN/TURN, SRTP, and SCTP paths.

She walks through fuzzing evolution—from mutating Chrome’s RTP output, through a lightweight C++ client, to an RTP replay tool with coverage—and parallel FaceTime and WhatsApp binary replay work. Examples include an STL iterator out-of-bounds issue, a FaceTime kernel heap corruption on answer, SCTP integration leaking and misusing heap pointers, and a small error-handling mistake in SCTP that became a widely shipped remote bug. She demonstrates varying exploitability on large Android apps, contrasting fully remote Duo-style behavior with one-click, contacts-only cases, and discusses SCTP data-channel exposure as an attack-surface knob.

Real-world WhatsApp and group FaceTime incidents reframed “pick up the call” assumptions, leading to six logic bugs that transmit audio or video without consent—state confusion in Signal and Messenger, misunderstood offer/answer handling elsewhere, and a Duo race that briefly enables video. She closes on vendor fixes, integrated fuzzing in OSS Fuzz, state-machine hardening, and using attacker economics to prioritize research.

talks.title: [WOOT2021] BadUSB-C: Revisiting BadUSB with Type-C
talks.teaser: Shows how a USB-C cable carrying video and input can give an attacker a live view and control of a phone.
talks.summary:
The talk revisits BadUSB, an attack in which a USB device pretends to be a keyboard, and extends it to USB Type-C connections that also carry video. The speaker explains the limits of the classic version: the attacker gets no feedback during the attack, cannot interact with graphical buttons, and may be caught by intrusion detection or firewalls. The proposed device uses the video channel to watch the victim's screen, adds a mouse emulator for on-screen interaction, and sends data over a separate wireless or cellular module. The prototype is built from a USB-C hub, a Raspberry Pi that reduces the video to frames before transmission, an auxiliary power bank, a capture card, and a keyboard and mouse emulator.

The speaker tests the prototype on a Huawei Android phone with 11 applications run under test accounts. Screenshots from a payment app showed financial status, a WeChat payment code could be used to make transactions, and a messaging app exposed chat history. The speaker also walks through a shared power bank scenario, where a tampered unit lets an attacker gain control of the device of a later user who plugs it in. Limitations include that the device cannot get past fingerprint authentication and needs DisplayPort over USB-C, a feature only some flagship phones support.

For mitigation, the speaker proposes isolated UI rendering, which keeps sensitive content such as passwords off external displays. The vendor issued a CVE entry and later added a requirement for user authorization before an external USB device can receive the video stream. The takeaway is that USB lacks strong device authentication, and that device makers should limit what external screens and connected devices can access.

talks.title: [WOOT2021] BlueMirror: Reflections on Bluetooth Pairing and Provisioning Protocols
talks.teaser: Reflection and cryptographic attacks break Bluetooth Classic, BLE and Mesh pairing and provisioning protocols.
talks.summary:
The talk examines the key agreement protocols that Bluetooth devices use to set up shared secrets: pairing in Bluetooth Classic and Bluetooth Low Energy, and provisioning in Bluetooth Mesh. The speaker explains that these share a common structure of feature exchange, key exchange, authentication and key distribution, with many variants. The focus is on the authenticated versions, which use a commitment check built from nonces and confirmation values.

Reflection attacks send the messages a device receives back to it, and the team applied them to these authenticated protocols. Against Secure Simple Pairing passkey entry, reflecting messages to the responder lets an attacker recover the passkey bit by bit, then impersonate the initiator and obtain the encryption key. This works on Classic and BLE. In Mesh provisioning, the team found a reflection flaw too, plus a cryptographic misuse: a block-size problem in the AES-CMAC confirmation values lets an attacker recover the authentication value and then a nonce. The attacker can then authenticate to the provisioner without knowing the authentication value, receive network secrets, and with further steps obtain a device key.

Across the three technologies, the team found seven flaws and disclosed them to the Bluetooth SIG; six CVEs have since been released. Reflection flaws can be patched in implementations, but the cryptographic problems need the specifications redesigned. Numeric comparison was not attacked. The takeaway is not to lean on Bluetooth's built-in security, and to pair and provision devices only in controlled environments.

talks.title: [WOOT2021] Evaluation of the Executional Power in Windows using Return Oriented Programming
talks.teaser: Quantifies how much computation an attacker can build from return-oriented gadgets in Windows 7 and 10 DLLs.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how much computation an attacker can achieve by chaining return-oriented programming gadgets, short instruction sequences already present in a Windows process's memory. It traces this code-reuse technique back to 2007 and asks how often such gadgets occur in real programs and whether they can express arbitrary computation. The adversary is assumed to know the memory layout, with randomization and control-flow integrity absent or defeated.

To answer this, the speaker defines a virtual language whose arithmetic, assignment, memory, logic and branching operations are each mapped to sequences of real gadgets. Conditional branching is the hardest to emulate, and the language is shown to be Turing complete. A Python tool, released under GPL version 3, disassembles binaries with Capstone and backtracks through candidate gadgets to resolve data dependencies and output a chain. The evaluation covers a subset of DLLs common to Windows 7 and Windows 10, in 32-bit and 64-bit builds.

Branching operations turned out to be the rarest, and 64-bit builds had no unconditional branch gadgets. Windows 10 and 64-bit systems yielded more operations than Windows 7 and 32-bit systems, and larger DLLs held more gadgets. On 32-bit systems the results depend on fixed base addresses, so randomization could shift them. Relaxing data dependencies with intermediate moves surfaced a few conditional branch results on Windows 10 but none on 64-bit Windows 7. The takeaway is that an adversary can chain simple gadgets to emulate most operations, though side effects remain unresolved and Linux and macOS are planned as future targets.

talks.title: [WOOT2021] Identifying Valuable Pointers in Heap Data
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for [WOOT2021] Identifying Valuable Pointers in Heap Data.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, James Roney presents research on enhancing memory cartography—a specialized data-oriented attack technique—to identify valuable pointers in heap memory without requiring heap spraying. In a standard memory cartography attack, an attacker with an arbitrary memory read vulnerability navigates through an application's address space along a pre-mapped network of pointers between memory regions (such as static data sections, heaps, and stacks) to leak arbitrary sensitive data without causing segmentation faults. While static data sections maintain deterministic relative layouts despite Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), transitioning from a dynamic, non-deterministic heap allocation to static data sections originally relied on heap spraying predictable objects. Roney and his collaborators introduce a method that uses signature-based byte filtering to reliably identify pointers from uncontrolled heap regions to static data sections.

### Key Topics
- **Data-Oriented Attacks vs. Control-Flow Hijacking**: Unlike traditional control-flow hijacking attacks (e.g., overwriting return addresses) that trigger modern defenses such as stack canaries or Control Flow Integrity (CFI), data-oriented attacks manipulate program variables and data pointers while strictly adhering to legitimate control-flow paths.
- **Memory Cartography Mechanics**: Originally introduced by Rogowski et al., memory cartography creates an offline map of deterministic pointers between memory regions. By chaining these references, an attacker can traverse from an initial leak to target data (such as browser session cookies) across fragmented memory spaces.
- **Heap Non-Determinism Limitation**: Previous memory cartography required spraying known objects into the heap to bridge the gap between dynamic heap memory and static sections. In environments where the attacker cannot control heap allocations, this method fails.
- **Signature-Based Pointer Identification**: An offline analysis technique that characterizes the byte patterns immediately surrounding frequent pointers to static destinations, generating simple byte-level filters that can identify target pointers during runtime heap scanning.

### Technical Details
- **Offline Signature Compilation**: The attacker executes the target application locally multiple times across independent runs with ASLR enabled. By inspecting boundaries (e.g., via Linux `/proc/self/maps`), the attacker tracks heap memory regions and maps all pointers referencing external targets (such as libc or program libraries). The method identifies the most frequently referenced destination offsets across runs. For each target destination, the algorithm inspects a window of bytes surrounding the pointers (preceding bytes, pointer bytes shifting due to ASLR, and trailing bytes) and establishes upper and lower bound value intervals for each position across all runs to construct a byte filter.
- **Online Attack Execution**: At attack time, the attacker scans memory starting from their local heap read vulnerability and evaluates aligned pointer-sized regions against the pre-compiled byte bounds. Once a match is detected, the attacker extracts the pointer to the known static destination, anchoring their memory cartography navigation without crashing the process.
- **Empirical Evaluation**: The approach was evaluated using 10-fold cross-validation across 10 memory dumps per target program:
  - *Vim*: Tested as a single-threaded baseline with a unified heap; identified pointers to top frequent destinations with over 99% precision.
  - *Firefox*: Characterized by complex, multi-VMA jemalloc heap chunks. By aggregating relevant jemalloc chunks matching the JavaScript heap, the filter identified pointers to `libxul` with high precision, maintaining strong performance even in the worst-case individual heap chunk.
  - *Apache with OpenSSL 1.0.1 (Heartbleed)*: Evaluated against a real-world read vulnerability scenario, demonstrating equally high precision.

### Takeaways
- **Expanded Threat Surface**: Attackers can reliably locate entry points into static data structures from heap memory using passive signature matching, eliminating the prerequisite of heap spraying.
- **Security Implications**: Highlights the critical need for strict process isolation and independent address spaces for mutually untrusted origins, as in-process mitigations and ASLR do not prevent data-oriented pointer mapping.
- **Assumptions & Future Directions**: The technique relies on stability of inter-region offsets between local analysis environments and victim targets. Future work aims to evaluate complete end-to-end exploits under real-world timing and bandwidth constraints.

talks.title: [DLS2021] 4th Deep Learning And Security Workshop -- Part 2
talks.teaser: Workshop sessions cover certifying neural networks against attacks, binary black-box malware evasion, and a trustworthy ML panel.
talks.summary:
The first session is a talk on building accurate models that are certified against attacks. It splits the task into specifying the attack space, such as norm-bounded noise or geometric transformations, and verifying that every input in that space keeps its label. The speaker argues that brute-force enumeration fails for these spaces, and that numerical abstract interpretation can be applied to neural networks. Certified training that pushes tight relaxations through the network can lower accuracy, so the talk proposes adversarial training on intermediate layers and combining a small certified network with a large standard one.

A second session studies binary black-box evasion of static malware detectors. The attacker sees only a pass or fail answer and has no access to model parameters. The method uses actor-critic reinforcement learning over discrete, functionality-preserving actions on executables, such as editing headers, sections and signatures, or appending bytes. A concrete-distribution relaxation makes sampling of these discrete actions trainable. Against a LightGBM-based detector and a CNN-based detector, the approach reached 37 percent more evasion than the baselines. Compression often came last in the action sequences, and the two detectors reacted differently to editing and additive actions.

The final panel discusses trade-offs among privacy, robustness, fairness and accuracy, and argues that some of these trade-offs can be challenged with better techniques. Panelists describe external audits of ad delivery that found skewed outcomes by gender and race, machine unlearning as approximate retraining, and models drifting when pandemic conditions changed production data. The main takeaway is that these properties are tightly linked and should be studied together.

talks.title: [DLS2021] 4th Deep Learning And Security Workshop -- Part 1
talks.teaser: Walks through adversarial attacks on antivirus engines, secure federated aggregation, prototype-based training and robocall blocking.
talks.summary:
The opening session of the Deep Learning and Security Workshop 2021 begins with organizer remarks on the year's submissions, then a keynote by Sadia Afroz on attacking commercial malware detectors. Her team modified Windows binaries in the problem space, adding sections, overlay bytes and renamed sections, with reinforcement learning choosing the changes. Adding sections often broke packed malware, so a sandbox check confirmed the functionality was intact and cut broken files to about four percent. Evasion against three commercial antivirus products reached roughly 30 to 50 percent, yet cloud-side detection caught many samples that resembled known malware.

Next, SafeLearn presents secure aggregation for private federated learning. It computes federated averaging with the ABY framework across two non-colluding servers, so only the aggregate is revealed, without a trusted third party. Accuracy matches plain averaging, and server communication for 500 models on a network intrusion task is about 8 megabytes. A prototype-based loss called IUPG treats benign samples as off-target data. On malware classifiers it reduced false negatives and roughly halved false positives on out-of-distribution inputs, and paired with adversarial training it held up best against appended benign content.

The last talk, RoboCallGuard, introduces a virtual assistant that answers unknown calls, asks who the caller wants to reach, and interrupts the caller to separate human telemarketers from robocalls. Against 79 clusters of real robocalls it blocked all of them and labeled about 98 percent correctly, and a 21-person user study found the added delay acceptable. The main limit is targeted calls from callers who already know the callee's name. Practitioners should take away that problem-space attacks and full-pipeline testing reveal more than feature-space or single-vendor evaluations.

talks.title: Ethics in Security and Privacy Research Panel
talks.teaser: Panelists weigh ways to identify and reduce harm in security research, from study design to conference review.
talks.summary: The panel discusses ethical risks in security and privacy research, using a withdrawn paper about submitting buggy code patches as a case study. Panelists consider human harm, research review, safer study designs, and the roles of program committees and advisory boards. They describe safety review efforts and discuss how conferences can make ethical reflection part of research and peer review.

talks.title: DP-Sniper: Black-Box Discovery of Differential Privacy Violations using Classifiers
talks.teaser: Finds differential privacy violations in black-box mechanisms with classifiers, including floating point flaws in Laplace noise.
talks.summary:
The talk presents DP-Sniper, a tool that hunts for violations of differential privacy in mechanisms that add random noise to released statistics. It opens with a hospital example and the Laplace mechanism, which perturbs a count before publication. Many real implementations leak extra information through floating point arithmetic, since low-order bits can reveal more than theory predicts. That flaw has been known for about eight years, yet existing verification and testing tools miss it and may certify vulnerable code as private.

The core idea is differential distinguishability, a measure of how far apart output distributions for neighbouring inputs can be. Input search reuses existing heuristics, while the attack is built by training a classifier to estimate how likely an output is to come from one input rather than the other. Training data is cheap to generate by running the mechanism. Outputs with high estimated likelihood form the attack, with a threshold chosen so that tiny probabilities are avoided. Assuming accurate estimates and a perfect classifier, the attack is approximately optimal, and the guarantee degrades gracefully otherwise.

Black-box testing suits floating point code, because the code is simply run and no model of the arithmetic is needed. Against a fixed baseline tool, DP-Sniper performs similarly on simpler algorithms but clearly finds higher distinguishability on more advanced state-of-the-art mechanisms, while running about 15 times faster. The approach is not limited to floating point flaws, and the code is publicly available.

talks.title: CanDID: Bootstrapping Decentralized Identity from Legacy Providers
talks.teaser: Shows bootstrapping signed credentials from legacy TLS sites with DECO proofs, committees, and Sybil-resistant deduplication.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with why conventional identity falls short: burdensome KYC, OAuth limited to login and amenable to tracking, dependence on issuing authorities that exclude stateless people, and large-scale breaches of centralized identity stores. Decentralized identity should improve usability, cut fraud, let users control credentials, and shrink enterprises’ stored personal data, yet issuers, key custody, and Sybil resistance with privacy and accountability remain unresolved.

A first speaker outlines CanDID’s goals, then Deepak introduces DECO: users prove statements about TLS-fetched web data to a verifier in zero knowledge without giving them the MAC key needed to forge transcripts, so legacy TLS sites need no redesign. CanDID uses a honest-majority committee. Alice picks web providers that expose attributes (e.g., age), proves claims via DECO, and receives signed credentials; the same pattern backs up and recovers secret keys via provider login proofs instead of OAuth, which would leak identity to committee nodes. Sybil resistance uses a PRF over unique identifiers such as social security numbers without revealing them, or fuzzy matching (e.g., edit distance via secure MPC and set shingles) for error-prone name-and-address cases, with related machinery for sanctions-style accountability checks.

Reported end-to-end measurements show credential issuance under twenty seconds including DECO from two legacy sites and deduplication; sanctions-style fuzzy checks took about twenty-five minutes once, with room to parallelize. Practitioners should see a concrete bootstrap path that turns existing TLS web accounts into issuers while addressing keys and duplicate identities cryptographically rather than through new central databases.

talks.title: SmartPulse: Automated Checking of Temporal Properties in Smart Contracts
talks.teaser: Shows how SmartPulse verifies smart-contract liveness via Smart LTL specs, program instrumentation, and Büchi-automata model checking.
talks.summary:
Cryptocurrency smart contracts have suffered costly bugs that break safety guarantees or strand user funds when liveness fails—users may never receive refunds or token payouts even though the contract should eventually honor them. Existing automated analyzers focus on safety, leaving liveness largely unchecked.

SmartPulse closes that gap. Practitioners write properties in Smart LTL, which extends familiar temporal operators with contract-specific atoms and constraints in quantifier-free logic, then supply Solidity code. The tool instruments the program with boolean flags for each atom, rewrites the spec as ordinary LTL, and feeds the result to a software model checker built on a CEGAR-style engine related to Ultimate Automizer. Verification walks Büchi automata, using emptiness checks and distinguishing terminating from non-terminating counterexample paths, with domain-specific refinements described further in the paper.

Evaluation on nine contracts with thirty-four properties, OpenZeppelin and on-chain samples, and comparisons to VeriSmart and KEVM-based checking, shows most liveness claims verified or falsified in roughly ten minutes on average, often outperforming prior tools on overlapping benchmarks. Reported counterexamples replay as concrete attack stories, including auction refunds failing when one bidder’s transfer reverts and blocking all payouts—aligning with reentrancy, gas denial-of-service, and overflow patterns from earlier incidents.

talks.title: Post-Quantum WireGuard
talks.teaser: PQ-WireGuard shows how Classic McEliece and a compressed Saber variant fit a quantum-resistant VPN handshake without extra round trips.
talks.summary:
Classical WireGuard relies on X25519 and optional pre-shared keys if users want confidentiality after large-scale quantum breaks, but shared-key assumptions are weak when both tunnel ends are not under the same control. The speakers motivate PQ-WireGuard: NIST level-3 quantum resistance, retention of WireGuard’s security goals, a single round-trip handshake, and payloads that stay under roughly 1100 bytes on IPv6 so firewalls do not drop fragments.

The design swaps Diffie–Hellman for KEMs—IND-CCA for long-term identity keys and IND-CPA for ephemeral material—adds explicit key confirmation, and patches gaps such as RNG compromise, unknown-key-share, and initiation authentication via sigma mixing, default pre-shared key from public keys, or user pre-shared keys. Proofs extend WireGuard’s computational and symbolic models to quantum adversaries. The concrete stack uses Classic McEliece plus a tweaked Saber variant called Dagger, implemented as a Linux kernel module with timing-resistant code.

Benchmarks on IPv6 report client and server handshake time rises of about 70% and 50% versus WireGuard, still dominated by public-key work. Compared with OpenVPN, IPsec, and Microsoft’s PQCrypto-VPN, PQ-WireGuard is faster on every metric except slightly more bytes than X25519 IPsec, while beating OpenVPN variants by orders of magnitude. Practitioners gain a deployable path to full quantum-resistant VPN handshakes without abandoning WireGuard’s packet economy.

talks.title: CRYLOGGER: Detecting Crypto Misuses Dynamically
talks.teaser: CRYLOGGER logs Android crypto API use, checks calls against misuse rules, and scales detection across Play Store apps.
talks.summary:
Android apps rely on Java cryptography APIs where algorithm choice, modes, padding, keys, IVs, and randomness must be configured correctly. Misconfigurations are widespread in production software, and most prior detectors are static analyzers that match code against cryptographic rules without proving those paths run at runtime.

CRYLOGGER uses a dynamic pipeline: Monkey drives each app on an emulator while twelve instrumented JCE/JCA classes log parameters from live calls to Cipher, MessageDigest, and related APIs. Offline analysis applies twenty-six rules through four checkers—validating allowed parameter values, spotting constants across repeated runs, assessing randomness (including NIST tests), and detecting dangerous reuse such as the same key and IV on different messages. On roughly 1,800 free Play Store apps (Android 9, about 30k Monkey events each), violations cluster around broken hashes, weak RNGs, bad keys and IVs, and weak passwords, though many hits involve non-sensitive contexts that are hard to separate automatically. Manual review of twenty-eight apps and feedback from eight developers and two library maintainers underscored that warnings are not always exploitable issues.

Compared with the static tool Cryptoguard, dynamic analysis sees executed crypto but depends on coverage, while static work scales yet can false-alarm on dead code or miss clipped paths. The takeaway is to triage CRYLOGGER output as security warnings, combine static and dynamic approaches, and improve test generation plus context-aware rules to cut false positives and negatives.

talks.title: Bitcoin-Compatible Virtual Channels
talks.teaser: Shows how virtual payment channels can be built on UTXO blockchains with limited scripting and no smart contracts.
talks.summary:
Most cryptocurrencies run on blockchains with fixed block sizes and block times, which limits throughput and pushes up fees. Payment channels let two parties pay each other off-chain, touching the chain only to open and close. Payment channel networks extend this through an intermediary who routes payments, but that intermediary charges fees and can see the amounts and parties involved, which weakens privacy. Virtual channels remove the intermediary from individual payments, yet existing constructions depend on smart contracts.

The talk presents a virtual channel construction for UTXO-based blockchains that support only limited scripting, such as time locks and signature verification. A virtual channel is opened by moving funds out of two ledger channels, and then the parties update it like any other channel. Two extra procedures handle failures: offload publishes the opening states on chain so the virtual channel is funded there, and punish penalizes colluding parties who try to revert a state while compensating the honest party. The security properties are formalized in the Universal Composability framework and a security proof is given.

A proof-of-concept builds the raw Bitcoin transactions and deploys them on a Bitcoin network to show compatibility. Opening, updating and closing a virtual channel incur no on-chain fees, while offload and punish do, with punish costing roughly what closing a payment channel costs. Communication overhead becomes lower than routing through a payment channel network once more than one payment is made, and the intermediary charges fees only at opening. Future work includes recursive virtual channels and support for users who go offline.

talks.title: PLATYPUS: Software-based Power Side-Channel Attacks on x86
talks.teaser: Shows how software-readable CPU power counters leak kernel layout, SGX secrets and AES keys.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Platypus, a set of software-based power side-channel attacks against Intel x86 CPUs. Intel's RAPL interface exposes energy readings for the core, DRAM and other domains, and on Linux it can be read from unprivileged user space. The speaker first showed that these readings reveal the energy cost of individual instructions, that operand values change consumption, and that loaded data and cache hits or misses are visible in the measurements.

Applied to security, the first case broke kernel address space layout randomization. By probing candidate addresses and watching for an energy drop on mapped pages, the attack located the kernel, and a demo showed this working. For a stronger attacker who controls the operating system, the team combined RAPL with an open-source Linux framework that single-steps SGX enclaves, measuring single instructions. This leaked key bits from a square-and-multiply RSA implementation and from the mbed TLS version, letting the full key be recovered. A user-space correlation power analysis also recovered AES key bytes from AES-NI encryptions, using Hamming weight and Hamming distance models over many blocks.

For mitigation, blocking unprivileged access to the counters is a one-line Linux kernel patch. Against a compromised OS, microcode updates coarsen the readings so data-dependent differences disappear, but enclave code still needs to be constant time. The speaker noted that other CPU vendors expose comparable interfaces that could be explored in similar attacks.

talks.title: CrawlPhish: Large-scale Analysis of Client-side Cloaking Techniques in Phishing
talks.teaser: Measures JavaScript cloaking in phishing sites that hides content from anti-phishing crawlers while showing it to victims.
talks.summary:
Penghui, a PhD candidate at Arizona State University, presents CrawlPhish, a framework for studying client-side cloaking in phishing sites. Blacklist-based anti-phishing systems judge content and URLs, so pages that use JavaScript to show different content to crawlers and victims can evade them. Prior work covered server-side cloaking, but JavaScript-based cloaking was poorly understood.

The pipeline starts with phishing URLs from the APWG eCrime Exchange and saves each page's source and screenshot. A JavaScript force-execution engine runs the page scripts, and the original and forced pages are compared on source and screenshot similarity. Sites whose forced results match are filtered out, leaving cloaked ones. Cloaks are labelled by meaning, and the web APIs and events in their code are stored in a database. Eight evasion types fall into three categories: user interaction (pop-up, mouse detection, click-through), bot behavior (timing, randomization) and fingerprinting (cookie, referrer, user-agent). Reused implementations dominate, with 20% of groups covering 74% of sites. Cloaked sites rose from 23% in 2018 to 34% in 2019, and code obfuscation from 21% to 24%.

Of 150 artificial sites with user-interaction cloaking reported to browser vendors, none were blacklisted except 21 blocked in Microsoft Edge a median of 3 hours later, because SmartScreen flagged the obfuscated JavaScript rather than the cloak. A 1000-worker study showed mouse-detection and click-through cloaks revealed hidden text to people, but only 43% saw text behind a notification-window cloak. Findings went to Google, Microsoft and Opera, who acknowledged them. The takeaway: crawlers should match the behaviors phishing kits expect, and the framework could be added to existing crawlers.

talks.title: BUFFing signature schemes beyond unforgeability and the case of post-quantum signatures
talks.teaser: Beyond-unforgeability captures malicious-key attacks on signatures; a BUFF transform adds these properties with modest overhead.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues that existential unforgeability is an incomplete benchmark for real deployments where adversaries may supply malicious public keys. Using Let's Encrypt's DNS-based domain validation as a concrete scenario, it shows how an honestly generated signature from an earlier run can verify a new challenge under an attacker-chosen key, yielding a certificate without breaking classical forgery definitions.

The speakers formalize this gap as beyond-unforgeability: strong destructive exclusive ownership, message-bound signatures, and non-resignability, noting these properties are independent. They introduce the BUFF transformation, which hashes the public key with the message before signing and checks that digest at verification, reducing attacks to hash collisions with only one digest worth of extra signature size and negligible hashing cost.

The analysis covers NIST post-quantum signature finalists from round three, marking which schemes meet each notion and presenting attacks where they fail. Lithium and Picnic satisfy all listed properties; Falcon and Rainbow are partial; GEMSS needs improvement; SPHINCS+ lacks full results for some notions. Practitioners can apply BUFF to harden schemes such as Falcon while keeping relative size advantages versus other finalists.

talks.title: Breaking the Specification: Certified PDF
talks.teaser: Shows how certified PDFs can be altered via annotations and signatures while suppressing viewer warnings.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how certified PDF documents protect their content, starting with the file structure: header, body objects, cross-reference table and trailer. It explains how incremental updates append changes to the end of a file without altering the original bytes. It then contrasts signed documents, which accept further signatures and annotations with warnings, with certified documents, where the certification sets a permission level (P1, P2 or P3) that limits what can be added later. At level P3, annotations can be added in most viewers without any warning.

The speakers present two attacks. The evil annotation attack places a white stamp over existing text, then a free text annotation with attacker-chosen content on top, and changes the annotation subtype so the annotation list in the third UI layer stays empty. The sneaky signature attack places an empty signature over the content, adds a visible signature with a white background and attacker text, then redirects object references and marks the field read only so viewers do not show it. Across 26 PDF applications on three operating systems, these stealthiness improvements raised the number of vulnerable applications, for example from 0 to 9 for sneaky signatures on UI layer 2 and from 0 to 50 for evil annotations on UI layer 3.

The conclusion is that unprotected incremental updates remain a problem for both certified and signed PDFs, and that features such as signatures and annotations can be misused. The speakers suggest that the specification allow signatures only in fields defined by the certifier before certification, and that annotation size and types be restricted, with an allow-list approach to reduce implementation flaws. They also offer a detector for both attacks.

talks.title: Self-Supervised Euphemism Detection and Identification for Content Moderation
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Self-Supervised Euphemism Detection and Identification for Content Moderation.
talks.summary: Wang Jung Joo presents self-supervised euphemism detection and identification for moderation: masked-language filtering removes generic drug contexts, then BERT fills masks to propose slang candidates on Reddit, Gab, and Twitter corpora, outperforming word2vec baselines on drug, weapons, and sexuality sets. A coarse classifier separates euphemistic versus literal mentions before a fine-grained multi-class head maps terms like weed or coke to target keywords using only unlabeled text and keyword lists.

talks.title: Randomized Last-Level Caches Are Still Vulnerable to Cache Side-Channel Attacks! But We Can Fix It
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Randomized Last-Level Caches Are Still Vulnerable to Cache Side-Channel Attacks! But We Can Fix It.

talks.title: When Function Signature Recovery Meets Compiler Optimization
talks.teaser: Shows how compiler optimizations skew binary function signature recovery and proposes fixes for more accurate CFI target policies.
talks.summary:
Indirect-call control-flow integrity depends on an accurate set of valid targets. Without source code, binary tools must infer function signatures from how arguments are passed in registers. The talk shows why this breaks: a 32-bit unsigned integer in the source can look like a 64-bit register value in the binary, so the recovered signature no longer matches what the code intended.

The speaker studied TypeArmor and TauCFI, both of which assume the standard 64-bit Linux calling convention with six integer argument registers. The team identified eight ways compiler optimization distorts that recovery and described two in detail. Unused arguments make optimized code read fewer registers, while unoptimized code usually reads all of them. Constants and pointers are often passed through narrower 32-bit writes or exclusive-or zeroing, so the recovered width shrinks. Across 552 C and 792 C++ executables built at several optimization levels, unused arguments were the largest contributor, especially in C++. Inlining and loop unrolling raised the likelihood of these cases at higher optimization levels.

The proposed refinements check whether a read of the third argument register follows a library call, which suggests a return value rather than an argument, and whether an argument register copied into another after being written is only a temporary. On the same programs they reduced overestimated argument counts and misclassified normal functions as variadic, without underestimating argument sizes, and they shrank the set of legal indirect-call targets compared with the existing tools. The takeaway is that binary CFI policies must model how optimized code really uses registers.

talks.title: A First Look at Zoombombing
talks.teaser: A measurement study maps how zoom bombing calls spread on social media and why insider access undermines common meeting passwords.
talks.summary:
Mass adoption of online meeting tools during the pandemic created a new disruption pattern: outsiders or coordinated groups join live sessions to harass participants, widely labeled zoom bombing. The presenters frame attacks through a four-phase model—call for attack, coordination, delivery, and harm—and illustrate it with a coordinated strike against a host’s meeting.

They gather public posts from Twitter and 4chan between January and July 2020, alongside monitoring of links tied to ten meeting platforms. Manual coding and annotation narrow thousands of posts to hundreds of bombing invitations on 4chan and Twitter. Quantitative work shows Zoom and Google Meet draw the most attention, activity spikes with quarantine and fades around school holidays, and most invitations aim at lectures and classes. Many posts include passwords, and large shares on both platforms appear to come from insiders with legitimate access, sometimes coaching attackers to mimic real student names. Coordination threads often imply meetings are live when posted, leaving little lead time for defense. NLP and qualitative review highlight class-related themes and some toxic language in thread discussions.

Most calls in the dataset target online instruction. Insider-driven sharing makes shared passwords and waiting rooms weak barriers. The talk argues for stronger access control: restricting participants to a single organization where feasible, per-participant or personalized join links, and platform features that trace who leaked access.

talks.title: Epochal Signatures for Deniable Group Chats
talks.teaser: Shows how replacing signatures with expiring epochal signatures makes efficient group chat protocols like MLS deniable.
talks.summary:
This talk looks at deniability in group chats, where a participant can later plausibly deny having sent a message or even having taken part in a conversation. Two-party deniability is well understood through MAC-based authentication, but that argument breaks down once more than one possible sender remains after verification. Pairwise workarounds still work for small groups, yet their communication overhead grows quickly with group size. The speakers present a formal security game for offline deniability, in which a judge receives finished transcripts and chooses instruction lists that mark each action as exposed, challenge, hidden or alternate reality.

Strong offline deniability, which forbids any state preserved between exposed and challenge actions, appears too costly to combine with efficient scaling and properties such as post-compromise secrecy. Weak offline deniability, which only forbids exposed and challenge actions in the same room, is too restrictive for practical use. The middle ground is hidden full interaction offline deniability, where exposed and challenge actions may coexist as long as every member has done something hidden in between, and the speakers show this notion can be achieved efficiently. To get there they introduce epochal signatures, which behave like ordinary signatures until an expiry date and can be simulated afterwards. Each signature carries the secret key of the least recently expired epoch, plus the current epoch key locked behind a timelock puzzle, so forgeries are not possible before the current key is revealed.

The authors show that a large class of group chat protocols, including MLS, becomes hidden full interaction offline deniable when its signatures are replaced with epochal signatures. They also note that the same idea can restore plain authenticity for email signatures that were unintended to allow later third-party verification. The practical takeaway is that deniability and efficient scaling can be combined in group messaging by changing only the signature component.

talks.title: SoK: Security and Privacy in the Age of Commercial Drones
talks.teaser: Surveys known attacks and defenses for commercial drones and the public, concluding the protective technology is not yet mature.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether the technology needed to protect drones and society from each other is mature enough for the growing number of commercial flights. The speaker presents a systematization of knowledge that reviews known attacks and countermeasures from two angles: the drone ecosystem itself, and the public exposed to drone-enabled threats. On the drone side, the attack surface covers the airframe and payload, onboard hardware, the ground control station, the first-person-view video link, the pilot and cloud services. The assumed attacker is a civilian using equipment that can be legally bought for a few thousand dollars.

Four methods were classed as severe, meaning a remote attacker at 15 meters or more can hit them with no effective countermeasure. GPS spoofing and jamming threaten autonomous navigation, while jamming the first-person-view link threatens remote control. The conclusion is that drones and their ecosystems are not yet adequately protected, with drones carrying organs to hospitals cited as an example. For society, individuals, organizations and national facilities face spying, cyber attacks, terrorism and smuggling. Facilities can be secured with dedicated hardware and organizations can rely on standard cyber defenses, but individuals lack consumer-grade detection and assessment tools.

Finally, the authors conclude that the required technology has not yet matured. Hardening drones against GPS spoofing, for instance, removes one way to disable a hostile drone, so drone security and public safety and privacy trade off against each other. The takeaway is to seek a reasonable balance between these interests and use it as a basis for criteria for safe and responsible drone deployment.

talks.title: Lightweight Techniques for Private Heavy Hitters
talks.teaser: Cryptographic protocols enable two servers to identify the most frequent client strings while hiding which client contributed each value.
talks.summary:
Organizations such as browser vendors often need aggregate telemetry—like which URLs most often accompany crashes—without building per-user browsing profiles. The talk frames this as private heavy hitters: many clients each hold a long string, two collection servers must discover which strings exceed a popularity threshold, and privacy holds if at least one server stays honest even under collusion with malicious clients or peers.

The presentation walks through a warm-up protocol where each client encodes its string as ones on a path through a binary tree, additively secret-shares every node, and sends one share to each server. Servers sum shares and traverse the tree breadth-first to prune subtrees below threshold until exact heavy hitters emerge with no counting error. Scaling to 256-bit strings rules out materializing the full tree; the work introduces incremental distributed point functions so clients send succinct keys with linear size and linear AES work per path instead of quadratic costs from standard DPFs. A second contribution, malicious secure sketching with algebraic manipulation detection, lets servers reject malformed submissions by checking that each layer’s shared vector has Hamming weight one.

The team implemented the full system in Rust, evaluated it with servers in distant cloud regions, and reports feasible latency-tolerant telemetry: for hundreds of thousands of clients and 256-bit strings, finding hundreds of top hitters needs under an hour of parallelizable server work and tens of gigabytes of cross-server bandwidth. The speaker positions the design as an MPC-style alternative to local differential privacy and notes related extractable DPF tooling and open releases.

talks.title: On the Just-In-Time Discovery of Profit-Generating Transactions in DeFi Protocols
talks.teaser: A research framework finds profitable DeFi transaction paths within block intervals using graph cycles and SMT solvers.
talks.summary:
Decentralized finance lets traders chain swaps, borrows, and other smart-contract actions into one atomic blockchain transaction, which creates opportunities to profit from price differences across platforms. With hundreds of protocols, varying pricing formulas, and state that changes every block—often on the order of thirteen seconds—spotting viable paths before the next block is mined is hard.

The work introduces DeFiPoster, with two complementary approaches. DeFiPoster-UP models token markets as a directed graph, maps exchange rates through negative logarithms, and uses Bellman-Ford to find negative cycles that correspond to profitable trade loops. DeFiPoster-SMT encodes richer action sequences—including borrowing and margin trades—symbolically, enforces constraints such as liquidity limits, and uses an SMT solver plus binary search to maximize profit per path, with heuristics to prune infeasible routes.

Over 150 days of historical blocks across ninety-six actions and twenty-five assets, the graph method surfaces weekly profit on the order of seventy thousand dollars versus roughly thirty thousand for the SMT variant; the latter also captures non-cyclic strategies and flags the January 2020 bZx opportunity. Results are replayed on chain to cut false positives. The closing analysis ties miner-extractable value to double-spending-style decisions, showing how large MEV can incentivize miners to fork the chain and weaken consensus—relevant for anyone modeling DeFi risk, MEV, or mining incentives.

talks.title: High-Frequency Trading on Decentralized On-Chain Exchanges
talks.teaser: Shows how transaction ordering lets attackers profitably sandwich traders on automated market makers on decentralized exchanges.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether high-frequency trading works on decentralized exchanges, which settle trades on public blockchains rather than through a central operator, and whether the market can be manipulated to the detriment of traders. Trading volume on these venues has grown sharply over the past year and now rivals large centralized platforms in some comparisons. Miners order pending transactions by publicly known rules, and traders must broadcast their orders over a peer-to-peer network first, so an observer who sees a trade early can insert its own transactions around it.

The focus is on automated market makers that price assets with a constant product formula, where each trade shifts the pool price along a curve. Traders set slippage protection thresholds that revert trades moving too far, and this is what enables sandwich attacks: the attacker trades ahead of a victim to worsen its execution price, then trades back for profit. The researchers derive a minimum profitable victim input, below which no sandwich attack can cover its costs, and propose disabling transactions above that level as a mitigation. Splitting large trades into smaller ones can also help, though it raises fees per transaction. Simulations with several attackers suggest they divide the revenue, and congestion makes break-even harder to reach. A variant where the attacker acts as a liquidity provider is also noted.

The closing point is that transparent blockchain exchanges, combined with the delay before transactions are processed, make market manipulation visible and exploitable. Anyone designing or trading on such venues should account for transaction ordering and slippage settings.

talks.title: Security of Multi-Sensor Fusion based Perception in Autonomous Driving Under Physical-World Attacks
talks.teaser: Shows printed roadside objects can hide obstacles from both camera and LiDAR fusion in self-driving cars.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether multi-sensor fusion, which combines camera and LiDAR data in autonomous vehicle perception, really protects against attacks on a single sensor. The speaker questions the assumption behind that defense, namely that an attacker cannot compromise all sensing sources at once. The attack uses a 3D-printed object shaped like a traffic cone or barrier, with its geometry optimized so that both sensors miss it and the vehicle drives into it.

The design had to produce physically consistent effects on both sensors and handle LiDAR preprocessing steps that are not differentiable. The team used differentiable rendering for LiDAR and camera, plus a smooth approximation of the point-in-cell test that feeds cell-level features. Demonstrations covered a miniature physical setup, a real vehicle with a 64-line LiDAR, and a simulation in Apollo, where a normal cone was detected and the car stopped while the adversarial object went unseen and caused a crash. Across four fusion algorithms and 100 real-world driving scenarios, the speaker reported over 91 percent success across object types and algorithms, over 95 percent average success across positions and angles, around 75 percent transfer between algorithms, at least 85 percent success in physical frames, and a 100 percent collision rate over 100 simulation runs.

The speaker reported that input-based and model-level defenses cut the attack success rate to 66 percent without harming benign performance, which is not enough. Adding more or different sensors would not fundamentally stop the attack. The team disclosed the findings to 31 companies, and 17 replied. The takeaway for practitioners is that fusion should not be treated as a general defense, and that stronger guarantees are needed.

talks.title: Is Private Learning Possible with Instance Encoding?
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Is Private Learning Possible with Instance Encoding?.
talks.summary:
### Overview
This presentation examines the viability of achieving privacy-preserving machine learning through instance encoding, focusing on the InstaHide scheme introduced at ICML. Instance encoding adds a pre-processing step where training data is converted into intermediate encodings intended to prevent information leakage while enabling models to train directly on the encoded data. The authors evaluate InstaHide's empirical security by completely breaking its official challenge dataset, present theoretical impossibility results bounding instance encoding privacy when combined with accuracy, and critically assess the role of security challenges in machine learning security research.

### Key Topics
- **Instance Encoding in Machine Learning:** The concept of transforming raw training data into privacy-preserving intermediate encodings that allow downstream algorithms to train without direct access to private samples.
- **InstaHide Architecture:** A mechanism combining linear combinations of private images with samples from an unlabeled public dataset, followed by random pixel sign flipping (masking).
- **Attack on the InstaHide Challenge:** A practical reconstruction attack utilizing neural-network-based clustering followed by image recovery to reconstruct private training images.
- **Theoretical Barriers:** Formal security definitions and impossibility theorems demonstrating fundamental trade-offs between instance encoding accuracy and cryptographic privacy.
- **Evaluation of Security Challenges:** The limitations of relying on static empirical challenges without formal, falsifiable security models and threat definitions.

### Technical Details
- **InstaHide Encoding Mechanism:** InstaHide draws images from both a private labeled dataset and an auxiliary public dataset, creates a linear combination of these images, and applies a masking layer that randomly flips the sign of each pixel with probability 1/2.
- **Challenge Reconstruction Attack:** The InstaHide challenge provided 50 encodings for each of 100 private images using an undisclosed public dataset. The attack operates in two phases: first, a neural network clusters encodings based on the underlying private images they encode; second, an image recovery step reconstructs the original images from each cluster, achieving near-perfect recovery of all 100 challenge images.
- **Alternative Threat Model Attack:** Assuming auxiliary knowledge where the attacker has access to the public dataset used during encoding, the authors developed an efficient attack that scales linearly with data size and reconstructs a private image from just a single encoding.
- **Theoretical Impossibility Bounds:** The authors formulated a security game where an adversary distinguishes which of two identically labeled instances was encoded. They proved that if a protocol achieves accuracy 1/2 + ε on encoded data across two concept functions, a polynomial-time adversary achieves advantage 1/2 + Ω(ε) in breaking privacy. When accuracy is defined on original data, the adversary's advantage is bounded by 1/2 + 1/n (where n is sample complexity), ruling out cryptographic levels of privacy.

### Takeaways
- **InstaHide is Insecure:** InstaHide fails to provide robust privacy, as demonstrated by the complete reconstruction of its official challenge dataset and efficient single-encoding recovery under public dataset knowledge.
- **Fundamental Incompatibility:** Strong cryptographic privacy and high utility/accuracy cannot be achieved simultaneously via instance encoding alone.
- **Challenges Cannot Replace Formal Models:** Security challenges should serve only as necessary conditions for security and cannot substitute for clear threat models and falsifiable claims. The broader machine learning security field must transition from informal evaluations toward rigorous, mathematically defined threat models.

talks.title: Poltergeist: Acoustic Manipulation of Image Stabilization towards Object Mis-Labeling
talks.teaser: Shows how injected sound into motion sensors blurs camera frames enough to hide, create or relabel detected objects.
talks.summary:
Cameras on autonomous vehicles, drones and robots feed object detectors that drive safety-critical decisions, so tampering with perception matters. Earlier attacks altered physical objects or added pixel-level noise to digital images. This work asks whether an attacker can reach the image through the sensors that drive camera stabilization.

Stabilizers rely on inertial sensors such as accelerometers and gyroscopes to measure motion. Earlier research showed these sensors respond to resonant acoustic signals, so injected sound can create fake camera motion. The attack models linear, radial and rotational blur, and tunes sound parameters with a gradient-free optimizer that needs only detector outputs. Three goals are covered: hiding an object, creating a non-existent one, and altering an object's label. In simulations on two driving datasets against four academic detectors and one commercial system, hiding reached 100 percent success on every detector tested, while creating and altering were harder, with creation from nothing the lowest. Real-world runs from a moving vehicle, using an ultrasonic speaker and a smartphone, showed all three attacks were visible, with hiding strongest across four road scenes.

The authors frame this as a new class of attack that combines hardware physics with adversarial machine learning into a system-level exploit. The reported attack power was 10 watts at one meter. Suggested defences include shielding the sensors and hardening stabilization algorithms. The main lesson is that the sensing chain belongs in the threat model for camera-based autonomous systems.

talks.title: SoK: Fully Homomorphic Encryption Compilers
talks.teaser: Compares compilers for fully homomorphic encryption and benchmarks them on genomics and neural network workloads.
talks.summary:
Fully homomorphic encryption lets a server run computations on data it cannot read, yet building such applications remains hard for non-experts. This systematization of knowledge reviews the tools that try to close that gap and examines what makes FHE development difficult. The speaker separates cryptographic challenges, such as choosing parameters and managing noise and bootstrapping, from computation-model challenges, such as replacing branches and secret-dependent loops with circuits and batching data into SIMD slots.

The talk compares libraries, general-purpose compilers and domain-specific frontends, showing the same program written at several abstraction levels in SEAL, EVA and nGraph-HE. Compilers are grouped by where they optimize: the input program, the generated circuit, or both. For a chi-squared test variant used in genome-wide association studies, EVA matched a hand-optimized implementation, though it works with approximate arithmetic over scalars. For MNIST networks, including CryptoNets and LeNet-5 with squaring activations, nGraph-HE and EVA beat a manual implementation on encrypted inference latency.

The takeaway is that broader adoption will depend on higher-level tools that automate parameter selection and the translation between computation models. The speaker argues that future tools should let developers move between abstraction levels and combine FHE with other secure computation techniques. The authors also provide code and Docker images for the tools they evaluated.

talks.title: Electromagnetic Covert Channels Can Be Super Resilient
talks.teaser: A memory-driven EM covert channel borrows LoRa chirp resilience to exfiltrate data across kilometers and through heavy shielding.
talks.summary:
Electromagnetic covert channels let malware turn an isolated machine into a radio that leaks secrets without touching the network, but prior work stayed inside roughly five meters and wilted against TEMPEST-style shielding orders of magnitude stronger than typical CPU memory leakage. The speakers revisit that assumption by asking whether LoRa’s attenuation-resistant chirp spread spectrum can be synthesized from involuntary memory electromagnetic emissions.

They present EM-LoRa, pairing a user-space transmitter that patterns memory traffic into approximate chirps with a customized receiver that refocuses dispersed spectral energy and adapts spread factor when CPU contention distorts timing. Experiments with inexpensive software-defined radio gear report large attenuation gains versus prior memory channels, multi-kilometer ranges on DDR3 desktop setups, resilience under video and mining load, building-scale pickup with moderate loss at some distances, field-style emulation sketches in Washington and Beijing, and partial success through a commodity Faraday cage around a shielded server.

Practitioners should treat air-gapped classification as insufficient if nearby adversaries can park receivers in public space, and should weigh detection research the authors flag for future work.

talks.title: SoK: All You Ever Wanted to Know About Binary Disassembly But Were Afraid to Ask
talks.teaser: Surveys how open-source x86 and x64 disassemblers recover instructions and functions, and compares their accuracy and coverage.
talks.summary:
Binary disassembly turns machine code back into assembly when source code is unavailable, which matters for analyzing and mitigating vulnerabilities in commercial, legacy and third-party software. The work asks how the tools work and how well they perform. To answer the first question, the team read the source code of open-source disassemblers and grouped their strategies into algorithms, which offer some correctness guarantees, and heuristics based on common patterns such as function-start signatures, which do not. They report 15 algorithmic strategies and 29 heuristics across four tasks: recovering instructions, functions, execution flows and pointers.

Several findings were highlighted. One tool combines recursive descent with linear sweep, starting with recursive descent and then scanning the gaps it leaves to balance coverage and precision. Another uses exception-handling unwinding tables, whose per-function entries give clues about function starts. A third concerns conditional non-returning functions, such as error and error_at_line, whose behavior depends on an argument; the speaker says every surveyed disassembler handled these incorrectly.

For the second question, the team built about 4000 binaries in C and C++ with known ground truth, and evaluated each tool and each strategy separately, reporting overall, per-strategy and error results. Every tool made some mistakes in every task, because heuristics are used to reach high coverage, creating a trade-off between accuracy and coverage. The takeaway is that current tools are not yet adequate for supporting vulnerability mitigation.

talks.title: Machine unlearning
talks.teaser: Describes SISA—sharded, isolated, sliced, aggregated training—to speed machine unlearning and meet formal data-removal guarantees.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens on tensions between growing model capacity, memorization, and privacy rules that let people withdraw data from systems that may have already absorbed it during training. The unlearning goal is defined in distributional terms: after removal, the model should match what retraining would yield if the forgotten points had never been included, despite stochastic training noise.

Existing options are surveyed briefly. Differentially private learning only fully unlearns at extremes that block useful learning; statistical-query methods suit simpler model classes but not typical deep networks. Retraining on the reduced dataset is the general baseline but costly. The core contribution is SISA—data split into shards with separate models whose outputs are aggregated, plus slicing that checkpoints incremental slice exposure so unlearning can restart from the right stage instead of the full shard history.

Evaluation across six datasets uses analytical retraining time tied to sample count. More shards accelerate unlearning until request volume grows but can hurt accuracy; slicing adds further gains with diminishing returns after a few slices. Logit aggregation beats naive label votes. When unlearning likelihood varies by user, distribution-aware sharding clusters higher-risk accounts to limit shard churn. The close emphasizes provable removal semantics, modest storage overhead, broad gradient-descent applicability, and efficiency gains when request patterns are known.

talks.title: Compositional Security for Reentrant Applications
talks.teaser: Shows how information flow control and integrity locks can stop reentrancy bugs across smart contracts and modular applications.
talks.summary:
Reentrancy happens when one module calls another, and that module calls back in before the first call has finished updating its state. The talk uses a simplified bank that pays out a withdrawal before it lowers the account balance, which is the pattern behind the 2016 DAO loss on Ethereum. It also covers the 2020 Uniswap attack, which exploited the interaction of two contracts that were harmless on their own. The problem is not limited to smart contracts: any two modules that can call each other without trusting each other, such as a host and an SGX enclave or a WebAssembly program in a browser, can show the same flaw.

Existing defenses target single smart contracts, so their definition of reentrancy depends on object boundaries and is not compositional. Refactoring a monolithic application into smaller modules can change whether the same execution counts as reentrant. The speaker instead defines reentrancy by integrity levels: an execution stack with two computations trusted at a given level, separated by one that is not. Security means a program's reentrant behaviour never allows anything its non-reentrant equivalent could not do, so developers can reason about correctness without thinking about reentrancy.

The approach enforces this with integrity locks. When untrusted code enters trusted code, the newly granted integrity level is locked, so a reentrant call cannot grant it again while ordinary calls still succeed. Locks can be checked statically with a type system, which costs nothing at run time but cannot cover unknown code, or enforced dynamically, which supports legacy code at a higher run-time cost. The talk combines both, requesting dynamic locks when calling unknown code. For the DAO example, the fix is either a dynamic lock on the send or reordering so the balance is decreased before the money is sent. The speaker notes that the paper contains formal proofs and a prototype type checker.

talks.title: Using Selective Memoization to Defeat Regular Expression Denial of Service (ReDoS)
talks.teaser: Selective memoization yields linear-time regex matching with practical space costs on hundreds of thousands of real-world patterns.
talks.summary:
Regular expression denial of service remains a practical threat because mainstream engines use depth-first backtracking that can explore exponentially many paths on malicious inputs. Engineers routinely apply regexes to untrusted text in web stacks, so a single slow pattern can tie up event loops or worker pools and harm other clients. The weakness sits in language runtime infrastructure rather than application logic alone, and linear-time engine alternatives exist but see limited adoption because of dialect complexity and compatibility risk.

The presentation proposes backwards-compatible memoization inside existing backtracking engines. During NFA simulation, recording failed vertex-and-offset pairs avoids revisiting the same ambiguous states. Full memoization guarantees linear steps but multiplies storage by automaton size and input length; selective schemes target only branching vertices or ancestors of back-edges, preserving linear time bounds with smaller tables. The formal model also accommodates lookaround assertions and backreferences through additional automaton edge types.

A prototype was evaluated against a dataset of roughly half a million patterns, including about fifty thousand with super-linear worst cases. Supported patterns covered eighty-four percent of the corpus and ninety-five percent of the super-linear set. Charts compared match times with and without memoization on patterns such as Microsoft username checks, Cloudflare rules, lookarounds, and backreferences. Space measurements on stack-overflow-sized inputs showed that combining vertex selection with efficient memo encodings often keeps overhead at practical, typically constant levels for most super-linear regexes under attack-like conditions.

talks.title: Ebb-and-Flow Protocols: A Resolution of the Availability-Finality Dilemma
talks.teaser: Researchers expose a liveness flaw in Gasper and introduce snap-and-chat protocols that balance availability with finality.
talks.summary:
Consensus systems face a tension between staying live when participation swings and staying safe under partitions. Longest-chain designs favor dynamic availability but can fork; classical BFT stays final under partitions but may stall when few nodes are online. The speakers relate this trade-off to Ethereum’s Gasper design, which nests Casper FFG finality on LMD GHOST, and ask whether one ledger can combine both behaviors via an available full chain and a finalized prefix that eventually aligns.

They report a liveness attack on Gasper in the synchronous network model: a small adversarial fraction can split honest committees with timed votes, sustain tied competing chains, and block decisions while risking safety as honest nodes oscillate. To capture the intended goal they formalize ebb-and-flow protocols, then present snap-and-chat constructions that compose an off-the-shelf longest-chain protocol with a partially synchronous BFT layer through snapshotting and flattening.

Under stated corruption bounds, the available ledger tolerates dynamic participation while the finalized prefix tolerates partitions, and the prefix remains consistent with the growing full ledger. Practitioners gain a modular template for combining availability and finality, clarity on Gasper’s failure mode, and criteria for optimal resilience when nesting ledgers.
