talks.title: Pegasus: Bridging Polynomial and Non-polynomial Evaluations in Homomorphic Encryption
talks.teaser: Pegasus switches HEAAN and FHEW modes to homomorphically evaluate polynomials and non-polynomials with far smaller keys than Chimera.
talks.summary:
Privacy-preserving collaboration often requires a model holder and a data holder to compute on sensitive inputs without exposing either the model or the data. Homomorphic encryption supports this goal, but practical schemes tend to favor either arithmetic on packed ciphertexts or Boolean-style evaluation, and non-polynomial steps such as division or comparisons usually force costly circuits or approximations.

The Pegasus framework bridges HEAAN-style arithmetic homomorphic encryption with FHEW-style lookup-table evaluation so polynomial work stays in one mode while non-polynomial functions use encrypted lookup tables after scheme switching. The design targets smaller keys and lighter computation than the Chimera baseline, with a public implementation built on Microsoft SEAL. Scheme switching homomorphically decrypts batched FHEW ciphertexts via an improved matrix–vector multiplication trick for tall matrices, and an extended homomorphic lookup table relaxes modulus constraints at the cost of controlled rounding error. Reported benchmarks show faster switching, roughly second-scale lookup evaluation, and large speedups on mean–index and encrypted sorting workloads.

Demonstrations include finding minima over encrypted arrays and running k-means on encrypted points, alternating polynomial distance updates with non-polynomial assignment and switching back for centroid averaging. The closing message is that practical cross-scheme switching materially widens what homomorphic encryption can run today, while efficiently bridging exact arithmetic schemes with exact lookup-table encryption remains an open challenge.

talks.title: Adversary Instantiation: Lower bounds for differentially private machine learning
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Adversary Instantiation: Lower bounds for differentially private machine learning.

talks.title: Compact Certificates of Collective Knowledge
talks.teaser: Introduces a compact certificate scheme that lets many weighted parties prove agreement on a fact with small, fast-to-check proofs.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a common problem: many parties, such as computers watching the same attack source, people seeing a rare event, or nodes in a blockchain tracking its state, want a short way to prove that a majority agrees on a fact. Bundling one signature per party works in principle, but the certificate grows with the number of parties and becomes expensive to check. The speaker presents a cryptographic primitive called a compact certificate scheme, designed to handle parties with different weights, faulty or malicious participants, and a verifier that does not need to trust the prover.

The construction commits to all signatures in a Merkle tree whose leaves also hold the start of each signer's weight range. The verifier keeps only a short commitment to the public keys and weights, and it sends random challenges sampled in proportion to weight. The prover opens the matching leaves. A prover who overstates the total signed weight must commit to some leaf that fails for at least one challenge, so enough queries expose the cheat. More signed weight means fewer queries are needed and smaller certificates. The scheme is made non-interactive with the Fiat-Shamir heuristic and is shown to be a random-oracle proof of knowledge, with certificate size polylogarithmic in the number of parties.

The implementation is about 1,200 lines of Go, using Ed25519 signatures and truncated SHA-512. At one million parties with 128-bit security, certificates range from under 100 KB to about 900 KB, compared with 11 to 77 MB for the naive approach, which makes them 50 to 280 times smaller. Verification takes roughly 10 to 80 ms, 300 to 4,000 times faster than the naive method at that scale. Generation stays under 60 seconds on a single thread and is at most twice the baseline cost. The speaker notes that the paper also covers use in blockchains with stake-weighted voting.

talks.title: Learning Differentially Private Mechanisms
talks.teaser: Covers learning and automatic sizing of differentially private mechanisms for queries, with validation and difficult-case examples.
talks.summary:
The presentation centers on differential privacy for database-style and analytics settings, where analysts need formal guarantees about how much any single participant can influence published results. A motivating question is how large the privacy impact of one individual's data can become under a chosen mechanism, and how to design releases that remain useful while respecting a privacy budget.

The speaker argues that satisfying the differential privacy definition alone is often easy if noise is cranked high, but that practical mechanisms must be sized and structured so utility loss stays controlled. The work sketches algorithm families and an automated design approach that derives mechanism scale from problem structure rather than manual tuning. Discussion touches deterministic query behavior, objective-driven mechanism selection, and constructing hard or worst-case instances to stress-test guarantees.

Later segments emphasize validation: state-of-the-art testing ideas, software checks on privacy settings, and workflows that generate candidate examples, rule out bad ones, and accelerate search. Benchmarking and timing of intermediate solutions appear as part of evaluating whether an automated pipeline can keep pace with realistic query workloads. The takeaway for practitioners is that private data release needs disciplined mechanism engineering—explicit objectives, testable privacy claims, and systematic search over mechanism size—not only textbook noise templates.

talks.title: Red Belly: a Deterministic Scalable Open Permissioned Blockchain
talks.teaser: Presents a leaderless, deterministic blockchain design that scales throughput through superblocks and sharded signature verification.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Red Belly, a blockchain designed around three goals: security under Byzantine failures with optimal resilience, fairness so that a correct user's transactions are committed even when a malicious user floods the system, and scalability that grows with the number of machines. It frames an "open" model in which any node can submit signed transactions, while block decisions are restricted to a set of temporarily permitted nodes.

The first technique removes the leader. Every replica proposes directly through a democratic BFT consensus, and transactions are ordered by their age in the mempool so the oldest are proposed first. To scale block decisions, the speaker proposes Set Byzantine Consensus, where the decided output is a non-conflicting union of the proposed sets, combined into one superblock. More participating nodes therefore mean more blocks decided per instance. The second technique shards signature verification: each transaction is checked by a subset of nodes, and f+1 matching answers establish validity, with extra checks when responses disagree.

The evaluation on AWS with 20 to 300 machines showed throughput rising with system size, with a peak near 660,000 transactions per second around 300 nodes, even though latency roughly doubled. Tests on geographically spread virtual machines found it outperforming a PBFT-based system, while HoneyBadger BFT runs became too slow beyond about 100 nodes. A 1000-VM deployment across four continents reported an average latency of about 3 seconds. The practical takeaway is that leaderless consensus, superblocks and verification sharding can let an open permissioned-style chain scale.

talks.title: Systematic Analysis of Randomization-based Protected Cache Architectures
talks.teaser: A generic prime-prune-probe technique undermines randomized cache defenses and shows why mapping design decides security.
talks.summary:
Modern CPUs rely on caches that speed up memory access but create timing side channels between programs. Randomized cache designs such as CEASER and Scatter Cache randomize set indexing and re-key periodically, and prior work argued attackers would need days or years of continuous probing to build useful eviction sets.

The presentation introduces prime-prune-probe, a general method to obtain partially congruent addresses and reliable generalized eviction sets despite randomization and partition selection. Applied to CEASER-S and Scatter Cache, the technique finds high-quality eviction sets within proposed re-keying windows, sharply reducing claimed security margins. An end-to-end demonstration against AES T-tables on an eight-megabyte sixteen-way last-level cache model recovers half-keys in minutes.

The talk closes with a mapping case study: a hardware-friendly linear Feistel round function yields key-independent shortcut equations, collapsing partial congruence back to full congruence across partitions. Practitioners should treat eviction-set construction and mapping instantiations as first-class design requirements, not parameters justified by older congruence-only analyses.

talks.title: DIANE: Identifying Fuzzing Triggers in Apps to Generate Under-constrained Inputs for IoT Devices
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding DIANE: Identifying Fuzzing Triggers in Apps to Generate Under-constrained Inputs for IoT Devices.

talks.title: "Many-out-of-Many" Proofs and Applications to Anonymous Zether
talks.teaser: Generalizes one-out-of-many proofs to hide sender and receiver indices in a private Ethereum payment contract.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the observation that standard cryptocurrencies such as Bitcoin lack privacy, and that earlier private payment systems focused mainly on keeping transactions small while neglecting the cost of running a wallet. Anonymous Zether instead stores encrypted account balances in one global table, so a wallet needs only a constant amount of data to check its balance or send funds, however long it was offline. A transfer names a ring of accounts including decoys, encrypts the balance changes, and attaches a zero-knowledge proof that the sender may spend, does not overdraw, and that every other account encrypts zero.

The core contribution is many-out-of-many proofs, a generalization of one-out-of-many proofs. Rather than hiding a single secret index, the prover shows that a secret, ordered subset of a committed list satisfies linear equations, while both the subset's contents and its order stay hidden. The construction commits to polynomials whose degree marks the secret position, then permutes the resulting vector to produce related evaluations. With shift permutations the operations form a circulant matrix that can be computed with the number theoretic transform. Proof size grows logarithmically with the anonymity set, while prover and verifier run time grows quasi-linearly. Examples include showing that a committed vector is a shifted basis vector without revealing the offset.

The speaker implemented anonymous Zether as a smart contract and reports performance comparable to standalone private payment cryptocurrencies. The main obstacle is gas use of around 7 million on Ethereum, which may make it prohibitive today, with later Ethereum versions suggested as a path to feasibility. The takeaway is that richer statements about committed vectors can be proven efficiently.

talks.title: Good Bot, Bad Bot: Characterizing Automated Browsing Activity
talks.teaser: Researchers deploy honeypot web apps worldwide to map bot traffic, TLS fingerprints, and gaps in public IP blocklists.
talks.summary:
Malicious and benign web bots dominate much of internet HTTP traffic, yet defenders struggle to label and study bot-only behavior on real sites mixed with human users. The presenters describe a honey-site platform that deploys full web applications on cloud instances worldwide, layered with browser, behavioral, and TLS stack fingerprinting, plus centralized log collection and analysis scripts.

Over seven months on one hundred quietly registered domains, the experiment captured tens of millions of requests from hundreds of thousands of unique addresses. Bots arrived via raw IP visits, domain-based discovery, or requests lacking host headers, and they concentrated on application-specific paths such as CMS login and admin endpoints. Traffic was split into benign, malicious, and gray intent; most requests looked malicious, public blocklists overlapped only a small fraction of those IPs, and many sources sat in residential rather than datacenter space. JavaScript ran on a tiny share of clients, while TLS fingerprints attributed far more activity and exposed widespread user-agent spoofing.

Practitioners should expect heavy daily bot noise even on obscure sites, treat fingerprinting beyond JavaScript as essential, and assume newly disclosed vulnerabilities draw exploitation within hours. The authors release their dataset for follow-on detection research.

talks.title: Hear “No Evil”, See “Kenansville”: Efficient and Transferable Black-Box Attacks on Automatic ...
talks.teaser: Presents an untargeted black-box attack that subtly alters audio to fool speech recognition and speaker identification systems.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces an untargeted attack on voice systems, where an audio clip is perturbed so that a human still hears the original command while a speech model outputs something other than it. The speaker explains why existing adversarial audio work, mostly targeted and white-box, is slow, does not transfer between models and breaks under noisy telephony channels. Use cases mentioned include evading transcription bots, telephony surveillance and content ID systems.

The attack targets the feature extraction stage instead of the model itself. It uses a discrete Fourier transform and a binary search over intensity thresholds to remove low-intensity frequencies, which the speaker argues the human ear largely ignores but the model relies on. Perturbation can be applied at word or phoneme granularity, and because voice models are context-dependent, changing a single vowel can corrupt a long stretch of the transcript. In one example, altering one vowel in "no evil" made Google's speech API output a different phrase, and a cosine similarity of about 0.8 was reported for a vowel change against Google.

The speaker reports that the attack needs less than 15 queries per adversarial sample and works against speech recognition and speaker recognition models in black-box settings. A listener study found transcription accuracy of about 98% for benign clips and about 96% for attack clips, suggesting audio quality is largely preserved. The takeaway is that protecting the model alone is not enough, since the signal-processing front end is a practical attack surface for any voice pipeline.

talks.title: ConDySTA: Context-Aware Dynamic Supplement to Static Taint Analysis
talks.teaser: Merges dynamic Android tests with context-matched static taint analysis to find missed privacy leaks and cut context false positives.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with how taint analysis tracks sensitive data from sources such as passwords or device identifiers to sinks like files or SMS APIs, and why purely static Android analyzers both over-report infeasible paths and under-report when flows cross third-party servers, dynamically loaded code, or other opaque regions.

The prior DySTA design instruments String-returning methods, rebuilds smali into test APKs, drives exploration with Monkey and adb, logs return values against a user profile to label intermediate sources, then feeds those sources into FlowDroid. ConDySTA adds calling-context matching so an intermediate source counts only when the dynamic call stack aligns with FlowDroid’s static context, avoiding leaks flagged when the same method returns benign data on other paths.

Evaluation on ReproDroid reports twelve additional taint flows missed by six bundled static tools, all judged true positives spanning native code, reflection, and intents. On forty-three apps with known safe flows, ConDySTA eliminates nine context-related false positives from DySTA. On one hundred Play Store apps it finds thirty-nine extra flows in twelve applications, including remote round-trips and cache read-backs.

talks.title: A Decentralized and Encrypted National Gun Registry
talks.teaser: Presents a design for a decentralized, encrypted national gun registry built on two-party computation and structured encryption.
talks.summary:
The talk presents a proposed federal bill for a voluntary national gun registry that keeps data encrypted and under local control. The speaker explains that tracing a firearm today is slow, often taking four to seven business days, and that the 1968 firearm owner protection act rules out a centralized registry but not a decentralized one. The team was asked whether such a design could work across the United States and whether the bill's requirements could map to concrete cryptographic protections.

Each county designates an official who holds a key, and that key encrypts the county's license and registration records in its own database. State servers only store and serve these encrypted databases. A global directory maps serial numbers to county IDs and is protected with structured encryption, with two custodians jointly generating query tokens through two-party computation so that no single party learns the query. Local queries follow a similar protocol, and officials can rate limit by refusing to decrypt large result sets. The threat model assumes semi-honest parties.

The team built the protocol end to end and tested it against an estimated 400 million guns. A directory insert took 377 milliseconds and a lookup averaged 247 milliseconds, both independent of directory size. Adding 100,000 records to a local database took under four minutes, and the directory would need 110 gigabytes of storage. The talk ends by noting possible misuse of such data by law enforcement and urging clear policy limits on what data can be collected before any deployment.

talks.title: Cross-Domain Access Control Encryption -- Arbitrary-policy, Constant-size, Efficient
talks.teaser: Presents a practical cross-domain access control encryption scheme with constant-size ciphertexts for arbitrary policies.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces cross-domain access control encryption, a variant where a central authority issues encryption keys and a separate receiver authority issues decryption keys. It targets malicious writers who might leak secrets through their own outgoing traffic, so cryptography enforces which senders can reach which receivers. A sanitizer rewrites ciphertexts in transit while remaining honest but curious.

Earlier constructions either replicated single-user schemes, which needs exponentially many copies for arbitrary policies, or relied on heavyweight functional encryption for general circuits. The proposed scheme represents the recipient set as one group element, called an aggregator, and combines structure-preserving signatures with identity-based broadcast encryption. Senders prepare a sanitization-ready ciphertext with proofs of well-formedness, so the sanitizer can work without any key and the ciphertext size stays constant. The cost is that encryption needs all other recipients, so a recipient can infer the central authority, a weaker anonymity notion the speaker considers sufficient.

The prototype uses a 462-bit BN curve without preprocessing. Setup, encryption key generation and decryption helper runtime grows linearly with the number of receivers, while other steps stay constant, and all run in seconds even for a thousand receivers. Security is selective, matching prior work, with adaptive security left open. The speaker closes by flagging post-quantum constructions as a remaining open problem.

talks.title: Birds of a Feather: A Hardware & Security Panel (Updated)
talks.teaser: Two academics argue whether fuzzing or formal verification is the better single method for finding security flaws.
talks.summary:
This lunchtime debate asks a practical question: if a team can use only one method to validate security, should it pick fuzzing or formal verification? The first speaker argues for formal verification, describing it as an umbrella of techniques including theorem proving, model checking, type systems and symbolic execution. The main point is that writing down security properties forces designers to clarify their security policy, so any counterexample points to a violation that already matters. The speaker adds that properties such as non-interference and speculative execution leaks can be checked formally, while random inputs may miss them.

The second speaker defends fuzzing as easy to run and easy to scale, noting that large vendors dedicate fleets of servers to it and that coverage-guided tools have found large numbers of bugs. The speaker raises the limits of formal methods, including scalability to large codebases and the gap between a verified model and real hardware, where side-channel attacks on commodity CPUs still apply. Both sides agree that the approaches work best together, for example when a fuzzer falls back on symbolic execution and an SMT solver to get past inputs that brute force cannot reach.

In rebuttals and audience questions, the first speaker argues that a flood of fuzzing reports is hard to triage, and that a small set of security-relevant counterexamples is more useful. Both speakers also acknowledge that formal tools need better usability and clearer output. For practitioners, the first speaker suggests symbolic execution as a low-barrier starting point, while the second suggests AFL++ as an accessible fuzzing framework. The closing takeaways contrast understanding a system through formal reasoning with finding bugs quickly through fuzzing.

talks.title: Panel 2
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Panel 2.
talks.summary: Ginger Wright of Idaho National Laboratory moderates an IEEE industry roundtable on how COVID-19 strained cyber supply chains and remote-work security. Diana Kelley describes Microsoft’s global work-from-home pivot, VPN and split-tunnel bottlenecks, COVID-themed phishing lures, and human-operated ransomware against hospitals. Nadia Bartol discusses BCG consultants’ remote collaboration, home-network guidance, and a deflected colleague-security survey. Dr. Gail Pomper explains Dreamport’s unclassified outreach, CMMC education going virtual, and integrating security into acquisition tiers. The panel closes on board-level cyber risk, IT–OT culture gaps, SDL practices, and certification frameworks like CMMC and IEC 62443.

talks.title: Panel 1
talks.teaser: Panelists examine provenance, microelectronics risk, and adaptable manufacturing for securing digitized global supply chains.
talks.summary:
The session opens with commodity and drone examples showing how one compromised overseas Wi‑Fi component can cascade into full system hijack, then broadens to multi‑tier networks, Industry 4.0 digitization, cloud and IoT exposure, and pandemic-era PPE flows that mix economic and political bottlenecks. Four panelists give position statements: adaptive, digitally integrated manufacturing with diversified suppliers, stockpiles, and component-level digital passports; near–real-time provenance and AI-enabled facilities beyond single “silver bullet” ledgers; historical supply-chain subversion and limits of isolation, including trusted-foundry ideas and game-theoretic risk framing via PRESTIGE; and permissioned distributed ledgers for traceability with tier‑two participation, IP, and privacy trade-offs.

Prepared and audience questions span hardware versus software commonalities, blockchain energy and geography concerns, contract liability, transparency versus trade secrets, bills of materials, counterfeits, workforce education, and quantifying risk under uncertainty. Closing prompts ask for one forward-looking metric; panelists highlight adaptability or agility, defined resilience, faster fault localization, quantitative risk assessment, and reduced counterfeits.

Practitioners should treat supply chains as opaque, adversary-rich attack surfaces where isolation alone fails, and invest in traceability, adaptable security instrumentation across supplier granularities, and measurable trust—not only efficiency.

talks.title: Identifying Ubiquitious Third Party Libraries in Compiled Executables Using Annotated and Translated
talks.teaser: Explains how function fingerprints from disassembled firmware reveal which open-source libraries and versions a device ships with.
talks.summary:
Jed Hale, a lead cybersecurity researcher at Idaho National Laboratory, presents research from a Department of Energy funded project aimed at defending embedded systems used in energy delivery, such as relays and smart meters. He frames firmware as an operating system assembled from many vendor and third-party components, where knowing which libraries are inside matters for vulnerability research and risk. A toolset for annotated and translated disassembled code analyzes binaries and stores the results in a graph database.

A motivating case involved BusyBox, which used an OpenNTP daemon with a vulnerability disclosed in 2009. The patched library did not reach BusyBox builds until 2016. To study this, the team compiled BusyBox releases across 14 architectures, two compilers and four optimization settings, producing about 2000 binaries. Each function was represented as a vector of counts of VEX intermediate-language instructions summed from its blocks. Plain matching of these vectors proved too imprecise because different functions collided, while classic classifiers and a convolutional neural network identified libraries and labeled functions with good accuracy.

The talk closed with limits and next steps. Supervised labels are unavailable for many closed platforms, classifiers cannot recognize code outside their training set, and the same source yields different counts on ARM and x86. The team is moving toward learned feature representations, cosine similarity lookup, transformer models, and symbolic and dynamic analysis. For practitioners, the takeaway is that automated enumeration of components can feed vulnerability database queries at scale, and the team is extending the approach to malware.

talks.title: Toward a Trustable, Self Hosting Computer System
talks.teaser: Shows an FPGA computer that rebuilds its own bitstream and software from source, judging trust by code instead of supply chain.
talks.summary:
Gabriel Sawa argues that judging hardware by who makes it and where is becoming an unreliable proxy for trust. He walks through the attack surface, from fabrication-time Trojans that insert about twenty transistors into a CPU die, to subverted design tools and bugs in source code. His alternative is to make trust a question about source code that the system owner can inspect and rebuild.

The core of the work is a self-hosting environment that extends down to the FPGA bitstream. Starting from a host Linux system, diverse double compilation checks that the C compiler and cross compiler are clean, and then the hardware toolchains and the target's kernel, libraries and compiler are built. The resulting clean-room target can rebuild its own bitstream and software. The prototype runs on a Lattice ECP5 FPGA using open-source toolchains and a RISC-V core, and it runs a RISC-V port of Fedora Linux. It is slow, about a third as fast as an original mid-1990s Pentium, which the speaker attributes to a low-end FPGA and to inefficient integration between the core and peripherals.

Scope limits include trust in RAM, which was left out, and the one-time bitstream load at boot, which is treated like firmware integrity. In the Q&A, the speaker noted that FPGA experiments reflect behaviour above register transfer logic but not silicon-level attacks. His takeaway is that buyers should demand full source so owners can field-strip and rebuild safety- and security-critical systems, and that the source bundle could be analysed with formal methods.

talks.title: On-Chip Randomization for Memory Protection Against Hardware Supply Chain Attacks to DRAM
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning On-Chip Randomization for Memory Protection Against Hardware Supply Chain Attacks to DRAM.
talks.summary: Brett Meadows proposes on-chip key registers that scramble DRAM addresses and data per power session, purging in nanoseconds to thwart cold-boot retention and row-hammer fingerprinting. Open-source SPICE simulations show faster erase than rewriting entire arrays and self-healing mappings after each boot.

talks.title: Binary Analysis with Architecture and Code Section Detection Using Supervised Machine Learning
talks.teaser: Presents a supervised machine learning tool that predicts binary architecture, endianness and code location from byte histograms.
talks.summary:
The talk presents a tool built at Idaho National Laboratory that applies supervised machine learning to compiled binaries before reverse engineering begins. Malicious code can reach both IT networks and operational technology, where firmware in water, power and gas systems is updated rarely, so the consequences can be severe. Identifying a file's architecture and where its code lives is the first step toward disassembly.

Each file is turned into a normalized byte histogram, which counts every byte value, and an endianness flag is added based on which multi-byte patterns dominate. Eight models were trained on binaries compiled for several architectures. Even with a partial file, an SVM model reached about 80 percent accuracy using only 20 percent of the original binary. Removing high-entropy regions, such as encrypted or compressed data, and low-entropy padding raised accuracy from 80 to 82 percent. To locate code, overlapping chunks of a larger firmware image were classified separately, and regions where the models agreed marked where instructions were concentrated.

Two firmware examples showed agreement on ARM64 in one case and PowerPC in another. Packed or compressed files were identified as a limitation, since they must be unpacked before the method can classify them. The speaker described the work as a proof of concept where speed was not optimized, with possible extensions including new architectures, a user interface and multithreading. The takeaway is that knowing a file's contents before or after it enters a network helps decide whether to admit it and how to recover.

talks.title: Modeling and Assessment of IoT Supply Chain Security Risks
talks.teaser: Shows how modeling errors in supplier structure can shift IoT supply chain risk more than uniform probability errors.
talks.summary:
The talk presents a method for system-level risk analysis of IoT supply chains, where a product's security depends on its own components and on the suppliers behind them. The model is graph-based: component and supplier nodes are linked by AND or OR logic describing how a component's security relies on its dependencies. A compromised supplier is assumed to compromise everything it supplies. Minimal cut sets, the smallest node combinations that reach an attack goal, are combined with per-node compromise probabilities to produce a risk value.

Since resources are limited, the work separates structural uncertainty, whether components and suppliers were understood correctly, from parametric uncertainty, whether the probabilities are right. Hypothetical mistakes of each kind were introduced and the change in risk measured. In a 25-node example with 53 minimal cut sets and every node at 0.05, baseline system risk was 40 percent. Flipping one node's logic type raised risk by about 0.15, and nodes nearer the attack goal mattered most. Omitting a high-level component lowered risk, while misplacing an edge caused only a slight increase.

Uniform overestimation of all probabilities produced a steady, linear rise in risk. Matching the effect of the single logic error would need roughly a 50 percent error across every probability. The presenter concludes with two practices: prioritize nodes closer to the attack goal, and get structure right before refining magnitudes. Q&A touched on weighting nodes by traffic data and testing redundancy for resilience.

talks.title: Birds of a Feather: Sharing Cybersecurity Research Artifacts To Accelerate Progress
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Birds of a Feather: Sharing Cybersecurity Research Artifacts To Accelerate Progress.
talks.summary: An NSF-backed birds-of-a-feather argues cybersecurity needs packaging, hosting, and support processes so labs can share reproducible datasets and tools without legal blockers from sensitive sponsor data.

talks.title: 3rd Deep Learning and Security Workshop Part IV
talks.teaser: A workshop covers enterprise adversarial ML readiness, lip-reading and k-NN attacks, sticker defenses, and patch detection.
talks.summary:
The session opens with an industry study based on interviews with 28 organizations, pairing machine learning engineers with security analysts. Despite hype around adversarial machine learning, only six large or government entities dedicate engineering headcount, while most teams lack tools and updated incident-response playbooks. Respondents rank data poisoning, model stealing, and model inversion above physical-domain evasion, and many analysts wrongly assume frameworks such as Keras or TensorFlow ship hardened against manipulation.

Subsequent papers walk through concrete attack and defense research. One group applies FGSM, iterative FGSM, and Carlini–Wagner optimization against LipNet on the GRID lip-reading corpus, achieving targeted mis-transcriptions with roughly 97.5–99.7% visual similarity. Another introduces a gradient-based, hinge-loss formulation to approximate minimum-norm adversarial examples for k-nearest neighbor classifiers and k-NN layers atop neural networks, scaling to larger k in minutes where quadratic-program baselines explode in cost; re-evaluation shows several published k-NN defenses look robust only under weaker attacks.

The closing presentations target localized physical threats. Clipped BagNet limits sticker influence by clipping patch logits before averaging and supports certified robustness for fixed sticker positions on ImageNet. SentiNet uses Grad-CAM masks, overlay tests, and curve fitting on flip rate versus confidence under random replacements to detect Trojan, backdoor, and adversarial-patch mechanisms without training on known attack samples, reporting high detection rates while discussing adaptive adversary limits and inference overhead.

talks.title: 3rd Deep Learning and Security Workshop Part III
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for 3rd Deep Learning and Security Workshop Part III.

talks.title: 3rd Deep Learning and Security Workshop Part II

talks.title: 3rd Deep Learning and Security Workshop Part I
talks.teaser: Opens the third Deep Learning and Security Workshop and features a keynote on shortcut learning behind adversarial examples.
talks.summary:
This session opens the third Deep Learning and Security Workshop in San Francisco. The chairs outline the programme: 33 submitted papers, 11 accepted (about 32%), four paper sessions, and two keynotes. Attendees submit questions in a chat, authors answer some right after each roughly 20-minute talk, and follow-up discussion moves to a per-paper Slack channel. Sponsor and related events are mentioned briefly.

The first keynote argues that adversarial examples are one symptom of a wider set of machine vision failures, all linked by shortcut learning. Networks trained on ImageNet lean on texture where humans rely on shape, shown with cue-conflict images that combine one object's shape with another's texture. A patch-based experiment showed that small image patches, with no larger spatial structure, could reach high accuracy on the task. Training on stylised images raised shape bias and improved robustness to some corruptions. The speaker also checked several proposed defences against whether they change the data, objective, architecture or learning algorithm, which is what shifts what a network learns. Adversarial training and Lipschitz constraints did, while others that left the learned features unchanged were broken.

The takeaway for practitioners is that no single architectural change is likely to fix adversarial robustness. Defences should be judged by whether they shift the features a model relies on. The Q&A touched on interpretability tools, scaling to larger datasets, and neuro-symbolic models, with the speaker noting that scale alone may not remove context biases.

talks.title: How Not to Prove Your Election Outcome
talks.teaser: Shows how trapdoor Pedersen commitments and a Fiat–Shamir flaw let mix servers forge shuffle and decryption proofs in Swiss e-voting.
talks.summary:
The presentation walks through Switzerland’s long-running internet voting stack, which promised complete verifiability via voter code sheets, control components, and mix servers that publish cryptographic proofs of honest shuffling and partial decryption. When source code became available during certification aimed at full cantonal use, reviewers found that stated assumptions were not enough to guarantee an honest election outcome.

The first issue sits in the shuffle proof’s Pedersen commitments: documentation showed H was derived as a known power of G, embedding a discrete-log trapdoor that lets a cheater open commitments arbitrarily. A short code change could exploit this while producing transcripts indistinguishable from valid proofs, fully breaking the chancellery’s verifiability requirement. Separately, the decryption proof applied the Fiat–Shamir heuristic without hashing the first ElGamal ciphertext element, allowing a malicious mix component to craft false equality-of-discrete-log proofs—sometimes with help from a cheating client—while verification still passes.

Practitioners should treat non-interactive zero-knowledge schemes as assumption-heavy: parameter generation, challenge derivation, and claimed properties must be proved, not hoped for. The talk contrasts Switzerland’s open evaluation—which paused May 2019 elections—with New South Wales deployments under secrecy laws, arguing transparency and independent review matter as much as the underlying mix-net mathematics.

talks.title: The Last Mile: High-Assurance and High-Speed Cryptographic Implementations
talks.teaser: Jasmin links fast crypto to certified compilation and proofs for correctness, constant-time behavior, and security.
talks.summary:
The presentation addresses a tension in cryptographic libraries: implementations must run fast, resist side-channel attacks, and still admit formal security guarantees. Optimizations and constant-time idioms complicate verification, and prior combined approaches often sacrificed performance.

The team presents Jasmin, a low-level language for efficient routines with explicit control over registers, loops, and x86 features including SIMD. A certified compiler preserves program behavior from source to assembly, and EasyCrypt-backed infrastructure supports proofs of functional correctness, cryptographic security, and constant-time properties. A stepwise methodology rewrites specifications into imperative form and chains equivalence proofs through many small hops, illustrated on ChaCha20 vectorization and TLS 1.3 components such as ChaCha20 and Poly1305, with benchmarks showing Jasmin near hand-tuned OpenSSL assembly.

Practitioners gain a model for marrying performance with assurance: certified compilation need not slow code when programmers control generated assembly, extensible instruction support matters for vectorized paths, and reusable proof steps can amortize work across primitives, including ongoing post-quantum case studies.

talks.title: Throwing Darts in the Dark? Detecting Bots with Limited Data using Neural Data Augmentation
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Throwing Darts in the Dark? Detecting Bots with Limited Data using Neural Data Augmentation.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Presented by Steve on behalf of a research collaboration between the University of Illinois, Virginia Tech, and Shape Security, this talk focuses on developing machine learning (ML) models for cybersecurity when labeled data is scarce. Using bot detection as a primary case study—covering threats like account takeover and web scraping—the presentation addresses three major challenges: the scarcity of ground-truth labels, concept drift caused by evolving attacker behavior, and the poor generalizability of highly customized domain features across different web services.

### Key Topics
- **Hybrid Bot Detection Strategy:** The architecture prioritizes rule-based detection for high-precision, low-cost coverage of common bots, deploying machine learning specifically to catch advanced bots that evade static rules by mutating their behavior.
- **Frequency-Based Feature Encoding:** Replacing raw application-specific features with generic network features (e.g., URL, cookie, browser), converted dynamically into frequency distributions using cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) over a sliding window.
- **Neural Data Augmentation:** A specialized dual-generator Generative Adversarial Network (GAN) architecture tailored for security contexts where benign data is representative, but malicious data is scarce, biased, and rapidly shifting.

### Technical Details
- **Dataset & Ground Truth:** The research evaluated 23 million network requests collected across three distinct websites (A, B, and C) spanning three months of data over a one-year period. Ground-truth labels were primarily established via user CAPTCHA interactions.
- **Feature Processing:** To avoid raw string dependencies and generalize across services, features are encoded based on frequency percentiles in an empirical CDF. A daily sliding window updates the distribution dynamically to handle unseen items and concept drift in real time.
- **Data Synthesis Architecture:** Standard GANs merely mimic existing samples, which fails against adapting bots. The proposed method splits malicious samples into clusters and outliers using DBSCAN:
  1. *Cluster Data Synthesis:* Synthesizes data near existing bot clusters by expanding boundaries cautiously, becoming less aggressive near benign data regions.
  2. *Outlier Data Synthesis:* Aggressively synthesizes data outward in the complementary space outside benign regions to anticipate future bot variants.
  3. *Discriminator Role:* Functions as the downstream classifier trained to differentiate benign users from both real and synthetic malicious bots.

### Takeaways
- **Rule and ML Complementarity:** Rule-based detection captured roughly 80% of bots, while adding the ML pipeline boosted detection to over 90%.
- **Robustness Under Extreme Label Scarcity:** When trained on just 1% of labeled data, the proposed method achieved F1 scores comparable to an LSTM trained on 100% of labeled data across evaluated services.
- **Mitigating Long-Term Model Decay:** Evaluating a model trained in August 2018 on data from January and September 2019 demonstrated that periodic model retraining with only 1% of new data per month effectively restores detection performance.

talks.title: Meddling Middlemen: Empirical Analysis of the Risks of Data-Saving Mobile Browsers
talks.teaser: Researchers empirically test nine data-saving mobile browsers on compression claims, bot detection, privacy leaks, and proxy security flaws.
talks.summary:
Smartphone users increasingly rely on data-saving mobile browsers that route traffic through cloud proxy servers to compress pages and cut cellular usage. The presentation outlines how that architecture interrupts end-to-end HTTPS, introduces gateway and endpoint proxy tiers, and forces users to trust operators with decrypted web traffic.

The team identified nine Play Store browsers that truly proxied requests, mapped large endpoint fleets with nmap, and measured savings on Alexa top sites and YouTube. Average compression fell near fifty percent rather than marketed ninety percent, and video often saved nothing. Shared proxy IPs correlated with lower reCAPTCHA v3 scores and demonstrated proof-of-concept IP reputation harm. Privacy testing found header stripping on Opera, device identifier exfiltration, outdated proxy software on several vendors, weaker cipher offerings with savings enabled, and Opera accepting certificates signed with the public Superfish key until disclosure.

Practitioners should treat data-saving mode as a security and privacy trade-off, not a benign optimization. The speakers argue for a redesigned model that loads primary HTML over direct HTTPS while proxying only bulky multimedia to preserve savings with less exposure.

talks.title: SEVurity: No Security Without Integrity
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of SEVurity: No Security Without Integrity - Breaking Integrity.

talks.title: Tactical Provenance Analysis our Endpoint Detection and Response Systems
talks.teaser: Shows how linking related EDR alerts into provenance graphs ranks true attacks higher and reduces log storage.
talks.summary:
The talk covers endpoint detection and response (EDR) tools, which collect system logs and raise alerts by matching events against MITRE ATT&CK techniques. The speaker argues these alerts are noisy, because techniques such as file deletion also occur in normal activity, so real intrusions get buried among false alarms. Analysts must also rebuild the chain of events behind each alert by hand, and short log retention can erase evidence from long campaigns.

To address this, the team presents RapSheet, which builds provenance graphs from system logs and alerts. For each alert, it traces backward through ancestry to find the first suspicious process, then orders causally related alerts by timestamp into a tactical provenance graph. Alerts are scored with MITRE severity and exploit likelihood, and a graph's score multiplies the alerts that follow the MITRE kill chain order. A separate log reduction scheme prunes stored logs while keeping the ability to link alerts.

The evaluation used a Symantec EDR deployment configured with 67 MITRE techniques and about 40 million events from 34 hosts. Of 58,000 alerts, 1,000 came from two attacks and 57,000 were false alarms. The pipeline produced 5 provenance graphs for true attacks and 676 for false alarms, and the true-attack graphs ranked higher. Using a threshold at the lowest-scoring true-attack graph would remove 98% of false alarms from consideration, and the 63% log reduction raised host buffer capacity. The takeaway is that provenance can strengthen commercial EDR triage and storage.

talks.title: SAVIOR: Towards Bug-Driven Hybrid Testing
talks.teaser: A bug-driven hybrid fuzzing framework steers testing toward sanitizer sites and uses symbolic execution to trigger violations efficiently.
talks.summary:
Coverage-guided fuzzing and concolic execution are often combined into hybrid testers that chase new branches and lines. The speaker argues that optimizing for code coverage alone can miss real defects—integer overflows may sit on already-covered lines—and can waste almost all cycles on code that rarely harbors bugs, echoing historically low industry defect densities.

SAVIOR replaces coverage-first guidance with bug-driven hybrid testing. At compile time it instruments targets with sanitizers, builds an interprocedural control-flow graph, and annotates basic blocks with counts of reachable sanitizer sites. At runtime a coordinator prioritizes fuzzer seeds by those bug-potential scores, then uses active property checking and SMT solving to satisfy bug-triggering conditions once sanitizer locations are reached. Scheduling also learns from past solver failures to avoid futile inputs.

Evaluations on LAVA-M and a real-world suite compare SAVIOR with AFL, AFLGo, Angora, and other hybrid tools. It reports roughly twice as many LAVA-M bugs, hundreds of sanitizer hits with many confirmed true positives and acknowledged fixes, and on average about 44.3% more bugs than the next-best tool in 24 hours despite modest coverage gains. Practitioners are invited to try the open-source release and treat sanitizer reachability as a practical proxy when hunting logic and undefined-behavior flaws.

talks.title: Measuring Legal Compliance of Banners from IAB Europe's Transparancy and Consent Framework
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Measuring Legal Compliance of Banners from IAB Europe's Transparancy and Consent Framework.

talks.title: FlyClient: Super-Light Clients for Cryptocurrencies
talks.teaser: FlyClient uses Merkle mountain ranges and randomized proof-of-work sampling so mobile wallets sync chains with megabytes, not gigabytes.
talks.summary:
Growing proof-of-work chains outpace what phones can download or verify. Full nodes must handle hundreds of gigabytes or more, while classic SPV clients shrink storage to headers yet still grow linearly with every block—roughly tens of megabytes on Bitcoin and multiple gigabytes on Ethereum, which breaks multi-chain and mobile use cases. Prior NiPoPoW constructions offer sublinear proofs but struggle with changing difficulty and can lose efficiency under adversarial conditions.

FlyClient restructures the chain header so each block commits to prior blocks through a Merkle mountain range, letting a client hold only the latest header yet reach arbitrarily old blocks with logarithmic hashes. To pick the honest chain without downloading all headers, the design assumes the adversary controls a known fraction of mining power and samples block headers at positions chosen from an optimized distribution. Invalid work on a forked chain appears as gaps; constant queries yield cryptographically small cheating probability, and recursive narrowing localizes forks before a short manual tail check.

Weighted Merkle trees extend the same sampling to variable difficulty, and Fiat–Shamir randomness makes proofs non-interactive. Reported Ethereum parameters land near 3.5 megabytes even under conservative adversary settings, versus about 2.2 gigabytes for conventional SPV, with growth staying logarithmic as history lengthens. The speaker notes practical deployments and paths that avoid hard forks by embedding the structure in transactions or contracts.

talks.title: KARONTE: Detecting Insecure Multi-binary Interactions in Embedded Firmware
talks.teaser: Shows how a static analysis tool traces user input across firmware binaries to surface bugs that single-binary analysis misses.
talks.summary:
Many IoT devices run Linux-based firmware, which the talk puts at 86% of samples, but they mix different CPU architectures and custom peripheral code, which makes dynamic testing hard. Existing static tools usually examine one binary at a time, and that approach can produce many false positives when a value that looks dangerous was already validated by another program. The talk presents Karonte, which follows user input from network-facing binaries into the other programs that receive it through shared channels such as environment variables, files, and sockets.

The pipeline unpacks each image with Binwalk and scores functions by how much they resemble network-facing parsers, using basic blocks, comparisons, branches and network-related references. Binaries with the highest scores become border binaries, and the tool links setter and getter binaries that share a data key. When a key is unknown, for example in stripped binaries, a generic module assumes the key is used as an index. Constraints are carried from setter to getter, and a taint engine built on BootStomp checks whether tainted data reaches memcpy-like sinks unsafely.

On 53 recent firmware samples from seven vendors, the analysis raised 87 alerts, and 51 were true positives, 34 of which were found because data was propagated across binaries. Investigating the alerts revealed 46 previously unknown bugs and five already known ones, all disclosed to vendors. In a larger run over 899 samples, nearly 40% were multi-binary, and in a random review of 100 alerts, 44 showed user data reaching a sink and 30 were multi-binary vulnerabilities. About 80% of samples were analyzed within a day. The takeaway is that firmware auditing should follow data across binary boundaries rather than inspecting each program in isolation.

talks.title: Krace: Data Race Fuzzing for Kernel File Systems
talks.teaser: Introduces a fuzzer that tracks cross-thread interleavings alongside code coverage to find data races in Linux kernel file systems.
talks.summary:
Data races happen when threads access the same memory location without locking or ordering, and at least one of those accesses is a write. The talk argues that the Linux kernel, and file systems such as Btrfs with many concurrent background threads, is a likely place for such bugs. Conventional kernel fuzzers rely on code coverage and usually notice only memory errors that crash the kernel. Data races often return a wrong error code without crashing anything, so a separate race checker is needed to flag them.

The talk presents Krace, which adds a second coverage dimension to fuzzing. Edge coverage alone cannot distinguish runs that hit the same branches in different thread orders. Tracking every instruction-level ordering is infeasible, so the tool records only cross-thread write-to-read pairs on shared addresses, which fit in a small bitmap. An interleaving generator injects delays before shared memory accesses to shift which thread defines a value another thread reads. Seeds that reach new bits are kept for further mutation. On Btrfs, concurrency coverage sometimes kept growing after edge coverage leveled off, and the approach also reached slightly more edge coverage than the baseline fuzzer.

Across Btrfs, ext4 and the virtual file system layer, the authors reported 23 bugs, at least 11 of which were confirmed as harmful. The effects included information loss, violated invariants, kernel crashes and performance degradation. The main takeaway is that for highly concurrent code, coverage should capture thread interactions as well as control flow. Future work includes structured input generation, seed selection and applying the approach to other applications.

talks.title: TRRespass: Exploiting the Many Sides of Target Row Refresh
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for TRRespass: Exploiting the Many Sides of Target Row Refresh.

talks.title: Fuzzing JavaScript Engines with Aspect-Preserving Mutation
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Fuzzing JavaScript Engines with Aspect-Preserving Mutation.

talks.title: xMP: Selective Memory Protection for Kernel and User Space
talks.teaser: Outlines Intel-backed memory domains and pointer binding that let Linux isolate sensitive data from data-oriented attacks.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with data-oriented attacks that corrupt non-control data while leaving control flow intact, making them hard to spot and citing Heartbleed as a case where sensitive data left the process without obvious traces. The speakers argue that practical operating-system primitives are needed to block read and write gadgets built from ordinary memory corruption.

They introduce selective memory protection (XMP) built on Intel second-level address translation and fast EPT view switching, without relying on a full hypervisor for policy. Three primitives partition sensitive regions into disjoint domains, enforce fine-grained permissions by switching LP2M-style views, and authenticate pointers with truncated SipHash HMACs bound to immutable context. The design is carried into Linux via buddy and slab allocators, thread state, new system calls for user-space isolation, and protections for page tables and credential structures; a prototype is demonstrated using Xen’s LP2M subsystem mainly to reduce engineering cost.

Evaluation on a Linux guest measures modest overhead on micro and macro benchmarks, including combined protections and many XMP namespaces for container-style isolation. Practitioners gain a model for coupling virtualization hardware to selective isolation of high-value kernel and user data, with part of the prototype released as open source.

talks.title: RAMBleed: Reading Bits in Memory without Accessing Them
talks.teaser: Shows how Rowhammer bit flips can leak RSA key bits from OpenSSH across security domains, even on ECC memory.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces RAMBleed, a technique that lets an unprivileged process read bits stored in memory it has no permission to access. Because DRAM places cells from different security domains next to each other, repeatedly activating neighbouring rows can flip bits in a victim row, and the flip pattern depends on the values stored around it. By hammering rows it owns and observing whether a middle bit flips, an attacker can infer the secret bits in the adjacent rows.

To make this practical, the speaker walks through an end-to-end attack on OpenSSH. The attacker uses a Linux allocator technique to exhaust small blocks until it obtains physically contiguous memory with a known DRAM layout, then applies a frame feng shui method to steer the server's RSA signing key into chosen frames by opening TCP connections to the daemon. In the demonstration, the attack recovered about 68% of a 2048-bit RSA key at roughly 0.3 bits per second with 82% accuracy. A probabilistic key-recovery algorithm then reconstructed the full key within a couple of hours.

The talk closes with ECC memory. ECC corrects flipped bits, but the correction path causes large read latency spikes that an attacker can time to detect a flip, so ECC slows the attack without stopping it. The takeaway is that Rowhammer threatens confidentiality as well as integrity, and that ECC alone does not prevent cross-domain data leakage.

talks.title: SoK: Understanding the Prevailing Security Vulnerabilities in TrustZone-Assisted TEE Systems
talks.teaser: Surveys over 200 reported TrustZone TEE vulnerabilities, sorting them into architecture, implementation and hardware flaws.
talks.summary:
TrustZone-based Trusted Execution Environments run on many mobile devices and protect items such as DRM and Android keystore data, yet attacks keep succeeding. The speaker's team collected over 200 reported vulnerabilities from CVE databases, proprietary sources, papers, online posts and repository history. They found that every major TEE had been compromised at some point, and that all secure software layers were affected.

The vulnerabilities fall into architecture, implementation and hardware classes. Architectural examples include a Widevine trusted application in one Qualcomm release exposing 70 commands, a Trustonic fingerprint driver reachable from almost every trusted application, and a Qualcomm system call that maps normal-world memory. Implementation examples include an overflow check in ARM Trusted Firmware that failed on 32-bit builds, a page table setting that made read-only pages executable, and an OP-TEE race between two trusted applications using the file system. On the hardware side, energy settings can be pushed to inject faults, and caches are shared between the worlds.

Attackers typically start in the normal world, reach a privileged driver, then pick a large trusted application and look for a flaw that gives them normal-world or trusted OS access. The talk ends by reviewing proposed mitigations, including isolated environments, encrypted memory, memory-safe languages, formal verification and hardwired safe voltage limits. The takeaway is that commercial TEE implementations deserve closer scrutiny.

talks.title: TARDIS: Rolling Back the Clock on CMS-Targeting Cyber Attacks
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding TARDIS: Rolling Back the Clock on CMS-Targeting Cyber Attacks.

talks.title: Efficient and Secure Multiparty Computation from Fixed-Key Block Ciphers
talks.teaser: Shows how fixed-key AES can securely and efficiently instantiate the hash functions used in MPC protocols.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at the bottom layer of secure multiparty computation: the concrete primitives that protocols rely on when they are actually implemented. Protocols such as garbled circuits and oblivious transfer extension depend on hash functions, usually modeled as random oracles and applied to short inputs, and implementations often swap in fast choices without careful analysis. The speaker compares costs: with batching, fixed-key AES needs about ten cycles per call, while SHA-based hashing is far slower.

The speaker then reviews existing constructions. Passive and active OT extension rely on correlation robustness, and the only known secure instantiation of that property uses a random oracle. Half-gates garbling relies on a circular variant that cannot be proven secure in the random permutation model, even though many implementations use fixed-key AES for it. The work formalizes correlation robustness and a tweakable variant, then shows that a simple fixed-key AES-based construction, π(x) XOR x, is correlation robust in the random permutation model. The resulting birthday-type bound is matched by an attack, so the proof is tight. Circular and tweakable versions are covered by similar results.

The takeaway is that fixed-key AES can give provably secure hashing for these protocols at roughly 20 cycles per tweakable hash, about 13 cycles for circular correlation robust hashing, and fewer for regular correlation robust hashing. Because the bound loses log Q bits of security for Q hash calls, a follow-up work reaches optimal security under the ideal cipher model. Implementations, including the EMP toolkit, are referenced as available.

talks.title: Semantic Understanding of Smart Contracts: Executable Operational Semantics of Solidity
talks.teaser: A complete K-framework operational semantics for Solidity enables specification-level verification and clearer secure contract design.
talks.summary:
Blockchain smart contracts in Solidity cannot be patched like ordinary software, and high-profile incidents such as the DAO attack show how costly semantic misunderstandings and vulnerability patterns in function calls can be. Much prior verification work targets EVM bytecode or translates contracts into intermediate languages, which forces tool builders and auditors to reason about compilation and equivalence and can introduce false positives when high-level and lowered representations diverge.

The presentation describes an executable operational semantics for Solidity formalized in the K rewriting-logic framework. The model defines syntax, a six-cell configuration (program state, control stacks, contract and function definitions, instances, and transactions), and rewriting rules for creating instances and for function calls expressed in a uniform format that covers internal and external calls, constructors, fallbacks, and delegate call context switching. The design is meant to be general enough for language evolution and blockchain-specific features such as value transfer and exception handling.

Coverage is evaluated against the Solidity compiler for documented high-level core features, with consistency reported against Remix for the supported subset; inline assembly and some fixed-point types are excluded. The takeaway for practitioners is that source-level semantics can underpin formal specifications, semantic security properties, and more trustworthy verification pipelines than bytecode-only analysis alone.

talks.title: TextExerciser: Feedback-Driven Text Input Exercising for Android Applications
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in TextExerciser: Feedback-Driven Text Input Exercising for Android Applications.

talks.title: Formal Modelling and Proof in the CHERI Design and Implementation Process
talks.teaser: Explains replacing prose CPU specifications with executable formal models and proofs of CHERI capability security properties.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the observation that memory safety bugs remain a major source of vulnerabilities, with 70% of Microsoft's patched vulnerabilities said to have a memory safety root cause. Testing catches common failures but misses small corner-case bugs, and mainstream hardware with C and C++ offers only coarse-grained memory protection, so small bugs escalate. The speaker's answer is to swap the prose architecture specification of CHERI for a formal architecture model. Being parsed, type checked and executable, the model lets software run directly on it and lets hardware implementations be tested against generated traces.

CHERI extends an existing processor design, with a MIPS prototype running on FPGAs, using capabilities that carry an address plus bounds and permissions, so an access outside the bounds traps. Capability tags are protected, and no instruction widens bounds or adds permissions. Sealed capabilities let compartments jump into each other's entry points. Because the documentation left monotonicity open to interpretation, the team defined formal security properties, built an abstraction of CHERI MIPS that keeps only memory accesses and capability manipulations, and proved it corresponds to the architecture. A theorem on reachable capabilities, under an assumption about system register access, supported a proof of a simple compartmentalisation scenario.

The main takeaway is that engineers without formal-methods training can write these models, and an executable specification makes it quicker to judge whether a design change is viable for hardware and software. The same methods are now being applied to the Arm variant of CHERI developed in the Morello project.

talks.title: Can Voters Detect Malicious Manipulation of Ballot Marking Devices?
talks.teaser: A mock polling-place study measures how often voters spot manipulated ballot printouts and which interventions raise detection.
talks.summary:
Ballot marking devices let voters choose races on a touchscreen and print a paper record they can verify before scanning. The talk explains that compromising the printer or interface can change printed choices while audits still match the wrong outcome, so security hinges on voters actually reviewing printouts and reporting errors.

The researchers ran a between-subjects mock election with 241 participants in a real Ann Arbor polling room, using modified commercial voting and scanning equipment. Every printed ballot contained a randomized manipulation in one race. Without interventions, only about 40% of participants reviewed their printouts and roughly 7% reported a problem. Passive signs and check-in instructions did not materially change outcomes, but having a poll worker engage voters at the scanner with a short script increased review and reporting somewhat. Supplying a written slate of intended choices together with those scripts drove review and reporting rates far above baseline, with statistically significant gains in the strongest condition. Ballot layout style did not matter much; errors higher on the ballot were detected more often; manipulation type showed little effect.

Limitations include a affluent, highly educated sample that may not generalize nationally, though related work in a more diverse city reportedly aligns. The closing message is that voters can find mistakes when they look, and targeted procedural interventions can help, yet catch rates may still fall short of what close elections would need for strong assurance.

talks.title: Neutaint: Efficient Dynamic Taint Analysis with Neural Networks
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Neutaint: Efficient Dynamic Taint Analysis with Neural Networks.

talks.title: ICAS: An Extensible Framework for Estimating the Susceptibility of IC Layouts to Additive Trojans
talks.teaser: Presents a framework that estimates how susceptible IC layouts are to fabrication-time hardware Trojan insertion.
talks.summary:
The talk examines whether an untrusted foundry could alter a chip's layout to add a hardware Trojan. Because fabrication is outsourced and finished chips are effectively black boxes, designers have little visibility into what gets built. The speaker argues that existing defenses against these additive Trojans are rarely deployed and asks why prevention falls short.

The presenter introduces ICAS, an open-source, extensible framework that reads a layout file and its final netlist to compute three metrics. Trigger space measures contiguous unused placement sites. Net blockage measures how much of the designer-marked security-critical nets are covered by nearby cells or wiring. Route distance combines both to gauge the routing paths an attacker would need. Across more than 60 layouts of an OR1200 processor, an AES accelerator and a DSP accelerator on a 45 nanometer process, lowering core density or tightening maximum transition time produced more compact layouts, yet thousands of insertion options remained. Filling unused sites near security-critical wires until chip density reached 95% helped further, but small Trojans still had many configurations.

The speaker concludes that placement-focused defenses cannot close the gap, since full 100% density is unattainable. Future protections, the speaker suggests, should focus on routing and guard the points where a Trojan could attach to unblocked security-critical wires.

talks.title: The Many Kinds of Creepware Used for Interpersonal Attacks
talks.teaser: Maps the ecosystem of apps that enable partner abuse, from spoofing and harassment tools to surveillance software.
talks.summary:
This measurement study, run with researchers from Cornell and New York universities and Norton LifeLock, examines apps that enable abuse between romantic partners. A 2020 survey cited in the talk found that 46 percent of U.S. adults admitted stalking a current or former partner. Building on earlier spyware research, the team seeded a graph-based method with 18 known surveillance apps and ran it over anonymized 2017 installation data covering about 27 million devices.

The method, called CreepRank, applies guilt by association: a device's score comes from the highest-scoring app it carries, and an app's score is the average of its devices. Rare apps were scoring too high, so a prior-based estimate was added to demand more evidence. Coders turned the top 1,000 results into a taxonomy, finding 143 with no creepware function. That was still a clear gain over a random walk with restart, which had more than two-thirds false positives. Categories included spoofing apps such as burner phone lines, harassment apps such as fake spying tools and SMS bombers, and control apps that knock victims off Wi-Fi.

Mitigation followed. Norton Mobile Security has warned users about surveillance apps since July 2019. The team reported 1,095 apps to Google, which agreed 813 of them violated its developer policies. Banned apps can persist in third-party stores. Open problems remain: notifications can reach the attacker who installed the app, support staff need training for safety planning, and United States law often fails to hold developers accountable.

talks.title: VeriSmart: A Highly Precise Safety Verifier for Ethereum Smart Contracts
talks.teaser: Shows how inferred transaction invariants let a verifier prove Ethereum smart contract arithmetic safe with few false alarms.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces VeriSmart, a safety verifier for Ethereum smart contracts that aims to prove arithmetic operations free of overflows and underflows. The speaker motivates the work with an April 2018 incident in which an overflow in a SmartMesh token contract let an attacker mint large amounts of tokens. The flaw slipped past the guard checks under a crafted input, and only one of four tested bug finders flagged it.

The central idea is inferring transaction invariants, global properties such as the total token supply equaling the sum of balances, that hold after construction and persist across transactions. On a worked token example, the speaker shows how such an invariant lets the tool prove that a subtraction cannot underflow even though the function has no direct check for it. The algorithm alternates a generator that proposes candidate invariants with a validator that uses them to prove safety, stopping once the contract is proven or the time budget runs out.

In experiments, it was compared with four bug finders on 60 contracts with known CVE vulnerabilities, finding all known issues with few false positives. Against two other verifiers on 25 contracts, it produced false positives on one contract, while the ascent checker produced them on 12. The tool also identified six incorrectly reported CVEs and was applied to access-control properties, where it found all simple bugs in that scenario. The takeaway is that inferring transaction invariants lets exhaustive verification stay precise for contract arithmetic safety.

talks.title: Plundervolt: Software-Based Fault Injection Attacks against Intel SGX
talks.teaser: Shows how undervolting Intel CPUs via an undocumented MSR induces faults that break SGX integrity and recover RSA and AES keys.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether software running with root privileges can induce hardware faults in Intel CPUs and whether those faults can defeat Intel SGX, the trusted execution environment meant to protect enclave code even from a root attacker. The speaker explains dynamic voltage and frequency scaling and identifies an undocumented model-specific register, 0x150, that allows voltage to be lowered from software.

By undervolting close to the crash point, the research produced repeatable multiplication errors, first as a single flipped bit and later as contiguous flips. Stability was best at mid-range frequencies such as 1 GHz. The same faults appeared while code ran inside an enclave, and identical bit positions showed up across machines and processor generations from Skylake onward. One faulty RSA decryption inside SGX, combined with the Lenstra attack against the Chinese remainder theorem optimisation, exposed a prime factor of the private key. Separately, a fault during AES-NI rounds allowed differential fault analysis to recover an AES key, and a fault in pointer arithmetic caused enclave data to be written to untrusted memory.

The speaker reports responsible disclosure to Intel, which placed the findings under embargo and mentioned other groups working on related attacks. The main takeaway is that the CPU is pushed outside its specification, which differs from the speculative-execution issue LVI, where the processor behaves as designed. Practitioners should see that trusted execution does not automatically shield enclaves from voltage and frequency manipulation by privileged software.

talks.title: Path Oblivious Heap: Optimal and Practical Oblivious Priority Queue
