talks.title: Browsing Unicity: On the Limits of Anonymizing Web Tracking Data
talks.teaser: Shows that generalizing web tracking data still leaves browsing sessions unique and easy to re-identify.
talks.summary:
Web tracking is widespread, and audience measurement firms that hold large browsing databases often rely on generalization to anonymize them. This talk asks whether that approach is a valid argument. It treats a unique pattern of behaviour as a kind of pseudonym, noting that an implicit identifier, such as a unique sequence of website visits, can count as one under the GDPR. Generalization is described as removing detail until records become indistinguishable, and k-anonymity is used as the goal to measure against.

The study used a one-week sample from a large German audience measurement provider. Coarsening timestamps alone left unicity around 30 to 40 percent at hour granularity, so other attributes had to be removed as well. Limiting session length had little effect, while dropping very short sessions of one or two clicks raised unicity. Average anonymity set sizes stayed below five even under heavy generalization. For identifiability, partial click traces often matched a single full session. In a shoulder-surfing scenario, two to three observations at minute precision uniquely identified well over half of the traces. In a dataset-overlap scenario, 30 percent overlap with minute-level timestamps identified 30 percent of traces.

The speaker concludes that generalization is not effective at anonymizing this kind of browsing data, since even the modest k-anonymity goal was not reached. Differential privacy is suggested as a method that may work better, though the talk sets aside why companies might not adopt it.

talks.title: MarkUs: Drop-in Use-After-Free Prevention for Low-Level Languages
talks.teaser: Presents MarkUs, a drop-in memory allocator that blocks use-after-free attacks in C and C++ at about 10% average overhead.
talks.summary:
Use-after-free bugs in C and C++ let an attacker reclaim memory a program has already freed and redirect control flow through a stale pointer. The talk presents MarkUs, an allocator that quarantines freed objects and releases them only when no dangling pointers remain. Once a quarter of the heap sits in quarantine, it scans the stack, data segments and registers for anything resembling a pointer, follows references through heap objects, and returns unmarked blocks for reuse.

Optimisations address the costs. Large allocations have their physical pages unmapped early, so memory is reused while the virtual address stays quarantined and stale accesses fault. Fully cleared small-object blocks are emptied to limit fragmentation, and marking runs only when enough memory is queued, trading memory for speed. On SPEC CPU2006 the prototype averaged about 10% execution overhead and 15% memory overhead, staying below 2x at worst.

The prototype works as a drop-in replacement loaded with preload commands and keeps the default allocator's interface. The speaker argues the same strategy suits any allocator, and the code is public on GitHub. Parallel marking added only about 2% CPU time on average, and multithreaded SPEC speed 2017 OpenMP runs showed similar slowdowns.

talks.title: OAT: Attesting Operation Integrity of Embedded Devices
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning OAT: Attesting Operation Integrity of Embedded Devices.

talks.title: Combating Dependence Explosion in Forensic Analysis Using Alternative Tag Propagation Semantics
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Combating Dependence Explosion in Forensic Analysis Using Alternative Tag Propagation Semantics.

talks.title: EverCrypt: A Fast, Verified, Cross-Platform Cryptographic Provider
talks.teaser: Presents a formally verified crypto library whose performance matches unverified providers like OpenSSL.
talks.summary:
Modern cryptographic providers such as OpenSSL are tuned hard for speed, and that tuning makes their code difficult to get right; the talk notes that OpenSSL had 24 vulnerabilities in three years. Earlier verification work tends to cover one algorithm or one piece of a routine, leaving the rest to the application developer. EverCrypt is presented as a comprehensive verified provider, built with performance in mind, that covers primitives and higher-level constructions.

The design centres on an agile, multiplexed API, so a client can move between hash or authenticated-encryption algorithms with a one-line change while its code and proofs stay the same. Abstract state types hide internal representations, and runtime checks guard against misuse of the initialise-update-finalise sequence. To verify hand-written assembly alongside C, the team wrote one generic specification for calls from C into assembly that covers several calling conventions, then used partial evaluation so the generic code specialises into plain imperative C. Benchmarks shown in the talk have the verified SHA-256 and AES-GCM implementations matching or beating OpenSSL's targeted versions.

A verified Merkle tree library built on the same hash interface serves as a case study. Its proofs show that a collision in the tree implies a collision in the underlying hash, and it handles insertions faster than Bitcoin's unverified implementation. Mozilla, Microsoft and the Linux kernel are named as early adopters. The takeaway is that agility and verified assembly need not cost speed, and that shared specifications let C and assembly be verified together.

talks.title: AdGraph: A Graph-Based Approach to Ad and Tracker Blocking
talks.teaser: Explores how graph-based cross-layer analysis in Chromium improves automated ad and tracker blocking beyond traditional filter lists.
talks.summary:
Online advertising supports free publishing, yet it drives privacy-invasive tracking, slower loads, malvertising on major sites, and cluttered pages. Widely used blockers depend on volunteer-maintained filter lists that lag new trackers, keep unused rules for years, and miss cross-layer behavior. Prior machine-learning blockers often judge only the network or JavaScript layer, which weakens accuracy because ads and trackers span HTML, network, and script activity together.

AdGraph addresses both accuracy and scale by instrumenting Chromium to record fine-grained interactions across those layers, representing each page as a graph, and training classifiers on structural and content features derived from that graph. Reported evaluation includes strong cross-validated precision and recall, cases where detections disagree with popular lists, and evidence that graph-based blocking can avoid some over-broad filter mistakes. Performance comparisons suggest many pages load faster than stock Chromium or extension-based blocking when network requests are stopped earlier.

The closing message is that cross-layer context matters beyond this one application. The speaker notes open-sourced instrumentation maintained for broader uses, including filter regeneration. Readers of the full paper get additional evaluations such as mistake-induced blocking leakage.

talks.title: ZEXE: Enabling Decentralized Private Computation
talks.teaser: Presents a system for private offline computation, with transactions that hide their program and verify in near-constant time.
talks.summary:
Public ledgers such as Ethereum, Tezos and EOS verify transactions by re-execution, so every node repeats every computation. This caps throughput at the weakest node and permanently exposes the program run, its inputs and its caller. Zexe, which stands for zero-knowledge execution, lets users compute offline and publish a proof of correctness instead. The transaction reveals none of the program, inputs or invoker, and checking it takes time independent of the underlying computation, with transactions under a kilobyte and verification under 50 milliseconds.

The talk starts from Zerocash, which hides senders, receivers and values through serial-number double-spend checks and a zero-knowledge proof covering membership, correct construction and value conservation. Generalising this to arbitrary data with one predicate per record allows value to appear from nothing, because a record's birth is never checked. Giving each record separate constraints for its creation and its consumption closes that gap. Since universal circuits are roughly 20 times slower, the implementation instead uses proof recursion, where the transaction verifies a proof that a predicate is satisfied.

Efficient recursion needs small circuits that verify SNARK proofs, which requires pairing-friendly elliptic curves. The team presents a way to sample recursion-friendly BLS12 curves, a new curve CP6 built with the Cox-Zimmerman method to verify BLS12-377 proofs, and Edwards curves that make Pedersen hashes and commitments efficient on both. All curves are implemented in a Rust library. The talk closes by pointing to the paper, which applies the model to private user-defined assets, stablecoins and decentralized exchanges.

talks.title: Are We Susceptible to Rowhammer? An End-to-End Methodology for Cloud Providers
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Are We Susceptible to Rowhammer? An End-to-End Methodology for Cloud Providers.

talks.title: Pseudorandom Black Swans: Cache Attacks on CTR_DRBG
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Pseudorandom Black Swans: Cache Attacks on CTR_DRBG.

talks.title: VerX: Safety Verification of Smart Contracts
talks.teaser: VerX automates safety checks on multi-contract Ethereum apps using specs, callback rules, and symbolic execution.
talks.summary:
Smart contracts on public blockchains often guard large balances and cannot be patched after deployment, so developers need ways to show that code matches intended behavior. The presentation introduces VerX, a verifier that takes a contract application plus a developer-written specification and either proves the spec holds for arbitrary transactions and inputs or reports a violating trace.

The speaker walks through natural-language-style requirements—access control, state relations, state machines, and ERC-20-style invariants—and shows VerX catching a crowdsale property violation with a concrete call sequence. A major thread is the specification problem when refunds send funds to another contract that can call back and return ether, which breaks naive balance properties. The work extends prior single-contract callback-freedom ideas to an effective external callback freedom rule suited to bundles of cooperating contracts.

On automation, the tool encodes contract bundles as programs with unbounded transaction loops, then combines a precise symbolic execution engine for EVM bytecode with predicate abstraction and SAT solving to tame infinite state spaces. The talk closes with examples where added predicates resolve false alarms and notes that VerX has been applied to real deployments, sometimes cutting verification effort to hours.

talks.title: SoK: Cyber Insurance - Technical Challenges and a System Security Roadmap
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for SoK: Cyber Insurance - Technical Challenges and a System Security Roadmap.

talks.title: Unexpected Data Dependency Creation and Chaining: A New Attack to SDN
talks.teaser: Shows how attackers can chain unexpected data dependencies inside SDN controllers to reach hidden APIs and find 18 vulnerabilities.
talks.summary:
Software-defined networking moves network logic into a central controller, which makes it a valuable target. An attacker who has only compromised a switch or host can often reach just the protocol message handler, while applications such as flow managers and web interfaces stay shielded. Earlier research reached such components by following existing data flows. This talk instead introduces data dependency creation and chaining, which builds new, unexpected dependencies so that attacker-supplied data reaches previously unreachable APIs.

Malicious content in a protocol field, sent by a compromised switch, creates a poisoned device object in the message handler. A sensitive method in the web UI then uses that object to send HTTP requests to the flow rule manager, which installs attacker-chosen flows and could enable man-in-the-middle attacks. To find such chains automatically, the team built a prototype that uses data flow tracking to pinpoint poisoning events and a small declarative language to reason about what each event can affect. Across four popular controllers they found 18 vulnerabilities, with effects including network manipulation, credential and file leakage, and denial of service, and some chains reached arbitrary command execution.

Suggested defenses include validating inputs to sensitive methods, enforcing dynamic information flow control, and centralizing protocol interactions so message formats and value ranges are checked at one point. The takeaway is that controller security depends on tracing how data moves between components, not only on checking each one alone. Most reported issues had been patched by the time of the talk.

talks.title: Kobold: Evaluating Decentralized Access Control for Remote NSXPC Methods on iOS
talks.teaser: Shows how generated test code probing iOS NSXPC methods exposed missing access control and led to three patched CVEs.
talks.summary:
Malware on iOS can escalate privileges by breaking access control, as the 2016 Pegasus spyware did with three chained vulnerabilities. Earlier papers analyzed the sandbox profile and daemon file access but skipped inter-process communication, a path for confused deputy attacks. Kobold closes that gap by combining sandbox rules with the entitlements daemons require to reveal what third-party apps can reach over NSXPC.

Analysis starts statically. Daemons come from the iOS firmware image, and pre-registered ports let the team map each daemon's ports without running it. Methods are found through NSXPC's object-oriented patterns, and when a daemon has several ports, methods are duplicated across them and pruned dynamically. The generated test app made about 3,000 invocations, roughly 1,500 of them unique, running on an iPhone. Of the 677 methods with completion handlers, 220 returned confirmations from daemons, and 139 of those did not appear to need an entitlement. Some calls produced audible effects or returned data, and several crashed daemons were reported but not exploited.

Three vulnerabilities were reported to Apple, which assigned CVEs and patched them. One activated mobile device management behavior on a device never enrolled, letting an app block websites across several browsers. Another started dictation without user action, waking the microphone for about a second with no access to recordings. The third let an app infer whether a file existed from differing permission and not-found errors, partly because a method exposed part of the file path. The takeaway is that privileged daemons reachable from third-party apps are an under-tested attack surface worth systematic analysis.

talks.title: SPIDER: Enabling Fast Patch Propagation in Related Software Repositories
talks.teaser: A static verification method labels security patches as safe to propagate across vendor forks without full regression testing.
talks.summary:
Open-source security fixes often land in upstream repositories long before they reach vendor forks, and many commits lack CVE identifiers, leaving integrators unsure what to cherry-pick. Attackers who study public patches can weaponize the underlying flaws in products that never received the fix.

The presentation introduces SPIDER, a lightweight static technique that classifies patches as safe when they do not widen the valid input space and preserve externally visible behavior for those inputs. Safe patches are verified from the original and patched source files alone, using path constraints from valid exit points, program dependence graphs, fine-grained differencing, and symbolic compilation; patches that materially change loop bodies are treated as unsafe.

Evaluation across tens of thousands of repositories and hundreds of thousands of commits finds a large share of changes—and many CVE-fixing commits—meet the safe criteria, including numerous unaudited security fixes absent from active forks. Practitioners can treat SPIDER as a filter to accelerate downstream propagation where full configuration testing is impractical, while respecting its alias, scope, and trusted-patch assumptions.

talks.title: Humpty Dumpty: Controlling Word Meanings via Corpus Poisoning
talks.teaser: Shows how poisoning a training corpus can shift word embeddings and steer search, translation and entity recognition.
talks.summary:
Word embeddings such as GloVe and SGNS place words in a vector space where distance tracks semantic closeness, and many language tasks reuse these vectors without retraining. The speakers ask what happens if an attacker can edit the public text used for training. Turning a desired shift in meaning into concrete corpus edits is difficult, since the link between word statistics and embedding distance is poorly understood.

The team compares first-order proximity, based on how often two words appear together, with second-order proximity, based on whether words share the same surrounding words. Second-order similarity matches trained embeddings closely, so it becomes the attack's objective, and a two-stage optimisation yields a small set of sentences to insert. In a translation system, invented English words are mapped onto chosen target words, and the edit works across languages without touching the target model. In named entity recognition, a made-up company can be pulled into the corporation cluster, or a real one pushed toward locations. In resume search, a few hundred inserted sequences tie a candidate's handle to a skill term, so the resume reaches the top ten results.

A language-model filter stops the naive version of the attack, but the attacker can join words with conjunctions to look plausible, or disguise inserted text using existing sentences. The second tactic makes the filter discard about 70% of the corpus while the attack keeps working. The takeaway is that embeddings from public text can be steered by small, hard-to-spot edits, so anyone reusing them should treat training data as untrusted.

talks.title: Ex-vivo Dynamic Analysis Framework for Android Device Drivers
talks.teaser: Shows how Android kernel drivers can be analysed and fuzzed inside an emulator, without porting them or emulating their hardware.
talks.summary:
Android device drivers run in the kernel with full privileges and account for many kernel bugs, while fast-moving phone releases leave less room for security. Dynamic analysis of these drivers usually means buying many handsets, and locked bootloaders can block reflashing them. The talk asks whether this analysis can move into an emulator without porting drivers or modelling their peripherals.

The central observation is that many driver code paths only need the peripheral or kernel to respond superficially, because returned values do not affect control flow. The framework is a modified Linux kernel that loads unmodified Android drivers. It fabricates device tree entries, redirects memory-mapped I/O to a zeroed buffer, replaces missing kernel functions with stubs, and corrects mismatched structure layouts. In the evaluation, 26 known bugs from 10 drivers were triggered in 80% of cases, and 62 other drivers were initialised up to the point of creating a device file in 77% of cases.

For finding new bugs, the team snapshotted initialised drivers and ran them under a user-space fuzzer in a CPU-only emulator. To handle ioctl inputs with nested pointers and size fields, they instrumented copy_from_user to learn where pointers and lengths sit within a structure. Across 32 drivers from two kernels, the work produced 29 findings, 12 confirmed as new bugs and 5 false positives. Limitations include a weaker fit for drivers whose malicious input does not come from user space, such as Wi-Fi drivers, and the possibility of false positives. The main takeaway is that driver bugs can be found without the physical peripherals.

talks.title: An Analysis of Pre-installed Android Software
talks.teaser: Measures pre-installed Android apps across hundreds of vendors, exposing unverifiable certificates, hidden permissions and privacy risks.
talks.summary:
Android phones often ship with extra system apps added by chipset makers, phone vendors, carriers and their partners. These apps sit on the read-only system partition, can run in the background, and usually cannot be removed without rooting the device. Because such apps are rarely published, the team built a freely available scanner app that, with user consent, collected pre-installed apps from devices. This gathered about 82,000 unique apps from more than 200 vendors.

The developers were mapped through signing certificates, but these are self-signed and cannot be checked against a trusted root, so a claimed owner means little. The team found over 90 certificates claiming to be from Google, and many apps whose company could not be identified. Advertising, analytics and social network libraries appeared in thousands of apps without user consent. Nearly 5,000 custom permissions were found, mostly undocumented, with about 10 percent not attributable to any company. Heat maps revealed partnerships, such as Facebook permissions spread across major vendors. Static analysis showed many apps could read sensitive data such as the IMEI, and some known malware families and rooting tools were present. Dynamic analysis was not run, so actual data leaks remain unconfirmed.

The speaker urged better documentation of custom permissions, published certificate hashes so fake signatures can be spotted, and tighter Google control over what gets preinstalled. Regulators also have a role to play. Part of the dataset is made available to the research community.

talks.title: A Stealthier Partitioning Attack against Bitcoin Peer-to-Peer Network
talks.teaser: Shows a low-traffic partitioning attack that isolates Bitcoin nodes by filling their peer tables with attacker-controlled addresses.
talks.summary:
Bitcoin nodes share blocks and transactions over a peer-to-peer network, and a partitioning attack cuts a victim node off from the rest of that network by taking over its connections. The speakers explain why this matters: a merchant isolated this way can be fed a view of the chain that serves the attacker, for example by accepting a payment that never reaches honest nodes. Earlier partitioning attacks needed control of an internet service provider and a prefix hijack to redirect the victim's traffic.

The talk presents a stealthier variant that avoids that kind of routing manipulation. The attacker makes the victim connect to "shadow" IP addresses, meaning any addresses whose traffic routes back through the adversary. Bitcoin nodes keep a new table and a tried table of peers and pick outgoing connections from them. Unreachable entries in the new table are evicted after 30 days, so the attacker sends low-rate traffic to keep its shadow addresses reachable, which lets them move into the tried table. Over time these addresses come to dominate the victim's outgoing slots, and the speakers argue the low traffic volume makes the attack hard to tell apart from normal activity and invisible to routing monitors.

The speakers estimate that several large network providers could mount the attack and note that at least 30 other cryptocurrency projects copy the same peer-to-peer implementation. They discuss countermeasures such as allowlisting trusted peers, proxies or VPNs, smaller peer tables, more outgoing connections, and fresh-data mechanisms, some of which are being tested. Because the attack exploits topology rather than a software bug, the speakers conclude that no simple patch fully mitigates it.

talks.title: The State of the Uniform: Attacks on Encrypted Databases beyond the Uniform Query Distribution
talks.teaser: Presents leakage-abuse attacks that recover encrypted range-query data without knowing the query or data distribution.
talks.summary:
Encrypted search lets a server answer queries over outsourced data without learning much about the query or the results. These schemes still leak information, mainly the search pattern (which queries repeat) and the access pattern (which encrypted records come back). Earlier attacks that turn this leakage into plaintext reconstruction depended on assumptions about how queries and data are distributed, such as uniformly random queries, densely populated databases, or known distributions, and those assumptions often do not hold in practice.

The work presents attacks that need none of these assumptions and combine search pattern and access pattern leakage. For range queries, observed query tokens are grouped by the records they return, and the number of distinct tokens in each group is estimated with nonparametric estimators (a jackknife and a Valiant-Valiant estimator). These estimates approximate products of gaps between plaintext values. The individual gaps are then recovered by solving a constrained least-squares problem in which the gaps sum to the domain size and stay positive. The speakers also revisit the earlier k-nearest-neighbor attack, aiming to need fewer observations and to scale to larger values of k.

In experiments with uniformly random queries across database densities from 10 to 90 percent, the range attack reached lower mean squared error than the prior state of the art, even though it knew nothing about the query distribution. With queries skewed toward short ranges, which earlier methods could not handle, the attack still performed well, because many short queries give more accurate estimates. The takeaway is that combining both leakage types can expose plaintext even when the classic assumptions are dropped, so designers of encrypted databases should treat leakage as a serious risk.

talks.title: Transys: Leveraging Common Security Properties across Hardware Designs
talks.teaser: Presents a tool that translates hardware security assertions between designs, with manual review still required.
talks.summary:
Hardware security teams write assertion-based properties by hand for each design and each new revision, which is slow and repetitive. This talk asks whether a property written for one design can be turned into a valid property for a second design that enforces the same policy, without a formal definition of the high-level policy. Differences such as pipeline depth, register layout and extra gating signals make a direct copy fail, even when the policy holds in both.

The tool, Transys, takes the Verilog of two designs plus properties that are valid for the first, and produces translated properties for the second in three phases. It first maps signals, ports and registers using features from the syntax tree and program dependency graph, combined with name similarity. It then adjusts arithmetic expressions and timing constraints, and finally refines the preconditions. Refinement treats validity as an unsatisfiability check on the design combined with the negated property, and adds constraints until that check holds without making the property trivially true.

Across AES and OpenRISC and RISC-V processor designs, the overall translation rate was 96%, and translating assertions from OpenRISC to RISC-V succeeded in 56% of cases. The average semantic equivalence rate was about 60%, while the AES translations reached 100%. Translation took about 70 seconds on average. The speaker concludes that the approach is practical for daily use, but that manual review of generated properties remains a required step.

talks.title: A Security Analysis of the Facebook Ad Library
talks.teaser: A security study of Facebook's political ad library measures disclosure gaps and surfaces undisclosed coordinated ad campaigns.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with election-related disinformation as the backdrop for Facebook's U.S. political ad transparency rules and the ad library's web portal and API. The researchers describe scraping daily ad library reports, querying the API for active advertisers, and validating their copy against Facebook's summaries. On roughly 3.7 million ads they find about 10,000 missing from their collection and 7,000 extra, and stress that disputed ads, policy changes, and technical limits mean the library is not a durable archive.

They then examine completeness and accuracy of disclosure strings. More than half of pages with political ads never provide one, yet those pages account for a small share of ads; nearly ten percent of ads run without disclosure, and long-running non-disclosing spenders include commercial advertisers and entities such as Xinhua. Enforcement appears weak. Estimated misattribution affects at least 17.7% of ads and 23% of strings break formatting rules, though Facebook later restricted how disclosures are entered.

To find misleading coordination, they cluster near-duplicate creatives with sim hashing and flag pages that repeatedly run similar content under different payers. Manual review of 172 clusters yields benign resharing, corporate astroturfing, dubious commercial schemes, clickbait, and inauthentic community pages tailored by geography or identity. The closing argument treats transparency platforms as security systems needing advertiser-level enforcement, verify-not-trust checks, and independent third-party auditing.

talks.title: Enabling Rack-scale Confidential Computing Using Heterogeneous Trusted Execution Environment
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Enabling Rack-scale Confidential Computing Using Heterogeneous Trusted Execution Environment.
talks.summary:
Zhu Jianping presents HETD, a heterogeneous trusted execution environment designed to enable rack-scale confidential computing in data centers without chip-level modifications. The motivation addresses the need to protect pooled computing resources (CPUs, GPUs, TPUs, FPGAs) commonly distributed across modern data centers, where existing TEE solutions either require hardware changes or cannot efficiently support such architectures.

The HETD system architecture consists of a sealed chassis containing a security controller (SSC based on MCPU and FPGA), PCI Express fabric for resource management, multiple proxy microservice nodes with accelerators, and untrusted external server nodes. The design separates security functions (in SSC) from computation (in HETD enclaves running standard software like TensorFlow and GPU drivers), minimizing the trusted computing base.

Key technical components include elastic resource allocation via PCIe fabric's software-defined and flexible topology properties, secure enclave lifecycle management through secure reboot procedures that clear memory and reset accelerators, and data protection using AES-GCM encryption with separate message queues for ciphertext and plaintext areas. An FPGA-based cryptographic controller enforces isolation, with no direct shared space between components. Trust establishment uses a two-layer public key design (endorsement key and attestation key) with remote attestation and symmetric key negotiation.

The threat model considers a strong adversary controlling the software stack and capable of side-channel attacks via network traffic analysis. Physical snooping on the host memory bus is in scope but not within the sealed HETD box. Covert channels, attacks on cryptographic algorithms, and denial-of-service attacks are out of scope.

The prototype integrates two Xilinx PX 9797 boards, one SC node, four processor nodes, and four NVIDIA GPUs. Performance evaluation shows throughput overhead under 5% for most workloads, with batch-size-dependent latency overhead reaching 42.96% for inference and 18.54% for training at batch size 8. Encryption overhead is small and stable. Multiple-GPU scalability matches the baseline, demonstrating that elastic resource allocation can improve single-enclave performance without sacrificing horizontal scalability.

The system provides four security guarantees in a Platform-as-a-Service model: isolation from other enclaves on the same proxy node, isolation from past and future users, protection from untrusted hosts, and protection from cloud providers. The design resists side-bleed attacks on sealed FPGAs and cold boot attacks when unauthorized chassis opening takes longer than power-removal-based memory extraction.

talks.title: Intriguing Properties of Adversarial ML Attacks in the Problem Space
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Intriguing Properties of Adversarial ML Attacks in the Problem Space.

talks.title: Flaw Label: Exploiting IPv6 Flow Label
talks.teaser: Shows how IPv6 flow label values leak a static per-device key that enables cross-browser tracking on Windows, Linux and Android.
talks.summary:
IPv6 adoption is growing, and modern operating systems prefer IPv6 when a server offers it, so many users send IPv6 traffic without knowing it. Since Windows 10 1703 and Linux 4.3, the 20-bit flow label field is filled with generated values rather than zeros. The researchers reverse engineered how each platform builds it. On Windows, the label comes from a Toeplitz hash of the addresses and ports, keyed by a 320-bit value that changes only at reboot. On Linux and Android, UDP labels come from a Jenkins hash keyed by a static 32-bit value, also set only at boot.

Because that key persists across browsers, network changes and temporary address rotation, it can act as a device identifier. The Toeplitz hash is bilinear, so an attacker who controls the destination fields can XOR inputs to isolate key bits, recovering more than 80 bits from a few crafted UDP packets or nine TCP packets. The generic case reduces to linear equations. For Linux and Android, the 32-bit key can simply be enumerated. An HTML snippet on any third-party page can trigger the needed traffic through WebRTC. A passive observer, such as a server or a man-in-the-middle, can derive the same identifier from ordinary IPv6 traffic and link past activity to a device. The attacks worked across 19 networks, including VPNs.

Windows 10 versions 1703 through 1903 were affected and fixed in the November 2019 update. Linux kernels 4.3 through 5.3.9 were affected and moved to a keyed hash with a 128-bit key. The authors argue that vendors should use strong cryptographic functions with adequate key sizes whenever attacker-observable values feed into identifiers.

talks.title: Binsec/Rel: Efficient Relational Symbolic Execution for Constant-Time at Binary-Level
talks.teaser: Presents a binary-level symbolic execution tool that checks constant-time cryptographic code for timing leaks compilers can introduce.
talks.summary:
Constant-time programming protects cryptographic code from timing side channels by keeping control flow and memory accesses independent of secret values. The speaker shows that compilers can break this property: a select function that is constant-time at optimisation level zero in Clang acquires a secret-dependent branch at level three. This makes automatic verification at the binary level necessary.

Existing tools work on source or LLVM code and can miss violations added later, or they run dynamically without bounded guarantees, or they over-approximate and report imprecise bugs. The authors' tool, Binsec/Rel, uses relational symbolic execution, which runs two program copies together so that work is shared between them. Plain self-composition did not scale in their experiments, so they add an on-the-fly memory model, untainting that collapses proven-equal expression pairs, and batching of solver queries per basic block.

Across 338 cryptographic implementations, 296 were verified constant-time with exhaustive bounded verification, covering 23 million instructions in under an hour. The tool was 700 times faster than standard relational symbolic execution in instructions per second and fully explored 14 more programs. A compiler study found that GCC at -O0 and backend passes of Clang introduce violations in code previously judged secure, which shows why reasoning at the binary level matters.

talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for JIT Leaks: Inducing Timing Side Channels through Just-In-Time Compilation.

talks.title: Towards Scalable Threshold Cryptosystems
talks.teaser: Shows how faster polynomial evaluation makes threshold signing and key sharing practical for far larger numbers of players.
talks.summary:
Threshold signature schemes split a secret key across several devices so that only a minimum number of them can jointly sign, which limits the damage from any single compromised device. The talk looks at why these schemes are hard to scale to very large numbers of players, with use cases ranging from crypto wallets and consensus protocols to random beacons and voting. The speaker walks through the building blocks involved: verifiable secret sharing, which lets a dealer split a key while players check their shares, and distributed key generation, which builds on it so that no one ever learns the full key.

The main bottleneck identified is computing proofs in polynomial commitment schemes. KZG commitments keep the commitment constant in size, but computing all the proofs naively takes time proportional to the number of players times the threshold. The speaker presents an authenticated multi-point evaluation tree that uses polynomial multi-point evaluation over roots of unity, trading larger proof sizes for much faster computation. In the reported experiments, dealing time improved by almost a factor of ten at 2,000 players, and the gains held at smaller scales too. For signature aggregation, the same evaluation technique replaces the quadratic cost of Lagrange interpolation with a near-linear one, substantially cutting aggregation time at large thresholds.

The takeaway is that the approach applies to any threshold system that relies on interpolation over a finite field, including threshold encryption. Open problems include the overhead of complaint broadcasting in the secret sharing and key generation protocols, and scaling the broadcast channel to millions of players.

talks.title: Leveraging EM Side-Channel Information to Detect Rowhammer Attacks
talks.teaser: Shows how DRAM clock electromagnetic emissions can reveal Rowhammer attacks despite spread spectrum clocking.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses detecting Rowhammer attacks, which repeatedly access the same DRAM rows to flip bits, by watching electromagnetic emissions rather than the attack itself. The speakers argue that the DRAM bus clock radiates a strong periodic signal that is amplitude-modulated by memory activity, so a hammering loop leaves symmetric sideband patterns around the clock frequency. Hammering through cache flushes, cache eviction and non-temporal instructions each produced such sidebands, and the rate of each method showed up at the matching spectral locations.

Two obstacles were described. Background noise can produce similar patterns, which the detector handles by looking for vertical sideband stripes that persist over the tens of milliseconds an attack needs. The larger problem is spread spectrum clocking, which is enabled by default to meet electromagnetic compatibility limits and smears the clock frequency so the sidebands become hard to recognize. The team counters this by characterizing the clock's phase behavior for each hardware platform in advance, aligning captured samples by cross-correlation, and restoring the hidden sidebands. This step also reduced background noise.

The resulting system, called the reader, uses a software-defined radio with a simple wire antenna, turns the signal into spectrograms with a short-time Fourier transform, and feeds them to a three-layer classification model. Tests covered single- and double-sided hammering across several methods, along with benign workloads such as random array access, video decoding and kernel compilation. The detector worked on platforms not used in training, including modified memory modules, and still flagged attacks that inserted random delays into each hammering iteration. The takeaway is that emission-based monitoring can offer a robust defense against evasive Rowhammer variants.

talks.title: Cornucopia: Temporal Safety for CHERI Heaps
talks.teaser: Shows how a CHERI heap allocator can revoke dangling pointers via concurrent sweeps, with modest overhead on SPEC benchmarks.
talks.summary:
The talk presents Cornucopia, a design for temporal memory safety in user-space heaps on the CHERI capability architecture. It frames memory safety as three properties: pointer provenance and integrity, spatial bounds on objects, and temporal lifetimes that end when memory is reallocated. CHERI capabilities are wide pointers carrying bounds and a tag bit, so hardware already enforces provenance and spatial limits, but stale copies of freed pointers can still alias reused memory.

The design builds on earlier quarantine-and-sweep ideas. Freed memory is held in quarantine instead of being reused, and once quarantine reaches a threshold the kernel sweeps memory for capabilities pointing into it and replaces them with null, using a shadow bitmap. Tag bits and a tag-read instruction let the sweep skip cache lines without capabilities, and trap-on-store tracking lets repeated passes revisit only pages that changed. Most of the work runs concurrently with the application, followed by a short stop-the-world pass. The changes span the kernel and malloc, and unmodified programs were run with a replacement allocator.

On SPEC CPU 2006 integer benchmarks, the single-threaded version had a geometric mean overhead of 5.8%, falling below 2% when sweeping was offloaded to a second core. Memory occupancy mostly held near the 33% target. Allocator-thrashing workloads saw memory traffic overhead of 15 to 30 percent, rising to 30 to 45 percent with concurrent revocation. Double-free and use-after-free test cases all aborted under the design. The takeaway is that sweeping revocation can be practical, that spatial safety lowers its cost, and that the work is aimed at mainline CHERI BSD.

talks.title: Automatic Uncovering of Hidden Behaviors from Input Validation in Mobile Apps
talks.teaser: Presents a static analysis tool that finds hidden keys, master passwords and secret commands in Android app input checks.
talks.summary:
Mobile apps sometimes contain behaviors that are never documented for users, such as easter eggs, word blacklists, or credentials that unlock protected data. The speaker explains that these behaviors often sit in the way apps validate user input. Examples include a news app that rejects nicknames on a keyword blacklist, a phone-loss protection app where a fixed string worked as a master password, and a translation app with a hidden access key that removed advertisements.

To find such cases, the speaker presents InputScope, a static analysis tool that takes an APK and flags suspicious validation logic. It tracks user input to equality checks, then uses backward slicing and string analysis to resolve the comparison value and where it comes from. Each check is described by how many values are compared and how many branches can follow, and four policies classify the results as access keys, master passwords, blacklists, or secret commands. Across 150,000 apps (100,000 from Google Play, 30,000 from Samsung firmware images and 20,000 from an alternative Chinese market), the tool found around 7,500 apps with access keys, 500 with master passwords and 6,000 with secret commands.

Manual review of popular apps showed access keys used for hidden admin logins, password resets and bypassing payment to remove ads. Some master passwords affected security-related apps, including a file-hiding app. Secret commands mostly enabled debugging modes or app-specific functions. The speaker suggests developers still place trust in client-side checks and sometimes leave debugging code in releases. Limitations include no coverage of WebView input or database-based checks, and some false positives. The practical takeaway is to validate security-relevant input on back-end servers and remove debugging code before release.

talks.title: SEIMI: Efficient and Secure SMAP-Enabled Intra-process Memory Isolation
talks.teaser: Shows how SMAP can isolate sensitive in-process memory faster than MPK-based designs, measured on real server applications.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from in-process memory isolation, a defense that shields sensitive data from memory corruption attacks. Software-based and hardware-assisted approaches already exist, but the speaker argues that existing hardware methods, including MPK-based designs, still cost too much when access rights must be switched often.

The core idea is SMAP, an x86 feature that stops supervisor-mode code from touching user-space pages. Because the instructions that toggle it are privileged, the team runs the target process inside a virtualized guest, where it gets its own privilege level and can change the permission cheaply. The speaker describes three challenges: separating reads and writes to isolated memory, protecting privileged structures such as page tables and descriptor tables, and preventing abuse of privileged hardware features. Their answers include a shared mapping that gives read-only access to isolated memory, redirecting interrupts and exceptions through the hypervisor, and checking privileged instructions before they run.

The system, called SEIMI, works in two phases: a setup phase that allocates the isolated memory region, and a runtime phase that monitors the target application and moves the current system into the virtualized mode. Evaluation on web servers and database applications showed an average overhead reduction of 33% compared to MPK-based isolation. The speaker also notes that frequent permission switches can make the design slower in some cases. The takeaway is that privileged CPU features can be reused safely for user-mode isolation when virtualization controls the sensitive paths.

talks.title: IJON: Exploring Deep State Spaces via Fuzzing
talks.teaser: Explains how annotations that add selective value feedback help fuzzers escape large equivalence classes and reach deeper program states.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Academic research on fuzzing predominantly focuses on fully automated approaches such as AFL and libFuzzer. While automation simplifies testing across diverse security scenarios, security practitioners often require finer control over fuzzer behavior. IJON (presented phonetically as Ejon) introduces an approach where human experts guide fuzzers using lightweight annotations. By combining standard code coverage feedback with selective value feedback on specific data points within the program's state space, IJON enables fuzzers to explore deep state spaces without becoming overwhelmed by state noise.

### Key Topics
- **Equivalence Classes and Feedback Limitations**: Modern fuzzers divide the input space into equivalence classes based on code coverage, discarding mutations that produce no new coverage. When equivalence classes are too vast—such as in complex state machines or arithmetic constraints—mutations fail to reach interesting states.
- **Selective Value Feedback**: Instead of tracking all program state (which causes noise and state explosion) or relying purely on code coverage, analysts add inline annotations to direct the fuzzer toward specific values or exploration goals.
- **Feedback Primitives**: IJON introduces feedback primitives such as state-tracking annotations and optimization feedback (e.g., maximizing coordinates or loop counters, minimizing arithmetic differences).
- **Limitations in Interactive Applications**: Long-running or interactive inputs face a severe cubic disadvantage: input queues expand, promising inputs become longer (leading to fewer mutations on critical bytes), and individual executions slow down drastically.

### Technical Details
- **Maze Solving**: In a modified maze game allowing revisiting of board positions, standard fuzzers and KLEE fail because code coverage is exhausted after pressing W, S, A, and D once. A one-line IJON annotation directing the fuzzer to treat new (X, Y) coordinate combinations as new coverage enabled AFL to solve the maze in seconds.
- **Protocol and Format Parsing (libpng)**: In stateful parsing (like FTP or chunk-based formats like PNG), identical code executes repeatedly across states. In `libpng`, tracking the last four observed chunk headers created artificial coverage that allowed AFL to discover a bug requiring a specific sequence of chunks without needing a full file format specification.
- **Maximization and Optimization**: In an integer factorization example, minimizing the difference between equation sides guided the fuzzer toward solutions. Applied to Super Mario Bros., maximizing the player's X coordinate turned AFL into an effective speed-running bot.
- **Vulnerability Discovery & CGC Evaluation**: An inline annotation targeting a `malloc` call quickly confirmed an integer overflow resulting in a zero-sized allocation. Evaluating undefeated DARPA Cyber Grand Challenge (CGC) binaries (via Trail of Bits' x86 port), IJON solved a third of inspected challenges by removing checksum checks during fuzzing and using AFL crash exploration mode with maximization annotations—replicating T-Fuzz results without symbolic execution. Other solved cases involved maximizing loop counters, single pointers, or bypassing string comparisons.

### Takeaways
IJON demonstrates that minimal, human-in-the-loop annotations can bridge the gap where fully automated coverage-guided fuzzers fail. It also highlights open challenges for automated fuzzing, including long-running interactive targets, loop counters, and deep checksum logic.

talks.title: A Comparative Usability Study of FIDO2 Passwordless Authentication
talks.teaser: Shows how users react to passwordless login with a FIDO2 security key, compared with ordinary text passwords.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether FIDO2 passwordless login, where a hardware security key is the only factor, can replace text passwords. The presenters describe it as a large-scale comparative usability study. They randomly split 94 participants into a password control group and a group that used a security key alone, then compared hands-on registration and login tasks on mock websites with survey responses.

Quantitatively, passwordless login was accepted more and rated more usable than passwords. Qualitatively, the burden shifted from remembering passwords to carrying a device, and key users worried most about losing the key or having it stolen. Several participants asked how to revoke or recover access, and phones without USB ports were a frequent complaint. Many participants lacked a clear model of how the key works. Of the passwordless group, 16 were unconditionally willing to use it privately, while 30 had concerns. A third group, shown no introduction videos, produced similar quantitative results but was more mistrustful.

The takeaways focus on adoption barriers. Recovery becomes harder at scale because one key is reused across many accounts, and users lack guidance for it. Users also need to know where token-based login cannot work. Since FIDO2 leaves the authenticator form open, future devices could be tailored to users, and mental models drawn from physical keys, such as keeping spare keys, could help build trust.

talks.title: BIAS: Bluetooth Impersonation AttackS
talks.teaser: Shows how Bluetooth Classic authentication and pairing flaws let an attacker impersonate devices without the pairing key.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at Bluetooth Classic, the high-throughput side of the standard, and asks whether its built-in authentication and session establishment hold up. The speaker presents BIAS attacks, which let an attacker impersonate a paired device during session establishment without knowing the long-term pairing key. The threat model involves two paired victims, and an outside attacker who lacks the key should be unable to impersonate either one.

The legacy secure connections authentication is examined first. It authenticates only the slave to the master, and a device can trigger a role switch before the procedure starts, so an attacker can take either role and skip the check. The Secure Connections procedure, which is mutual, is also shown to be vulnerable. Its protocol choice is not integrity protected, and Secure Connections support is not enforced during pairing and session establishment, so an attacker can force a downgrade to the legacy method. A hypothetical stricter mode that blocks downgrades is still open to role-switch and reflection attacks.

The attacks were built on off-the-shelf hardware, a Linux laptop with a development board, using patches to the operating system kernel and board firmware. Testing against 31 devices with 28 unique Bluetooth chips found that nearly all were vulnerable, regardless of Bluetooth version, chip maker or operating system. Combined with a previously demonstrated key negotiation attack, the impersonation can also reduce session key entropy and enable brute forcing. The speaker recommends mutual authentication during session establishment, integrity protection with the pairing key, and enforcing Secure Connections across pairing and session establishment. The Bluetooth standard has been updated, but many deployed devices, such as cars, may never receive a patch.

talks.title: Transparent Polynomial Delegation and Its Applications to Zero Knowledge Proof
talks.teaser: Presents a transparent polynomial delegation scheme that enables fast, post-quantum zero-knowledge proofs without trusted setup.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with zero-knowledge proofs, where a prover convinces a verifier that a computation on a secret input gives a claimed output without revealing that input. Completeness, soundness and zero knowledge are the core guarantees, and proof generation time, proof size and verification time are the main efficiency measures. The speaker points to Zcash, which validates transactions on a public blockchain while keeping addresses and amounts hidden. Its zk-SNARK, however, needs a function-specific trusted setup, has slow proving, and its security depends on discarding a secret generated by a trusted party.

The talk then turns to interactive proofs based on the GKR protocol, which have fast proving but were made zero-knowledge only through polynomial commitments that required a trusted setup or were not post-quantum secure. The speaker's work builds a transparent zero-knowledge polynomial delegation scheme. It removes the trusted setup, relies only on symmetric-key primitives, and is a candidate for post-quantum security. The key idea is to have the prover handle the computation of the evaluation vector for the inverse and forward transforms through a small GKR circuit, so the verifier avoids doing that work directly. The prover runs in near-linear time, while verification time and proof size are polylogarithmic.

In experiments, the new scheme's prover was about 8 to 10 times faster than the commitment scheme used in Libra, taking about 12 seconds for a polynomial of size 2^20, though its proofs are larger. Plugging it into Libra yields Virgo, a transparent zero-knowledge proof system. For a Merkle tree with 256 leaves hashed with SHA-256, Virgo generated a proof in about 53 seconds and verified it in about 15 milliseconds. The speaker also notes the scheme could support verifiable secret sharing with active security. The takeaway is that transparent, post-quantum-friendly proofs with fast proving are feasible, at the cost of larger proof sizes.

talks.title: Sync HotStuff: Simple and Practical Synchronous State Machine Replication
talks.teaser: Presents a simple synchronous BFT replication protocol that commits within two message-delay bounds in steady state.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Sync HotStuff, a synchronous Byzantine fault tolerant state machine replication protocol. The speaker starts with why replicated state machines matter for decentralized services and sets out the threat model: up to a minority of replicas may behave arbitrarily. Synchronous protocols have long been considered impractical because their rounds wait on a conservative latency bound, which real networks can occasionally exceed. Proof-of-work chains and partially synchronous designs such as HotStuff serve as points of comparison.

The protocol builds a chain of blocks, with quorum certificates proving that f+1 votes exist for a block. In the steady state, an honest leader proposes each block carrying the certificate of its predecessor, so a new block appears one round trip after the last. Each replica starts a 2Δ commit timer on seeing a proposal and commits the block when the timer expires, rather than moving in lockstep. Forwarding proposals lets honest replicas catch an equivocating leader within 2Δ, and a view change keeps replicas synchronized within Δ.

The talk also covers a weaker sluggish model, where most replicas may briefly exceed the delay bound, and optimistic responsiveness, which advances at network speed when three-quarters of votes arrive. A single-fault prototype reaches over 280 Kops/sec, comparable to HotStuff. Safety rests on two lemmas about committed blocks and certificates across views, so a synchronous protocol can match partially synchronous performance when the common case avoids lockstep rounds.

talks.title: HydRand: Efficient Continuous Distributed Randomness
talks.teaser: Presents HydRand, improving continuous distributed randomness for blockchains with stronger delivery guarantees and better scalability.
talks.summary:
Publicly verifiable, bias-resistant randomness underpins cryptography, security protocols, and many Proof-of-Stake ledger designs. Continuous random beacon protocols must keep producing unpredictable values on a steady cadence even when participants misbehave, without leaning on a trusted dealer at setup time.

HydRand is built on publicly verifiable secret sharing so each beacon output stays verifiable, unpredictable, and resistant to manipulation. The protocol targets guaranteed output delivery on regular, predictable intervals despite adversarial actions. Relative to prior PVSS-style beacons with similar goals, communication complexity drops from cubic to quadratic in the number of parties, improving scalability. The speakers position HydRand against leader rotation, encrypted recovery messaging, and the interaction pattern needed to advance from one random value to the next.

They sketch application settings such as secure lotteries, gaming, and leader selection, and report prototype benchmarking along continuous-operation paths. The presentation also offers a structured comparison of recent random-beacon designs, and notes limited time for full industry scenarios before questions. Practitioners evaluating beacon choices for distributed systems should weigh delivery guarantees, setup trust assumptions, and communication cost at scale.

talks.title: Replicated State Machines without Replicated Execution
talks.teaser: Shows how a replicated system can skip re-executing transactions by checking zero-knowledge proofs of state changes instead.
talks.summary:
Replicated state machines, such as blockchains, have every node re-run the same transactions, which becomes very costly at large scale. Earlier fixes either change consensus so that fewer nodes are trusted, or execute transactions off the global state, and both weaken safety or liveness. This talk presents Pepper, which lets a single prover execute a batch of stateful transactions and publish a succinct proof together with a transcript of the state changes. Other nodes only verify the proof and apply those changes, so the expensive execution is not repeated everywhere.

The speakers explain how they extend the earlier Spice system, which delegates stateful computation to a prover using zero-knowledge SNARKs and audits a key-value store with incremental hashes. Pepper's added step proves that the published state changes match the audited state. Hashing the difference between old and new state means a value rewritten many times in a batch appears only once, and data such as signatures drops out entirely. Further optimizations, such as a signature scheme that is cheap to verify in a circuit and hashed batch inputs, are mentioned only briefly.

The prototype is tested against an ERC-20 style payment service on Ethereum. In synthetic benchmarks, verification becomes cheaper than the baseline for batches of 64 transactions or more, with break-even near 10,000 replicas at large batch sizes. In the Ethereum test, cost per transaction fell by more than a factor of five and network traffic dropped nearly threefold. The main takeaway is that proof machinery can cut the costs of real systems, and that privacy and lightness need not be opposed.

talks.title: SoK: A Minimalist Approach to Formalizing Analog Sensor Security
talks.teaser: Presents a transfer-function model that groups analog sensor attacks into shared steps, then predicts new attacks and defenses.
talks.summary:
The talk begins with the growing number of systems that depend on sensor data, from manufacturing and automotive to IoT, and the risk when physical signals corrupt that data. The speakers describe transduction attacks, which use lasers, ultrasound, radio frequency and other signals to make sensors such as microphones, accelerometers, gyroscopes and LiDAR report false values. Attacks from different labs looked unrelated because their terminology differed, which motivated a systematization.

The core is a simple model in which a sensor is a chain of cascading transfer functions, one per component such as transducer, amplifier, filter and converter. Each stage takes a regular input and a noise input, so an adversary's signal can enter at any stage and propagate to the output. Every attack is split into signal injection and measurement shaping. Shaping relies on properties such as saturation, aliasing, filtering, intermodulation distortion and envelope detection. Dolphin Attack and Ghost Talk, both on microphones, look different but share out-of-band injection, intermodulation distortion and filtering.

For defenses, the talk groups them by the step they mitigate, split into detection and prevention categories such as filtering, shielding, sensor fusion and saturation detection. As a predictive exercise, the speakers combine Dolphin Attack's injection with Walnut's shaping steps into a hypothetical microphone attack. They argue that an IMD defense for one attack should also block the other. The takeaway is that shared steps can hint at future attacks and at defenses that transfer across sensors.

talks.title: Understanding and Mitigating Security Risks of General Messaging Protocols on IoT Clouds
talks.teaser: Examines security gaps in MQTT messaging across eight IoT cloud platforms, from stale sessions to guessable client IDs.
talks.summary:
IoT cloud platforms relay messages between connected devices and user apps, and many run on MQTT, a lightweight messaging protocol that offers little built-in authentication or authorization. The researchers studied eight leading IoT clouds, assuming an attacker who holds an ordinary user account or temporary access to a device, such as one in a rented hotel setup.

Several weaknesses emerged. Retained last-will messages stayed live after a device changed hands, so a former user could register one and choose when it fired, even after losing access. Persistent subscription sessions kept delivering a device's topic data to an attacker after a reset revoked the previous owner's permissions. Client IDs, often derived from MAC addresses or serial numbers that are not secret, were not bound to authentication, so one account could take over another device's ID or kick off clients to cause denial of service. One platform showed a single identity holding multiple connections. A wildcard subscription could receive messages from all topics. Captured status messages from an air conditioner also revealed a household's daily pattern.

The authors argue that general-purpose protocols need a security model tailored to adversarial IoT settings. Their recommendations include tying client IDs to authenticated platform identities, updating session state whenever permissions change, and defining how retained messages are accepted and who may trigger them. Practitioners building on MQTT should not assume the protocol enforces these checks.

talks.title: SoK: Differential Privacy as a Causal Property
talks.teaser: Shows differential privacy bounds a person's causal effect on outputs, not correlation or what an adversary learns.
talks.summary:
The talk examines a long-running disagreement about whether differential privacy needs assumptions about the data. The speaker, presenting a systematization paper with two co-authors, argues it is best understood as a causal property. The guarantee limits how much one person's record can shift an algorithm's output distribution, but it does not cap the correlation between that record and the output, or what an observer can learn about it.

A survey about a genetic mutation, with two participants named Ada and Bob, illustrates the point. A randomized counting mechanism that flips each answer with probability one quarter achieves log three differential privacy. If Ada is Bob's mother and the mutation is inherited maternally, their records become correlated, and conditioning on one reveals a factor of nine rather than three, reflecting two changed inputs. That makes the associative version strictly stronger, requiring extra assumptions such as a strong adversary who knows every other record or independent records, both judged unrealistic. Intervening on the underlying DNA rather than the recorded value shows why records do not affect one another even when correlated.

The causal reading explains the disagreement in prior work and why the guarantee appears in fairness and secure learning. Associative definitions would block valuable studies, such as one showing smoking causes cancer, while causal definitions permit them but also allow contested work like a model inferring sexual orientation from photos. The speaker concludes that privacy, as a normative topic, should not be reduced to either property.

talks.title: SPECTECTOR: Principled Detection of Speculative Information Flows
talks.teaser: Presents a semantic notion of speculative non-interference and a symbolic tool that flags Spectre v1 leaks in compiled code.
talks.summary:
The talk asks how to tell whether a program stays secure when it runs on a CPU that uses speculative execution, with branch prediction as the running example. It recaps how mispredicted work is rolled back at the architectural level while cache changes persist, which is the basis of Spectre variant 1. The speaker proposes speculative non-interference, a semantic security property requiring that a program leaks no more under speculative execution than under ordinary in-order execution. The model combines a standard semantics, a speculative semantics parametric in a branch prediction oracle, and an attacker who observes memory addresses, program counter changes and the start and end of speculation.

To find leaks, the approach symbolically executes a program under the speculative semantics with an always-mispredict oracle, producing symbolic traces that pair path conditions with observations. A leak is a pair of states that agree on non-speculative observations but differ on speculative ones. The tool, SPECTECTOR, translates x64 assembly into an intermediate language and uses an SMT solver. In a first case study, 15 Spectre v1 variants were compiled with three compilers under different mitigations and optimization levels, giving 240 programs. Leaks appeared in unprotected builds, a previously reported Microsoft compiler issue was confirmed, and most speculative load hardening builds were proven secure, except two with minor leaks.

A second case study examined scalability on a large real-world codebase. Challenges included obtaining realistic security policies, covering a broad instruction set and handling path explosion, and the trade-offs made to cope with them affected soundness and completeness. Across tens of thousands of traces, checking the property took roughly the same order of time as discovering the symbolic paths, so the approach adds no fundamental bottleneck beyond those of symbolic execution. The tool is available on GitHub.

talks.title: ICLab: A Global, Longitudinal Internet Censorship Measurement Platform
talks.teaser: Describes a longitudinal platform that spots DNS tampering, injected resets, and block pages across many national networks.
talks.summary:
The presentation motivates automated, repeatable censorship measurement where qualitative press-freedom reports cannot scale. It walks through how blocking can occur at DNS resolution, via injected TCP resets or FINs, or through served block pages, and why single-country snapshots and single-technique probes leave gaps in a global picture.

ICLab is positioned as continuous monitoring since October 2016 across 62 vantage points, mainly commercial VPNs with location validation, compared against three control nodes in the United States, Japan, and the Netherlands. Measurements exercise shared test lists, capture stack-layer evidence, and classify DNS manipulation (including CDN disambiguation via URL-to-IP ratios), packet injection, and block pages (regex plus clustering of HTML tag frequencies and LSH). Applied at scale, the pipeline reports on the order of 15,000 DNS manipulations, 143 thousand packet injections, and 230 mm block pages.

Findings stress that the chosen URL list changes perceived policy, that censors mix methods by content category (with Turkey as an example), and that longitudinal data show evolving filters—including a Turkey spike tied to political timing—while the same breadth surfaces non-censorship interference such as geo-blocking, tracking injection in South Korea, and cryptocurrency mining injection. Practitioners gain a comparative-control design pattern and concrete detectors they can study via the project site.

talks.title: Are Anonymity-Seekers Just like Everybody Else? An Analysis of Contributions to Wikipedia from Tor
talks.teaser: Compares edits from Tor users on Wikipedia with other editor groups, measuring reversion, persistence and quality.
talks.summary:
Many user-generated content sites block contributions from privacy proxies such as Tor, mainly over concerns about vandalism, spam and abuse. Wikipedia has restricted Tor editing since as early as 2005, yet the researchers found over 11,000 English Wikipedia edits from Tor exit nodes between 2008 and 2018, plus edits in other languages.

The team traced how Wikipedia's blocks worked. Early on, administrators and bots blacklisted individual Tor exit addresses for fixed periods, and a MediaWiki block extension was later used, which by late 2013 largely stopped Tor edits. The unreliable early blocking likely explains the spikes of edits that got through. Comparing Tor edits with IP editors, first-time editors and experienced registered editors, Tor edits were reverted more often, yet when reverting others' work was set aside they matched first-time editors. Tor edits also kept more persistent text than IP and first-time editors. A machine learning quality classifier rated Tor, IP and first-time editors similarly, with registered editors higher. Topic modelling showed Tor editors focusing more on politics, technology and religion and less on sports.

The takeaway is that Tor users resemble other anonymous and new editors in many ways, but they revert others far more often and engage in back-and-forth editing more, especially on discussion pages. Their topic choices also differ. The authors argue that the potential value of Tor contributions is being lost, and they encourage the community to explore ways for Tor users to contribute with added safeguards.

talks.title: Hijacking Transient Execution through Microarchitectural Load Value Injection.
talks.teaser: Explains Load Value Injection, which hijacks transient execution by injecting attacker-chosen values into a victim's CPU loads.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces Load Value Injection (LVI), a new class of transient execution attacks that builds on Spectre and Meltdown. It begins by recapping Spectre variant 1, where a bounds check is speculatively bypassed to read memory outside an array, and Meltdown, where unauthorised memory is encoded during transient execution before the fault is handled.

The middle of the talk covers Meltdown variants that depend on address computations and on microarchitectural buffers, showing how data held in those buffers can be observed transiently. A toy example then reverses the direction: the attacker first places a chosen value into a buffer, and a victim's load transiently picks it up, so the victim's own instructions and control flow are steered into leaking data through a gadget.

The speaker explains that a straightforward mitigation, stalling the pipeline by inserting serialising instructions after loads, is effective but expected to carry very high performance overhead. The practical takeaway is that any load in victim code can become an injection point, so defences need to account for buffer-based data flow and not only the memory-access checks that addressed earlier attacks.

talks.title: Detection of Electromagnetic Interference Attacks on Sensor Systems
talks.teaser: Presents a method that detects electromagnetic interference attacks on sensor systems by randomly switching the sensor on and off.
talks.summary:
Sensor wires can act as unintended antennas, so an attacker can use electromagnetic interference to inject a signal that changes a sensor's reading, and a microcontroller that trusts that reading has no way to tell. The talk considers this for automotive sensors and nuclear plant temperature monitoring, where a falsified value could drive a harmful decision. Shielding and filtering reduce the injected signal but cannot remove it, so the system must be able to detect attacks itself.

The proposed method switches the sensor off and on in a secret, randomised pattern. The bias voltage is generated by encoding an n-bit secret sequence in Manchester code, and the analog-to-digital converter takes two samples per clock cycle: one while the sensor is powered, expected to be non-zero, and one while it is off, expected to read zero. Without an attack, all non-zero samples match and all zero samples are zero. An attacker who does not know the secret must guess the transition direction in every cycle, so a wrong guess shows up as a mismatched or non-zero sample. The speaker argues that the chance of evading detection over the whole sequence is negligible.

For signals that change too quickly to treat as constant, the method can still flag samples that fall outside the signal's known bandwidth as outliers, so an attacker must alter many samples at once. The practical demonstration uses a thermistor-based temperature sensor in a lab at about 25 degrees. Without detection, an attacker can steer the reading by adjusting the injected power. With detection, a continuous attack is flagged at once, and an attacker who guesses wrong in a single cycle is also caught. The key point is that the sensor can verify its own measurements by switching off at random, provided the secret sequence stays hidden.

talks.title: WaveSpy: Remote and Through-wall Screen Attack via mmWave Sensing
talks.teaser: Shows how a mmWave probe can read liquid crystal responses to infer screen content through walls.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the usual defence against screen snooping: put a device in an isolated zone, with no line of sight, no nearby access and no signal path. Earlier side-channel work on screens, including electromagnetic and finger-movement methods, assumed that isolation held. The speakers argue it does not, and set out to test that claim.

The attack relies on the fact that displayed content is set by the orientation of liquid crystal molecules. A continuous-wave millimeter-wave probe aimed at a screen returns a modulated response whose subcarrier reflects that liquid crystal state. Building this required handling sub-millimeter liquid crystal spacing, millisecond refresh intervals and covert operation. Preliminary tests on an LED monitor, a Samsung phone and an on-screen keyboard showed distinct response patterns for different activities and keys. The WaveSpy pipeline applies a wavelet transform, classifies content type with an SVM, and then uses a sequence model to reconstruct sensitive text. A live demo showed through-wall recognition, keystroke detection and cursor tracking.

Across more than 100 content types on 30 screens, the team reported 99% accuracy for content-type recognition and 87.77% for top-three sensitive information retrieval in realistic conditions. Results held across display resolutions and cover materials. They acknowledged the attack is not perfect but said it greatly reduces an attacker's time and the entropy of a password. Countermeasures were grouped into hardware and software protections. The takeaway is that isolation alone should not be trusted to protect sensitive screens.
