talks.title: The Value of Collaboration in Convex Machine Learning with Differential Privacy
talks.teaser: Presents a differentially private gradient descent method that lets data owners jointly train a model without sharing raw data.
talks.summary:
Banks and similar institutions hold valuable but sensitive records. Pooling them would yield a better model, yet raw data cannot be shared. The running example is several lenders training a model that maps applicant salary, employment status and credit rating to historically approved interest rates. Three approaches are compared: secure multi-party computation and encryption, which add heavy computation and communication overhead; centralized training with differentially private noise; and a distributed approach that keeps each owner's data in place.

The proposed method is a differentially private gradient descent algorithm in which each data owner computes noisy subgradient responses locally and the learner aggregates them. The learning rate is tied to the total number of iterations so the privacy budget holds across the whole training horizon. For general convex losses, the analysis uses a slower decaying rate with iterate averaging. The predicted performance of the shared model depends on data set size and privacy budget, and a single owner with an extremely small budget can degrade results for everyone.

Experiments with three financial institutions show that larger privacy budgets make owners more willing to share and improve accuracy, as the theory predicts. Owners with small data sets or small budgets gain little from collaboration, while those with large data and budgets benefit most. A linear SVM fraud detection case on credit card data further supports the results. The takeaway is that collaboration pays off only when participants hold enough information to overcome the added noise.

talks.title: Towards a Natural Perspective of Smart Homes for Practical Security and Safety Analyses
talks.teaser: Generates realistic smart home automation scenarios with language models to specify security policies and test platforms.
talks.summary:
The talk, given by snail, looks at how to analyse the security and safety of smart home automation when prior work relies on hand-written use cases, random events and marketplace apps. The speaker argues that routines users build directly in the platform interface are largely missing from that work. A preliminary survey found that 42 percent of user-created routines were not covered by marketplace apps. Collecting real execution traces was rejected because they are noisy and highly privacy-invasive.

The team instead generates synthetic but natural scenarios. A survey of 40 participants supplied 273 routines written in plain English, plus timing and frequency hints, which were tokenized and arranged into month-long timelines. An n-gram language model trained on this corpus showed that home automation sequences were more predictable than English and programming-language corpora. The framework, named Hylian, generates both likely and deliberately unlikely scenarios, and an execution engine on SmartThings runs them as test cases with snapshots of device and platform state.

Across 260 sampled histories, the method found 27 security and safety violations, leading to 17 policies, such as a device acting while the user was away. Test runs also exposed dropped device commands, deleted apps that kept running, and an auto-lock feature implemented as an inconsistent default. In a study with 16 evaluators, generated routines were rated nearly as reasonable as user-made ones, while unlikely ones were seen as invalid. The takeaway is that smart home analysis must look beyond marketplace apps toward end-user programming.

talks.title: CrypTFlow : Secure TensorFlow Inference
talks.teaser: Presents a system that compiles TensorFlow inference into secure multi-party computation, scaling to ImageNet-sized networks.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a privacy conflict in machine learning inference. A hospital wants to keep its proprietary model secret, and a patient wants to keep their medical data private. Secure multi-party computation can resolve this, but earlier work has struggled with three things: low-level circuit representations that are hard to write and debug, manual conversion from floating-point to fixed-point numbers, and small datasets and models that do not reflect ImageNet-scale networks. Most prior work also assumed honest participants rather than malicious ones.

The speaker presents CrypTFlow, an end-to-end system built from three parts. Ethos is a compiler that takes TensorFlow inference code, generates metadata, and converts floating-point values to fixed-point automatically by sweeping a scale factor and tuning it on a validation set. It then emits semi-honest MPC protocol code through a modular backend, currently ABY and Porthos. Porthos, a three-party protocol for neural network inference, is mentioned but not covered in depth. Aramis turns any semi-honest protocol into a maliciously secure one by having participants run inside Intel SGX and rely only on its integrity guarantee, since confidentiality attacks such as Foreshadow and Plundervolt break the stronger hardware-based approach.

Reported results on ImageNet networks, ResNet-50 and DenseNet-121, run in about 25 seconds in the semi-honest model on a LAN with commodity hardware. Malicious security adds less than 3x overhead, and compilation takes around 40 seconds. For ResNet-50, the chosen scale factor keeps accuracy at the plaintext level. The takeaway is that large, malicious-secure inference is becoming practical, and the authors provide the paper and code.

talks.title: This PIN Can Be Easily Guessed: Analyzing the Security of Smartphone Unlock PINs
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of This PIN Can Be Easily Guessed: Analyzing the Security of Smartphone Unlock PINs.
talks.summary: Researchers motivate PIN study despite biometrics: knowledge factors still back up Face ID and remain guessable under coercion. A 1,200-person survey shows two-thirds still use PINs; prior work proves four- and six-digit choices are predictable, while blacklists help but need smartphone-specific balancing of security versus usability across treatment arms.

talks.title: NetCAT: Practical Cache Attacks from the Network
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for NetCAT: Practical Cache Attacks from the Network.
talks.summary: Michael Schwarz presents NetCAT, using Intel DDIO to place NIC DMA into the last-level cache and remotely prime-probe SSH keystroke arrival times without malware on client or server. Timing fingerprints plus typing-pattern statistics leak shell commands; the talk contrasts prior cache attacks that required co-resident code execution on shared hardware.

talks.title: Message Time of Arrival Codes: A Fundamental Primitive for Secure Distance Measurement
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Message Time of Arrival Codes: A Fundamental Primitive for Secure Distance Measurement.

talks.title: Nicholas Carlini: Making and Measuring Progress in Adversarial Machine Learning
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Nicholas Carlini: Making and Measuring Progress in Adversarial Machine Learning.

talks.title: Exploring Adversarial Examples in Malware Detection
talks.teaser: Shows how appended and slack-space byte injections evade neural malware classifiers and what makes them vulnerable.
talks.summary:
Machine learning classifiers that separate malware from benign files increasingly learn directly from raw bytes, avoiding hand-built features. This talk asks whether one shallow convolutional architecture can be evaded by adversarial examples. Naive gradient-based noise breaks executables, so the work focuses on modifications that keep files runnable. Models were trained on a large production dataset and a smaller public one. The speaker showed that a simple attack appending bytes from benign files succeeded far more against the small-dataset model, suggesting that limited training data can produce skewed estimates of attack effectiveness.

A single-step gradient attack that appends perturbation bytes was more effective against the model trained on the larger dataset. The speaker attributed this to the architecture: non-overlapping convolution windows and max pooling without positional information mean appended features cannot be told apart from those at the start of the file. A second method, slack-space FGSM, writes perturbations into the gap between a PE section's raw and virtual sizes, a region not loaded into memory. At the same number of modified bytes it was roughly 40 percent more effective than appending, although the available slack capacity is limited.

The takeaways were that representative training data matters when measuring robustness, that architectural choices such as positional encoding can introduce vulnerability, and that realistic attacker capability requires reasoning about program semantics. Questions raised limits: functionality preservation cannot be fully guaranteed without execution, the approach may depend on the compiler and platform, and simple header-consistency checks could detect such edits.

talks.title: On the Robustness of Deep K-Nearest Neighbors
talks.teaser: Delivers differentiable attacks against k-nearest neighbor and deep k-nearest neighbor for white-box robustness evaluation.
talks.summary:
The presentation motivates security evaluation for k-nearest neighbor (KNN) and deep k-nearest neighbor (DkNN) classifiers, which are nonparametric and not differentiable, so standard gradient-based adversarial attacks do not apply directly. Prior work suggested these models may resist adversarial examples and support error detection, yet little work had systematically attacked them under a white-box setting where all training data is known.

The speakers describe a simple mean-direction baseline that pushes inputs toward the mean of another class until misclassification occurs, then a gradient-based method that targets a small set of nearby opposite-class training points. A hard distance threshold is relaxed with a sigmoid so the objective becomes differentiable and can be minimized under an Lp perturbation budget and valid input bounds. On MNIST with cosine KNN (k=75), the new attack matches the baseline’s success while using much smaller L2 perturbations; many failures show semantically shaped noise. For DkNN, distances are summed across neural representation layers; the gradient attack drives accuracy to zero with mean L2 around 2.1–2.2, far below the mean attack’s 44.4, and some changes are nearly imperceptible despite similar norm.

Practitioners should treat norm size alone as a weak proxy for human-visible risk when perturbations carry semantic structure. The work argues DkNN still shows some defensive promise relative to ordinary classifiers, while credibility scores for detection remain imperfect. Ongoing directions include pairing DkNN with more robust networks and stronger KNN variants; experiments also extend beyond MNIST to richer datasets such as CIFAR-10.

talks.title: Targeted Adversarial Examples for Black Box Audio Systems
talks.teaser: Presents a gradient-free genetic attack that makes a speech recognizer transcribe chosen phrases from near-unchanged audio.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at targeted adversarial examples against automatic speech recognition, where a small change to audio makes the system transcribe a chosen phrase while a listener hears no difference. Targeted attacks are harder than untargeted ones, and black-box attacks assume only the model's output logits are visible, not its architecture or gradients. The speaker reviews two prior approaches: a black-box genetic algorithm limited to single-word classes, and a white-box method that uses CTC loss to handle full phrases.

The proposed attack combines these ideas into a gradient-free genetic algorithm that works on full sentences against the open-source DeepSpeech model, using Common Voice clips sampled at 16 kHz. Each generation keeps the top ten of a population of 100 candidates, ranked by CTC loss, and applies crossover and mutation, with the added noise high-pass filtered. A momentum-style mutation rate rises when scores stall and falls when they improve. Once the decoding is within a Levenshtein distance of two from the target, the attack switches to gradient estimation over randomly chosen sample indices to fine-tune the result.

On the first 100 clips, with randomly generated two-word targets run for 3000 generations, the attack reached a targeted similarity of 89.25 percent, and the average similarity to the benign input was 94.6 percent by cross-correlation. Only 35 percent of samples matched the target exactly, though many were within a few edits. The speaker compares this with a white-box attack that reached full success but needed model internals, and with single-word black-box work. Stated limitations include transferability, sample efficiency, runtime cost and no robustness testing against room noise. Replaying prerecorded, predictable audio is the most realistic scenario mentioned, and the work is presented as a proof of concept.

talks.title: Activation Analysis of a Byte-Based Deep Neural Network for Malware Classification
talks.teaser: Explains which features a byte-based neural network learns for Windows malware classification, and how data volume changes them.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at what a deep convolutional network learns when it classifies Windows PE files from raw bytes, without hand-built features. Three variants were compared: a baseline trained on about 15 million samples skewed toward malware, a smaller model trained on half that data with a balanced split, and a dropout version of the baseline. The data came from VirusTotal and ReversingLabs feeds.

The analysis worked up the network in three stages. Clustering the embedding layer showed that outlier byte patterns mattered more than clusters. Inspecting high-activation regions in the first convolutional layer showed the small model using few, flexible filters, while the dropout model used nearly all of its filters yet matched very specific strings. Shapley attribution showed the small model gathering evidence across many PE structures, while the dropout model relied on about three.

The small model generalized better on held-out data from 2018 despite less training data. The speaker concluded that these networks behave like learned antivirus signatures, where broader patterns work better than narrow ones, and that capturing malware indicators matters more than modeling PE structure in general. Future work includes separate branches for PE sections.

talks.title: Efficient Evaluation of Activation Functions over Encrypted Data
talks.teaser: Demonstrates efficient evaluation of activation functions on encrypted data using table lookups and modular selection.
talks.summary:
Sensitive machine learning still typically requires decrypting data at processing time, which conflicts with goals such as protecting training data, inputs, model weights, and outputs. Homomorphic encryption supports addition and multiplication on ciphertexts, but standard activations like sigmoid and ReLU are not polynomial, so prior work often swaps in x squared or polynomial surrogates that may fail to converge or misbehave when outputs must stay in valid probability ranges.

The work targets evaluation of arbitrary functions over a bounded discrete range on encrypted inputs using an RLWE-based integer scheme with fixed-point encoding. A malicious server learns nothing about inputs or outputs; a semi-honest server still yields correct results to the client. The core idea builds encrypted index vectors, uses rotations and multiplications to place a single nonzero entry, then applies precomputed modular factors so one slot becomes an encrypted one before dotting against a precomputed function table. The procedure needs on the order of log n plus two multiplications and scales linearly with table size.

Experiments replace sigmoid and ReLU in a variational autoencoder on MNIST and in a merger classifier, tuning precision via truncation or rounding. Sigmoid inputs often take only tens of distinct values, so modest tables suffice. Takeaway: encrypted inference is largely numerical analysis—map activation inputs, pick precision deliberately, and prefer faster polynomial activations when they converge; otherwise this lookup path trades speed for generality while community efforts chase larger-scale HE performance.

talks.title: Membership Inference Attacks against Adversarially Robust Deep Learning Models
talks.teaser: Shows adversarial training makes models more vulnerable to membership inference, revealing a security-privacy tension.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how defenses against adversarial examples affect privacy, specifically membership inference attacks, where an adversary tries to tell whether a given input was part of a model's training data. Prior work usually treats these security and privacy questions separately. Membership inference is tied to overfitting and to how sensitive a model is to any single training point.

The argument is that adversarial training, which keeps predictions stable within a small perturbation radius around each training point, makes the model more sensitive to individual training examples. The speaker compared loss distributions for members and non-members and found a wider gap for the robust model. Using a shadow-model attack and a fixed threshold on prediction confidence, the speaker tested two defenses: adversarial training and a provable defense. Adversarial training made membership inference noticeably easier, and larger perturbation budgets leaked more. The provable defense did not increase membership inference risk in these experiments, but it cost a large drop in clean accuracy.

The takeaway is that robustness and privacy should be evaluated together, since a defense that improves one can worsen the other. A follow-up mentioned in the Q&A trained robustly on only part of the data; it kept accuracy close to the robust model while inference accuracy fell between the natural and robust results.

talks.title: Deep in the Dark - Deep Learning-based Malware Traffic Detection without Expert Knowledge
talks.teaser: Shows how deep learning on raw packet and flow bytes can detect malware traffic without hand-built features.
talks.summary:
Gonzalo presents work on detecting malware in network traffic with deep learning, aiming to cut the manual feature engineering that classic machine learning pipelines depend on. Expert-designed features must be rebuilt for each problem, which takes time and makes results hard to compare. The team asked whether neural networks could learn directly from raw bytes and how they would fare against shallow models.

They tested two input forms: raw packets, where each packet's bytes form one sample, and raw flows, where the first two packets of a flow are combined into one sample. Labelled data came from public Stratosphere IPS captures, with malware and normal traffic recorded under controlled conditions, giving about 250,000 packet samples and about 68,000 flow samples. The packet model pairs convolutional layers with an LSTM, while the flow model uses a smaller convolutional network with dense layers. The deep model beat a random forest given the same raw bytes. The raw-flow model caught about 88% of malware with a false positive rate under 0.2%. A random forest using about 200 expert features reached roughly 97% accuracy with a false positive rate under 1%, so the raw-flow model came close to that baseline rather than clearly beating it.

Questions from the audience focused on labelling: the captures were built by infecting some devices by hand, so the ground truth reflects a lab setup, and transfer to other networks is unproven. The main takeaway is that raw bytes can reduce manual feature work and that flow-level inputs allow fast detection, but generalization to real traffic remains the open challenge.
