talks.title: Resident Evil: Understanding Residential IP Proxy as a Dark Service
talks.teaser: A large-scale probe of five residential proxy vendors verifies IP types and maps recruitment, abuse patterns, and LAN exposure risks.
talks.summary:
The presentation compares traditional anonymization proxies with marketed residential proxy services that promise cleaner, geo-distributed egress and fewer blocks. The researchers describe a gateway model in which customer traffic is relayed through peers that stay hidden from buyers, and they purchase access to five major providers to measure the ecosystem.

Their clients sent more than 60 million successful probes and collected more than 6 million unique IPv4 addresses spanning more than 200 countries and tens of thousands of autonomous systems. A random-forest residential IP classifier built from high-confidence labels and features such as DNS and WHOIS traits supports the providers’ residential claims. Overlap with public Tor and web-proxy lists is negligible, and only about 2% of observed addresses correlate with common threat-intelligence blacklists—yet downstream flow analysis still flags a meaningful share of destinations as malicious. Device profiling surfaces routers, cameras, printers, and other IoT hosts; industry telemetry helps tie 67 unwanted programs across all five vendors to relay traffic, with most flagged malicious by antivirus engines.

Further findings include shared infrastructure between certain brands, heavy use of advertising and affiliate destinations, and alarming provider behavior that relays customer traffic to loopback or private LAN addresses—exposing home gateways and printers. Practitioners should treat residential proxy pools as scalable abuse infrastructure, watch for covert recruitment, and harden local networks against lateral traffic injected through compromised or volunteered peers.

talks.title: New Primitives for Actively-Secure MPC over Rings with Applications to Private Machine Learning
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of New Primitives for Actively-Secure MPC over Rings with Applications to Private Machine Learning.

talks.title: On the Security of Two-Round Multi-Signatures
talks.teaser: Shows that known two-round Schnorr multi-signature schemes can be forged, and offers a repaired, provably secure variant.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces multi-signatures, which let a group of signers jointly produce one compact signature that anyone can check against their combined public key. It starts from the basic Schnorr signature and the usual way of extending it into a two-round protocol. Rogue-key attacks are long known, but a subtler obstacle appears in security proofs, where simulating signing queries breaks down because an adversary can control the product of the commitment values.

The speaker argues that every known two-round Schnorr-based scheme, including BCJ, MWLD, CoSi and MuSig, is insecure. Forgeries apply Wagner's algorithm to lists of hashes, so that challenge values sum to the hash of a different message and signatures can be combined without the secret key. With 127 signing queries, the attack needs roughly 2^45 steps. Proving these schemes secure under the one-more discrete-log assumption is shown to be unlikely with known techniques, which exposes flaws in several published proofs.

As a repair, the speaker presents mBCJ, a modified BCJ scheme proven secure under the discrete-log assumption in the random-oracle model. In a CoSi-based implementation, 16,000 signers signed a message in under two seconds, with a slight bandwidth rise and a 75% increase in computation. The talk closes with three-round discrete-log schemes or BLS-based schemes as alternatives, and urges care when dropping proof steps and better tools for checking complex proofs.

talks.title: Kiss from a Rogue: Evaluating Detectability of Pay-at-the-Pump Card Skimmers
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Kiss from a Rogue: Evaluating Detectability of Pay-at-the-Pump Card Skimmers.
talks.summary: Researchers extend earlier overlay and deep-insert skimmer taxonomy work to pay-at-the-pump internal devices installed after attackers unlock pumps with weak or default keys. EMV rollout stalls because licensed payment retrofits can cost thousands of dollars per nozzle, leaving magnetic stripe fraud economical. The team coded three years of Florida Agriculture inspections and found intact anti-tamper seals on most compromised pumps, showing seals fail as consumer-facing controls when attendants reapply them without inspection or criminals swap rolls cheaply. A teardown of seven mobile skimmer-detector apps finds brittle Bluetooth name and MAC-prefix heuristics, heavy advertising, and iOS inability to scan classic Bluetooth modules common in seized hardware. Lab tests against six real skimmers show trivial serial reconfiguration evades matching rules. Recommendations emphasize hardened pump locks, terminal disable-on-open designs, and interruptive UI patterns instead of unaided seal glances.

talks.title: SoK: Shining Light on Shadow Stacks
talks.teaser: Examines shadow stack designs for return-address integrity, performance, and deployment alongside forward-edge CFI mitigations.
talks.summary:
Memory corruption in C and C++ often lets attackers overwrite code pointers and hijack control flow. Forward-edge protections such as control-flow integrity narrow indirect call targets, but backward edges—returns—remain weakly defended; stack canaries fail when overflows corrupt pointers that write past the canary. Shadow stacks copy return addresses out of the data-heavy program stack and check them at return time, giving precise backward-edge integrity without huge static target sets.

The presentation surveys indirect versus direct shadow-stack mappings, implements multiple designs in LLVM, and benchmarks them on SPEC CPU2006 plus workloads such as Phoronix suites and Apache. Indirect mapping with a dedicated general-purpose register holding the shadow stack pointer delivers about 3.65% average overhead while using less memory than mirror stacks. Compatibility topics include threading, C++ exception unwinding, setjmp/longjmp, and calling uninstrumented code, with incremental deployment argued as practical.

Integrity enforcement for isolated shadow metadata is also compared: software randomization adds modest cost, Intel MPX lands near 12%, and MPK can spike severely in some cases. The closing argument is that deployed CFI must be paired with shadow stacks for complete control-flow hijacking defense, with stronger intra-process isolation likely needing better hardware than today's MPX and MPK shortcuts.

talks.title: LBM: A Security Framework for Peripherals within the Linux Kernel
talks.teaser: Presents a Linux kernel framework that filters USB, Bluetooth and NFC traffic using eBPF rules before the stack.
talks.summary:
Peripherals such as USB devices, Bluetooth gadgets and NFC readers can carry reprogrammed firmware that acts like a keyboard or sends malformed packets to a host. Examples include a USB device that injects keystrokes and a malicious charging station. Packet firewalls do not map well onto these buses, so the speaker asks how a host can defend against them.

The proposed answer is LBM, a Linux kernel module described as a generic security framework for peripherals. It places hooks in the USB, Bluetooth and NFC I/O paths, covering both transmit and receive, as low in each protocol stack as practical. Filter rules are written in a short DSL that compiles through an abstract syntax tree into eBPF instructions and loads into the kernel. Adding NFC support reportedly took about 100 lines of changes or fewer. Demonstrations included dropping malformed USB enumeration packets from a USB hardware tester, allowing only a trusted keyboard to type, enforcing charging-only mode on a port, and dropping the offending L2CAP configuration response packet to block a Bluetooth kernel overflow.

Benchmarks on a USB 3.0 hard disk showed a worst-case overhead below 1.8 percent compared with the stock kernel, and filter-count scaling was measured with a USB Wi-Fi adapter. Limitations include that BPF memory writes are disallowed, so packets cannot yet be modified, filters are mostly stateless, and vendor or product ID rules can be bypassed by reprogrammed firmware. The main takeaway is that filters can patch peripheral behaviour on a running kernel without waiting for vendor fixes or a reboot.

talks.title: Stealthy Porn: Understanding Real World Adversarial Images for Illicit Online Promotion
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Stealthy Porn: Understanding Real World Adversarial Images for Illicit Online Promotion.
talks.summary:
### Overview
This presentation examines real-world adversarial images used for illicit online promotion (termed "APIs" or adversarial promotional images) that bypass state-of-the-art illicit content detectors on major online forums. These images typically feature promotional text or QR codes alongside explicit, adult material designed to lure users into following redirection chains leading to sexual live streams or illicit services. The study represents collaborative research between the Chinese University of Hong Kong, Indiana University, and the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

### Key Topics
- **Characterizing Adversarial Promotional Images (APIs):** Distinguishing real-world APIs from theoretical adversarial examples (which rely on imperceptible mathematical noise) and cropped images. APIs retain promotional information and at least one clearly visible explicit region designed to attract human attention while evading machine detection.
- **The Malina Detection Framework:** Design and implementation of a sequential detection pipeline that achieved 91% precision and 85% recall on empirical data.
- **Ecosystem and Campaign Measurement:** Analysis of 4 million images across 76,000 posts collected from China's two largest social networks—Tieba (over 200 million users) and Weibo (over 400 million users)—identifying over 4,000 manually confirmed APIs.
- **Underground Infrastructure and Distribution:** Investigation into attacker campaigns, account types (compromised vs. dedicated accounts), and contact channels (such as WeChat IDs and QR codes).

### Technical Details
- **Malina Architecture:** The Malina framework operates using four components:
  1. *Preprocessor:* Identifies image formats and splits animated GIF files into individual frames.
  2. *Promotional Content Identifier:* Extracts promotional identifiers categorized into text and QR codes. Text is extracted using PixelLink. For QR codes, because standard detectors struggled across diverse styles and embedding the heavy WeChat client was impractical, the authors filtered images using an adaptive threshold before detection.
  3. *Regional Illicit Content Detector:* Uses a region proposal network to locate candidate human regions with high confidence scores, crops them, and passes them to a neural network to evaluate whether explicit content is present.
  4. *Evasiveness Checker:* Tests candidate images against current detectors to confirm whether they successfully bypass detection.
- **Visual Evasion Techniques:** The authors identified seven primary visual manipulation techniques: noise, blur, texture generalization, occlusion, rotation, and color manipulation. The top three most common techniques observed were noise, rotation, and occlusion. Testing against two prominent commercial detectors from Google and Yahoo revealed severe fragilities: rotating explicit images by 45° or 135°, adding slight noise, or transforming images to a green color tint caused both commercial detectors to fail.
- **Promotion and Campaign Tactics:** WeChat IDs represented the primary promotional vector, often disguised using obfuscated terms or secret signals (such as "VX" to represent WeChat). Adversaries frequently engaged in asset reuse: 37% of promotional content appeared across multiple APIs, and 91% of explicit content was reused across different promotional targets. Grouping these overlapping assets revealed coordinated illicit campaigns, the largest of which produced more than 13,000 posts. Over half of the accounts utilized were aggressive, automated "dedicated accounts" posting more than 30 times a day with meaningless text, while the remainder were compromised existing accounts posting on hot topics.

### Takeaways
- **Prevalence and Evasion:** Real-world illicit promotional images are widely deployed across major social networks and routinely defeat deployed commercial detectors through straightforward spatial and color transformations.
- **Model Hardening:** Deployed neural network models urgently need hardening, which can be accomplished by fine-tuning classifiers on augmented datasets incorporating realistic visual manipulation patterns (rotations, noise, color transformations).
- **Holistic Ecosystem Defense:** Mitigating illicit campaigns requires addressing the wider operational ecosystem—including blocking external promotional channels (such as WeChat handles) and implementing platform behavioral rules to restrict high-frequency automated dedicated accounts.

talks.title: Dominance as a New Trusted Computing Primitive for the IoT
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Dominance as a New Trusted Computing Primitive for the IoT.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In large-scale IoT deployments—such as smart cities, supply chains, and Industry 4.0—thousands of identical devices are deployed across wide geographic areas. Because these devices share identical software and configurations, an attacker exploiting a single software vulnerability or weak password can compromise an entire fleet, sever communication with central management hubs, and recruit devices into botnets. Recovering such fleets currently requires costly manual servicing, such as dispatching field workers to manually reflash firmware. To solve this problem without manual intervention, the speaker presents Cider, a system designed to establish "dominance" over IoT devices.

Dominance is defined as the capability of an IoT hub to force a remote device to execute arbitrary code (such as a patched firmware) within a bounded timeframe (e.g., within four hours of discovering an attack), even under a strong adversarial model where application software, network communications, and the OS kernel have been fully rooted.

### Key Topics
- **Dominance as an IoT Security Primitive**: Allowing a central management hub to unconditionally regain control and patch compromised IoT devices.
- **Minimal Hardware Primitives**: Building root-of-trust and recovery guarantees using read/write latches, read-write latches, and authenticated watchdog timers instead of heavyweight trusted execution environments.
- **Isolation in Time**: Alternating between trusted and untrusted software states rather than relying on complex concurrent hardware isolation.
- **Unconditional Recovery Guarantees**: Enforcing recovery via cryptographic attestation and watchdog-driven hardware resets when an attacker refuses commands.

### Technical Details
Cider assumes only the underlying hardware is trustworthy and introduces three core guarantees built on simple hardware primitives:
1. **Execution of an Unaltered Bootloader**: Devices must always reboot into an untampered trusted bootloader (the Cider bootloader). This is achieved using hardware write latches that block write access to the bootloader's flash/eMMC storage blocks before control transfers to untrusted firmware.
2. **Firmware Attestation and Patching**: Bootloader verification ensures only hub-approved firmware runs. To prevent a compromised firmware from stealing the device attestation key, the key is consumed during boot and immediately locked down using a read-write latch that blocks all further reads and writes until the next hardware reset. To minimize the Trusted Computing Base (TCB), the networking stack is isolated into an untrusted recovery module treated like standard firmware.
3. **Unconditional Device Reset via Authenticated Watchdog Timers**: Conventional watchdog timers can be spoofed by malicious software writing expected constants to registers. Cider replaces this with an authenticated watchdog timer requiring nonces signed by the hub (certificates/tickets). If a device is compromised and fails hub verification, the hub stops issuing tickets, causing the timer to expire and triggering an unconditional hardware reset back into Cider's trusted bootloader.

The authors implemented Cider across high-, mid-, and low-end evaluation boards (SolidRun, Raspberry Pi 3, and STM32). The authenticated watchdog timer can be realized either by repurposing existing onboard hardware (such as TrustZone, physical timers, or MPUs) or by attaching an external microcontroller costing under one dollar.

### Takeaways
Cider demonstrates that dominance over IoT devices can be enforced with minimal performance overhead—runtime delays are negligible since watchdog check-ins occur only every few hours or days, and boot overhead is minimal unless downloading full patch images. By prioritizing temporal isolation ("isolation in time") over complex runtime hardware isolation mechanisms (which require MMUs, context switching, and multi-threading susceptible to speculative execution and side-channel attacks), Cider provides a practical, low-cost cornerstone for resilient IoT security.

talks.title: Drones' Cryptanalysis - Detecting Privacy Invasion Attacks Conducted by Drone
talks.teaser: Shows how intercepted Wi-Fi drone video traffic can reveal whether a drone is secretly spying on a victim.
talks.summary:
Drones are increasingly used to spy on spouses, neighbours and celebrities, and the talk argues that geofencing, which detects a nearby drone with radar, cameras or hybrid systems, cannot reveal a privacy invasion. A drone's position says little about where its camera points, and open-skies rules allow more flying over populated areas.

The approach targets the video downlink of Wi-Fi first-person-view drones. Although the payload is encrypted, packet sizes remain visible. A receiver several kilometres away builds a time series from these sizes, and frequency analysis of the bitrate reveals the frame rate, from which resolution can be estimated. Combined with motion detection, this classifies a link as a drone camera within about three seconds. To connect the stream to a victim, the method exploits H.264 compression: a light flickering at the target changes how much data is encoded, and that pattern appears in the traffic. The flicker is hidden by alternating between two brightness levels the human eye cannot distinguish.

Demonstrations used a siren in a moving car and a smart film on a living-room window, with a legitimate flight facing away as a control. A fixed threshold flagged attacks in about two and a half seconds at a low false-positive rate. Frequency analysis was preferred over time-domain analysis, which produced more false alarms. The paper also covers locating the drone with one receiver, countermeasures, and the effects of wind and ambient light. The takeaway: defenders should examine what the video link reveals about camera use, not just where the drone is.

talks.title: Dangerous Skills: Understanding and Mitigating Security Risks of Voice-Controlled Third-Party...
talks.teaser: Shows how voice skills with confusable invocation names can be hijacked, and proposes checks to detect masquerading.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at third-party skills on voice assistants such as Amazon Alexa and Google Home. Users reach these skills by saying an invocation name rather than installing an app, and the platform's routing decides which skill answers. The speaker sets out security requirements for this routing and identifies two attack classes: skill squatting, where a malicious skill claims a name that sounds like a popular one, and masquerading, where a skill impersonates the system or another skill during a conversation. Possible consequences include access to bank balances or home devices, spread of misleading information, phishing through notifications, and damage to the victim skill's reputation.

The researchers tested how reliably each platform recognizes invocation names, using human speakers and text-to-speech recordings. Recognition error rates were high on both platforms, and Google performed noticeably better than Alexa. They then published attack skills with names close to a popular skill, and many of them were invoked instead of the victim skill, especially on Alexa. A scan of the skill market found that more than nineteen percent of skills collide with others through identical pronunciation, 2.7% use sound-alike names with different spelling, and 1.8% exploit longest prefix matching to compete with existing skills.

To counter masquerading, the authors propose two components. A user intention classifier decides whether a request is a context switch or a continuation of the current interaction. A secure response checker compares each skill response against a blacklist and flags responses with high similarity as suspicious. The speaker notes that both platforms acknowledged the reported cases and discussed mitigation plans. The practical takeaway is that invocation-name collisions are a real routing risk that voice platforms must handle at registration and at runtime.

talks.title: SoK: Security Evaluation of Home Based IoT Deployment
talks.teaser: Presents a framework that grades consumer IoT devices across their device, mobile app, cloud back-ends and local network.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a consumer question: is a connected home device safe to own? Prior work has studied individual devices, home networks, voice interfaces and cloud integrations, but rarely the whole ecosystem. The speaker, a Georgia Tech PhD student, proposes a framework that grades each device across four components: the device itself, its mobile app, its cloud back-ends and the local network.

For each component the framework runs specific checks, such as how a device pairs and whether it updates automatically, how many back-ends it contacts and how its TLS is configured, whether the app contains hard-coded secrets, and whether local traffic is encrypted and resistant to interception. One device contacted twelve first-party back-ends and had a remote code execution flaw in one of them. A speaker's local traffic was largely unencrypted. Scores varied sharply between components of the same device, and across devices from one manufacturer. Devices that were cloud managed, updated automatically and encrypted local traffic using authenticated services tended to score highest.

The evaluation covered 45 devices, with about 70 now in the lab. The team plans a longitudinal analysis to see how grades shift as updates and CVEs arrive, along with more realistic deployments that simulate household activity. Scorecards and the dataset are published online.

talks.title: PhishFarm: A Scalable Framework for Measuring the Effectivness of Evasion Techniques Against...
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of PhishFarm: A Scalable Framework for Measuring the Effectivness of Evasion Techniques Against....
talks.summary:
## Overview
PhishFarm is a scalable framework for measuring the effectiveness of evasion techniques against modern anti-phishing blacklists, developed through collaboration between Arizona State University and PayPal. The research addresses a critical gap in understanding how phishing attacks bypass browser-based defenses. Phishing attacks rely on social engineering but are difficult to mitigate at scale due to an extensive ecosystem supporting their deployment. While browser blacklists—including Google Safe Browsing, Microsoft SmartScreen, and Opera's protection—represent a key defense mechanism, attackers actively employ evasion techniques to circumvent them.

## Research Methodology
The study was conducted in two phases. Preliminary experiments deployed 400 sites (6-7 per technique, 10 entities each) to understand anti-phishing entity behavior and refine the testing approach. Full-scale experiments deployed approximately 2,000 sites (66 per technique, 4 batches per entity) with continuous monitoring. The framework enabled end-to-end automation: configuration, deployment to cloud infrastructure, reporting to anti-phishing entities, and real-time blacklist monitoring across desktop and mobile browsers. Researchers used both random and deceptive URLs. After disclosure meetings with browser vendors and anti-phishing providers, a written report was shared with other organizations.

## Cloaking Techniques Tested
Six primary techniques were evaluated: (1) no cloaking (control), (2) mobile-targeting (Android/iOS), (3) geolocation-based filtering (US vs. non-US desktop), (4) real-world phishing kit data with IP addresses and user agents, (5) JavaScript-based rendering requirements, and (6) htaccess dataset fingerprinting. These techniques were chosen to represent real-world attacker practices and user populations.

## Key Findings
Cloaking reduced the likelihood of blacklisting by approximately 50% and doubled the time to blacklisting. A critical finding was that iOS and Android cloaking techniques resulted in zero blacklisting—mobile users visiting mobile-targeted phishing sites received no warnings, while desktop blacklists did not protect mobile platforms. US-only geolocation filtering successfully bypassed Google Safe Browsing, and similar region-specific patterns emerged for other entities. Real-world phishing kit data was more likely to be blacklisted, possibly due to fingerprinting. JavaScript cloaking effectively delayed long-term blacklisting. Significant blacklist changes occurred after approximately 2 hours, with variation by entity.

## Monitoring Results
Over 72 hours, the framework collected over 20,000 blacklist timestamps and recorded over 2 million web hits from security crawlers. Google Safe Browsing proved fastest at blacklisting, though coverage gaps existed on mobile. Microsoft SmartScreen was the only entity using proactive heuristics on page content and URLs without verifying content first. Limited data sharing occurred between Google and Microsoft, though clearinghouses like the aPWG facilitated some coordination. Opera showed very limited coverage.

## Security Implications and Outcomes
Following disclosure to Google before September 2018, mobile blacklisting issues were addressed. Users visiting known malicious sites on mobile subsequently received proper warnings, and other cloaking techniques became more detectable. The research revealed that hosting providers took an average of 17 hours to respond to abuse reports, and remediation was often ineffective initially. The ease of automated phishing site generation means that even 24-hour mitigation windows provide little value to defenders, as attackers deploy hundreds of sites per hour.

## Recommendations
Cloaking prolongs attacker opportunities, particularly with geo-specific filtering. Current mitigations are insufficiently fast. The researchers recommend improved blacklist and hosting infrastructure responses, continuous testing and verification of defenses, enhanced data sharing between entities, trusted reporting channels from phishing victims, and proactive detection techniques leveraging intelligence beyond content analysis. These should complement multi-layer strategies including two-factor authentication and user training.

## Takeaways
PhishFarm demonstrates that evasion techniques significantly degrade blacklist effectiveness and revealed a critical protection gap on mobile platforms. The framework supports ongoing security testing and baseline verification. The research emphasizes the need for faster, more coordinated responses and proactive detection rather than reactive blacklisting alone.

talks.title: Measuring and Analyzing Search Engine Poisoning of Linguistic Collisions
talks.teaser: A large-scale study measures search poisoning when other-language word collisions let misspellings skip autocorrect on Google and Baidu.
talks.summary:
Web users often reach sites through search rather than URLs, and search engines use autocorrect and partial result rewriting to fix typos. Attackers have long abused misspelled queries for SEO, but those defenses push them toward linguistic collision misspellings: edits that still form real words, often in another language, so engines neither warn nor correct. The presenter describes measuring this problem on Google for English and Baidu for Chinese across spam-heavy and brand-like keyword sets drawn from Alexa rankings and thirteen categories.

The methodology generates edit-distance-one typos—keyboard-adjacent swaps for English and pinyin ambiguity, tones, and fuzzy dialect input for Chinese—then checks which queries skip autocorrect and which first-page results VirusTotal flags as poisoned. Roughly 1.8 million candidate misspellings yield about 1.2% poisoned among non-corrected collisions. Drugs, adult, and gambling terms see far higher targeting than other buckets; Chinese shows lower poisoning partly because Baidu surfaces reputable domains more often. A character-level RNN filters viable misspellings about 2.8 times better than random sampling, and poisoned typo traffic skews mobile.

Poisoned listings lean on malvertising and cheap third-level hosting. Google Translate language tagging helps explain why some English drug terms escape English-centric correction, with collisions spanning dozens of languages. Practitioners should treat plausible alternate-language tokens as a bypass for typo defenses, not a solved problem.

talks.title: Why Does Your Data Leak? Uncovering the Data Leakage in Cloud from Mobile Apps
talks.teaser: Shows how leaked keys and misconfigured permissions in mobile apps expose cloud backend data at scale.
talks.summary:
Many mobile apps rely on cloud backends offered as mobile backend-as-a-service, such as AWS, Google Firebase and Microsoft Azure. The talk frames data leakage as an access control problem: an app key identifies the app, a user credential proves who is calling, and a privileged root key lets developers manage the backend. The speaker identifies two root causes: privileged keys shipped inside client apps, and permission rules too loose to separate one user's records from another's.

To find these problems at scale, the authors built LeakScope. It locates SDK calls that take a key, recovers the key strings through value set analysis, and then sends a request for existing data using that key. The error response decides the outcome: an authorization failure means the check held, while a "data does not exist" reply means the key passed and the permission check was reached, without reading anyone else's data. Applied to 1.6 million apps, the tool flagged more than 15,000 vulnerable apps across six vulnerability types, some with over 100 million installs.

After disclosure, the providers responded. Microsoft updated documentation that had shown root keys in examples, Google planned friendlier permission configuration tooling, and Amazon added a new permission check. The takeaway for practitioners is to keep root keys off the client and default to restrictive permissions. The study covers only three providers, and the speaker points to future work on other software stacks and vulnerability classes.

talks.title: Formally Verified Cryptographic Web Applications in WebAssembly
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Formally Verified Cryptographic Web Applications in WebAssembly.

talks.title: The Code That Never Ran: Modeling Attacks on Speculative Evaluation
talks.teaser: Builds a formal model of speculative execution that covers Spectre-style leaks and demonstrates new attacks on real compilers.
talks.summary:
Speculative evaluation is a hardware optimization meant to stay hidden at the architectural level, yet Spectre showed it can bypass dynamic array bounds checks and expose memory from inside JavaScript. Compiler reordering adds to the problem. The talk sets out a high-level formal model that captures speculative execution without low-level timing or cache detail.

The authors formalize the model with partial orders and offer compositional semantics in the style of C11. It captures Spectre, Spectre-Prime and attacks on transactional memory, along with fencing-based mitigations. Building it also exposed an information-flow property tied to compiler optimizations: when a secret equals one, a compiler can float an assignment out of an if statement, removing a dependency that would otherwise form a cycle and allow a leaking execution.

Craig then explained how to build such compiler attacks on real GCC and Clang. The setup is unrealistic: the secret must be a compile-time constant while the permission check stays dynamic. A second thread keeps writing to a shared variable, and a short delay of up to 30 straight-line instructions makes the load and store reordering more likely. One attack reached 99.99% bitwise accuracy at 300k bits per second, and a dead-store elimination variant hit 99.99% at 1.2 megabits per second on both compilers. Just-in-time compilers were not aggressive enough to reproduce the attack yet. The work concludes that compiler optimizations alone can leak secrets, and the model helps reason about these cases.

talks.title: SoK: General Purpose Frameworks for Secure Multi-Party Computation
talks.teaser: Compares nine general-purpose secure multi-party computation frameworks on expressiveness, build complexity and documentation quality.
talks.summary:
Secure multi-party computation lets mutually distrustful parties compute a function over their combined inputs while keeping those inputs private. Real deployments, such as a Danish beet auction and a study of gender and racial wage gaps, have shown the approach is practical. Early projects, however, needed teams of cryptographers to build custom engines. The talk surveys general-purpose end-to-end frameworks, which pair a compiler that turns a high-level function description into an executable representation with a runtime where the parties run the protocol together. The survey covered nine such frameworks and two circuit-only compilers, grouped into garbled circuit protocols, multi-party circuit protocols based on linear secret sharing, and hybrid protocols with optimized sub-protocols.

To compare them, the team wrote three sample programs in every framework and recorded protocol features, supported data types and usability criteria. The sample programs, along with complete build environments, were published in an open repository. Most frameworks were open source and could express the samples, but build systems were often complicated, and some required compiling specific library versions or setting up certificate authorities, which took one to two weeks on average. Documentation was the other main gap. One compiler required undocumented variable naming rules, another rejected common names as reserved keywords, and a third needed extra parentheses that its tutorial did not show.

The speaker argued that the level of abstraction in a framework's language matters when choosing one, since some expose raw circuit primitives while others offer custom operators for common functions. Maintainers were advised to provide several kinds of documentation and an online issue tracker, which can serve as a living FAQ. Involving programming-language researchers in language design was also recommended. The talk closed with a few framework recommendations for general use and for more specialized needs.

talks.title: Simple High-Level Code for Cryptographic Arithmetic -- With Proofs, Without Compromises
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Simple High-Level Code for Cryptographic Arithmetic -- With Proofs, Without Compromises.

talks.title: On the Feasibility of Rerouting-Based DDoS Defenses
talks.teaser: Shows how adaptive attackers can learn the BGP detours that rerouting defenses rely on against link-flooding DDoS.
talks.summary:
Link-flooding DDoS attacks target the links between autonomous systems rather than the victim's servers, and they are hard to filter because attack flows look like normal traffic. A recent proposal uses BGP poisoning so a destination can reroute its critical traffic around a congested link without help from other networks. The speaker asks whether that defense still holds against an adaptive attacker.

The talk describes a learning attack in three steps: detect the reroute in near real time through periodic path measurements, learn the new detour path by choosing bots whose paths are close to the detour, and then target that path. The attacker reportedly identifies the correct detour about 94% of the time. The defense works best when the detour is isolated, meaning no other networks learn about it, which requires poisoning many autonomous systems. Analysis of the BGP specification, router implementations and ISP practice shows that a single message can carry many ASes in theory, but some routers cap it at 250, and most observed messages carry fewer than 30.

The takeaway is that poisoning enough networks to isolate the detour is practically infeasible, so the attack remains effective against this defense. The speaker also argues that protocol specifications alone do not predict real behavior, because implementations and configurations change the outcome. The suggested direction is a middle ground: minimal BGP changes that let destinations control critical traffic during emergencies.

talks.title: Touching the Untouchables: Dynamic Security Analysis of the LTE Control Plane
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Touching the Untouchables: Dynamic Security Analysis of the LTE Control Plane.

talks.title: Breaking LTE on Layer Two
talks.teaser: Shows how LTE's missing user-plane integrity lets an attacker on the radio link redirect a victim to a malicious website.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at which security protections apply on the radio link of LTE mobile networks, focusing on the Packet Data Convergence Protocol at layer 2. Control-plane traffic gets both encryption and integrity protection, but user-plane traffic, which carries the phone's ordinary IP data, is encrypted without integrity protection. The speakers presented three attacks that use this layer.

The first attack links a subscriber's temporary identity to the radio identifier used during a connection. The base station sends the temporary identity back for collision avoidance, which can be observed from the downlink, and the speakers showed this works in a commercial network. The second attack is website fingerprinting from unencrypted layer 2 metadata. A classifier trained on recorded website visits reached about ninety-five percent success in a controlled lab with simple scenarios, and a follow-up study in a commercial network looked at factors such as browser, operating system and subscription type.

The third attack is an active man-in-the-middle relay. Because the stream cipher XORs a keystream with the plaintext, an attacker can flip chosen bits in the ciphertext and know which plaintext bits changed. The relay rewrote DNS responses to point a victim at a malicious server, redirecting an HTTP session where credentials could be captured. The takeaway is that LTE user-plane integrity is absent and 5G only offers it as optional, so this attack surface is likely to remain, and upper-layer protections such as HTTPS are not a complete answer.

talks.title: Learning to Reconstruct: Statistical Learning Theory and Encrypted Database Attacks
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Learning to Reconstruct: Statistical Learning Theory and Encrypted Database Attacks.

talks.title: Threshold ECDSA from ECDSA Assumptions: The Multiparty Case
talks.teaser: Presents a multiparty ECDSA threshold signing protocol that relies only on assumptions native to the signature curve.
talks.summary:
Threshold signing splits an ECDSA private key into fragments held by several devices or parties, so a signature needs a qualifying group to cooperate. The output must look like an ordinary ECDSA signature, and no coalition below the threshold should be able to sign or learn the key. The talk covers the full multiparty case, where an adversary may corrupt all but one participant. ECDSA is hard to split because its nonce inversion step is non-linear, and earlier schemes relied on homomorphic encryption or zero-knowledge proofs, which add computational cost or extra assumptions.

The speaker extends a previous two-party construction to many parties. Multiplication is done with two-party protocols built on oblivious transfer with OT extension, instantiated in the same elliptic curve as the signature, so the only assumption is that computational Diffie-Hellman is hard in that curve. Key generation is fully distributed. The main contribution is a consistency check that verifies the shares in the exponent before they are revealed. It costs about five exponentiations per party, does not grow with the party count, and avoids zero-knowledge proofs. A randomized target, revealed only after the adversary commits, prevents hidden additive cheating. Security is proven in universal composability against a static adversary, in a synchronous network with a broadcast channel.

Benchmarks on cloud nodes and low-power devices show that three Raspberry Pi devices can sign in under 100 milliseconds, and that 16 parties spread across the world sign in just over three seconds. Bandwidth is the main cost, at a few hundred kilobytes per party. The speaker argues this suits human-initiated mobile signing but is less suited to high-throughput automated systems. A practitioner gets a threshold ECDSA design that is light on computation, avoids extra assumptions, and trades communication for speed.

talks.title: Data Recovery on Encrypted Databases with k-Nearest Neighbor Query Leakage
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Data Recovery on Encrypted Databases with k-Nearest Neighbor Query Leakage.

talks.title: Blind Certificate Authorities
talks.teaser: Shows a blind certificate authority that binds an email address to a public key without learning who holds it.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how a certificate authority can confirm that someone controls an email address without learning who that person is. Conventional authorities record the identity of every registrant, which is risky for whistleblowers and others who need anonymity. The speaker presents a blind CA that issues an X.509 certificate binding a chosen public key to an email address while keeping the account name hidden.

The building block is secure channel injection, where a third party inserts a private message into another party's TLS-protected traffic without either endpoint noticing. Here the authority injects a challenge into an SMTP message the user sends from her own account to a mailbox she controls, proving ownership without revealing the address. For the SHA-256 and AES parts, the speaker avoids a generic MPC circuit, which would be very large and slow, by noting that intermediate compression outputs look random and reveal nothing, so only full AES blocks need secure computation. Certificate issuance uses zero-knowledge proofs over commitments that link the certificate to the hidden account.

The prototype uses malicious-secure two-party computation libraries and was tested against standard mail servers and Gmail, with small overhead for certificate generation and verification since much of the work runs offline. A side analysis of eight thousand SMTP session durations showed a long tail, with 15 percent lasting over 20 seconds, so session length is unreliable for anomaly detection. The takeaway is that identity checks and anonymity can coexist, which could help bootstrap systems where no participant is identified. The Q&A raised extending the approach to other authentication methods.

talks.title: Bitcoin vs. Bitcoin Cash: Coexistence or Downfall of Bitcoin Cash
talks.teaser: Shows how miners switching between Bitcoin and Bitcoin Cash can starve the weaker chain of loyal hash power.
talks.summary:
Bitcoin Cash split from Bitcoin in 2017, and since both use compatible proof-of-work, miners can point the same hardware at either coin. The talk asks which coin a rational miner should choose when profit depends on both price and difficulty. This leads to what the speaker calls fickle mining, where miners switch coins only when difficulty changes. The speaker models a game among miners choosing between strategies and a committed faction that keeps mining Bitcoin Cash regardless of profit, then maps hash power shares on a triangle diagram to find equilibria.

The model yields either coexistence or a downfall where only the committed faction keeps mining the weaker coin. Tracing historical data, the speaker found Bitcoin Cash often lacked loyal miners until a difficulty adjustment change on 13 November 2017 moved it toward coexistence. Before that, the speaker described blocks taking up to four hours, five miners and two accounts producing 70% of blocks, and double-spend susceptibility with only 1 to 2% of computing power. Automatic mining, where miners switch in real time, was shown to push the system toward losing loyal miners once about 5% of total hash power joins it, and the later hash war between Bitcoin ABC and Bitcoin SV matched this analysis.

The same analysis, the speaker argues, applies to any two coins with comparable mining algorithms, such as Ethereum and Ethereum Classic. The takeaway is that a larger coin can weaken a rival's security and decentralization by moving shared hash power.

talks.title: "Should I Worry?" A Cross Cultural Examination of Account Security Incident Response
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning "Should I Worry?" A Cross Cultural Examination of Account Security Incident Response.

talks.title: IEEE S&P 2019—TC Business Meeting
talks.teaser: Reviews the technical committee's year, new test-of-time awards, and feedback on the symposium's rolling paper submission model.
talks.summary:
This business meeting of the IEEE Computer Society technical committee on security and privacy, held during the 2019 symposium, opened with a status report on the committee's activities. Its roughly sixty-six thousand dollar budget went mostly back to the conferences it co-sponsors, including the symposium, CSF, EuroS&P, SecDev and HOST. Awards were presented, including the first round of the new test-of-time awards, which covered papers from 2007 to 2009, and recognition for volunteers who had built the awards process. Bryan Pernod was then elected vice chair for 2020 and 2021.

The meeting then covered the symposium's move to a multi-track format for 2019, which added about thirty thousand dollars in costs, and the rolling monthly submission model adopted in 2018. Organisers said the model gave authors flexibility and made accepted papers available sooner, but the program committee faced continuous review load, and the single review round left some papers without enough expertise. For 2020 the committee grew to 122 members split into five groups, each reviewing in three cycles, though this fragmented expertise in some areas.

For 2021 the organisers floated a longer review cycle of about two and a half months, a second review round for papers needing extra expertise, and a move to quarterly or bimonthly deadlines. Attendees asked for faster changes, early decisions, published data on acceptances by topic, better reviewer matching, and caution about growing the committee too far. The organisers said they would write a full proposal and gather community input before deciding.

talks.title: IEEE S&P 2019—40th Celebration Plenary Session: Test of Time Awards
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in IEEE S&P 2019—40th Celebration Plenary Session: Test of Time Awards.

talks.title: IEEE S&P 2019—40th Celebration Plenary Session: Panel: Reflections on four decades of the symposium
talks.teaser: A plenary panel traces how the symposium began, grew, and still shapes security research culture today.
talks.summary:
The session opens with the moderator inviting four longtime researchers to reflect on roughly forty years of the IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy. Dorothy Denning and Peter Newman describe how George Devito and IEEE's Technical Committee on Security and Privacy launched the 1980 meeting, linking it to earlier gatherings in Paris, Rio, and Atlanta, and to the later split that helped feed a separate cryptography community while keeping broad coverage here.

Deb Franken and Dick Kemmerer share graduate-student memories of a smaller, face-to-face community, then trace how public awareness, dual-track scale, and specialization changed what researchers can read and validate. Stories range from Risks Digest and early intrusion detection through Claremont venue lore, selective attendance debates, and candid audience exchanges on whether security is winning.

The conversation returns often to openness versus responsible disclosure, trustworthy whole systems versus point fixes, education, maintenance of shared tools, and existential risks from complex and life-critical deployments. Practitioners hear that progress is uneven and perpetual, yet relationships, scientific scrutiny of deployed systems, and layered defenses have materially improved everyday safety compared with the 1980s.

talks.title: IEEE S&P 2019—40th Celebration Plenary Session: A Wild Ride Through Time
talks.teaser: A retrospective charts four decades of submission trends, topic clusters, and cultural shifts at a leading security symposium.
talks.summary:
The plenary opens with a personal look at how reviewing four decades of symposium proceedings revealed shifting hot topics and community growth. Submission and acceptance statistics show rising volume, acceptance settling around twelve to fifteen percent, and pragmatic shifts such as dual-track scheduling. Lighter analysis covers title colons, abstract length, growing author lists, prolific repeat authors, and informal “slam” metrics across top-tier venues.

The speaker applies machine learning to titles, abstracts, and keywords, surfacing long-running themes such as access control, information flow, malware, web and crypto protocols, privacy, and software security, plus faded clusters like multi-level security and formal methods that spun into their own communities. A decade-by-decade narrative ties cultural milestones to research waves: eighties optimism about provable end-to-end security, nineties internet and language-based security with early fuzzing and side channels, two-thousands cloud and virtualization with privacy on large datasets, and the recent decade’s blockchain, machine learning in security, browser exploitation, and measurement studies.

The close credits program and general chairs across forty years, points listeners to the System Security Circus visualization and prior write-ups, notes ongoing celebration CTF activity, and transitions to a separate panel on symposium reflections.

talks.title: Self-Encrypting Deception: Weaknesses in the Encryption of Solid State Drives
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Self-Encrypting Deception: Weaknesses in the Encryption of Solid State Drives.

talks.title: Using Safety Properties to Generate Vulnerability Patches
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Using Safety Properties to Generate Vulnerability Patches.

talks.title: SensorID: Sensor Calibration Fingerprinting for Smartphones
talks.teaser: Shows how phone motion sensor calibration data can uniquely fingerprint devices from websites and apps without permissions.
talks.summary:
Device fingerprinting builds a unique identifier for a device and is mostly used by advertisers to follow users. Mobile operating systems already block some hardware identifiers such as phone numbers and MAC addresses, but motion sensors remain open. The accelerometer, gyroscope and magnetometer can be read from apps or websites without any permission or user interaction. Manufacturing imperfections cause systematic errors, and factory calibration stores correction matrices in non-volatile memory, where they stay constant over time.

The proposed calibration fingerprinting attack infers these matrices from raw sensor outputs in under a second, using around 100 samples. Subtracting successive readings removes the offset, and integer ADC quantization, anchored to a nominal gain from a datasheet or the spacing between steps, lets the gain matrix be estimated. Uncalibrated sensors stay flat within a quantization step, while calibrated ones fluctuate. Fingerprints were obtained from iOS gyroscopes and magnetometers and a Pixel 3 accelerometer. Across 870 iOS devices, the gyroscope fingerprint carried about 42 bits of entropy and the magnetometer about 25 bits, for iPhone 6 and 6s models.

Proposed mitigations were adding noise, rounding outputs to a multiple of the nominal value, or removing sensor access, the most secure option. Apple added noise and disabled sensor access in Mobile Safari by default, while other browsers still expose the data, and Google had not yet addressed the Pixel issue. The takeaway is that calibration data, usually treated as a utility trade-off, is a real privacy exposure.

talks.title: Tap 'n Ghost: A Compilation of Novel Attack Techniques against Smartphone Touchscreens
talks.teaser: Shows how an NFC lure and injected electrical noise can trick an Android phone into approving a Bluetooth pairing.
talks.summary:
The talk presents Tap 'n Ghost, an attack chain against Android smartphones that combines an NFC lure with manipulation of the touchscreen. A device hidden under a wooden table holds an NFC emulator and a metal sheet. When a phone is placed on the surface, the emulator asks it to pair with the attacker's Bluetooth device, and a confirmation dialog appears. The metal sheet then injects electrical noise into the touchscreen's receiver electrodes, producing phantom touches that select the confirm button without the user's input.

The speaker described the two components. The ghost touch generator targets mutual capacitive touchscreens, where injected noise creates false touch events along the receiver lines. It succeeded on five of seven tested models, and the effective noise frequency varied by model, so the attacker must identify the handset first. The NFC stage handles that step: a dynamically changing emulated tag sends the phone to a website that reads the user agent to identify the model, then the tag is rewritten to request the Bluetooth pairing.

To test feasibility, the researchers seated 16 participants at such a table without telling them about the device. Fifteen of them presented several chances to be attacked within 15 minutes of normal phone use. Based on this, the team estimated a 71 percent success probability for 30 people with three attempts each. Proposed countermeasures include requiring user approval before an NFC tag opens a website and detecting the spatial patterns of false touches. The researchers informed several manufacturers, and one confirmed the attack worked on its latest model. In questions, the speaker noted that NFC range is about four centimetres, so holding a phone farther away is a practical defence.

talks.title: Understanding the Security of ARM Debugging Features
talks.teaser: Shows how ARM hardware debug features can break TrustZone isolation without physical access, and how to defend against it.
talks.summary:
Hardware debugging on ARM processors usually requires a physical JTAG connection, and debug authentication signals are meant to keep malicious debug hosts out. The talk questions both assumptions. It shows that one processor on a chip can debug another through memory-mapped debug registers, which removes the need for physical access. A survey of development boards, IoT devices, cloud hardware and phones found that many devices leave debug signals enabled, and that the controls are often undocumented or locked by one-time programmable fuses.

The core attack lets a low-privilege host ask a target core to enter debug state, then switch it into a higher-privilege state, so the host reaches secure-world resources while still running in the normal world. Demonstrations include inferring AES keys from secure configuration registers, running a payload from the normal world, and extracting fingerprint sensor data from a commercial phone's secure RAM, which was then reconstructed into an image. The findings were reported to ARM and affected vendors.

Simply disabling the debug signals is not a practical fix, because many debugging and program analysis tools depend on them and the signal management mechanism is not publicly documented. The talk proposes layered defenses: ARM should account for the privilege of both debug host and target in inter-process debugging, SoC vendors should improve signal management and add hardware access control to debug components, and OEMs and cloud providers can apply software-based access control. The overall message is that components treated as safe in single-core systems can become vulnerable in multi-core designs.

talks.title: Security of GPS / INS based On-road Location Tracking Systems
talks.teaser: It shows how GPS–INS road tracking can be evaded with spoof routes, escape paths, and a real-time spoofer that fools monitoring centers.
talks.summary:
Commercial GPS remains unauthenticated and weak at the receiver, so spoofing with higher-power fake signals is a well-studied risk for ships, drones, and consumer apps. On-road tracking often pairs GPS with inertial navigation because IMU data resists jamming and naive spoofing, yet fused systems still trust sensor noise bands. The work asks whether a driver under route monitoring, or someone on a GPS–INS ankle monitor, can reach unintended destinations without raising alarms.

The attack pipeline builds a city road graph with turn angles, curvatures, and travel times, then ranks spoof routes—extensions of depth-first search scored by how closely turn and curvature patterns match common city geometry (notably 90-degree turns and straight segments). Those spoof routes seed escape routes whose deviations stay within error thresholds derived from open sensor recordings on 140 routes (75th percentile accelerometer, bearing, turn, and curvature errors). A real-time integrated spoofer maps true to fake position, computes spoof location and bearing within about 5 milliseconds (up to 60 milliseconds in Boston driving tests), and drives parallel GPS and magnetometer spoofing aligned with stops, turns, and traffic. Simulations across Manhattan, Chicago, London, Paris, and other hubs show many routes with displacement above 10–20 kilometers and coverage fractions of city area when escape destinations vary; grid cities fare worst.

Countermeasures discussed include military signed GPS (which breaks the spoofing assumption) and a secure-routes algorithm that inverts the spoof-route scorer to pick paths exposing fewer escape destinations, plus more accurate sensors over time. Deployments such as ride-sharing must accept that the defense is probabilistic rather than a guarantee on every network.

talks.title: Synesthesia: Detecting Screen Content via Remote Acoustic Side Channels
talks.teaser: Shows that screen rendering noise picked up by nearby or remote microphones can reveal displayed websites, typed keys and text.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether the faint acoustic noise a computer screen makes while rendering content can reveal what is shown on it. The presenters explain that such sound can be captured by built-in webcam or laptop microphones, by a phone or smart speaker placed nearby, or from about 10 meters away with a parabolic microphone, and that it survives compression and transmission during video calls. A zebra-stripe test displayed on many screens produced a consistent spectral component tied to the refresh pattern. The team later traced the source to the screen's power supply, where power draw changes with pixel intensity.

To make the signal usable, the researchers aligned and averaged the repeated refresh cycles despite timing drift and jitter. They then built three attacks on convolutional neural networks. In website distinguishing, a classifier identified which of about 100 popular sites was open, and a smaller test with 10 sites worked even on the remote end of a video call. A second attack distinguished individual on-screen keyboard keys, and the results narrowed typed words to a shortlist of about ten. A third attack extracted text, recovering exact words in over half of cases in an open-world setting.

The talk closes by noting that a model trained on screens of the same model transfers reasonably well, and that training on more screens reduces overfitting. Countermeasures would mostly need changes to how screens are built, such as shielding, or software that keeps pixel-line rendering consistent. The practical takeaway is that microphones near a screen, including ones in video calls or voice assistants, may expose on-screen content.

talks.title: Port Contention for Fun and Profit
talks.teaser: Port Smash exploits SMT execution-port contention to leak ECDSA keys from OpenSSL TLS and Intel SGX enclaves.
talks.summary:
The presentation introduces Port Smash, a side channel that targets contention on shared execution ports in simultaneous multithreading. After outlining how modern cores pipeline micro-operations onto numbered ports, the authors show that two logical threads on one physical core can observe each other's port usage through latency shifts, extending a line of SMT resource attacks beyond caches and TLBs.

Laboratory experiments on an Intel Core i7-8700K establish a covert channel between paired processes, then a spy process infers secret-dependent branches in a victim by matching instruction footprints to specific ports. Unlike many cache-oriented techniques, the approach retains usefulness when victim data sits within a single cache line. The team then attacks ECDSA signing in OpenSSL 1.1.0 over TLS, filtering traces to spot double-and-add peaks, assembling partial nonce information, and finishing with a lattice step to recover the long-term key. Separate traces show the same leakage inside Intel SGX enclaves because the execution engine remains shared.

Practitioners should treat SMT-hosted cryptographic code as exposed unless branches and operations are timing-stable, and should weigh disabling hyper-threading or stronger isolation where latency matters. The work received a CVE, prompted hardened OpenSSL releases, and ships as a proof-of-concept implementation others can adapt to new port layouts.

talks.title: Attack Directories, Not Caches: Side Channel Attacks in a Non Inclusive World
talks.teaser: Shows how directory conflicts enable prime-and-probe cache attacks on Intel processors with non-inclusive cache hierarchies.
talks.summary:
Prime-and-probe cache attacks are well established on inclusive last-level caches, where evicting a shared-cache line also evicts the victim's private copy. Newer Intel server processors use a non-inclusive hierarchy, and many expected conflict-based attacks to fail there. The talk explains why they are harder in this design: a victim's line is not duplicated in the shared cache, so filling that cache cannot push out the private copy.

The research shifts the target to the directory that tracks which private caches hold each line. After reverse engineering the traditional and extended directory structures on Skylake-SP class processors, the researchers showed that directory set conflicts can force a victim's line out of its private L2 into the shared cache, and that an attacker can detect this through reload latency. A demonstration against a square-and-multiply routine produced clearly separated timing traces that reveal each key bit. Additional contributions covered an adapted eviction-set construction, a multithreaded evict-and-reload variant, and results that did not carry over to AMD machines.

The takeaway is that the directory is the shared structure behind these attacks, and that simple fixes are impractical. Very high directory associativity is too costly, and way partitioning does not scale to server parts with many cores. Any secret-dependent memory access remains observable through this channel. A follow-up secure directory design was presented as a defense.

talks.title: Hard Drive of Hearing: Disks that Eavesdrop with a Synthesized Microphone
talks.teaser: Shows how a hard drive's head-position signal can capture speech, turning storage hardware into an eavesdropping microphone.
talks.summary:
The talk asks how well a hard drive can approximate a microphone, a sensor it was never designed to be. The speaker's threat model assumes an attacker with malware on the machine who can reflash the drive's firmware, which matters when a device's microphone is disabled or physically disconnected. The head is kept on track using a position error signal read from servo sectors. Sound waves appear to nudge the head similarly, so that signal can approximate microphone output. At 7,200 rpm with 288 servo sectors per track, the sampling rate reaches about 34.5 kHz.

In the lab, a diagnostic port exposed the position signal, and a 2.6 kHz whistle produced the expected extra energy. With a speaker about ten inches away and the drive in an enclosure, platter eccentricity, thermal drift and head turbulence added heavy noise. Linear and nonlinear DSP reduced it enough for muffled but recognizable Harvard sentences at 85 dBA. A case study played The Trooper by Iron Maiden into the Shazam app, which recognized the song at 90 dBA even though the filtering did little. Averaging across drives or aligning repeated words could raise the signal further.

For defenders, ultrasonic masking can hide speech on deployed drives, since the low sampling rate aliases the noise into the audible range. Requiring signed firmware would block unauthorized reflashing, though few drives the authors examined used signatures. The talk concludes that everyday devices can still sense the physical world.

talks.title: F-BLEAU: Fast Black-box Leakage Estimation
talks.teaser: Shows how machine learning estimators can measure how much a black-box system leaks about its secret inputs.
talks.summary:
The talk covers how much a black-box system reveals about its secret inputs, without any knowledge of its internals. The system takes a finite secret and returns an output drawn from an unknown distribution. The goal is to estimate the Bayes risk, the error probability of the best possible adversary, from queries alone. Leakage measures such as min-entropy leakage are derived from that value.

The existing approach counts how often each output follows each secret and takes a majority vote. This breaks down for continuous outputs and for large output spaces, because every output value must have been observed. The speaker argues that nearest-neighbour classifiers, with small modifications, asymptotically approximate the Bayes risk, and that k-nearest-neighbour extends this to continuous outputs. More broadly, a class of universally consistent machine learning rules has the same property given enough queries. In location privacy experiments with geometric and Laplacian noise, only the nearest-neighbour approach converged within about 20,000 queries. On a mechanism with very few possible outputs, the methods performed about the same as the frequency approach.

Synthetic experiments with up to a million output values showed that nearest-neighbour methods scale well when the output has a usable metric, such as timing. A no-free-lunch argument shows that no single estimator is best for every system, so the practical choice is the one that converges fastest for the system at hand. The speaker released F-BLEAU, which currently implements nearest-neighbour methods. The takeaway is that leakage can be measured without modelling a system's internals, and future work targets membership inference against machine learning models.

talks.title: Full speed Fuzzing: Reducing Fuzzing Overhead through Coverage-guided Tracing
talks.teaser: Explains how tracing only coverage-increasing test cases cuts fuzzing overhead and raises test case throughput.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Coverage-guided fuzzing is a premier software testing technique used to discover vulnerabilities across modern applications. Typical coverage-guided fuzzers execute test cases against a target application and record coverage metrics to identify inputs that explore new execution paths. However, conventional implementations trace code coverage for every executed test case. Stefan Nagy, presenting joint research with Dr. Matthew Hicks from Virginia Tech, shows that over 90% of fuzzer execution time is spent on tracing and executing test cases, even though over 99.99% of generated inputs fail to discover new coverage and are discarded. To address this inefficiency, the authors introduce coverage-guided tracing through a framework called UnTracer, which filters out non-coverage-increasing inputs at native execution speed and restricts expensive tracing strictly to inputs that discover new coverage.

### Key Topics
- **Overhead Analysis in Fuzzing:** Profiling popular tools like AFL and Driller across diverse benchmarks reveals that tracing adds severe performance costs, while the rate of coverage-increasing inputs decays exponentially to fewer than 1 in 10,000 test cases over a 24-hour run.
- **Coverage-Guided Tracing Concept:** Instead of indiscriminately inspecting every test case, the execution framework places lightweight detection mechanisms on untaken basic blocks to detect coverage increases without continuous tracing.
- **UnTracer Architecture:** Utilizing software interrupts (e.g., modifying the first byte of basic blocks) in an instrumented binary, the framework identifies new block visits. Once hit, the input is traced via a separate binary (using Dyninst), and the triggered interrupts are removed dynamically so future executions run with zero overhead.
- **Complementary Optimization:** The approach isolates tracing performance and works orthogonally alongside test case generation and mutation engines such as Angora and VUzzer.

### Technical Details
Standard coverage-guided fuzzers hook every basic block to update shared tracking structures (such as AFL's coverage bitmap), introducing instruction overhead across long execution paths and tight loops. UnTracer instead statically rewrites the target binary by inserting interrupt instructions at the beginning of basic blocks. When a test case executes, the common case—inputs that do not increase coverage—encounters no interrupts and runs at native speed with zero tracing overhead. 

When a novel test case triggers an interrupt, UnTracer identifies it as coverage-increasing, runs that specific test case on a separate tracing binary built with Dyninst to extract full coverage information, and clears the corresponding interrupts in the interrupt binary so subsequent executions do not fire them again. Over time, as coverage saturates, the interrupt binary sheds interrupts and runs at native execution speed.

In experimental evaluations across eight diverse benchmarks over five days worth of test cases and 24-hour trials, UnTracer reduced tracing overhead to approximately 0.3%. It achieved a 36% overhead reduction compared to AFL Clang assembly-time white-box tracing, and boosted total fuzzer throughput by 70% to 616% when evaluated with QSYM.

### Takeaways
- Tracing every generated test case represents an enormous resource waste in coverage-guided fuzzing because the vast majority of test cases yield no new coverage.
- Filtering out redundant executions with dynamic interrupt removal permits the common execution path to run at native speed, cutting overhead to near zero.
- Coverage-guided tracing provides massive throughput speedups (70%–616%) while maintaining modularity and compatibility with existing test case generators and modern hybrid fuzzers.

talks.title: ProFuzzer: On-the-fly Input Type Probing for Better Zero-day Vulnerability Discovery
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning ProFuzzer: On-the-fly Input Type Probing for Better Zero-day Vulnerability Discovery.
talks.summary: Wu presents ProFuzzer, probing input byte types on the fly so mutation-based fuzzers stop wasting millions of blind tweaks on structurally meaningless fields. The approach improves AFL-class coverage on formats where naive bit flips plateau after hours.

talks.title: Razzer: Finding Kernel Race Bugs through Fuzzing
talks.teaser: Presents a kernel fuzzer that enforces thread interleavings at race windows to find kernel race bugs faster than syzkaller.
talks.summary:
Kernel race conditions are hard for fuzzers because a bug fires only when two threads touch the same memory inside a narrow timing window that the kernel scheduler controls, which coverage-guided fuzzers ignore. The talk walks through a file-name cloning case where one thread sizes a buffer, another lengthens the name, and the copy overflows. In a restricted experiment, syzkaller failed to trigger three known race bugs in ten hours.

The tool, Razzer, pairs a static analysis with fuzzing. An inclusion-based points-to analysis of the kernel produces about three million race candidates; its false positives are acceptable because the fuzzing stage rejects them. A single-thread phase extends coverage and flags inputs whose two system calls reach a candidate, then splits them into two threads. A multi-thread phase uses a hypervisor-based deterministic scheduler to pause threads at breakpoints set at the end of the race window, and virtual machine introspection confirms whether both accesses hit the same address. A timeout discards inputs where a lock blocks the second thread.

Running the tool on the Linux kernel for about a month yielded 30 new race vulnerabilities, many with serious impact such as heap overflows, use-after-free and double free. On three known race bugs, the tool found every one within about 7 to 26 minutes, while syzkaller missed them in 10 hours. The takeaway is that controlling thread interleaving, not only coverage, makes kernel race discovery practical.

talks.title: Helen: Maliciously Secure Coopetitive Learning for Linear Models
talks.teaser: A training system lets competing banks jointly learn fraud models without sharing raw data or trusting a central party.
talks.summary:
Organizations that compete yet need shared machine learning—such as banks detecting fraud across institutions—cannot pool customer data in plaintext or rely on an expensive, breach-prone trusted aggregator. The speaker introduces coopetitive learning in a malicious threat model where up to all but one party may deviate, and where participants must not leak intermediate global models, only the agreed final weights.

Prior maliciously secure MPC training via general platforms like SPEEDS is impractical; estimating stochastic gradient descent for a modest four-party lasso problem suggested months of runtime and failed from memory limits. Helen targets regularized linear models and combines three ideas: an ADMM formulation that scans data once into a summary, scalable zero-knowledge proofs of summary correctness using reduced representations from singular value decomposition, and a mixed protocol pairing local homomorphic encryption with MPC for coordination steps.

The workflow covers one-time threshold homomorphic key setup, decentralized summary preparation with proofs, alternating local encrypted optimization and MPC aggregation, then joint decryption of final weights. On four EC2 parties spanning Oregon and Virginia, Helen matches baseline accuracy while cutting runtime on a UCI sound-prediction dataset—roughly a nine-hundred-fold gain at one hundred thousand samples per party versus SPEEDS-based SGD. Practitioners gain a concrete path to high-assurance collaborative training on linear models where generic MPC alone does not scale.

talks.title: Neural Cleanse: Identifying and Mitigating Backdoor Attacks in Neural Networks
talks.teaser: Presents a way to detect hidden backdoor triggers in neural networks, then filter inputs and patch the model.
talks.summary:
Deep neural networks are hard to inspect, and testing them on a fixed set of samples says little about how they will behave on inputs never tried. The talk focuses on backdoor attacks, in which an attacker poisons the training data so that a hidden trigger, such as a small yellow sticker on a traffic sign, pushes inputs into a chosen target class while normal behaviour stays intact. The defender is assumed to hold a small set of clean samples and no poisoned data.

The detection idea rests on the observation that reaching the target label of a backdoored model takes a much smaller change to the input than reaching any other label. For each label, the method reverse-engineers the smallest trigger that causes misclassification, then runs outlier detection on the trigger sizes. In tests on four models with the BadNets-style injection and two models from a second injection method, infected models scored above the threshold of 2 while clean models stayed below it. The infected label consistently had the smallest trigger, and the recovered triggers matched the original attack's success rate and fired similar internal neurons.

For mitigation, the recovered trigger is used in two ways: as an input filter that rejects samples activating the same neurons, and as training data to unlearn the backdoor and patch the model. The speaker notes that enlarging the trigger until it covers a large part of the image can defeat detection. The takeaway for practitioners is that backdoors can be found and removed without poisoned samples, with further variants such as multiple triggers covered in the paper.

talks.summary: The speaker describes a two-level sketching method for estimating how identifying records are within a dataset and how much two datasets overlap, without exact counting. Attendees learn how the method uses compact approximate-counting sketches, how it performed on uniqueness and containment estimates, and where its accuracy weakens for datasets of very different sizes. The talk also discusses its use in large-scale analysis and regression testing, along with possible improvements.
