talks.title: An Extensive Formal Security Analysis of the OpenID Financial grade API Pedram Hosseyni
talks.teaser: Presents a formal security analysis of the Financial-grade API, uncovering attacks on its OAuth-based flow and proposing fixes.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at the Financial-grade API (FAPI), a hardened profile of OAuth for high-risk settings such as open banking, already adopted by banks in the UK and considered for European payment rules. The speaker starts with the basic OAuth authorization code flow, using a workflow tool that gains access to a cloud storage account as an example. They then cover FAPI's stronger attacker model and how mutual TLS token binding is meant to make stolen tokens useless.

To check the protocol, the authors used the Web Infrastructure Model, a detailed formal model of browsers, servers, DNS and network attackers. They built a model of FAPI with its configuration options, defined security properties for authentication, authorization and session integrity, and attempted proofs. The proofs initially failed, exposing four attacks on FAPI and on underlying security mechanisms. The talk details one: a malicious authorization server in a multi-server setup lets an attacker inject a stolen, token-bound access token into a second flow, so the bound client uses it on the attacker's behalf.

The proposed mitigation has the client tell the resource server which authorization server issued the access token, letting it spot the injected token and stop the flow. With fixes for all four attacks in place, the authors report that FAPI is secure within their model. They are also working with the OpenID Foundation and the IETF to update the standard.

talks.title: True2F: Backdoor resistant authentication tokens Emma Dauterman
talks.teaser: Shows how security key tokens can resist backdoored or buggy hardware while staying compatible with existing U2F servers.
talks.summary:
The talk targets a trust gap in hardware security keys built on the U2F standard. These keys resist phishing and browser malware, but users must still trust the token itself, which may contain implementation bugs or be tampered with in the supply chain. The speaker points to a 2017 random-number-generator flaw in smart cards and a recent Bluetooth stack bug in a Google security key as examples of how fragile these elements can be.

The talk introduces True2F, which keeps U2F protections and also holds when either the browser or the token is malicious. Browser and token jointly contribute randomness during a new initialization step that creates a master key pair, so the master secret stays on the token. At registration, the browser verifies each site-specific public key derived from that master key, and authentication uses firewalled ECDSA signatures so the token cannot leak secrets through signature randomness. Only the token and browser change, not the server.

The system was implemented on Google hardware. Unoptimized authentication took 446 milliseconds versus 23 milliseconds for standard U2F. With optimizations it dropped to 57 milliseconds, about 2.5 times slower, but because much of the time is spent in browser middleware, users see only 20 to 30 milliseconds of extra delay. The takeaway is that backdoor-resistant tokens can be practical on commodity hardware while staying compatible with existing servers.

talks.title: Reasoning Analytically About Password Cracking Software Alex Liu
talks.teaser: Shows how to estimate password strength for rule-based cracking tools like Hashcat without enumerating every guess.
talks.summary:
Password strength can be judged by its guess number, the count of guesses an attacker makes before reaching a target password. Researchers have fast ways to estimate this for probabilistic password models, but the rule-based cracking tools that practitioners use, such as John the Ripper and Hashcat, lacked comparable methods. Running the tool until the password appears does not scale, and these tools also need careful configuration of word lists and rules.

The talk introduces two operations for these tools. Rule inversion works backwards from a target password to find the dictionary words that a transformation rule would turn into it. Guess counting then determines how many guesses each rule produces without enumerating them, with dependencies such as rejection rules handled in a tensor-based structure processed in one pass. On a large word list and rule set producing about three times ten to the fourteen guesses, the speaker reported that the analysis took seconds after a one-time preprocessing step, while full enumeration would need three petabytes of data stored on disk.

The techniques are then applied to configuration. Ordering rules by cracks per guess, with the order trained on one set of leaked passwords and tested on another, comes close to the best achievable ordering. Analysis of the leaked data also surfaces missing pre-images that should be added to word lists, including site-specific terms, generalizable words, and short strings that pair well with rules. The main takeaway is that researchers can model attacker configurations more rigorously, and the speaker noted that the code is open source.

talks.title: Using Safety Properties to Generate Vulnerability Patches Zhen Huang

talks.title: Towards Automated Safety Vetting of PLC Code in Real World Plants Mu Zhang
talks.teaser: Shows how timed event sequences expose PLC safety violations that ordering-only testing misses in factory test beds.
talks.summary:
Industrial control systems on factory floors are increasingly targeted, and attackers aim for physical damage and safety hazards, not only profit. Programmable logic controllers (PLCs) sit at the core of these floors, and faulty code, whether introduced by mistake or by an attacker, can lead to hazards. Prior work mostly checked individual PLCs in isolation, overlooking that a PLC constantly exchanges signals with robots, CNC machines and conveyors.

The speaker walks through a pallet-loading cell from a physical testbed built with domain experts from Rockwell Automation. A robot signal that is ended within 0.5 seconds to save time is safe at normal speeds, but when events arrive early it can end before the PLC registers the other event. The stopper then never retracts, violating a safety rule that requires no more than 30 seconds between pallet arrival and departure. Reordering events alone could not reproduce this, because two sequences with the same order behaved differently depending on timing.

The proposed approach combines program analysis, which builds a causality graph among events, with data mining of timing invariants collected from the testbed. Time ranges are then discretized into slices to generate timed event sequences. In evaluation on two testbeds and ten real-world scenarios, ordering-only generation found no safety violations, while the timed approach found them. Finer time granularity also narrowed the speed ranges in which errors occurred. The takeaway is that PLC code is event-driven and timing sensitive, so safety testing must model timing as well as event order.

talks.title: CaSym: Cache Aware Symbolic Execution for Side Channel Detection and Mitigation
talks.teaser: Introduces a cache-aware symbolic execution tool that finds, localizes and verifies cache side channels in C code.
talks.summary:
Cache side channels leak secret data through the state of the CPU cache, and the attacks can be fast enough to matter in enclaves and cloud settings. Finding them in code is hard because microarchitectural behaviour is subtle. The speaker reviewed earlier tools: a 2013 abstract-interpretation approach that bounds leakage without pointing to the offending line, and a 2017 symbolic-execution tool that localizes leaks but can miss paths because some inputs must be concrete, and that offers no fixes.

CaSym runs symbolic execution on every variable, public and private alike, and duplicates the program so an SMT solver can compare the final cache states under two different secrets. It takes C source through clang and LLVM IR, checks verification conditions with Z3, and produces a localization report naming the line and the reason for the leak. Three cache models trade precision for speed: an infinite model, an age model and an LRU model. On crypto benchmarks under a trace-based attack model, the infinite model found 269 unique vulnerable points in about 200 seconds, while the age model found one more but took an order of magnitude longer.

The talk showed preloading and pinning as mitigations, which let the tool verify the absence of side channels under certain models. The speaker also reported over 20 new vulnerabilities found in PostgreSQL. In questions, the speaker noted that page-table effects are not modelled yet, and that pointers are supported only when they refer to one memory region at a time.

talks.title: Iodine: Fast Dynamic Taint Tracking Using Rollback free Optimistic Hybrid Analysis
talks.teaser: Presents Iodine, a taint tracking tool that uses rollback-free optimistic hybrid analysis to cut monitoring overhead.
talks.summary:
Dynamic information-flow tracking can enforce security policies by following tainted data from sources to sinks, but it often slows programs by an order of magnitude, which keeps it out of production use. Static analysis can remove many unneeded tracking monitors, yet to stay sound it must account for a large over-approximation of program states, which limits the gains. The talk presents optimistic hybrid analysis, which profiles a program to learn invariants that usually hold and uses them to make the static analysis more precise.

When an invariant fails at runtime, the optimized analysis must recover missing taint metadata. Earlier approaches roll back execution to do this, which is impractical on live systems. The key insight is to elide only monitors proven to be no-ops, so the metadata stays identical to a conservative analysis. The system can then switch from the fast path to a conservative slow path at the point of failure without any rollback. The tool, Iodine, is built on LLVM for C programs and was evaluated on email integrity in Postfix and on overwrite attacks against nginx.

Results showed an average 4.4x speedup over conservative tracking, and nearly half of the monitors were elided under a generic policy. Profiling on existing test suites delivered most of the benefit, with additional beta-style inputs adding more. Implicit flows were left out because they would taint too much state, a point also raised during questions.

talks.title: Asm2Vec: Boosting Static Representation Robustness for Binary Clone Search...
talks.teaser: Presents a static, machine-learning approach to finding similar assembly functions across obfuscated and optimized binaries.
talks.summary:
Reverse engineers often need to know whether a disassembled function has been analyzed before, by themselves, a teammate, or as a known library routine or variant. The talk treats this as an information retrieval problem and presents Camino, an open-source platform that acts as a shared repository of assembly functions that teams can index and search. Matches are split into exact copies, the same logic compiled differently, and minor edits.

Optimization and obfuscation make the hard cases. The speaker compared an original function with an optimized build, a control-flow-flattened version, and one protected by virtualization and just-in-time execution. Dynamic execution was ruled out because users cannot wait minutes per query. The proposed model, Asm2Vec, borrows word and paragraph embedding ideas: it predicts an instruction from its neighbors in a sliding window and weights rare patterns more heavily, since those draw analysts' attention.

In the reported tests, the static method matched original and optimized binaries more accurately than graph-based and dynamic baselines, though sample sizes were too small for a significance claim. It reportedly found no false positives on a vulnerability dataset, returning results in a few hundred milliseconds per query. Matching survived virtualization and partly JIT execution, but failed when all protections were stacked. Limits include hard-to-explain similarity scores, dynamic jump tables, and an assumption of one architecture family. The code is open source and can run locally or on a Spark-backed cloud deployment.

talks.title: Characterizing Pixel Tracking through the Lens of Disposable Email Services
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Characterizing Pixel Tracking through the Lens of Disposable Email Services.
talks.summary:
### Overview
In this talk, Han from Virginia Tech presents a measurement study examining disposable email services and email pixel tracking. While email addresses serve as critical personally identifiable information (PII) connecting online activity to real-world identities, users increasingly encounter tracking pixels embedded in messages. To protect privacy and prevent user profiling or targeted phishing, users often turn to disposable email services (e.g., maildrop.cc, guerrillamail.com, mailinator.com). Han investigates why users rely on these services, the security risks associated with them, and leverages the collected email dataset to conduct an empirical analysis of email tracking prevalence and techniques.

### Key Topics
- **Risks of Disposable Email Services**: Many temporary email platforms provide public, shared inboxes without authentication, meaning anyone using the same username can read incoming messages. Furthermore, providers often fail to delete messages within their promised retention periods.
- **Sensitive Data Exposure**: Analysis of inboxes revealed critical PII, including credit card numbers, Social Security numbers (SSNs), and Employer Identification Numbers (EINs), as well as sensitive account notifications.
- **Account Hijacking Risks**: Across the dataset, 86,000 emails were related to account creation, registration, password resets, and authentication codes—including messages from healthcare.gov, the Air Force, and iOS document scanners.
- **Email Pixel Tracking**: Senders embed 1x1 or hidden tracking pixels to determine if and when an email is read, the recipient's location, and device details.
- **Evasive Tracking Methods**: Trackers often conceal pixel dimensions by omitting size attributes or route through extensive redirect chains via hidden third-party trackers.

### Technical Details
- **Data Collection**: The researchers monitored 70,000 disposable inboxes across 7 popular disposable email services from October 2017 to January 2018. They selected 10,000 popular usernames (e.g., `info`, `john`, `admin`) derived from prior data breaches. In total, they gathered between 2.3 and 2.7 million messages from approximately 210,000 sender domains.
- **Tracking Detection Criteria**: An image was classified as a tracking pixel if either:
  1. The image URL contained a recipient identifier (either raw email address or a hash; evaluated using 32 hash function types and over 33,000 combinations).
  2. The image had an exact display or rendered size of 1x1.
- **Evasive Techniques Identified**:
  - *Size Hiding*: 24.9% of tracking images omitted size attributes in the HTML markup, requiring the researchers to dynamically fetch pixels to confirm their actual dimensions.
  - *Redirection Chains*: 54.8% of tracking URLs used redirects. In total, 2,825 hidden trackers were identified, with Google-owned `doubleclick.net` being the top hidden tracker (appearing in over 96,000 emails).
- **Tracking Prevalence**:
  - 24.6% of all analyzed email messages and 5.5% of all senders utilized email tracking.
  - Tracking was far more prominent among popular senders: nearly 50% of domains in the Alexa top 10,000 performed tracking.
  - First-party tracking was slightly more common than third-party tracking.
  - Unlike web tracking (where Google tracks ~80% of top 1M sites), email tracking was less concentrated: the top 10 trackers accounted for 31.8% of tracking senders.

### Takeaways
Public disposable email services present major security risks due to shared inbox visibility and inconsistent message deletion policies, exposing sensitive PII and account recovery mechanisms. Concurrently, email tracking is prevalent among major senders, employing redirect chains and dynamically rendered pixels to monitor recipients. Proposed defenses include HTML filtering, preloading images, and email client proxying (such as techniques deployed by Gmail) to shield individual user IP addresses and browsing environments from trackers.

talks.title: Towards Practical Differentialy Private Convex Optimization
talks.teaser: A deployable private optimizer and large empirical study show strong accuracy for differentially private convex learning on real data.
talks.summary:
The presentation argues that published differentially private convex optimization methods often assume an exact loss minimizer or a bespoke optimizer, which blocks use with ordinary training stacks. It introduces AMP (approximate minimum perturbation), a four-step procedure that splits the privacy budget, regularizes the loss in a spirit similar to objective perturbation, runs any off-the-shelf optimizer until the iterate lies in a gradient-norm region controlled by gamma, then adds noise before release. The speaker motivates privacy with membership inference against released models, reviews epsilon and delta, and notes prior families: objective perturbation, in-training noise, and output perturbation.

Formal utility claims are summarized rather than derived: AMP supports standard convex losses beyond GLMs, matches objective perturbation’s asymptotic utility order when gamma is small, and improves n-dependence versus private permutation SGD and output perturbation. Experiments cover logistic regression on thirteen datasets—low- and high-dimensional synthetics plus Uber collaboration sets—with delta fixed at one over n squared and epsilon from 0.01 to 10, tuned methods versus a hyperparameter-free AMP schedule tuned only on synthetic data, and a non-private baseline over ten runs.

On high-dimensional realsim and rcv1, tuned and hyperparameter-free AMP often beat other private methods. On large real-world sets, private methods sometimes exceed the non-private baseline, and AMP stays near baseline even at strict epsilon. The takeaway is that large n can make privacy cheap in practice, AMP is meant for deployment, benchmarks and code are released open source.

talks.title: Postcards from the Post HTTP World: Amplification of HTTPS Vulnerabilities in the Web Ecosystem
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Postcards from the Post HTTP World: Amplification of HTTPS Vulnerabilities in the Web Ecosystem.
talks.summary: Researchers quantify how broken TLS on included hosts undermines apparently healthy HTTPS home pages. They formalize known attacks as boolean attack trees, classify channels as tainted, leaky, or partially leaky, then crawl Alexa top sites with headless Chrome, subdomain enumeration, and existing TLS scanners mapping onto those trees. Scanning one target often pulls in more than one hundred related hosts. About five percent expose channel weaknesses, yet roughly ten percent of home pages risk script injection because three quarters load JavaScript from third parties with bad TLS. Baidu and Akamai vulnerable edges alone taint hundreds of sites. Session cookies on more than four hundred properties leak confidentiality via shared subdomain scopes, and five hundred show low integrity though host-only and __Host- cookie fixes would shrink exposure yet remain rare. Tracking pixels on leaky TLS enable cross-site profiles amplified when attackers inject scripts. TLS 1.3 adoption is expected to help but is not a complete fix.

talks.title: Fidelius: Protecting User Secrets from Compromised Browsers
talks.teaser: Shows how a hardware enclave and dongles keep typed secrets hidden from a fully compromised browser and operating system.
talks.summary:
Users routinely type sensitive data such as social security or bank account numbers into web pages, and malware that has taken over the browser or the whole operating system could capture it. This talk presents Fidelius, which keeps typed secrets away from that software by running a small trusted component inside a hardware enclave while the browser stays outside. The prototype uses Intel SGX, but the design does not depend on it. Developers add a secure attribute to sensitive tags and a server-generated signature, so existing sites need only minimal changes.

The enclave code, about 8,500 lines of C++, is the part that must be audited, since keeping the browser out avoids moving millions of lines into the enclave. Input and output travel over a trusted path built from Raspberry Pi dongles attached to a keyboard and a display. In trusted mode the keyboard dongle emits encrypted packets at a fixed rate, and the display dongle overlays encrypted sensitive text on the pass-through video, with indicator lights and a green banner showing the origin. A demo compared what the user saw with what malware could capture. The prototype took about 200 milliseconds from keypress to visible change, which the speaker attributed mostly to prototype overhead rather than the design.

The speaker was clear about limits. Side-channel attacks on enclaves are not addressed, and a server that sends secrets back insecurely is not protected against. An operating system could also skip the enclave, but the missing indicator would alert a careful user. Audience questions covered hypervisor-based alternatives and automatic labelling of sensitive inputs. The takeaway is that the trusted path can be reused on its own for any enclave that needs user input and output.

talks.title: "If HTTPS Were Secure I wouldn't Need 2FA" End User and Administrator Mental Models of HTTPS
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in "If HTTPS Were Secure I wouldn't Need 2FA" End User and Administrator Mental Models of HTTPS.

talks.title: EmPoWeb: Empowering Web Applications with Browser Extensions
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of EmPoWeb: Empowering Web Applications with Browser Extensions.

talks.title: Does Certificate Transparency Break the Web? Measuring Adoption and Error Rate
talks.teaser: Measures Certificate Transparency adoption and Chrome error rates, and draws lessons for rolling out ecosystem-wide security changes.
talks.summary:
Certificate Transparency (CT) is a system of public, cryptographically auditable logs for spotting misissued certificates quickly. Emily Stark explains that browsers could not require CT from every site at once without breaking many of them, so Chrome rolled it out in stages. The study combines Chrome telemetry, active scans of popular websites and an analysis of Chrome help forum threads.

The main metric is the CT compliance rate, which asks whether sites that Chrome requires to support CT actually do so. Adoption reached 71% of HTTP requests in Chrome, partly because Cloudflare enabled CT for its sites by default, which accounted for 1600 of the Alexa top 10,000. Compliance stood at 99.7 percent when required, but the speaker argues it cannot be assumed: some popular sites adopted a custom CT option by mistake, and some CAs shipped buggy or no CT. Errors matter because users clicked through CT errors about twice as often as certificate errors overall, and 60% of help forum threads about them contained an incorrect explanation or fix.

Staged enforcement limited the damage, moving from EV certificates to specific CAs, an opt-in reporting mode, and finally all certificates issued after April 2018. Under EV enforcement, less than 4% of connections lost the EV indicator at any time, though some CAs kept issuing EV certificates without CT. The reporting mode caught a large website's misconfigured SCTs before users were affected. Remaining challenges include the heavy implementation burden on browser vendors, since 19% of forum threads described users switching browsers to reach a site that did not enforce CT. The takeaway: ecosystem-wide changes need staged rollouts and monitoring rather than a single flag day.

talks.title: XCLAIM: Trustless Interoperable Cryptocurrency Backed Assets
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of XCLAIM: Trustless Interoperable Cryptocurrency Backed Assets.

talks.title: Lay Down the Common Metrics: Evaluating Proof of Work Consensus Protocols' Security
talks.teaser: Finds no proof-of-work consensus protocol that beats Nakamoto consensus on all three attacks, using a Markov decision process model.
talks.summary:
Proof-of-work blockchains depend on a consensus protocol to decide which transaction history is authentic. Nakamoto consensus has imperfect chain quality, so an attacker with less than half the mining power can still succeed at selfish mining, double spending and censorship attacks. Many successor protocols claim stronger security, so the talk sets out a framework that compares them on four metrics: incentive compatibility, subversion gain, double-spending resistance and censorship susceptibility.

The protocols fall into two families: those that try to raise chain quality directly, and attack-resistant designs that rely on reward distribution, punishment or content-based rewards. The method models each protocol as a Markov decision process, computes the attacker's optimal strategy, and compares the resulting utility with Nakamoto consensus. Two examples were covered. Fruit chains treat some attacker blocks as risk-free, which makes them worse on incentive compatibility and subversion gain, though they resist censorship better because orphaned blocks can be re-embedded later. Reward splitting, which lets blocks reference orphaned uncles, performs better on incentive compatibility, with subversion bounties of 102 for Nakamoto consensus, 346 for reward splitting and zero for fruit chains at 10% attacker power and six confirmations. It also gives weaker attackers a new censorship tool.

The conclusion is that no protocol clearly outperforms Nakamoto consensus, since each gain on one attack tends to weaken another. Designers should avoid protocols too complicated to analyse, test against more than one strategy and incentive, and avoid unrealistic parameters, favouring practical assumptions such as network awareness or loosely synchronised clocks. The speaker also notes that protocol analysis does not establish the security of live cryptocurrencies, which depends on many other factors.

talks.title: Ouroboros Crypsinous Privacy Preserving Proof of Stake
talks.teaser: Introduces Crypsinous, a proof-of-stake protocol that keeps stake hidden using zero-knowledge proofs and private transactions.
talks.summary:
Proof-of-stake systems pick block producers according to how much stake each participant holds, which uses far less energy than proof-of-work and resists takeover by rented mining power. Most designs, however, need to know every party's stake, clashing with the goal of hiding who transacts. The talk introduces Crypsinous, presented as the first protocol to keep stake hidden while still electing leaders.

The speaker recaps Ouroboros Genesis, which divides time into epochs and slots and lets a participant lead a slot when a random evaluation falls under a stake-dependent target. Zerocash supplies the privacy layer: coins are tracked through commitments and serial numbers, and spending is proven in zero knowledge. Crypsinous combines them by proving leadership inside a zero-knowledge statement. Two problems follow. Spent coins sit out until the next epoch so they cannot be linked to a proof, and replacement coins are derived deterministically so an adversary cannot grind for a win. For adaptive corruptions, forward-secure signatures give way to a Merkle tree of keys erased after use, and non-committing encryption gives way to forward-secure encryption relying on bounded delays.

The result is a private proof-of-stake protocol modeled under adaptive corruptions, with a new private ledger functionality in the UC framework. The speaker noted that the Merkle-tree key erasure could also strengthen earlier protocols, at the cost of a bounded number of keys that is usually acceptable in practice.

talks.title: Proof Of Stake Sidechains
talks.teaser: Outlines proof-of-stake sidechains moving one currency between settlement and computation layers via compact Ouroboros Merkle certificates.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames a problem familiar from live networks: users want Bitcoin-like safety on one chain and Ethereum-like smart-contract richness on another, without forcing a single monolithic codebase. The proposed architecture names a settlement layer for savings-style transfers and limited policy, plus an independently evolving computation layer for richer contracts, sharing one currency through paired destroy-and-mint moves.

Moving value into the computation layer is straightforward when nodes watch both ledgers. Returning value is harder because settlement-layer validators should stay simple and not ingest the full computation chain. The approach aligns Ouroboros epochs across layers, elects a stake-weighted committee from late-epoch slots, and posts compact Merkle-backed certificates with aggregatable signatures so settlement nodes can confirm remote burns without direct peering. An inductive committee handoff carries stake evolution, and a firewall rule caps inflows so settlement-layer supply cannot exceed what previously left, even if the computation layer fails catastrophically.

The work is cast in a formal sidechain security definition the authors argue others should reuse, with a Cardano-oriented implementation noted as the motivating proof-of-stake case. The closing discussion clarifies that asset identity stays constant across chains, committee honesty follows the honest-majority stake assumption rather than a fixed federation, and computation-layer bugs harm only computation-layer balances.

talks.title: Redactable Blockchain in the Permissionless Setting
talks.teaser: Presents a way to redact harmful blockchain data through miner voting, with no trusted authority or heavy cryptography.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses a problem with permissionless blockchains such as Bitcoin: data is immutable, so harmful content written into a block stays there. Jurisdictions disagree on whether running a full node that holds such data is acceptable, and law enforcement has taken notice. Forking the chain is costly when data sits deep in history, and miners who quietly drop data leave hash links that new users cannot verify. Earlier redaction proposals depended on a trusted authority or a permissioned committee, which do not suit an open network.

The proposed protocol makes redaction a policy-governed vote. A policy sets how much agreement a change needs. Anyone can publish a candidate replacement block by putting its hash on the chain, and miners signal support by including that hash in the blocks they mine. If the votes meet the policy threshold within a fixed voting period, the original block is swapped for the candidate. Block headers gain a second Merkle root, creating an old link and a new link, so the original proof of work can still be checked after a redaction. Edits at transaction level are allowed, provided monetary details such as addresses and amounts stay unchanged.

The protocol keeps public, accountable records of who requested and who voted, and claims no trust assumptions beyond those of the underlying consensus. A proof-of-concept implementation showed validation overhead of up to three percent for a chain with up to five thousand redacted blocks, compared with an unredacted chain. Audience questions covered bribery risks and why miners would take part in voting.

talks.title: PERUN: Virtual Payment Hubs over Cryptographic Currencies
talks.teaser: The presentation introduces Perun virtual payment channels for fast, cheap micropayments without routing each payment through a hub.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with why on-chain cryptocurrency payments are slow, fee-heavy, and poorly suited to tiny transfers, and sets a target for micropayments that stay cheap, fast, usable with limited connectivity, and as strong as ordinary ledger transactions. Smart contracts on platforms such as Ethereum can hold locked funds, but every on-chain touch still pays gas and waits on block time, so the work centers on off-chain channel designs.

Ledger payment channels follow fund, update, and close phases familiar from Lightning-style designs: parties exchange signed state tuples off-chain and fall back to the contract only to settle disputes. For hub networks, hash time-lock routing forces the intermediary into every payment and limits throughput. Perun’s virtual payment channel locks collateral on both sides of the hub once, then lets Alice and Bob update balances directly while the hub stays financially neutral at close. The construction is backed by formal analysis, including proofs in the UC framework, and an Ethereum proof of concept with measured open, update, and close costs.

Compared with per-payment hash time-lock routing, virtual channels shift hub compensation toward locking time rather than per-transfer fees, preserving micro-payment behavior for updates. Extensions mentioned include state channels for logic inside channels and multi-party variants. Practitioners should weigh when hub lock fees beat per-route fees, plan periodic blockchain monitoring or watchtower-style helpers for offline exchange, and treat promised coin amounts as volatile rather than fiat-priced options.

talks.title: RIDL: Rogue In-Flight Data Load
talks.teaser: Shows how the RIDL speculative execution attack leaks in-flight data from CPU fill buffers across security boundaries.
talks.summary: Stefan Guo demos RIDL, leaking in-flight data across CPU privilege boundaries despite Meltdown and Spectre mitigations—extracting /etc/shadow hashes from unprivileged code and spanning kernel, hypervisor, SGX enclaves, and browser processes.

talks.title: LBM: A Security Framework for Peripherals within the Linux Kernel...
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for LBM: A Security Framework for Peripherals within the Linux Kernel....
talks.summary: Researchers present LBM, a Linux-kernel security framework for peripherals, motivated by real-world cryptographic storage devices whose ARM-based firmware must be analyzed because integrated self-encryption is not trustless magic.

talks.title: Exploiting Correcting Codes On the Effectiveness of ECC Memory Against Rowhammer Attacks
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Exploiting Correcting Codes On the Effectiveness of ECC Memory Against Rowhammer Attacks.

talks.title: Theory and Practice of Finding Eviction Sets
talks.teaser: Presents a linear-time group testing method for finding cache eviction sets, with benchmarks across browsers and hardware.
talks.summary:
Modern CPUs cache memory in sets, and an eviction set is a group of addresses that all map to the same cache set, enough of them to fill it. Such sets are a building block for attacks like Prime+Probe, Rowhammer, and speculative-execution attacks, which need to push specific data out of the cache. Finding them is hard because an attacker often cannot see how physical addresses map to cache sets, and from JavaScript only array indices are available.

The usual method gathers a large set of randomly chosen addresses that probably contains enough colliding ones, then shrinks it by testing elements one at a time. That reduction needs a quadratic number of memory accesses. The speakers treat reduction as a threshold group testing problem, a generalisation of classic group testing. Each round splits the candidate set into subsets of associativity plus one and discards at least one of them, so the cost grows linearly with the initial set size. When the attacker knows nothing about the set-index bits, the earlier approach takes minutes per set, while the new one finishes in under two seconds. Some modern replacement policies break the test's assumptions and cause errors, which repetition and backtracking heuristics handle at a small cost. A browser-based JavaScript demo found 73 eviction sets in a few seconds and reduced each to a minimal set.

The main takeaway is that minimal eviction set discovery is a threshold group testing problem, which matters when designing countermeasures. Randomising the cache index hides the mapping, but the set must be recomputed whenever the mapping changes, and dynamic remapping would also slow legitimate programs. The speakers suggest that noisy group testing variants could reduce the overhead of the heuristics.

talks.title: SoK: The Challenges Pitfalls and Perils of Using Hardware Performance Counters for Security
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding SoK: The Challenges Pitfalls and Perils of Using Hardware Performance Counters for Security.

talks.title: Spectre Attacks Exploiting Speculative Execution
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Spectre Attacks Exploiting Speculative Execution.

talks.title: AI and Security: Lessons, Challenges, and Future Directions
talks.teaser: Surveys lessons, open challenges and future directions where AI meets security, from a 2018 deep learning workshop keynote.
talks.summary:
This keynote by Dawn Song looks at the relationship between artificial intelligence and security under the heading of lessons, challenges and future directions. It was presented at the first workshop on deep learning and security, held on May 24, 2018, alongside the 2018 IEEE Symposium on Security and Privacy in San Francisco.

The framing treats the subject as a broad survey rather than a single technique or tool. The talk's stated focus covers what has been learned so far, the problems that remain open, and where the work may head next, so it is aimed at orientation rather than step-by-step method.

A reader who wants context before going into the technical papers from the workshop would find the keynote's overall framing useful. The page records only the title and the event details, so specific examples and conclusions are not summarised here.

talks.title: FP-Stalker: Tracking Browser Fingerprint Evolutions
talks.teaser: Antoine Vastel examines FP-Stalker: Tracking Browser Fingerprint Evolutions.

talks.title: On the Economics of Offline Password Cracking
talks.teaser: Predicts how many stolen password hashes a rational attacker cracks, and how memory-hard hashing changes the outcome.
talks.summary:
Stolen password hash files let an attacker guess offline with no lockout, so the only real limit is the cost of each guess. The talk looks at key stretching, which makes each hash more expensive to compute. It covers iterated hashing such as PBKDF2 and bcrypt, and newer memory-hard functions such as scrypt and Argon2id. The speaker revisits four breaches, Dropbox, Ashley Madison, Yahoo and LastPass, where the deployed settings became known afterwards. LastPass, for example, used PBKDF2 with SHA-256 and 100,000 iterations, above the NIST guidance of 10,000 iterations cited in the talk.

The model treats the attacker as untargeted and rational: they know the password distribution but nothing about a given user, and they stop guessing once the marginal cost exceeds the marginal reward. Guessing cost is estimated from Bitcoin mining hardware, putting PBKDF2 at 100,000 iterations at roughly 70 cents per billion guesses. Reward depends on black-market prices, which fall as more passwords are cracked. Password frequencies in a set of 70 million Yahoo passwords fit a Zipf-style law. Even with assumptions that favour the defender, the modelled settings fall in a region where the attacker cracks essentially all passwords. A pessimistic case with memory-hard functions still predicts about 20% cracked.

Memory-hard functions force the attacker to allocate memory for the full run, so cost grows with both time and memory rather than time alone. The talk closes with advice: move away from PBKDF2 and bcrypt toward memory-hard functions, use distributed password hashing for organizations, and enable two-factor authentication for users instead of relying on more complex passwords.

talks.title: Mouse Authentication without the Temporal Aspect
talks.teaser: A 2D CNN maps mouse curves to images for authentication, outperforming classical and sequence baselines on public behavioral datasets.
talks.summary:
Behavioral mouse dynamics can authenticate users without extra hardware, but many public mouse corpora are too small for deep sequence models trained from scratch. The work reframes mouse traces as static curve images and trains a two-dimensional convolutional network, using transfer learning rather than preserving full temporal structure in the input.

The method adapts GoogleNet with joint multi-label training over per-user binary decisions, then compares against a classical sixty-six-feature model, a one-dimensional CNN on normalized sequences, and an LSTM baseline. On Pallavi and a second public collection evaluated with cross-validation, the two-dimensional model leads consistently; averaging predictions across consecutive curves improves reliability. Robustness experiments weaken performance only slightly when curves are recentered, but hurt sharply when train and test screen resolutions differ—a gap the authors flag for real deployment. Layer-wise relevance propagation heat maps show which plotted segments support or oppose a decision; the network tends to down-weight long straight strokes and crossing artifacts introduced by rasterizing paths.

Takeaways for practitioners include treating resolution shift as a serious operational risk, using interpretability maps to verify the model is not keyed on plotting artifacts, and recognizing limitations around task stability and long-term behavior left for future datasets and follow-on work.

talks.title: Is "Adversarial Examples" an Adversarial Example?
talks.teaser: Questions how adversarial examples are defined and argues that defenses should follow from adversary goals and costs.
talks.summary:
The talk asks what counts as an adversarial example and argues that common definitions are weak. An adversarial example is an input an adversary crafts on purpose, which is hard to use as a working test. In malware, the true class can be checked by running the sample, while for images it rests on human perception. The dominant image definition uses a small distance bound, which the speaker says assumes too much about both perception and adversary goals.

A malware case study used evolutionary search over PDF structure to evade a detector, finding evasive variants for every seed tested, often by inserting simple content. Hiding the classifier score still allowed attacks using only binary outputs. For images, feature squeezing reduces input precision and compares model outputs on original and squeezed inputs, separating many adversarial inputs on MNIST and giving reasonable detection on ImageNet. Adaptive attacks that fold the defense into the loss needed larger perturbations but still succeeded. For black-box attacks, query costs varied widely across seeds, and targeting easy seeds first came close to the best possible cost.

The speaker argues that security usually treats a small success rate as a serious break, while this field accepts high rates, so evaluation must change. Defenses should follow from a clear model of adversary goals, and evaluation should measure the cost of finding many examples rather than average success. The talk ends by comparing the field to early alchemy: useful experiments, but no solid theory yet.

talks.title: Defense Against the Dark Arts
talks.teaser: Explains why published defenses against adversarial examples break and what evaluation games practitioners should demand.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens on a crowded literature where many claimed defenses against adversarial examples are quickly overturned, and frames clarity as the goal rather than a new attack paper. It contrasts classical machine learning’s independent-and-identically-distributed training with security settings where attackers choose inputs, including tiny perturbations that flip deep network labels, graffiti on stop signs, and domain shifts such as apples in mesh bags.

The core of the talk maps the problem as explicit defender–attacker games: action spaces, costs, white-box versus varied gray-box access, and transfer of attacks across models so substitute networks can fool black-box targets. Norm-bounded perturbations are described as convenient lab benchmarks—not faithful models of physical attacks—while defender-first dynamics explain why training on a fixed attack set often fails against adaptive adversaries. Trade-off curves mix clean and adversarial traffic; one example puts the crossover near 7.1% adversarial inputs. A staged pipeline of failure modes runs from ineffective methods through clean-accuracy loss, non-adaptive robustness, overfitting to one optimizer, gradient masking, and robustness trapped inside a single threat model, with historical examples such as dropout, weight decay, cropping, defensive distillation, and adversarial training variants.

Practitioners are urged to state threat models clearly, prefer reactive attackers in evaluation, weigh deployment-time adversary rates, and pursue indirect regularizers alongside direct adversarial training. Future work emphasizes better benchmarks beyond vision, certification beyond local norm geometry, domains with crisp ground truth, and security goals—mistake cost, confidence on errors, transfer resistance—that diverge from plain accuracy. The talk closes with the Clever Hans metaphor and an open-source library named for that story.

talks.title: Security Risks in Deep Learning Implementation
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Security Risks in Deep Learning Implementation.

talks.title: When Your Fitness Tracker Betrays You: Quantifying the Predictability...
talks.teaser: A framework quantifies how biometric traits leak across devices, helping compare systems and harden authentication choices.
talks.summary:
Popular biometric authentication often assumes an attacker already possesses a victim’s enrollment-quality signals. The presentation reframes the first stage of cross-context attacks: commodity sensors on watches, straps, and everyday phones continuously leak behavior that may differ from the sensor used for login. Position and device type reshape gait, touch, eye, ECG, and related features, so smartwatch accelerometer traces need not resemble phone traces even for the same walk.

The researchers learn a universal transfer mapping from paired population data—sources and targets that exclude the victim—to minimize distribution distance between contexts. From that mapping they derive per-feature and aggregated unpredictability scores; lower scores mean an attacker can approximate target-context features more closely. They built a multi-biometric, multi-context dataset with thirty participants measured across two sessions and applied the metric to compare biometrics, sessions, and source devices.

Eye movement and touch dynamics proved more predictable across contexts than gait; stale sessions raised scores; ECG prediction eased when source contexts resembled the authenticator. Finer touch sensors on higher-end phones lowered predictability. Practitioners can use the scores to rank systems, flag risky enrollment contexts, prioritize protected data sources, and select features that resist cross-device inference.

talks.title: Towards Security and Privacy for Multi User Augmented Reality
talks.teaser: Presents a user study of HoloLens pairs that surfaces privacy and security concerns in shared augmented reality experiences.
talks.summary:
The talk examines security and privacy risks for augmented reality when several people share an experience, an area the speaker says earlier work largely overlooked. Prior research mostly treated apps on a user's own headset as the threat and seldom asked people what worried them. The team ran a qualitative study with 22 participants, recruited as 11 pairs who already knew each other, trying Microsoft HoloLens for the first time.

Each pair used a single-user shell, then three apps: a shooter game, Skype for HoloLens with a tablet partner, and a block-building app the team built because few shared apps existed. Interviews followed on three open adversarial scenarios: harassment, untrusted apps, and bystanders. Participants found the experience more immersive than expected and often reacted physically to virtual objects. They assumed the environment would be shared by default, altered each other's appearance with virtual props, and disputed ownership of virtual blocks. Concerns included physical harm, such as a digital object distracting a driver, and photorealistic content that could be mistaken for a real hazard. For shared settings, participants proposed access control with separate view and edit permissions.

The takeaway is that multi-user AR is growing and its defenses should be designed while the platform is still malleable, with user perspectives guiding that work. The speaker argued that today's hardware is already immersive enough to produce these concerns, so the risks do not wait for future advances.

talks.title: Learning Universal Adversarial Perturbations with Generative Models
talks.teaser: Shows how a generative model can be trained to produce universal adversarial perturbations that fool image classifiers.
talks.summary:
Adversarial examples are inputs nudged to make a classifier err. A universal adversarial perturbation (UAP) is one image-agnostic change that, added to most inputs in a dataset, flips a model's prediction while staying within a small norm bound. Earlier work built these with iterative attacks, which must be rerun for each new perturbation. This talk asks whether a neural network can learn to generate UAPs instead.

The method samples random noise, passes it through a generative model that outputs a perturbation, scales it into a fixed epsilon ball and adds it to random dataset images. Training pushes the top class down and the runner-up up, with a confidence margin and a norm penalty. After training, producing new perturbations is nearly free. On three ImageNet classifiers, accuracy on the crafted examples falls well below clean accuracy. The same approach can target a chosen class, such as golf ball, and on a ten-class dataset the speaker produced targeted perturbations for every class.

The speaker also ran an alternating game against adversarial training, retraining the target on generated examples and then regenerating attacks. Accuracy settled into an equilibrium after roughly 20 to 30 rounds. Questions covered sample diversity, which a related paper handled with an extra penalty on similar outputs. The takeaway is that a learned generator can make cheap, reusable attacks, so defenses should be tested against adaptive generators.

talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Routing Around Congestion: Defeating DDoS Attacks and Adverse Network Conditions via Reactive....

talks.title: HeNet: A Deep Learning Approach on Intel® Processor Trace for Effective Exploit Detection
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning HeNet: A Deep Learning Approach on Intel® Processor Trace for Effective Exploit Detection.

talks.title: Machine-Learning DDoS Detection for Consumer Internet-of-Things Devices
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Machine-Learning DDoS Detection for Consumer Internet-of-Things Devices.
talks.summary: Rohan describes a home-router middlebox that segments per-device flows, extracts lightweight IoT-specific state features plus stateless packet stats, and classifies Mirai-style HTTP/TCP/UDP floods with random forests and small neural nets. Stateful endpoint-count features raise F1 scores beyond pure packet-size classifiers.

talks.title: Audio Adversarial Examples: Targeted Attacks on Speech-to-Text
talks.teaser: Shows near-inaudible audio perturbations that force DeepSpeech to transcribe chosen phrases from speech, music or silence.
talks.summary:
Carlini explains how an end-to-end speech recognition network, trained on raw audio waveforms with CTC loss, can be attacked by slightly altering an input clip. The attack is framed as a constrained optimization: keep the change small, measured in decibels relative to the original audio, while steering the network toward a chosen target phrase. Plain gradient descent struggles with the constraints, so the approach instead minimizes a CTC-based loss toward the target.

The attack is run against Mozilla's open-source DeepSpeech implementation in a white-box setting. Demonstrations include a spoken sentence made to be recognized as a long literary passage, a short Bach cello piece transcribed as a sentence claiming speech is embedded in music, and a speech clip made to register as the empty string. The speaker notes that erasing speech is easier than inserting it into silence or music, which requires larger and more noticeable changes. He also says the attacks are not expected to survive playback over speakers, because the physical channel distorts the perturbation.

The talk argues that properties known from image adversarial examples, such as transferability, appear to hold for audio as well. Open questions include over-the-air attacks, transfer between models, universal perturbations, and whether image defenses and detectors carry over to audio. The takeaway for practitioners is that optimization-based attacks are very effective against speech models, and defenses should be evaluated beyond image domains.

talks.title: Black-box Generation of Adversarial Text Sequences to Evade Deep Learning Classifiers
talks.teaser: Shows a black-box method that makes small character-level edits to words, flipping deep learning text classifier predictions.
talks.summary:
Text classifiers deployed on cloud servers, such as toxicity detectors, are usually reachable only through an interface, so attackers see predictions but not the model itself. Most earlier adversarial work assumed white-box access or targeted images. Because text is discrete, the presented approach changes words through small character-level edits, with edit distance measuring the size of the perturbation.

The method has three parts. A scoring function estimates which words matter most by querying the model with and without each word, comparing the outputs, and also considering the words that follow it. The words are then ranked by score, and the top-ranked words are modified with small character edits that typically turn them into out-of-dictionary tokens the model cannot map to meaning. Across several text classification datasets, the approach outperformed random word selection and a gradient-magnitude baseline, and it needs no iterative loop, so it runs faster than prior methods. Adversarial examples also transferred between models using different embeddings, dropping accuracy from around 90 percent to between 20 and 50 percent.

Modifying roughly 10 to 20 words sharply reduced accuracy. Adversarial training recovered some accuracy, but only partially. An autocorrect defense recovered much accuracy against simple attacks, yet stronger attacks that remove two characters within a word still caused large drops. The takeaway for practitioners is that character-level perturbations are a cheap, practical threat to deployed text classifiers, and spelling correction alone is not a sufficient defense.

talks.title: Detecting Homoglyph Attacks with a Siamese Neural Network
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Detecting Homoglyph Attacks with a Siamese Neural Network.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Daniel Grant presents research conducted with Hiram Anderson and Jonathan Woodbridge on detecting homoglyph attacks using computer vision and Siamese neural networks. Homoglyph attacks exploit visual similarities between different characters to deceive users and security systems. These deceptive techniques appear in both domain spoofing (leveraging the Internationalized Domain Name / IDN system) and process spoofing on operating systems, such as replacing characters in system binaries like `svchost.exe` (e.g., using a zero instead of an 'O') in real-world threats like the Beta Bot trojan and SMB worm.

### Key Topics & Limitations of Prior Art
Traditional approaches to identifying spoofed strings rely heavily on text-based metrics such as Levenshtein edit distance or weighted edit distances. However, standard edit distance generates significant false positives and is trivially bypassed by attackers making edits just outside the detection threshold. While weighted edit distance attempts to account for character visual similarity (such as digraphs like 'rn' mimicking 'm'), manually defining pairwise similarity across tens of thousands of Unicode characters is largely intractable. In text embeddings, accented or lookalike Unicode codepoints have numerical values completely unrelated to their ASCII counterparts, failing to capture visual closeness directly.

### Technical Details
To address these challenges, the researchers convert text strings into visual images (rendered using an Arial-based font) and use deep learning to generate feature vectors where visual similarity corresponds to small Euclidean distance:
- **Architecture**: A Siamese neural network composed of convolutional networks (ConvNets) with max pooling, flattening, and dense layers. Twin networks share weights and are trained on paired images.
- **Training**: Pairs of potential spoof variants (e.g., `google.com` vs. a spoofed version) are labeled 0 (small target distance), while unrelated pairs (e.g., Google vs. Facebook) are labeled 1.
- **Dataset & Indexing**: The pipeline ingests approximately 50,000 common domains (such as top domains from the Alexa 1M list) and 50,000 common process names. The 32-dimensional output feature vectors are indexed using KD-trees (leveraging non-deterministic/randomized trees) to perform fast approximate nearest neighbor lookups rather than brute-force search.
- **Evaluation**: Dimensionality reduction via PCA demonstrated clear visual clustering of spoof variants (e.g., variations of Twitter clustering together). Area Under the ROC Curve (AUC) showed significant detection gains over standard edit distance and visual edit distance heuristics. In process spoofing, standard edit distance performed near random chance (~0.5 AUC), whereas the Siamese network achieved superior discrimination, despite a small false-positive challenge with short legitimate names that resemble each other (such as `java` and `javac`).

### Takeaways
Visual representations provide an effective, automated method to capture deceptive lookalike strings without manually mapping Unicode tables. The approach is released under the Endgame Inc GitHub repository (`endgameinc/homoglyph`). Future work highlighted during the talk and audience Q&A includes diversifying font coverage (handling serif versus sans-serif fonts) and addressing collisions between short legitimate process names.

talks.title: Adversarial Examples for Generative Models
talks.teaser: Shows how tiny perturbations redirect generative model outputs to chosen targets, and how GANs craft stealthy adversarial inputs.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at adversarial examples aimed at generative models, which it separates clearly from attacks on ordinary classifiers. A generative model typically has an encoder that compresses high-dimensional data into a lower-dimensional latent space and a decoder that rebuilds the data from that space. The threat is an attacker who adds a small perturbation so that, after encoding and decoding, the output becomes a chosen target.

The attack is framed as an optimization problem: keep the perturbed input as close as possible to the original while steering the reconstruction toward the target. Distance is usually measured with an Lp norm, though the speaker notes it is a weak proxy for visual realism, so alternatives such as total variation loss are used. Demonstrations covered face images, where a face was mapped to a target person, and handwritten digits, where each digit could be redirected to a chosen target. Attacks can also operate directly on the latent space using standard classifier-style gradient methods.

The second half flips the idea and uses a GAN to produce adversarial examples against other classifiers. A generator outputs a perturbation, a discriminator keeps the result looking like genuine inputs, and the total loss combines an adversarial term for the target classifier, a GAN term for realism, and a closeness term to the original. ImageNet examples showed perturbations that were not visible on close inspection. The takeaway is that generative models are an attack surface in their own right and can also be used to craft more realistic adversarial inputs.

talks.title: PIR with Compressed Queries and Amortized Query Processing
talks.teaser: Shows how compressing PIR queries into one ciphertext cuts network cost for private database retrieval.
talks.summary:
Private information retrieval lets a client fetch one file from a server's database without revealing which file it wants. Downloading the whole database is private but expensive, and the talk focuses on the computational variant, which avoids the non-collusion assumption that multi-server schemes need. The starting point is a 1998 protocol in which the client sends an encrypted selection vector with one entry per record. That vector is large, and the server's homomorphic operations over it are costly.

The proposed technique compresses the selection vector into a single ciphertext. The client encodes its choice as coefficients of one polynomial, and the server expands it back into the vector using an extract step built from ciphertext addition, plaintext multiplication and a substitution operation. This avoids the expensive homomorphic multiplications that a fully homomorphic approach would need. Compared with the XPIR baseline, query size drops by up to two orders of magnitude and client computation falls, while the server pays roughly 6 percent extra for decompression. In a group messaging case study, the speaker reported a 56 times reduction in network cost from compression, and up to 40 times from the separate batching technique.

The talk closes with the trade-offs. Server work still grows linearly with database size, but it parallelizes well across hardware. The speaker also argued that a fully homomorphic alternative would likely cost far more server time than it saves in bandwidth. The main takeaway is that PIR becomes practical for mobile clients on constrained networks.

talks.title: A Tale of Two Studies: The Best and Worst of YubiKey Usability
talks.teaser: A paired lab and four-week field study exposes YubiKey setup pitfalls and daily-use strengths for everyday accounts.
talks.summary:
Password replacement and two-factor authentication remain central goals, yet strong cryptography only helps when real people adopt it. The presenter describes twin studies of YubiKey usability: a laboratory session where thirty-one campus recruits learned about the keys and tried to enable U2F on supplied Google, Facebook, and Windows 10 accounts without coordinator help, and a four-week longitudinal study where twenty-five participants used YubiKey Neo or Nano devices on personal accounts after guided setup.

Laboratory outcomes were uneven. Google registration succeeded for eighty-three percent of participants and Facebook for seventy percent, but many who registered a key on Facebook never toggled the separate control that actually enabled two-factor authentication at login. Windows proved far harsher: twelve participants pursued the wrong tool, and only five of nineteen who used Yubico’s login software completed setup, with some risking lockout from reboots and registry issues. Open responses criticized instructions; the System Usability Scale scored setup near fifty, below typical acceptability.

After coordinators handled setup, longitudinal scores landed in the seventies and daily use proved smoother, though sharing accounts, nano size, lost keys, and accidental keystrokes from keyboard-emulation still frustrated users. The closing recommendations stress standardized setup, clear success confirmation, test drives, backup keys, and OS integration—changes the speaker notes the ecosystem has begun to address.

talks.title: Secure Device Bootstrapping without Secrets Resistant to Signal Manipulation Attacks
talks.teaser: Presents a pairing protocol for groups of devices that uses radio signal cancellation limits to resist man-in-the-middle attacks.
talks.summary:
The talk covers how a group of wireless devices can establish trust with a central hub when they share no secrets and have no advanced user interface. Such groups appear in drone swarms, body area networks and field deployments, where preloaded keys leak and unauthenticated key exchange is open to man-in-the-middle attacks. The speaker shows that an adversary's chance of breaking at least one pair grows with group size, and asks whether the number of devices can instead strengthen the pairing.

The threat model lets an adversary join as an extra member, hijack a legitimate session, or pose as a rogue hub, using overshadowing or signal cancellation. The defence relies on on-off keying with Manchester coding, so each bit depends on energy being present or absent, and on random transmissions the adversary cannot predict. Cancelling one device's signal at two receivers is possible only at specific points, while cancelling it at three receivers requires an intersection that geometry rules out. Experiments reported by the speaker found cancellation probabilities below 10 to the power minus 4 at a detection threshold of minus 50 dBm.

The protocol exchanges key primitives in sequence, after which all devices simultaneously send a hash of the protocol transcript. If an attacker has altered a device's transcript, the mismatched device raises an alarm by transmitting energy in the off slots, corrupting the exchange. The speaker concludes that the scheme gives physical-layer integrity verification resistant to overshadowing and cancellation, and that its security improves as more devices take part.

talks.title: On the Economics of Offline Password Cracking
talks.teaser: Models how many passwords a rational attacker cracks after a breach, using Yahoo password data and key-stretching costs.
talks.summary:
The talk asks whether key stretching can make offline password cracking expensive enough to limit what a rational attacker gains from a stolen hash file. Offline attackers face no lockout, so their effort is bounded only by the resources they invest. The speaker revisits breaches at Dropbox, Ashley Madison, Yahoo and LastPass, noting that each company had deployed some form of key stretching, with LastPass using PBKDF2 and 100,000 iterations. The analysis uses a decision-theoretic model of an untargeted attacker who stops once marginal guessing costs exceed marginal rewards.

Guessing costs are estimated from Bitcoin mining hardware, where a SHA-256 ASIC performs 14 trillion hashes per second, which leads to roughly 70 cents per billion PBKDF2 guesses at 100,000 iterations. Password popularity is modeled with Zipf's law, fitted to a dataset of 70 million Yahoo passwords. Under optimistic assumptions, including diminishing returns and the lowest black-market value found, the speaker reports that a rational attacker cracks every password. A pessimistic case, with a four-dollar value per password and no diminishing returns, still predicts that only about 20% of passwords fall when a memory-hard function is used.

Memory-hard functions such as scrypt and Argon2id make attack cost scale quadratically with running time, unlike the linear scaling of bcrypt and PBKDF2. Matching that protection with PBKDF2 would take about two minutes per hash, which the speaker considers unacceptable for usability. Recommendations include moving organizations toward memory-hard functions and distributed password hashing, and having users enable two-factor authentication and use different passwords per account rather than more complex ones.

talks.title: Study and Mitigation of Origin Stripping Vulnerabilities in Hybrid-postMessage Enabled Mobile Apps
talks.teaser: Exposes origin stripping in hybrid app postMessage bridges, with a detection tool and a mitigation evaluated on popular apps.
talks.summary:
Hybrid mobile apps embed a WebView so web content can run alongside native code. The postMessage API lets web frames exchange messages, but in hybrid apps the bridge to native code offers no reliable way for senders and targets to be specified and validated, so origin information gets lost. The speaker walks through attack cases: a malicious subframe or compromised web content can reach the native side, and an attacker can either monitor messages sent to the mobile platform or inject messages into it.

To study the problem, the team built a dynamic detection solution. It instruments an app to tag messages crossing from the web side to the mobile side, then checks whether origin data survives the trip. Running it on 1000 popular hybrid apps, it flagged vulnerable apps. A case study covered a popular React Native framework used by many apps, along with an app for shopping lists and Google Cloud Print. Reported impacts ranged from silently monitoring a microphone to triggering data races that cause crashes. The developers found the framework issue difficult to fix after disclosure.

The team then proposed a mitigation that provides a hybrid postMessage API with origin checks and supports customization for framework and library developers. Its evaluation covered effectiveness, performance and ease of use. The main takeaway is that standard web postMessage defenses do not cover the hybrid bridge, so developers of hybrid frameworks need explicit sender and target checks on the native side too.
