talks.title: The Spyware Used in Intimate Partner Violence
talks.teaser: Researchers map intimate-partner spyware in app stores and show commercial anti-spyware fails to flag dual-use trackers.
talks.summary:
Intimate partner surveillance turns phones into tools for stalking and control because abusers often have brief physical access, know passwords, or supply the device itself. The presenter describes a first systematic study of the spyware ecosystem aimed at intimate partners, motivated by prior victim reports and a need to see what tools exist online, how abusers find them, and whether developers know or encourage misuse.

The team used snowball search across Google and app-store APIs, growing query sets from search suggestions until limits were reached. They identified overt off-store spyware plus thousands of store-listed apps, including more than 3,500 on Google Play and hundreds on Apple’s store after machine-assisted screening and manual verification. Apps range from overt trackers to dual-use programs marketed for anti-theft, family, or employer monitoring but repurposed in forums and guides. Developer behavior spans explicit promotion, affiliate funnels, paid ads on partner-tracking queries, and customer-support responses that mostly facilitate hidden installation. Disclosure led Google to remove some couple-tracking offerings and tighten policy enforcement on explicit terms, yet most danger remains in dual-use software stores still allow.

Evaluating forty consumer anti-spyware products showed none reliably flag dual-use trackers, leaving victims with weak heuristics. Practitioners should treat IPS as a mobile abuse problem intertwined with store policy, marketing, and detection design—not only overt malware. Ongoing work targets victim-facing detection with industry partners and raises a design challenge: reducing repurposing risk without banning every legitimate tracking feature.

talks.title: Distance-Bounding Protocols: Verification without Time and Location
talks.teaser: Replaces timing with event ordering to automatically verify distance-bounding protocols, exposing flaws in two published designs.
talks.summary:
Distance-bounding protocols defend against relay attacks, in which an attacker forwards messages between a car key or payment card and its reader so that a distant device appears to be nearby. The protocols time a challenge-response exchange and reject a device whose round trip suggests it is too far away. The talk recaps an earlier formal model that treats distance as a primitive and checks claims over protocol traces. That model depends on timing assumptions that are hard to guarantee in practice, because the tag's computation time is unknown and an attacker could overclock it.

The new result removes time and location from the model and reasons only about the order of events in an execution trace. The proposed definition requires that, between the reader sending a challenge and receiving the response, the tag performs some activity of its own. If a response can be produced before the challenge arrives, the protocol violates this causal ordering, and the speaker showed that an early response implies a very early one. The condition was encoded in the Tamarin model checker, which allowed the checks to run automatically.

Applied to protocols from the literature, the method confirmed that known flawed designs failed and that correct ones passed. It found new attacks on two protocols, and it explained why a protocol previously proven correct by its authors was not sound, pointing to a weaker attacker model in that proof. In audience questions, the speaker noted that bit-by-bit response channels may need a finer causal model, and that a probabilistic version of the analysis is future work.

talks.title: Learning from Mutants: Using Code Mutation to Learn and Monitor Invariants of a CPS
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Learning from Mutants: Using Code Mutation to Learn and Monitor Invariants of a CPS.
talks.summary: Researchers learn invariants of the SWaT water-treatment testbed by mutating PLC logic, simulating tank levels, and training SVM classifiers that flag abnormal time-series pairs—physical attestation when vendor PLC code cannot be audited directly.

talks.title: Sonar: Detecting SS7 Redirection Attacks With Audio-Based Distance Bounding
talks.teaser: Audio timing can expose redirected calls, though short detours may be difficult to distinguish from normal route variation.
talks.summary: The speaker describes Sonar, a system that uses audio distance bounding to detect SS7 call redirection. The talk covers a testbed with geographically varied call routes, measurements of mouth-to-ear delay, and tests of actual redirections that showed substantially higher latency. Attendees learn how route distance affects detection and why small route changes and call-path variation limit accuracy.

talks.title: The Rise of the Citizen Developer: Assessing the Security Impact of Online App Generators
talks.teaser: Measures how online app generators used by non-developers produce Android apps with shared code and weak security.
talks.summary:
The talk examines citizen developers, individuals with minimal software engineering background who build apps with online app generators through point-and-click interfaces and predefined modules. The speaker reports that about 250,000 apps, more than 11% of the Google Play sample of 2.3 million, were generated this way. A classifier that maps Android apps back to their generating service exposed large clusters of near-identical apps, which prompted a closer look at the generation model.

To study that model, the researchers subscribed to 13 generators, seven free and six paid, and built three test apps from each. Merkle-tree hashes over class hierarchies showed that only two generators produced module-dependent code, while eleven emitted monolithic boilerplate containing every available module. In those monolithic apps the configuration is either bundled or fetched over unencrypted HTTP, enabling a reconfiguration attack that lets a network attacker read or alter API keys, URLs and enabled modules. Other findings included over-privileged apps requesting 7 to 21 permissions and one generator's tracking libraries issuing more than 250 web requests in five minutes.

The speaker's conclusion is that the main problem is monolithic boilerplate generation rather than generation itself. Producing only the selected modules follows least privilege and would improve security and privacy across the ecosystem, and Android App Bundles and Instant Apps were offered as ways to split functionality. The talk ended by arguing that Apple's removal of these template apps from the iOS App Store is the wrong response, and that pressuring the few generators involved to produce safer output would have a better effect.

talks.title: T-Fuzz Fuzzing by Program Transformation: Hui Peng
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of T-Fuzz Fuzzing by Program Transformation: Hui Peng.

talks.title: SoK: "Plug & Pray" Today - Understanding USB Insecurity in Versions 1 through C
talks.teaser: Surveys forty USB attacks and thirty defenses across layers, and formally checks the USB Type-C authentication protocol.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at USB security over roughly two decades of research. The speakers reviewed 40 attacks and surveyed 30 defensive solutions, then sorted both into four layers: human, application, transport and physical. Attacks range from baiting people with dropped flash drives and abusing autorun, to firmware changes that make a drive inject keystrokes, to snooping on bus traffic and high-voltage devices that can destroy a host.

Several patterns stood out. Users and operating systems trust a USB device by default, based on its appearance. Attacks that begin at the transport or hardware layer still usually target application data or sensitive user information. Single-layer defenses fall short, and software alone cannot stop voltage-based injection unless the host controller has overcurrent and overvoltage protection. The USB implementers forum's Type-C authentication protocol was its first official response to these security problems. The team formally verified that protocol and found that a cached certificate chain allowed spoofing, and that an attacker who writes their own key and certificate into firmware could bypass it. The protocol also lacked certificate verification and accepted self-signed certificates.

The takeaway is that hardware-anchored trust helps but is not sufficient alone. Future work includes combining defenses across layers, supporting authentication in both directions so the host is checked as well, and deciding whether to reuse an existing policy language or design one for USB peripherals.

talks.title: Crowd-GPS-Sec: Leveraging Crowdsourcing to Detect and Localize GPS Spoofing Attacks
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Crowd-GPS-Sec: Leveraging Crowdsourcing to Detect and Localize GPS Spoofing Attacks.

talks.title: Blue Note: How Intentional Acoustic Interference Damages Availablity and Integrity -
talks.teaser: Acoustic attacks disrupt magnetic hard drives via head resonance and shock-sensor spoofing, causing OS failures and integrity loss.
talks.summary:
Connor Bolton presents research on turning acoustic interference into a deliberate attack on spinning magnetic hard drives. Prior incidents—from a 2008 data-center shouting video to a 2016 fire alarm knocking out bank storage—motivate two threat models: abusing built-in speakers near the drive, or placing cheap ultrasonic emitters the victim cannot hear.

The work isolates two physical mechanisms. Audible energy resonates the platter and read/write head, pushing positioning nanometers off track until writes and then reads fail; amplitude and frequency matter sharply, with resonant peaks far more damaging than others. Ultrasonic energy instead fakes the drive’s drop-protection shock sensor, triggering a binary decision to park the head and killing throughput abruptly. Demonstrations trace fallout up the stack: surveillance DVRs buffer seconds of video in RAM before losing footage, sustained I/O delays trip driver timeouts that persist after the sound stops, Linux queries return implausible capacity figures, and Windows can crash—including from attack audio played through a laptop’s own speakers via a web page.

Passive shielding proves awkward because low frequencies bend around foam and full encapsulation raises heat problems. The proposed fix adds firmware-side feedback that anticipates periodic acoustic displacement and nudges the head to stay within read/write thresholds, recoverable as an update suited to legacy disks still common in safety-critical settings.

talks.title: Speechless: Analyzing the Threat to Speech Privacy from Smartphone Motion Sensors
talks.teaser: Tests whether smartphone gyroscopes and accelerometers can pick up speech, finding leakage only from loud sources on shared surfaces.
talks.summary:
The talk examines whether smartphone motion sensors, which apps and web content can read without any permission, can pick up speech and so threaten speech privacy. The speaker notes earlier work that used these sensors to infer keystrokes and driving routes, and that gyroscopes or accelerometers have recovered some speech traits. Press coverage framed the sensors as eavesdropping microphones. The main limit is sampling: Android caps motion sensor output near 200 Hz, far below the rate needed to capture speech as a microphone does.

The study builds a threat model across audio source, propagation medium and loudness. Sources included external loudspeakers, vehicle speakers, laptop and phone speakers, and live human speakers, with the phone placed on the same surface, a different surface, or reached only through air. Using single-word recordings from a digit corpus, the researchers compared frequency spectra and time-domain peak ranges with and without speech. A loudspeaker on the same surface produced a clear effect on both sensors, most visible on the accelerometer, while a different surface produced none. Laptop speakers caused only minimal accelerometer change, and normal or loud live speech into a phone lying on a table showed no detectable difference.

The takeaway is that the effect appears to come from vibrations travelling through a shared surface rather than from airborne speech, so the threat is confined to restricted settings and does not extend to ordinary phone conversations. The accelerometer seemed more sensitive than the gyroscope. Future work includes measuring surface vibrations with a laser Doppler vibrometer and considering attackers who can bypass the operating system's sampling limit.

talks.title: The Cards Aren't Alright: Detecting Counterfeit Gift Cards Using Encoding Jitter
talks.teaser: The presentation shows how encoding jitter distinguishes cloned gift cards from factory-issued ones using cheap hardware.
talks.summary:
Gift card fraud often ends with stolen track data rewritten onto blank magnetic cards using inexpensive encoders that mimic legitimate factory gear. The speaker outlines how frequency/double-frequency encoding embeds clock and data on the stripe, and how factory lines use precise linear optical positioning while handheld writers rely on lower-resolution rotary encoders and uneven manual swipes.

At the University of Florida, researchers imaged cloned versus authentic stripes with a quantitative magnetic microscope, then built a commodity reader tied to audio gear to record waveforms and compute jitter variance from peak spacing. After discarding the first tenth of each swipe, they tested hundreds of Walmart gift cards and clones across high and low coercivity stocks, reporting roughly 98.5–99.9% separation on high-coercivity media and somewhat lower but still strong results on low coercivity. A smaller study on worn credit and debit cards supported the same signal, with majority voting across repeated swipes improving performance.

Practitioners can treat elevated jitter variance as a fraud flag alongside existing checkout risk signals rather than a sole decline rule. The talk also notes that affordable motorized encoders do not erase cloning artifacts and that chip-based gift cards raise cost and deployment barriers, while urging integration into payment terminals and broader card studies with industry partners.

talks.title: Double-efficient zkSNARKs Without Trusted Setup
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Double-efficient zkSNARKs Without Trusted Setup.

talks.title: vRAM: Faster Verifiable RAM With Program-Independent Preprocessing
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding vRAM: Faster Verifiable RAM With Program-Independent Preprocessing.

talks.title: xJsnark: A Framework for Efficient Verifiable Computation
talks.teaser: Presents a framework that compiles high-level code into efficient zk-SNARK circuits, automating field arithmetic and memory choices.
talks.summary:
Verifiable computation lets a client hand work to an untrusted party and check a short proof of the result. Building these proofs depends on compiling a program into arithmetic circuits, and the cost model is unusual: multiplying circuit values is far pricier than multiplying by constants, and bitwise operations are expensive. Existing high-level compilers often produce larger circuits than hand-built ones and leave bit-width, overflow and reduction decisions to the programmer, while low-level libraries require manual gadget design.

xJsnark is presented as a Java extension on the JetBrains MPS platform that adds parameterized native and non-native types, so the programmer picks field sizes while the tool handles chunking, subtraction, division and reduction. Its backend adds integer, read-only memory and polynomial minimization optimizations. For lookups with secret indices into constant tables, a square-root partitioning scheme that uses cheap constant multiplication and prover-supplied witnesses is said to beat linear scans, permutation networks and Merkle trees on small memories. External code blocks let programmers use prover witnesses, such as a sort verified by a permutation check.

Benchmarks on SHA-256, RSA and AES yield smaller circuits than earlier compilers, with SHA-256 and RSA matching hand-written versions. The sorting example gains orders of magnitude from the permutation check, and a Zerocash-style application reaches the performance of a manual implementation. The main limitations are the need to learn the new environment and the lack of built-in hard-coded gadgets. Future work covers more front-ends, backends and automated checks for missing constraints.

talks.title: Mobile Application Web API Reconnaissance
talks.teaser: Shows how mismatched input checks between Android apps and their web APIs let attackers send requests servers should reject.
talks.summary: Abner Mendoza presents WarDroid, which slices Android apps for HTTP templates, mutates parameters beyond client checks, and flags servers that accept illegal transfers, SQLi logins, or negative Shopify cart prices. Ten-thousand-app evaluation found millions of users exposed when server validation lagged the mobile client.

talks.title: A Formal Treatment of Accountable Proxying over TLS
talks.teaser: Presents a provably secure design that makes TLS middleboxes visible and accountable, and exposes flaws in mcTLS.
talks.summary:
TLS was designed as an end-to-end protocol, so middleboxes such as parental filters or web application firewalls must run their own handshakes with each side and are usually invisible to at least one endpoint. The talk examines accountable proxying, starting with mcTLS from 2015, which made middleboxes visible and gave them fine-grained read or write access to HTTP contexts. The authors show that mcTLS omits finished messages, so a network attacker can make a middlebox believe it serves content for one origin while the content actually comes from an attacker's server.

The authors then propose a generic, modular design that works with any authenticated key exchange that can export keys, with TLS 1.3 as an example. Independent handshakes run between the client, each middlebox and the server, and exported keys produce binders that tie the sessions together. Endpoints exchange these binders with the proxy configuration and permissions over encrypted messages, then derive access keys per HTTP context so read-only middleboxes receive only read keys. The security model adds configuration soundness, and proofs show that a network adversary cannot forge the configuration and that middleboxes can detect malicious endpoints.

Read-only middleboxes are shown to be harmless, while read-write middleboxes are not guaranteed to be. A prototype with TLS 1.3 and one middlebox showed some performance degradation. The takeaway is that accountable proxying is hard to achieve, the guarantees are modest, and a practitioner should place the most sensitive middlebox closest to the server and expect efficiency costs.

talks.title: Enumerating Active IPv6 Hosts for Large-scale Security Scans via DNSSEC-signed Reverse Zones
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Enumerating Active IPv6 Hosts for Large-scale Security Scans via DNSSEC-signed Reverse Zones.

talks.title: Tracking Certificate Misissuance in the Wild
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Tracking Certificate Misissuance in the Wild.

talks.title: Angora: Efficient Fuzzing by Principled Search
talks.teaser: Presents Angora, a fuzzer that uses gradient descent to solve path constraints and reach deeper program branches.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses a limit of coverage-guided fuzzing: random mutation of inputs struggles to pass path constraints, such as checks on multi-byte values or a minimum input length. Angora, the tool presented, instruments a program to track branch coverage and uses taint tracking to find which input bytes influence each branch predicate. It then treats the predicate as a black-box function of those bytes, so the input can be adjusted toward the value that satisfies the branch.

Solving works by minimizing the distance to the required condition with gradient descent. The program has no analytical form, so the gradient is estimated numerically by running the program on the original input and again on a slightly perturbed one. Angora also infers the minimal input length a path needs and treats multi-byte values as single arguments. In the evaluation on LAVA-M and open-source programs, it found more unique crashes and covered more branches than the compared fuzzers, and it found all bugs in one LAVA-M program within ten minutes. Some bugs behind nested conditionals were still missed.

The closing summary listed four key components: taint tracking, gradient-based constraint solving, input length and type inference, and the value of exploration alongside solving. In questions, the speaker noted that the gradient approach does not apply to non-numeric operations, where the tool falls back to random mutation. Practitioners get a view of how combining taint tracking, numerical optimization and mutation can reach program paths that mutation alone cannot.

talks.title: Precise and Scalable Detection of Double-Fetch Bugs in OS Kernels
talks.teaser: Presents a way to find double-fetch bugs in OS kernels with static analysis and symbolic checking, cutting manual review.
talks.summary:
Double-fetch bugs happen when kernel code reads the same user-space value more than once, and another thread can change that value between the reads. The talk explains why this pattern is common: kernel developers often fetch a size or header from user memory, validate it, then fetch the full structure again, which leaves a window for the value to change. Examples include a size-check pattern, an ioctl path where the two fetches end up using different device numbers, and a protocol version check that can be altered after it passes. Earlier detection work relied on static analysis that flagged many candidate pairs, each needing manual verification.

The approach combines static analysis with symbolic checking. Fetch pairs are found bottom-up, starting from each copy-from-user call and following reaching definitions, and inlining functions that hide a fetch. A double fetch is defined as two overlapping fetch regions where a control or data dependence on an overlapping value cannot be shown to hold after the second fetch. Each code path is then checked symbolically. The speaker walked through a small example in which a size variable is fetched twice and no constraint proves the two values match. Across Linux, Wine and FreeBSD, the work reported 24 bugs, with some patched, others pending review, and some marked as won't fix.

For practitioners, the talk covers the mitigation patterns the authors used: overwriting the second fetch with the first value, aborting if the user-supplied data changed, switching to incremental fetches, or using a single large fetch. No generic fix emerged, and some cases need significant refactoring or interface changes. Stated limitations include path explosion, loop unrolling done only once, and imprecise pointer-to-object mapping. The speaker suggested that the formal modeling approach could extend to hypervisors and trusted computing bases, where privilege boundaries are similarly clear.

talks.title: Tracking Ransomware End-to-end
talks.teaser: Estimates ransomware revenue from Bitcoin blockchain data and flags exchanges and affiliates as possible takedown choke points.
talks.summary:
Ransomware encrypts a victim's files and demands Bitcoin, usually paid to a wallet address unique to each victim. This talk asks how much revenue ransomware families earn and whether their operations can be disrupted. It walks through a typical infection, from distribution and encryption to the ransom note, the victim buying Bitcoin on an exchange and paying.

Because payments are not labeled, the method starts with known paying victims and follows co-spent wallet addresses that likely share an owner. Payment amounts matching a family's fixed ransom increments are counted as ransom. For one family without reported victims, the researchers paid about ten dollars to their own infected sandbox to start the money flow. Across ten families, the estimate is at least 16 million dollars over two years, about 90 percent of it from two families. Tracing outgoing coins showed roughly 40 percent of one family's revenue going to a single exchange, which law enforcement has since seized.

A second part reverse engineers the command-and-control protocol of another family, whose infected machines send traffic to many IP addresses. Listening on one address for two weeks showed that about three percent of affiliates were responsible for half of the infected addresses. Audience questions raised that the total is a lower bound, since some payments were excluded, and that search trends and binary sightings suggest missed wallets. The takeaway is that exchanges, affiliates and network operators could be useful points to disrupt ransomware.

talks.title: Surveylance: Automatically Detecting Online Survey Scams
talks.teaser: Describes an automated pipeline that crawls, classifies, and completes online survey scams to map their ecosystem at scale.
talks.summary:
Online survey scams lure people who search for free or discounted digital goods through malicious ads and risky sites into gateway pages, then survey publishers, before denying the promised content. Victims often install unwanted software, open malicious documents, or hand over personal or workplace details. The speaker argues this human-centered ecosystem is serious yet understudied compared with machine-targeted web attacks, with prior work mostly ad hoc rather than systematic.

The Surveylance framework combines a Chromium-based crawler, a classifier using fourteen features across three categories, and a browser extension that auto-fills surveys from a catalog to observe post-submit behavior with limited manual effort. Seeding uses deception-oriented keywords from Google Trends and builds on prior malvertising research. Early reachable gateways numbered in the hundreds even with safe browsing enabled; larger runs reported on the order of fifty-five thousand gateways leading to hundreds of thousands of publishers and more than one hundred thirty thousand completed surveys. Roughly forty-five percent of gateways traced back to entry points reachable from Alexa top thirty thousand sites. After submission, outcomes span reward phishing, fake player updates, and downloads; unwanted programs dominated analyzed cases at about forty-two percent, and a fifth of collected binaries were new to VirusTotal.

Practitioners should treat survey funnels as a distinct malvertising and social-engineering channel that complements classical ad malware paths, and that benefits from automated gateway detection and blacklisting. CAPTCHAs blocked full automation in some campaigns, and survey answers may be harvested even when no malware is served.

talks.title: Impossibility of Precise and Sound Termination-Sensitive Security Enforcements
talks.teaser: Shows secure multi-execution falls short for termination-sensitive non-interference and proves no sound, precise enforcer exists.
talks.summary:
The talk tackles enforcing confidentiality in programs where termination itself can leak secret information. Using a simple deterministic imperative language with input and output channels, the speaker defines termination-sensitive non-interference, where confidential inputs must not change whether a low-security observer sees a program terminate. A small example that loops forever on a confidential input value shows how the policy can be violated.

The speaker then examines secure multi-execution, a mechanism from 2010 that runs one copy of the program per security level and orders those copies with a low-priority scheduler. An example shows that this scheme can terminate on one input and diverge on another, so it does not enforce the policy soundly and precisely. The main result is an impossibility proof: no sound and precise enforcement mechanism exists for termination-sensitive non-interference. The argument is first made in a simpler setting of partial functions over natural numbers, where the policy concerns whether programs diverge on confidential input, and then carried over to the input-output language.

The closing section turns to a weaker policy, indirect termination-sensitive non-interference, in which the observer cannot directly see termination. The speaker reports that secure multi-execution with a fair scheduler can enforce this policy soundly and precisely, while the low-priority scheduler version does so only when the security lattice is totally ordered. The takeaway is that termination behaviour has to be treated as part of the policy. In the question round, the speaker said related progress-sensitive work is similar in spirit, differing mainly in whether it considers finite or infinite traces.

talks.title: Hackers vs. Testers: A Comparison of Software Vulnerability Discovery Processes
talks.teaser: Compares how professional testers and bug bounty hackers find software vulnerabilities, and what each group can learn from the other.
talks.summary:
Dana presents a study of how professional software testers and external white hat hackers search for vulnerabilities. The problem is that expert reviews tend to happen late in development, when fixes are costlier, and that a small pool of experts brings limited perspectives and often produces noisy bug bounty reports. The team interviewed 10 testers and 15 hackers, recruited through 106 contacted organizations, and used task analysis to map each participant's discovery process along with the tools, skills and communities involved.

Both groups followed a similar six-step process: gathering information about the program, building a mental model of how it works, mapping its attack surface, exploring it with varied inputs, recognizing a likely vulnerability largely through intuition, and then reporting it in a way that convinces developers to act. The two populations differed mainly in two factors. Hackers had far more discovery experience, having examined many programs, taken part in many exercises and read reports from many sources, which gave them broader ideas and recognizable patterns. Testers had more access to the development process, including internal documentation and direct contact with developers. That access gave them a head start on understanding the system, but it could also carry over flawed assumptions.

The talk closes with recommendations. To build testers' experience, Dana suggests training in their own codebase, such as exercises that use past fixes from the company's diffs. To strengthen hackers' relationships with developers, companies could assign a single point of contact who builds shared language with external reviewers. Dana also notes that a mix of insiders and outsiders appears most useful.

talks.title: AI2: Safety and Robustness Certification of Neural Networks
talks.teaser: Shows how abstract interpretation proves neural networks stay stable under small input changes, scaling past SMT solvers.
talks.summary:
Neural networks often change their output when an input image is altered slightly, as the road sign and panda examples in the talk illustrate. Heuristic defenses improve robustness only a little, and far less work has tried to prove that a network behaves correctly around a given input. The speaker presents an automated method that aims to show that no such robustness violations exist within a region around a specific image, and that scales to realistic networks.

The method uses abstract interpretation, a technique that over-approximates what a program can do. Each abstract element stands for a set of possible values, and abstract transformers propagate these sets through the network. The speaker compared box, zonotope and polyhedra domains, and the polyhedra domain was too slow to finish. Transformers were defined for fully connected, convolutional and max pooling layers, while ReLU is handled by splitting the abstract element on each neuron's sign. The result is sound but incomplete, so some properties that actually hold may not be proven.

On a convolutional network, the zonotope-based version with up to 64 zonotopes verified more properties than an SMT-based baseline within a one-hour timeout, and the SMT approach showed steep growth in running time. The implementation began on the Apron library and later moved to an in-house library. The speaker closed with ongoing work on more activation functions, specialized transformers, and using abstract interpretation during training.

talks.title: Stealing Hyperparameters in Machine Learning

talks.title: A Machine Learning Approach to Prevent Malicious Calls Over Telephony Networks
talks.teaser: Shows how client-side call labels and a machine learning model can block malicious calls without network data.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses telephony spam and scam calls, which the speaker says cause large financial losses worldwide. Much prior work on voice-over-IP services depended on network infrastructure data, which is not available on a traditional telephony network. The proposed approach is client-side: a mobile app called TouchPal lets users label calls as malicious or benign, and a number tagged by more than a threshold of users goes onto a blacklist. That simple method lets many unwanted calls through before it triggers, so the team set out to predict malicious calls earlier with machine learning.

The team collected call logs over three months in 2016 in China, comprising more than nine billion records. A measurement study showed that malicious call volume dropped on holidays and weekends and followed a work-hours pattern, and that call-count distributions differed across the categories. From these results the speaker described 29 features covering the current call and historic records for the same number. These included static attributes and features relating calls to each other, such as the time gap between consecutive calls and whether a call is a redial. Several models were compared by AUC, with random forest performing best, and the results held on data from a different province.

To measure early detection, the authors introduced a metric counting how many calls must be seen before a number can be predicted malicious while keeping benign precision high. At a benign precision of 0.9999, the average was about three to four calls, against the 30 to 100 unblocked calls under the blacklist threshold, which the speaker described as a reduction of over 90%. An ablation analysis showed that the ten most-used features performed close to the full set. The takeaway is that call-log behaviour alone can support an effective client-side blocker without network data, while caller ID spoofing was left as future work.
