talks.title: SymCerts: Practical Symbolic Execution For Exposing Noncompliance in X.509 Certificate Validation
talks.teaser: Uses symbolic execution to find certificate validation flaws in small TLS libraries, such as misread UTC years.
talks.summary:
Certificate chain validation in TLS requires checking signatures, names, validity periods and extensions, and the speaker argues that small C libraries used on IoT devices and increasingly in desktop apps may depart from RFC 5280. The proposed white-box approach keeps tag and length fields concrete while making certificate fields and extensions symbolic. Each library's validation code is symbolically executed to capture the certificates it accepts and rejects, and pairwise comparisons with an SMT solver surface certificates that one library accepts while another rejects.

Across nine implementations from four library families, the team reports 48 instances of non-compliance. One library reads two-digit UTC years with a boundary that pushes 1995 expiry dates to 2095. Another compares extended key usage by summing encoded bytes rather than matching identifiers exactly, so unrelated values can collide. Some libraries ignore country, state and locality when matching names, one sanity check can never reject input because its conditions are unsatisfiable, and a missing break in the extension parser causes some extensions to be handled wrongly. A reversed comparison in one library rejects valid certificates at the edge of their validity period, and some libraries do not check path length constraints at all.

The scope is certificate semantics rather than the full handshake, and small libraries were chosen partly because new ones keep appearing. For app developers, the practical advice is to move to newer versions of the TLS libraries they embed, since those usually carry more bug fixes and stricter validation logic.

talks.title: HVLearn: Automated Black-box Analysis of Hostname Verification in SSL/TLS Implementations
talks.teaser: Shows an automated black-box method that learns how TLS libraries match hostnames to certificates and flags spec violations.
talks.summary:
Hostname verification is the step where a TLS client confirms that the name it requested matches the server's certificate. Matching draws on the common name and subject alternative name fields, and each identifier type, such as DNS names, IP addresses and emails, has its own rules for wildcards, internationalized names and case. The specification leaves several cases unclear, and implementations span many languages, so manual testing scales poorly.

The speaker presented HVLearn, a black-box framework that pairs automata learning with differential testing. An active learner infers an automaton of the host names each implementation accepts for a certificate, using a reduced set of representative characters to limit queries. Comparing the learned models exposes names that one implementation accepts and another rejects. Against random black-box testing and grey-box fuzzing, the learner reached higher code coverage, taking up to five minutes per certificate.

The team reported RFC violations and inconsistencies across several libraries and applications. Examples included checking the common name before the subject alternative name even when an IP address was present, allowing wildcards in internationalized domain names, and inconsistent case sensitivity for domain names and email local parts. Developers were notified and some have shipped fixes. The approach is language independent and could extend to other pattern-style checks, such as certificate issuance.

talks.title: CRLite: A Scalable System for Pushing All TLS Revocations to All Browsers
talks.teaser: Presents CRLite, which pushes TLS revocation status for all certificates to browsers using filter cascades instead of per-site checks.
talks.summary:
The talk opens with the history of TLS certificate revocation. Certificate revocation lists can be tens of megabytes, so browsers cannot fetch one on every handshake, while OCSP adds latency and tells certificate authorities which sites a browser visits. OCSP stapling is easy for a network attacker to strip and was used by only a small share of certificates in 2016. Browser-maintained lists such as Chrome's CRLSet and Mozilla's PRL cover only a few high-priority revocations, so they are incomplete and not auditable.

The core of the talk is CRLite, which ships revocation status for all certificates to clients so that checks happen locally and fail closed without contacting authorities. A plain Bloom filter yields false positives that could block legitimate sites. Because certificate transparency logs and scans now provide nearly every valid certificate, the presenters can compute every false positive in advance and store them in a cascade of alternating filters. Lookups need at most about 20 hashes. The January 2017 build covered 43 million certificates in roughly 10 megabytes, and daily updates, made by XORing yesterday's cascade with today's and compressing the result, average about 580 kilobytes.

The talk closes with the audit log of valid certificates and signed CRL and OCSP responses, which lets third parties verify the filters and rebuild them. A back-end pipeline and a Firefox prototype exist, though Firefox's deprecation of the needed API limits the add-on. In questions, the presenter explained that clients who miss updates can receive a combined diff, and that periodic resizing is needed because new certificate issuance outpaces revocations.

talks.title: Catena: Efficient Non-equivocation via Bitcoin
talks.teaser: Explains how chaining Bitcoin transactions makes a published log hard to equivocate, with cheap client verification.
talks.summary:
Public key directories, certificate logs and software transparency systems publish a digest at each time period. The problem is equivocation: a malicious server can show different digests to different users, so an impersonation can go unnoticed, because the victims cannot compare their views without a secure channel. Earlier Bitcoin-based logs embedded statements in transactions without constraining how those transactions relate, so verifying them meant downloading full blocks.

The talk presents Catena, which relies on Bitcoin's rule against double spending. Each new statement sits in a transaction that spends the output of the previous one, so two conflicting statements would require a double spend that miners prevent. A client only needs the log's genesis transaction, the 80-byte block headers it checks for proof of work, and a Merkle proof for each statement, about 600 bytes per statement. The speaker described a Java implementation with open-source code and covered the costs: a statement can be issued only about every ten minutes, clients wait around six confirmations, and fees had risen since the paper.

To avoid overloading the Bitcoin peer-to-peer network with client connections, the design adds a relay network that fetches block headers and serves them to clients. A compromised relay alone cannot cause equivocation, although it could make adversarial mining easier. In the Q&A, the speaker admitted that how hard Bitcoin is to fork under heavier use is an open question, and that Ethereum was set aside for its larger headers and the lack of light verification at the time. The takeaway is that public key distribution and transparency logs can gain non-equivocation at low bandwidth cost.

talks.title: Hijacking Bitcoin: Routing Attacks on Cryptocurrencies
talks.teaser: BGP hijacking can partition Bitcoin or delay block propagation, exposing the network to double-spending and denial of service.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens with well-known Internet routing hijacks against payment brands and a mining-pool theft tied to prefix manipulation, then argues that such events are routine. Analysis of six months of BGP data shows thousands of hijacks per month, mostly from misconfiguration but still capable of steering live traffic.

Despite Bitcoin’s decentralized design, mining capacity and node traffic concentrate in a handful of autonomous systems. That concentration makes two BGP-based threats practical. A partition attack advertises more-specific prefixes to pull peers apart, enabling denial of service, orphaned mining work, and double spending; the speakers estimate that splitting half of mining power needs fewer than a hundred hijacked prefixes and that diverting a test node’s traffic took under two minutes. A delay attack intercepts block announcements and alters get-data requests so victims miss new blocks—often invisibly—wasting hash power or enabling fraud; experiments show most clients sit where a single AS-level adversary could do this.

Short-term mitigations include routing-aware peer choice and anomaly monitoring on delays. Longer fixes—encrypted transport and secure routing such as BGPsec or RPKI—address different sides of the problem. The Q&A stresses that hijacks need ISP BGP access, that prefix theft happens daily at scale, and that protocol forks are not the only path to meaningful risk reduction.

talks.title: IKP: Turning a PKI Around with Decentralized Automated Incentives
talks.teaser: Presents IKP, a smart-contract platform that uses automated payouts to deter rogue TLS certificate issuance.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at misissued TLS certificates, where a compromised or misbehaving certificate authority can issue a certificate for any site and enable man-in-the-middle attacks. The speaker argues that CAs lack incentives to invest in security, and that manual reporting is so tedious that few people bother. Browsers cannot simply distrust a CA, as the Symantec case showed, because benign sites would become unreachable.

The presenters introduce IKP, where domains publish certificate policies listing the criteria their certificates must meet, and CAs sell reaction policies that pay out when an unauthorized certificate appears. CAs escrow funds, detectors who report bad certificates earn a bounty, and a refundable fee discourages spam reports. Checker and reaction programs run the logic, and threshold signatures protect policy updates.

The prototype runs as Ethereum smart contracts written in Solidity, handling SHA-256 and RSA certificates, so no central authority must be trusted. The deployment cost was about 450, with per-operation costs a small fraction of typical certificate prices of several hundred dollars. The speaker noted costs had been roughly a tenth of today's when the paper was submitted, because the Ether price had risen. Future work covers incentive analysis with mechanism design and game theory, richer policies, and external data feeds. The takeaway is that automated penalties could realign CA behavior, though deciding what counts as legitimate remains up to each domain.

talks.title: Securing Augmented Reality Output
talks.teaser: Presents Aria, an AR operating system that enforces policies to limit harmful or buggy application output.
talks.summary:
Augmented reality systems take in sensor data from the user's surroundings and draw virtual content over the physical world. That means a buggy or malicious app can hide real-world hazards such as pedestrians or road signs, or startle and disorient the user. The talk notes that prior security work has focused mostly on input privacy, leaving output largely unexamined. The speaker introduces Aria, an AR operating system built with output security as a primary goal. Instead of rectangular windows, Aria manages virtual content at the level of individual AR objects, and a trusted output module intercepts display requests and applies policies to them.

Policies are written as if-then rules: a condition, such as an object containing a pedestrian, paired with an action, such as making that object transparent. Policy mechanisms act as intrusiveness bounds, such as maximum opacity, size, or speed, so when several policies apply, Aria applies the least intrusive combination. Policies that keep triggering each other are identified as a key design challenge. The policies were adapted from automotive road-visibility guidelines and HoloLens developer guidelines, which the speaker notes are not technically enforced.

The prototype ran in Unity on a desktop across three scenes: a home, a car windshield, and an office, each with apps that behaved maliciously or buggily. Policies stopped one app's objects from occluding another app's content, removed world-locked objects, limited abrupt movement, removed ads covering pedestrians while keeping billboard ads, and kept objects from covering an exit sign. The speaker closes by pointing to future work on noisy sensor input, richer constraint solving, latency, end-user involvement, and who should be allowed to define policies.

talks.title: Norax: Enabling Execute-Only Memory for COTS Binaries on AArch64
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Norax: Enabling Execute-Only Memory for COTS Binaries on AArch64.
talks.summary: Norax rewrites commercial AArch64 binaries so text pages become execute-only, blocking dynamic memory disclosure that harvests ROP gadgets after an initial pointer leak—bringing xom-style protection to COTS without source.

talks.title: SysPal:System-guided Pattern Locks for Android
talks.teaser: Proposes Android unlock patterns that must include a few random points, and measures guessing resistance and memorability.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from the weakness of user-chosen Android unlock patterns, which earlier work showed are often predictable. It reviews attempts to fix this, such as larger grids, that still left patterns guessable, and introduces SysPal, a scheme where the system requires a small number of randomly selected points that users may place anywhere in their pattern.

The study compared the existing Android policy with three SysPal variants that mandate one, two or three points. An online study of 1,717 participants measured recall after 24 hours, and a follow-up field test had people use a screen-unlock app on their own phones for a day. Guessing resistance was estimated with a Markov model, because the collected sample was too small to analyse the full pattern space directly. The one- and two-point policies were cracked significantly less often than the original policy, while the three-point variant did not improve on it. The one- and two-point versions also showed no significant drop in recall.

The speaker noted that starting points stayed biased toward the upper-left corner, even though they were more evenly spread than before, and that mandated points were often used early in a pattern. The main takeaway is that one or two mandated points offer a practical security gain without a clear memorability cost. The Q&A raised participant drop-out between sessions, the remaining starting-point bias and alternative placement policies as open questions.

talks.title: Multi-touch Authentication Using Hand Geometry and Behavioral Information
talks.teaser: Presents a touchscreen login that combines hand geometry with behavioral traits from one multi-touch swipe.
talks.summary:
Phone and tablet unlock methods such as PINs and pattern locks are exposed to shoulder surfing and smudge attacks, fingerprints raise privacy concerns, and behavioral biometrics are hard to rely on because a person's touch changes over time. The speaker presents an authentication method for multi-touch screens in which a user performs one swipe with several fingers moving together. The method records both the hand geometry and the behavioral characteristics of the touch trace and uses them together for verification.

The data came from 161 subjects, with hand images from 144 of them, collected on one device across seven sessions spread over more than two months, with at least a week between sessions. Hand geometry features were found to be the most discriminative, and fusing them with selected behavioral features gave an EER of 5.84% with five training samples, improving to 1.88% with enough training. In the time-based evaluation, the behavioral-only features degraded over the weeks, while the combined and selected features stayed stable.

Security tests covered zero-effort attacks, smudge attacks, shoulder surfing and statistical attacks. The results indicated resilience to these threats, with the zero-effort risk rising for pairs of users with very similar hand shapes. A usability study with 158 undergraduate students compared the gesture with PINs and pattern locks, and authentication took under a second on average. The main takeaway is that pairing hand geometry with behavior can make touch-based login more stable over time.

talks.title: SoK: Exploiting Network Printers
talks.teaser: Shows how PostScript and PCL features let attackers capture print jobs, halt devices and reach stored data on network printers.
talks.summary: James Miller systematizes exploiting PostScript and PCL as Turing-complete print channels: infinite-loop DoS, factory-reset via PJL, hooking operators to alter others’ jobs, capturing spool data, and NVRAM wear on twenty printers tested with the PRET toolkit. Web attackers can POST malicious PostScript to port 9100 from browsers; EPS converters and ImageMagick thumbnails leak directory listings. He notes shared data/code paths mean anyone who can print can administer.

talks.title: IoT Goes Nuclear: Creating a Zigbee Chain Reaction
talks.teaser: Shows how a Zigbee flaw in Philips Hue bulbs lets an attacker take over lights and spread a worm between them.
talks.summary:
The talk examines Philips Hue smart lights, which communicate over the Zigbee Light Link standard inside an encrypted personal network. A proximity check is meant to stop distant attackers from taking over bulbs. The researchers found that the transaction ID in a factory reset message was compared against a stored value that defaulted to zero, so sending a zero ID switched the lamp into an older protocol mode without that check. Using a drone carrying cheap transceivers, they took over lights roughly 300 metres away.

To run code on the bulbs, they targeted the over-the-air update mechanism. Updates were encrypted with symmetric keys shared across a lamp model and held in a secure chip. Correlation power analysis revealed the CCM mode with AES, and attacking the verification step instead of the stream cipher exposed both keys. With them, the team built custom firmware, demonstrated with bulbs that kept only one light on at a time by sending multicast messages to their neighbours.

The speakers estimated that roughly 15,000 randomly placed lights could let a worm spread across a city like Paris, and listed possible effects such as blackouts and Wi-Fi jamming. Philips fixed the protocol bug through the same update mechanism, but the update process remained vulnerable. The speakers argued that ad hoc IoT networks form an unmonitored communication medium that needs protection, and that threat models should include physical key extraction.

talks.title: How They Did It: An Analysis of Emission Defeat Devices in Modern Automobiles
talks.teaser: Analyzes software defeat devices in diesel ECUs and argues emissions compliance needs firmware verification, not chassis dyno tests alone.
talks.summary:
The presentation reframes Dieselgate through system security: modern diesel engines rely on exhaust aftertreatment (oxidation catalysts, particulate and NOx storage filters, EGR, optional SCR) managed by an engine control unit under tight trade-offs between NOx, soot, filter lifetime, and urea refill intervals. Because regulators use standardized, publicly known driving cycles on chassis dynamometers, manufacturers can tune software to recognize those profiles.

For Volkswagen’s acoustic or profile-check logic, the ECU compares engine parameters such as time since start and distance traveled against published upper and lower curves; inside the matched “white” interval the car runs in a compliant tuning mode, while outside it does not. The speakers built a Pië and IDA Pro–based analyzer that lifts Bosch EDC7 firmware to SSA and reports which test cycles each image targets, processing over 900 firmware images from 2009–2016 in minutes per run and finding more than 300 that detect at least one cycle. A Fiat 500x case study shows parallel “homologation” versus “wheel driving” NSC regeneration paths, with only the more polluting path active after 1,600 seconds—aligned with typical test duration.

Portable on-road emissions measurement still leaves timer-based or environmental cheats possible. The takeaway is that compliance is increasingly a software verification problem: large-scale firmware analysis can screen ECU images faster than repeated physical tests, and black-box dyno testing alone cannot surface hidden dual-mode engine logic.

talks.title: An Experimental Security Analysis of an Industrial Robot Controller
talks.teaser: Shows how an industrial robot controller can be manipulated to skew accuracy, misreport safety state and corrupt control parameters.
talks.summary:
Industrial robots are multi-axis mechanical arms driven by a controller and programmed through a handheld teach pendant, and many are reachable over networks. The talk opens with a survey of robot users that found weak access control, direct internet exposure and rare vulnerability assessments. Starting from the accuracy, safety and integrity requirements of these robots, the speakers define robot-specific attacks, including tampering with control loop and calibration parameters, altering production logic, and falsifying the robot state shown to operators.

For a case study, the team examined an ABB IRC5 controller and its teach pendant, which runs Windows CE. They found several vulnerabilities, including buffer overflows that lead to remote code execution and authentication bypasses. Chained together, these let them disable user access control, upload a malicious DLL to the pendant, and reboot into a state where the pendant can command the controller. Three proof-of-concept attacks followed: an accuracy violation in which tuned parameters made a straight-line path drift by a few millimetres, a safety violation in which the pendant showed manual mode while the arm ran automatically with motors on, and an integrity attack that would make the arm collapse on itself. The integrity attack was verified with robotics experts rather than run on hardware, for cost and safety reasons.

The speakers conclude that standards should address active attackers, not only accidental safety failures, and that real-time operating systems need attacker detection and hardening. They also warn that collaborative robots, whose safety depends on software rather than physical cages, will need further security work.

talks.title: SoK: Cryptographically Protected Database Search
talks.teaser: A systematization maps leakage types, attack models, and scheme classes for encrypted database search at scale.
talks.summary:
Organizations depend on searchable data, yet storing and querying it exposes breach risk that encryption at rest or in transit does not fully address when the database server itself must remain untrusted. The presentation reframes cryptographically protected search—covering symmetric searchable encryption and property-preserving schemes—as a deliberate trade between functionality and compromise risk, noting wide research, product, and government interest without treating popularity alone as rigor.

Because efficient schemes necessarily leak, the speakers argue prior work lacked comparable security statements. They introduce a shared leakage vocabulary—structure, identifiers, predicates, ordering, and full data revelation—plus when leakage appears at initialization versus per query. A hospital-style toy attack shows how query patterns and return counts, combined with public statistics, can recover field values; follow-on work exploits correlations across fields. Legacy wrappers atop existing engines, custom rebuilt stores, and oblivious multi-server designs differ in performance, when they leak, and fit for high-entropy sparse data versus queries returning large fractions of the database.

On utility, instrumentation and terabyte-scale benchmarks separate performance from expressiveness. Rather than full SQL, coverage is judged against union, difference, join, projection, and selection as combinable base queries—with join as a notable gap—while warning the field lags several database paradigm shifts. Practitioners should treat commercial legacy products as initialization-heavy leakers, match scheme class to data entropy and query selectivity, and pursue cross-paradigm base-query efficiency instead of restarting crypto for each new datastore model.

talks.title: Comparing the Usability of Cryptographic APIs
talks.teaser: Tests whether usability-focused Python cryptography libraries lead to more secure code in an online developer study.
talks.summary: Yasemin Acar reports a 256-participant online study where Python developers implemented symmetric and asymmetric crypto tasks with PyCrypto, M2Crypto, cryptography.io, pyca/nacl, and keyczar. Manual grading shows certificate validation and secure key storage fail most often; simplifying APIs does not guarantee usable or secure code—keyczar scored worst on task success yet best on security when experts read source. Documentation quality and full feature coverage matter more than stripping options; 20% of working submissions were believed secure when they were not.

talks.title: Obstacles to the Adoption of Secure Communication Tools
talks.teaser: Presents an interview study explaining why people adopt or abandon secure messaging apps.
talks.summary:
The talk examines why people do not adopt secure communication tools, despite expert advocacy and built-in features such as WhatsApp's end-to-end encryption. The researchers interviewed 60 people recruited around University College London, starting with 10 unstructured interviews that shaped a script for 50 semi-structured sessions averaging 90 minutes. Each session covered tool choice, contacts, shared information, perceived protection and adversaries, and reasons for quitting an app.

Usability was not the main barrier, as people kept using apps despite complaints. Fragmented user bases made it hard to reach all contacts, and Apple-only tools such as iMessage and FaceTime were avoided for lacking cross-platform support, even when seen as secure. Missing features also drove choices: Telegram's secret chats do not support groups, so most participants used the default mode. Poor call quality was read as a sign an app was insecure, and many trusted phone calls over texts. Some assumed powerful adversaries could defeat any tool because providers know the scheme. When ranking apps, people relied on popularity and service quality rather than security, and they did not grasp the EFF scorecard's terms such as forward secrecy.

The authors recommend defining utility for secure tools and improving apps that already have mainstream users rather than launching new ones. They also suggest cutting latency and dropped packets, improving interface design, and running public campaigns to correct misconceptions about what encryption can protect against.

talks.title: SoK: Science, Security, and the Elusive Goal of Security as a Scientific Pursuit
talks.teaser: Examines what the scientific method means for security, and why untested assumptions undermine many security claims.
talks.summary:
The talk surveys the push to make security research more scientific, noting interest from funding agencies and pessimistic remarks from senior figures about whether the field is making progress. Rather than deciding which work counts as science, the speaker looks at how other disciplines define the term, drawing on philosophy of science. The central criterion is falsifiability: a claim should be testable against observation and refutable by some conceivable result.

The speaker separates deductive statements, which follow from axioms, from inductive statements about the real world. A proof about a formal model says nothing certain about a deployed system, because whether the system satisfies the model's assumptions is an empirical question. The speaker illustrates this with decades-old password composition rules, which were adopted on untested assumptions and only checked much later, and with the advice to change passwords every 90 days. For the latter, the speaker asks what evidence would refute the claim, arguing that many security claims hide implicit assumptions that should be listed explicitly and tested.

In the question round, the speaker accepted that measurement is hard when user behavior and conditions shift, but argued that this difficulty does not justify replacing observation with invented assumptions about attackers, and that studies should be repeated as often as needed. A second question on engineering led to the view that building systems is not enough without a feedback mechanism, such as real-world use, that separates sound practices from unsound ones. The takeaway is that security claims should be stated precisely and tested against evidence.

talks.title: Is Interaction Necessary for Distributed Private Learning?
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Is Interaction Necessary for Distributed Private Learning?.
talks.summary: Pradeep Mitra presents distributed private learning with local differential privacy: devices randomize outputs before a server trains classifiers, and fully parallel one-round protocols exist for low-dimensional statistics via a median-reduction trick. For higher-dimensional models, prior adaptive algorithms need as many interaction rounds as devices; their work cuts adaptive rounds to logarithmic while still touching each device once, yet impossibility arguments show non-interactive schemes cannot reach minimally accurate high-dimensional models without adaptivity. He cites Apple emoji-frequency and Google RAPPOR deployments as motivation.

talks.title: SecureML: A System for Scalable Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning
talks.teaser: Shows how linear and logistic regression can be trained on data split between two servers without revealing the inputs.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses how companies can train machine learning models on sensitive user data without seeing that data. Each user splits their data into shares and sends one share to each of two non-colluding servers, so neither server alone learns the inputs. The servers then run a two-party secure computation to produce the model, and users can go offline after submitting their data.

The work proposes protocols for linear regression, logistic regression and neural networks under this model. A key obstacle is that secret sharing works over integers, while regression needs decimal arithmetic. The authors keep decimal multiplication accurate with a truncation step that still works on shared values, adding only a tiny error in the last decimal place. For logistic regression, a simpler bounded activation replaces a costly polynomial approximation of the sigmoid and is cheap to evaluate with garbled circuits.

Experiments on a LAN and a wide-area link between US coasts show offline precomputation as the main cost. With 100,000 records and 500 features, the online phase took about 1.4 seconds on the LAN. Logistic regression was reported to scale to a million records with 5,000 features, and a neural network with two hidden layers of 128 neurons took about 25,000 seconds end to end on the LAN. The takeaway is that combining these techniques makes privacy-preserving training orders of magnitude faster than prior work.

talks.title: Caradoc: a Pragmatic Approach to PDF Parsing and Validation
talks.teaser: A whitelist PDF validator uses formal grammar, type inference, and graph checks to reject ambiguous or malicious document structures.
talks.summary:
Portable Document Format files underpin contracts and tax workflows, yet reader implementations disagree on syntax and semantics. The presenter notes more than five hundred Adobe Reader vulnerabilities over seventeen years, polymorphic files that open differently as PDFs or archives, and outline loops that hang or crash Foxit, Adobe, and Poppler while other tools detect or mishandle the same bytes.

The Caradoc approach rejects blacklist-only malware scanning in favor of accepting only documents that pass layered checks: a BNF formalization of PDF syntax, restrictions that drop incremental updates and linearization, semantic type inference from the trailer through catalogs and page trees, and graph verification to forbid destructive loops. A strict parser, relaxed normalizer, and cleaning step were tested on ten thousand web-sampled files; fourteen percent passed strict parsing initially, and normalization roughly tripled fully type-checked acceptance while surfacing real-world typos parsers had silently corrected.

Live demos showed cyclic outlines repeating pages or crashing readers and polymorphic payloads rendering vendor-specific text from one file. Practitioners gain a concrete whitelist validation pipeline, identifiable parser discrepancy risks, and a roadmap to extend types, compression filters, and graphics grammars before deployment.

talks.title: In Search Of Shotgun Parsers In Android Applications
talks.teaser: Proposes a definition of the shotgun parser anti-pattern and measures how far untrusted input spreads through Android apps.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces a stricter definition of the "shotgun parser" anti-pattern, where untrusted input is used while it is still being validated, so that it can be detected with automated static analysis. The definition rests on three properties: how far tainted data spreads relative to the size of the control flow graph, whether input is used before full recognition, and how many program state variables become tainted.

The research applied the first property to Android apps. The team modified FlowDroid to record the path length of each taint source and analysed 56 apps from 12 Google Play categories. Normalised path length histograms showed a common shape, with many short paths where data is used immediately and a long tail of data that travels through a large part of the graph. In one comic reader app, two clusters of several thousand paths spread over about 80 percent of the graph diameter, and the speaker pointed to these as the places to focus on the other two properties.

The speaker then compared three other cases. In ImageMagick, raw arguments passed through about seven function calls and were used in five functions before parsing, and the sanitising step only checked printable ASCII, which let shellcode through. Heartbleed was described as a lack of length validation rather than intermixed use and validation. The Mongrel HTTP request parser was presented as a good example, with a finite state machine that rejects input outside its grammar. The work is an early foundation, limited by a one-semester timeline and a small sample, with future goals of automating recognition checks and classifying known vulnerabilities.

talks.title: An Incremental Learner for Language-Based Anomaly Detection in XML
talks.teaser: Shows how an incremental automata learner flags XML signature wrapping attacks that standard schema validation misses.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses XML-based web service protocols, where digital signatures in WS-Security headers can be abused through signature wrapping attacks. The speaker recalls that an earlier analysis found many implementations vulnerable, and explains that business logic often selects the signed body in ways that are hard to pin down. The problem is framed as learning which XML documents an interface should accept, without relying on hand-written schemas.

The approach represents the accepted language as a data-typed automaton and learns it incrementally from training documents. States are named from the document prefix, the typing context and the left siblings, and two states are merged when they are locally the same under specified parameters. Each time the learner revises its model, this is counted as a mind change, and the speaker showed that many changes happen early and then taper off. If the learner has absorbed an attack by mistake, the attack can be simulated and its edges decremented, with a trim step dropping edges whose counts reach zero. On one signature wrapping dataset, the learner usually reached a usable representation after only a few examples.

Across the experiments, the learned model detected all of the signature wrapping attacks, while traditional schema validation detected none of them because of protocol extensions. The method also produced some false positives and false negatives tied to data types. The speaker positions it as a protection layer for XML exchanges, particularly in systems built from composed schemas, and mentions an XML firewall for web services that is in development. The main takeaway is that automata learning can supply a practical, data-driven check on XML messages where fixed schemas fall short.

talks.title: A Posteriori Taint-tracking for Demonstrating Non-interference in Expressive Low-level Languages
talks.teaser: Shows how taint tracking inside an abstract interpreter can prove that secrets do not leak in Android bytecode.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how to prove that sensitive data, such as GPS coordinates or passwords, cannot flow to observable outputs in Android apps. The analysis works on Dalvik bytecode, a low-level language with functions and exceptions, and aims to cover every possible execution rather than a single run. The starting point is classic taint-flow tracking, which is dynamic, and the speaker explains why it was moved into a static setting by running it inside an abstract interpreter.

Implicit flows through branches on secret values are tracked with a set of context taints, and post-dominators identify where control flow reconverges. The speaker then demonstrates a bypass: a program can branch on a secret and reveal it by checking stack depth, which a control-flow graph alone does not capture. The fix is to add stack height to the projected graph, with a wildcard when the height cannot be computed. A first version timed out on all twelve benchmark apps, so the design was reordered: abstract interpretation first, then taint analysis over the finished state graph.

With the revised design, five of the twelve apps gave correct results with no false negatives, and some had reasonable false positive rates within a day. The speaker presents this as ongoing work. Separating the two phases could let a fresh abstract interpreter targeting another language reuse the taint stage, though that is still future work.

talks.title: The State of Hammer: Ready for ICS
talks.teaser: Shows how a parser combinator grammar was built for the DNP3 industrial protocol, and what fuzzing and isolation revealed.
talks.summary:
The talk revisits Hammer, a parser combinator library for C, and its use on DNP3, an industrial control protocol. The speakers explain that the DNP3 specification is large, and that a regular expression can describe the layered application structure but misses constraints between header flags, function codes, object groups and variations. Some rules live in prose descriptions rather than in the formal tables, and some constraints, such as relative timestamps needing a common reference time, are never stated. Writing the grammar by hand raised open questions, such as whether a Select request may carry no blocks at all.

To test the approach, the team built a validating proxy that intercepts TCP traffic, parses both directions with the grammar, and drops invalid messages. They ran it under a memory isolation mechanism that keeps code from touching sections it should not access. Hammer's allocations were not tracked by that mechanism, so they wrote a custom allocator over a large overcommitted region, and Linux overcommit accounting got in the way. Testing combined unit tests, Valgrind, AFL and a DNP3-focused fuzzer. Fuzzing exposed a Hammer problem where a large count field triggered huge allocations, which was fixed, and an integer overflow of the kind common in DNP3 implementations.

The main takeaway is that a grammar-first design decomposes naturally into testable pieces and helps separate parsing from processing for privilege isolation. The downsides are speed and memory. Ordered choice combinators try alternatives one by one, which is slower than the table lookup a context-free generator would produce, and generic semantic values can expand tightly packed bit fields into large structs. The speakers also suggested a recognizer-only variant that skips building semantic values as a future direction.

talks.title: Research Report: Analysis of Software for Restricted Computational Environment Applicability
talks.teaser: Explores LLVM-based analysis that labels Linux kernel code as Turing-complete or sub-Turing-complete for restricted runtimes.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames MOCHA, a follow-on to the CREMA effort, which asks how much of a large codebase can execute in a sub-Turing-complete setting versus full Turing completeness. Turing-complete fragments can accept arbitrary inputs and drift into ill-defined states; sub-TC regions promise bounded, analyzable behavior, aligning with a langsec mindset even before full enforcement is practical.

The workflow compiles a trimmed Linux kernel with LLVM and Clang, then applies custom analysis and transformation passes on intermediate representation to separate clearly bounded loops from ambiguous cases such as buffer-sized induction limits or recursion. Metrics track source volume and classification outcomes, with manual review reserved where halting-style questions remain. Early scans highlight dense loop activity under arch, drivers, and core kernel areas, while include trees show little loop structure. Reported figures cite on the order of 350,000 lines, mostly ANSI C, with a modest share of functions still undecided relative to the unlooped bulk of the tree.

Practitioners should treat much of the kernel as already amenable to restricted execution models, and prioritize folders where unbounded-looking loops concentrate for deeper review. Transformation passes can surface hidden bounds without changing runtime semantics. The speaker argues for extending the same measurement approach to user-space and application code, where style and recursion may skew results compared with the refined kernel.

talks.title: Mitigating LangSec Problems With Capabilities
talks.teaser: Shows how a capability-based supervisor shrinks the damage LangSec bugs can do in web apps, using a sample of past CVEs.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why web applications are hard to secure when many of them share one server. Apps on such a machine usually inherit broad ambient authority: shared system users, readable system files, unrestricted network access, and a single database user that stands in for every account. Login and permission logic is rebuilt inside each application, so a language-security bug such as path traversal, code injection or a leaked cookie can reach far beyond the flawed code.

The speaker presents Sandstorm, which replaces the web server with a supervisor that tracks users and their rights. Each document starts private to its creator, who can delegate subsets of their access, and the supervisor records who granted what and can revoke it. Every document runs in its own sandbox with a read-only copy of the application, no native network access and a heavily filtered set of system calls, so all outside communication passes through the supervisor. Across a sample of 20 CVEs from ported applications, including Tiny Tiny RSS, WordPress and Roundcube, only one, a cross-site scripting bug in Roundcube, was not mitigated. Of 27 Linux kernel CVEs examined from a set of 224, system call filtering blocked 24.

The speaker stresses that this is a safety net rather than a fix. Applications still need correct authorization checks and output filtering, and the surviving XSS shows the limits. The takeaway is that authorization can be treated as a parsing question, with the parser deciding whether a request is permitted, much as parsers have long decided what data to trust.

talks.title: Some musings on the deduplication weird machine
talks.teaser: Details how copy-on-write deduplication timing and Rowhammer combine to drive Microsoft Edge exploitation from JavaScript.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames memory deduplication in hypervisors and recent Windows releases as a “weird machine” that extends beyond the one-bit confirmation described in the authors’ IEEE Security and Privacy work. Prior browser-facing Rowhammer research made bit flips reachable from JavaScript, but building privilege escalation there remained awkward because it depended on spraying file-backed pages and steering paging behavior.

The speakers describe a chain against Microsoft Edge on Windows 10 that first abuses deduplication’s copy-on-write timing: identical pages merge, and a write that triggers deduplication is measurably slow even from script. They show how alignment and staged probing can leak ASLR-related JIT code addresses despite high entropy, and how a birthday-style mass of guessed object pages reduces the cost of finding a useful heap pointer. Megabyte-aligned probes recover pointer candidates across the address space.

Rowhammer then flips an array element so it references a crafted fake object, yielding arbitrary read and write from the browser. The closing message is that deduplication leaks are richer than a single presence bit, and that combining them with Rowhammer makes credible in-browser exploitation practical for defenders to reckon with.

talks.title: Panel: Toward a LangSec Software Development Lifecycle
talks.teaser: Panelists debate how to make language-theoretic security practical for developers through checks, hiring and standards.
talks.summary:
This panel at a language-theoretic security workshop asked how software teams can be pushed to reason about untrusted input before flawed parsing becomes exploitable behavior. The panelists questioned whether code metrics or pre-commit checks could flag risky patterns without burying developers in false positives, and they agreed that any automated check needs a concrete guarantee attached to it.

Much of the discussion centered on people and incentives. Panelists noted that hiring developers who can build correct parsers is hard, and that this gap might be measured through longitudinal studies with hard numbers rather than anecdotes. They compared parsing to cryptography, where bugs became specialist knowledge, and pointed to SQL injection as a case where bound parameters largely replaced string concatenation. Other examples included XML external entities, which many parsers can disable with a single setting, and unsafe deserialization and eval of user data in several languages. Protocol buffers were cited as a widely available library that makes safe serialization the easy path.

For practitioners, the takeaways were to make parser generators and parser combinator libraries approachable, to map each vulnerability to the specific language-theoretic failure behind it, and to get such failures into penetration test reports, coding standards and static analysis rules. Penetration testers and standards bodies were named as possible channels for that change. The panel closed by inviting proposals for a secure development workshop.

talks.title: The Cracked Cookie Jar: HTTP Cookie Hijacking and the Exposure of Private Information
talks.teaser: Shows how plaintext HTTP requests leak session cookies that expose email, search history and accounts across major services.
talks.summary:
The talk covers HTTP cookie hijacking, in which a passive attacker on the same network captures a session cookie sent over plain HTTP and replays it to take over the victim's account. The attack has been known since a 2010 public demonstration. Moving to HTTPS helps only partly, because a visit that begins with a plain request before redirecting still leaks any cookie not marked secure.

Of 25 major services studied, 15 exposed sensitive data or account functions from the cookie alone. Search engines revealed profile details, search and visited-result history and saved locations, and a Q&A site exposed who had posted anonymous questions. Retail sites that encrypted only login and checkout leaked account names, carts, purchases and shipping addresses. Ad network cookies revealed browsing history and interest categories. Monitoring campus Wi-Fi for 30 days, using hashed cookie values under ethics approval, found about 280,000 vulnerable accounts, which were reported to the services. Tor traffic, observed without collecting cookies, still showed many plain HTTP connections, suggesting anonymous users were exposed too.

Existing defences fall short. The Secure flag blocks leaks but breaks sites that personalise over HTTP on purpose. HSTS and its preload list close the first-visit gap, yet adoption is partial, with some account subdomains preloaded while main domains are not. HTTPS Everywhere relies on hand-written rules that miss URLs and need exclusions. The key lesson is that mixing HTTP and HTTPS on one site is risky, and a single plain request carrying a cookie is enough for an attacker.

talks.title: pASSWORD tYPOS and How to Correct Them Securely
talks.teaser: Shows how login systems can accept common typos like stray Caps Lock without weakening password security.
talks.summary:
Login systems hash the submitted password and compare it with a stored digest, so a small slip such as a missed capital letter fails outright. The proposed relaxed checker runs the normal exact check first and, on failure, tries a few correctors on the input. The stored hash database stays unchanged, and the operator picks which typos to tolerate. Because hashing is deliberately slow, the correctors must be a small set.

To choose those correctors, the team gathered transcriptions of more than 100,000 passwords from 4,300 workers on Amazon Mechanical Turk. Common errors were an accidental Caps Lock press, an extra trailing character, and a flipped first-letter case, together about 20% of typos. A Dropbox production study logged how many failed logins these fixes would have rescued, without granting any extra logins. About 3% of users in a 24-hour window hit one of these three typos.

Server breaches give an attacker nothing new, since the stored hashes are unchanged. Online guessing gets extra guesses per query, but success depends on the probability mass of guesses, not their count. Simulations using phpBB and MySpace leaks as stand-ins for real password distributions showed a small gap for the basic approach. Skipping corrected guesses that are very popular, based on the free correction theorem, cut the gap to about 0.02% when RockYou data estimated the distribution. Targeted attacks were not studied. Typo tolerance can raise login success with almost no security cost when risky corrections are filtered.

talks.title: SoK: Towards Grounding Censorship Circumvention in Empiricism
talks.teaser: Maps real-world censor behavior against circumvention research and urges user-centered empirical evaluation.
talks.summary:
The talk frames nation-state censorship as a practical threat to users who need fast web access across jurisdictional borders, using blocked Wikipedia-style browsing and Tor with obfuscation when relays are denied. It deliberately limits scope to conventional, channel-based circumvention rather than every possible design.

Drawing on 31 measurement studies and 55 circumvention papers, plus analysis of thousands of Tor bug reports and blog posts, the speakers characterize real censors as often on-path, stateful, blacklist-driven, and timed to political events. They document 34 Tor-blocking incidents worldwide, mostly via IP blocklists and protocol or certificate properties, with rare active probing. Deployed tools tend to disguise connection setup through polymorphism, while much unpublished research targets usage patterns with steganography and assumes more aggressive, usage-phase attacks that over-block under packet loss compared with passive real-world sensors.

The conclusion argues research threat models lag live censorship, evaluation metrics are fragmented and technique-focused rather than user- and context-specific, and the field needs grounded success criteria, maintenance and usability awareness, open datasets, and automated pre-deployment tests against the simple blocking heuristics censors already use.

talks.title: A Tough call: Mitigating Advanced Code-Reuse Attacks At The Binary Level
talks.teaser: Presents Type Armor, a binary-level CFI scheme that matches argument counts at indirect calls to block code-reuse attacks.
talks.summary:
Control-flow integrity restricts where indirect calls in a program may go, but schemes that work on compiled binaries struggle to resolve the exact targets of those calls, because the type information available in source code is missing. As a result, attackers who control an indirect call can still chain many functions together through a loop gadget, as in the COOP style of code-reuse attack, and binary-level defenses leave a set of permitted targets that is too broad.

The approach presented, Type Armor, tries to approximate source-level precision from the binary alone. It recovers argument counts at indirect call sites by finding the argument registers that are written before a call, and recovers the expected argument count at each function by finding the argument registers that are read before being written. Under the x86-64 calling convention, the tool then allows an indirect call only to functions whose expected argument count does not exceed what the call site prepares. Checks inserted before indirect calls and IDs placed at function entries enforce this at runtime. The speaker reported that the argument counts were determined precisely for most call sites and functions in memcached, lighttpd, Engine X and MySQL, with a geometric mean overhead below three percent on SPEC. MySQL was the worst case at 24 percent overhead.

The speaker stated that Type Armor stops the published advanced code-reuse attacks that were examined, while being more precise than existing binary-level solutions though less precise than source-level ones. The team plans to release the tool as open source. The main takeaway for practitioners is that binary-level control-flow integrity can be made considerably tighter by reasoning about function arguments, at a modest performance cost.

talks.title: Users Really Do Plug in USB Drives They Find
talks.teaser: Presents a university field study measuring how often people plug in USB drives they find, and what makes them do it.
talks.summary:
The talk revisits a well-known anecdote in which planted USB drives are picked up and plugged into work computers, and asks whether that really works. The researchers dropped 297 photographed drives at 30 spots across the University of Illinois campus over three days, at morning and afternoon times. The drives came in five styles, including unlabeled ones, ones marked confidential, and ones with keys or a return label. Each held realistic documents, and the only code was an HTML file that loaded a remote image when someone double-clicked it.

About 290 drives were picked up, and 135 showed files being opened, so the researchers set a lower bound of 45 percent. Because plugged-in drives with no file opens went untracked, they estimated the true rate lies between 45 and 98 percent. The median time from drop to first file open was about 6.9 hours. Changing a drive's appearance or the time of day did not raise success, but a return label lowered it. Of the 62 survey respondents who opened files, most said they wanted to return the drive, yet many opened the winter break photos first, which points to curiosity. Most took no precautions, and their demographics and security habits resembled the wider university population.

The main takeaways are that found drives are very likely to be plugged in, that appearance and timing matter little, and that a return label discourages opening. Because curiosity drives many people, organizations should treat found media as a threat. The study ran on a campus, though graduate students and staff also picked up drives.

talks.title: You Get Where You're Looking For: The Impact Of Information Sources On Code Security
talks.teaser: Compares how Android developers' lookup sources, like Stack Overflow and official docs, affect whether their code ends up secure.
talks.summary:
Developers who search for a coding problem often land on a Stack Overflow answer, and an earlier study had tied such snippets to insecure Android apps, including custom trust managers that accepted any host. To see how developers really find help, the team surveyed Android developers whose addresses came from those apps. Roughly 300 of 50,000 emailed developers replied, and about 70% said they used Stack Overflow, usually after a search engine.

A lab study followed with 54 Android developers recruited in the US and Germany. Participants were randomly given Stack Overflow only, official Android documentation only, books only, or free choice starting from Google, and they had 20 minutes per task. The tasks covered storing login credentials, switching to HTTPS with a hostname check, a phone call with minimal permissions, and restricting an activity to apps from the same developer. Stack Overflow users produced the most functional code, 67%, but also the most insecure code, while documentation and book users wrote more secure solutions. Only 16% spoke about security while coding, though 60% said afterwards they had considered it.

The authors conclude that Stack Overflow is quick and usable while official documentation is secure but harder to use, so the two need to be combined. Suggested options include security ratings on Stack Overflow, a security-focused Q&A site that appears in search results, Q&A inside official documentation, and secure snippets for common trouble spots. Limitations include opt-in bias among volunteers and the artificial lab setting.

talks.title: PhotoProof: Cryptographic Image Authentication for Any Set of Permissible Transformations
talks.teaser: Shows a cryptographic proof approach that keeps cropped, rotated, or otherwise edited photos verifiably authentic.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses how to tell whether an edited photograph is genuine. Signing camera output breaks once a permitted change such as cropping or brightness adjustment alters the pixels, and earlier robust-hash schemes support only a few transformations, are often inefficient, and give weak accuracy. The speakers present PhotoProof, which uses proof-carrying data to attach to each derived image a succinct, zero-knowledge proof that the edit was permitted. Anyone can verify these proofs and extend the chain with further permitted edits.

The construction treats an image's life as a distributed computation, with a compliance predicate checking each step's source image, output image and parameters. Because the underlying cryptography works over arithmetic circuits, the speakers hard-code transformations, such as rotation built from shearing matrices implemented with barrel shifters, and supply trigonometric values as advice that is cheaper to check than to compute. For 128 by 128 pixel images, key generation took about four minutes and produced roughly four gigabytes of public keys, proving one transformation took about five minutes, and proofs were a few kilobytes that verified in under a second.

In the question period, the speakers noted that their scheme only covers processing after the sensor, so staged scenes and substitution of a different photo remain open. Sensor-level checks, such as analog signatures or focus information, could catch some of that. The main takeaway is that proof-based authentication can cover any efficiently checkable set of edits, though larger images still need engineering work.

talks.title: Cinderella: Turning Shabby X.509 Certificates into Elegant Anonymous Credentials with ...
talks.teaser: Shows how X.509 certificate validation can run as a zero-knowledge proof, so holders disclose only chosen fields.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at two weaknesses of X.509 authentication. Certificates are often sent in full, which reveals the holder's identity and every field inside it, such as national ID data, and the verifier runs validation logic that differs by application. The speaker presents Cinderella, which keeps existing PKI and credentials unchanged but moves certificate validation off the verifier's machine. A validation policy, specialised to a class of issuers, is compiled with the Pinocchio toolchain into an arithmetic circuit, producing an evaluation key and a verification key. The certificate holder runs the policy locally and returns a constant-size proof that discloses only the fields they choose.

The work covers templates with fixed-length bounds on variable fields, a compiler that turns these templates into validators, and libraries for hashing, ASN.1 formatting and RSA PKCS#1 signature checks. Two applications are built on it: TLS client authentication with OCSP revocation checking, and an e-voting scheme built on Helios that uses Estonian ID card templates. Reported timings put verification at about 8 milliseconds, comparable to native checks, while evaluation takes several minutes. The largest full benchmark, covering TLS with two intermediates and OCSP, finishes within 10 minutes. Verification keys are a few kilobytes, but evaluation keys can reach 1 GB for complex policies.

In the Q&A, the main concerns were a trapdoor in key generation, which must be destroyed or distributed to avoid undetectable impersonation, and the loss of certificate visibility, which could be partly addressed by checking transparency proofs inside the policy. The takeaway for practitioners is that verifiable computation can make X.509 validation private and practical without changing issuers or protocols, while key setup and distributing large evaluation keys remain open problems.

talks.title: Revisiting Square Root ORAM: Efficient Random Access in Multi-Party Computation
talks.teaser: Revisits square-root ORAM to cut MPC random-access startup cost and outperform linear scan on many practical data sizes.
talks.summary:
Multi-party computation lets parties jointly compute on private inputs without revealing intermediates, but ordinary array indexing exposes which element is read. Scanning the whole array hides the index yet makes each access linear in array length, while oblivious RAM offers polylogarithmic access but heavy setup and per-access cost that can dominate real workloads.

The presentation compares prior MPC-oriented ORAM, including a recent CCS construction, against linear scan and shows that asymptotically better schemes are often slower in practice for modest element counts. It revives the classic square-root ORAM idea by removing per-access secure hash evaluation, using periodic reshuffles, bounded batches of accesses, and a two-party protocol to update position maps via masked permutations without revealing them.

Evaluation across benchmarks such as binary search, stable matching, and hash-like random access highlights much lower initialization cost—often two orders of magnitude—and earlier breakeven with linear scan. The takeaway is that concrete MPC application design should weigh startup time and break-even parameters, not asymptotics alone, when choosing how to hide memory access patterns.

talks.title: TaoStore: Overcoming Asynchronicity in Oblivious Data Storage
talks.teaser: A formal model of adaptive async obliviousness, Curious gaps, and TaoStore for concurrent oblivious storage are delivered.
talks.summary:
Companies increasingly outsource data to untrusted clouds while many employees read and write concurrently. Encryption alone does not stop access-pattern leakage, and classical oblivious RAM designs target a single client. Parallel systems such as PrivateFS, OblivStore, and Curious add proxies and partitioning, yet earlier models weakly capture asynchrony: a network adversary may delay messages, schedule adaptively, and observe response times.

The talk introduces adaptive asynchronous obliviousness so pairs of time-inconsistent executions stay indistinguishable, and argues that Curious is not secure under that model. Concurrent requests to the same logical item use fake accesses; when responses can reorder on asynchronous links, timing reveals whether accesses collide on one item. TaoStore is proposed as a fully asynchronous, concurrent tree-based oblivious store with atomic semantics, non-blocking write-back via subtree invariants, partitioning as an add-on, and a sequencer that replies in arrival order to close the fake-access timing channel.

Evaluation on a one-gigabyte dataset with a UCSB proxy and AWS storage reports on the order of forty operations per second at ten-way concurrency, with throughput limited by bandwidth. Memory utilization can stay near two to five percent of the dataset without much throughput loss. Practitioners should treat response-time channels as first-class when hardening parallel oblivious cloud storage.

talks.title: SoK: (State of) The Art of War: Offensive Techniques in Binary Analysis
talks.teaser: Surveys offensive binary analysis techniques and evaluates them on a shared framework using DARPA's Cyber Grand Challenge binaries.
talks.summary:
A UC Santa Barbara team presents a systematization of offensive binary analysis, examining how well current techniques find and exploit vulnerabilities in compiled code. Growing binary firmware in smart devices raises the stakes, while many published tools are unreleased, rigid, or hard to combine. To compare techniques on equal footing, the team built anger, a modular and open-source binary analysis framework.

The framework provides a binary loader, multi-architecture lifting and a common data-domain layer. The team reimplemented core techniques from prior work, including control flow recovery, symbolic execution, value set analysis and symbolically assisted fuzzing, and tested them on 131 binaries from the DARPA Cyber Grand Challenge qualification event. Those binaries range from a few kilobytes to about ten megabytes and come with ground-truth vulnerabilities. In this dataset, the AFL-based fuzzer found almost three times as many vulnerabilities as any other single technique and more than all the others combined. The speaker links this to crashes that lie deep in execution, around 10,000 to 100,000 basic blocks in, where symbolic execution hits state explosion.

The authors argue that a shared base makes it possible to tell whether gains come from a technique or from its implementation. The project is released as open source with documentation and a Docker image. The speaker also notes that many published tools cannot be checked against originals, and that the team has used anger in CGC and capture-the-flag competitions.

talks.title: Back in Black: Towards Formal, Black Box Analysis of Sanitizers and Filters
talks.teaser: Shows how symbolic automata learning can infer regular expression filters from queries and bypass web application firewalls.
talks.summary:
The talk covers black-box analysis of sanitizers and filters, the components that block or clean untrusted input to stop injection attacks such as cross-site scripting and SQL injection. Testing them often has to happen without source code, whether for policy reasons or cost. The focus is regular expression filters, which can be modeled as deterministic finite automata, and the question is whether their structure can be learned by querying them.

The method relies on exact learning from queries, where a learner asks membership questions and equivalence questions. Classic automata learning tests every transition, which is impractical over large alphabets such as Unicode. The authors use symbolic automata instead, grouping transitions into guards learned from a sample of symbols, and add a counterexample processing step that distinguishes a wrong guard from a missing state. They also introduce grammar-oriented filter auditing, where an attacker with a context-free grammar of attacks searches for strings the learned model lets through and checks them against the live filter with one membership query.

In experiments on 15 regular expression filters from popular web application firewalls, using an alphabet of 92 symbols, symbolic learning needed about 15 times fewer queries than the classical algorithm on average, and about 35 times fewer with grammar-oriented auditing. Live tests against ModSecurity and a PHP intrusion detection system produced bypasses, including an authentication bypass using the LIKE operator and an attack that retrieves data, both acknowledged by the ModSecurity team. The speaker stresses that the learned models are approximations meant for assisted black-box testing, not a point-and-shoot tool.

talks.title: CaSE: Cache-Assisted Secure Execution on ARM Processors
talks.teaser: Shows how ARM processors can keep decrypted code and data inside the cache, shielded from memory-dump and compromised-OS attacks.
talks.summary:
The talk presents CaSE, a design for running sensitive ARM code hidden from an attacker who combines a physical memory-disclosure attack, such as cold boot on a lost phone, with a compromised normal-world OS. Earlier defenses rarely considered this combined threat. The goal is confidentiality and integrity for code, data and runtime state, using the processor cache as the protected execution space.

In secure mode, encrypted binaries are decrypted inside the secure cache and kept there across context switches. The non-secure mode pauses the normal OS, loads the application into the non-secure cache, and verifies the execution environment, including address translation state, since redirected virtual addresses could bypass content checks. Context is re-encrypted before it leaves the cache. Cache locking is done one way at a time, and self-modifying code is handled by writing decrypted content directly into the unified L2 cache.

Tests used an integrity checker and a cryptographic library covering RSA, SHA and AES, compiled for size to fit one cache way. A single RSA decryption per environment setup added 25% overhead, which shrank as more work ran per cycle. System overhead was about 3% with one L2 way and roughly 20 to 30% with all seven. Open work includes OS calls into an untrusted OS. A DMA-capable device can modify memory but was verified not to rewrite the locked cache contents.

talks.title: Shreds: Fine-grained Execution Units with Private Memory
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Shreds: Fine-grained Execution Units with Private Memory.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Modern application development frequently integrates multiple third-party libraries and components within a single process. However, the standard OS model only distinguishes between processes (separate address spaces) and threads (shared address space). This shared address space enables 'in-process memory abuse,' where compromised or malicious components access sensitive data (such as OpenSSL private keys or login passwords) or invoke private internal APIs belonging to other components within the same process.

To address this limitation without paying the high IPC overheads of process-level isolation or the usability constraints of Intel SGX and ARM TrustZone, the researchers present 'Shreds.' Shreds are fine-grained execution units that represent arbitrary scoped execution segments of a thread, augmented with private memory pools (termed 's-pools') isolated from the rest of the process.

### Key Topics
- **In-Process Memory Abuse**: Malicious or compromised in-process components stealing secret data or executing private code.
- **Limitations of Existing Defenses**: Process-based isolation incurs expensive IPC and complex multi-process re-architecting; software fault isolation (like Google Native Client) cannot easily handle dynamically generated or external code; hardware enclaves (Intel SGX, ARM TrustZone) suffer from semantic gaps or strict restrictions like forbidding system calls.
- **Shreds & S-Pools**: Introducing segmented thread execution with dedicated private memory pools allocated from the shared address space.
- **Hardware-Assisted Domain Isolation**: Utilizing ARM Memory Domains (and Intel Memory Protection Keys) to enforce memory isolation efficiently without multiple page tables or nested paging.

### Technical Details
The Shreds architecture consists of two primary components:
1. **S-Driver**: An OS module responsible for runtime events, access control, and memory isolation.
   - **Memory Domain Binding**: ARM architecture provides 16 memory domains checked via domain access control registers. Because domains are scarce, S-Driver statically binds an accessible domain to each CPU core and reuses it across multiple s-pools.
   - **Critical Path Optimization**: Instead of altering page table entries and invalidating TLBs, S-Driver controls access by fast manipulation of domain access control registers (a single-instruction operation). Domain faults are resolved lazily via a domain fault handler to distinguish legitimate accesses from attacks.
   - **Secure Stacks and Interfaces**: Provides each shred with an isolated stack allocated inside its s-pool and intercepts system interfaces (like debugging or physical memory/IO access) that could bypass domain checks.
2. **S-Compiler**: A compiler module that verifies proper API usage, associates s-pools with valid shred enter call sites at compile time (storing metadata in a dedicated ELF section to prevent unauthorized s-pool access), hardens control flow, and checks data flows to prevent sensitive data leakage.
3. **API Design**: Developers use lightweight APIs including `s_enter` and `s_exit` (for scoping shred execution) alongside pool management functions (`s_alloc`/`s_free` wrappers, such as `sds_init` and `sds_free`). Multiple shreds can also securely share an s-pool when explicitly configured.

### Evaluation and Takeaways
The system was evaluated on a Raspberry Pi 2 (ARM Cortex-A7, 1 GB RAM) across 5 different software packages, including the lighttpd web server and OpenSSL. Key evaluation takeaways include:
- **Adoption Effort**: Minimal developer intervention was required—an average of 21 lines of code changed and roughly 32 minutes to instrument each application.
- **Performance**: Shred execution introduced less than 5% execution slowdown and less than 1% memory overhead. Shred creation/entry APIs ran slightly faster than `clone()` (about twice the runtime of `getpid()`), while s-pool allocation ran comparably to `mmap()`.

talks.title: Cache Storage Channels: Alias-Driven Attacks and Verified Countermeasures
talks.teaser: Shows how cache inconsistencies on ARM let attackers break formally verified software integrity and leak secrets.
talks.summary:
The talk starts from a gap in formal verification of low-level platforms such as hypervisors: the models usually leave out cache behaviour, so timing and similar channels fall outside the proofs. The focus is mismatched cacheability attributes, where two virtual mappings of the same physical memory differ, one cacheable and one not. Architecture manuals advise against this, but a powerful untrusted component can set it up, and the result is incoherent cache behaviour.

The first attack targets a reference monitor. The attacker writes through a non-cacheable alias, the victim reads through a cacheable alias so a stale value gets cached, and after the cache line is evicted the victim fetches the attacker's value after its policy check, bypassing the policy. The second attack leaks secrets: the attacker detects a victim's secret-dependent evictions by probing its own memory, with no timing measurement needed. Both were demonstrated on a formally verified ARM hypervisor, where Linux could inject page tables and take control, and on an AES implementation running in ARM TrustZone.

Countermeasures include flushing the cache on entering critical sections, which cost roughly 800% overhead for the hypervisor, or evicting only the affected lines, which is faster but needs extra verification constraints. For confidentiality, avoid secret-dependent accesses or map lookup tables as non-cacheable. The takeaway is that formal models must account for cache coherence, and software should be verified against this channel where the hardware does not guarantee it.

talks.title: HDFI: Hardware-Assisted Data-Flow Isolation
talks.teaser: Presents a hardware-enforced one-bit tagging scheme that isolates sensitive data such as return addresses from memory corruption.
talks.summary:
Memory corruption bugs such as stack buffer overflows remain a leading cause of remote code execution. The talk reviews why existing return-address defenses fall short. Stack canaries can be bypassed by arbitrary writes or information leaks, encrypted return addresses raise key management problems, and software shadow stacks force a trade-off between slow isolation and fast schemes that have been broken. Hardware shadow stacks are narrow in scope and struggle with setjmp and longjmp, deep recursion and kernel stacks.

The speaker introduces HFI, a hardware-enforced data-flow isolation mechanism inspired by data-flow integrity. Each machine word gets one tag bit, managed by three instructions: a store that sets the tag, and loads that check whether the tag is zero or one. Ordinary loads are unchanged, which keeps existing binaries compatible. Because tags sit in an in-memory bitmap, the design adds a tag cache, avoids fetching tags for loads that do not check them, and skips all-zero table lines. Return-address protection needs only a single policy, and the same mechanism covers vtable and code-pointer protection, kernel data, non-control data and information leak prevention.

Evaluated on a RISC-V Rocket core, the optimizations bring runtime overhead to a negligible level, and all synthesized attacks were defeated. A shadow stack port needed only a few compiler changes. Questions covered overhead from fetching extra tag bits and how tags from separate protections can coexist. The answer was that sensitive data is tagged distinctly, though some cases would need runtime memory safety checks.
