talks.title: Security Analysis of Emerging Smart Home Applications
talks.teaser: Examines how third-party apps on Samsung SmartThings gain excess privileges, spoof events and inject commands in a smart home.
talks.summary:
The talk examines programmable smart home platforms, which let third-party apps coordinate devices through a hub and cloud service. Using Samsung SmartThings as a mature case with hundreds of apps and design principles shared by newer frameworks, the researchers asked how such homes can be attacked. Their method combined hand-built test apps, an analysis of 499 real apps, and proof-of-concept attacks. Because the platform is closed source, they filled gaps in capability documentation using network traces and built their own analysis tool for Groovy.

The core findings are design weaknesses. Automatic over-privilege means a coarse capability such as lock also grants unlock, and picking one device during enumeration grants every capability that device supports. About 55 percent of apps leave granted operations unused, and 43 percent receive capabilities they never requested. The event system also lets apps subscribe to events from any device they can reach, monitor a device through its 128-bit identifier, and spoof physical device events. Other issues include an OAuth 2.0 weakness, Groovy injection through unfiltered strings, and SMS and internet APIs usable without any capability.

The proof-of-concept attacks chain these issues. One popular lock-control app was made to program a PIN code into a door lock through injection. A battery-monitoring app was reconfigured at runtime to snoop PIN codes and leak them over SMS. Spoofed events disabled vacation mode and triggered a fake CO alarm, with no capabilities required. The speaker recommends least privilege with risk-based capabilities, since turning an oven on is riskier than turning it off, along with strong event identity and access control. SmartThings said it updated its vetting process and best practices after disclosure.

talks.title: Algorithmic Transparency via Quantitative Input Influence ...
talks.teaser: Presents quantitative input influence, a causal measure of which inputs drive a classifier's decisions for individuals or groups.
talks.summary:
Learning systems now drive decisions about credit, policing and other areas with real consequences, yet they are often opaque. A rejected applicant may have no idea why, and group disparities, such as men being approved far more often than women, are hard to explain. The talk places this within algorithmic transparency, where explanations help diagnose harms from inappropriate information use.

Correlated inputs make it hard to tell which features a classifier actually uses. The proposed remedy is quantitative input influence, a family of metrics built on causal interventions: an input is replaced with random values from its population while the others stay fixed, and the change in a chosen quantity is measured. That quantity can describe one person, a group, or a gap between groups. Because single features may show no effect alone, the method evaluates sets of inputs and divides credit among them using a cooperative-game summation, which can be approximated by random sampling.

Two test applications were built: a predictive policing model using a youth survey, and an income classifier using census data, both with standard machine learning algorithms. Two people with similar profiles received different explanations, showing that alike individuals can be denied for different reasons. The measures can also be made differentially private at low cost. The takeaway is that causal reasoning is needed to find which inputs a model truly uses, and that the approach works without constraining model design.

talks.title: A Method for Verifying Privacy-Type Properties: The Unbounded Case
talks.teaser: Presents conditions that let symbolic verification prove unlinkability and anonymity for unbounded sessions and users.
talks.summary:
Electronic passport RFID protocols can let an eavesdropper link a holder's sessions, which breaks privacy. Designing such protocols safely is hard, and existing automated tools can check unlinkability only for a fixed number of users and sessions, often reporting false attacks. This talk verifies unlinkability for an unbounded number of users and sessions in the symbolic model.

The attacker controls the network and can eavesdrop, deduce and inject messages, while cryptography is assumed perfect. Unlinkability is cast as trace equivalence between runs with repeated sessions and runs where each user plays once. Two leak types are shown. A tag sending its identity under a fixed symmetric key can be traced with an equality test on two eavesdropped messages, and a challenge-response variant falls when an attacker injects a constant challenge. A reader that aborts or answers depending on a decryption outcome leaks which tag it serves. Two conditions address these: outputs must be indistinguishable from fresh nonces, and a conditional must succeed for a user only when that user's own session produced the input.

The speaker proves these conditions imply unlinkability and anonymity for a class of two-party protocols. The conditions can be checked with existing symbolic verifiers, and a prototype tool automates this. Applied to RFID protocols, the method proves basic access control in passports unlinkable and finds new attacks on other protocols, typically within five minutes. Group-signature and anonymous credential protocols fall outside the two-party class.

talks.title: Synthesizing Plausible Privacy-Preserving Location Traces
talks.teaser: A generative framework delivers plausible synthetic location traces via geographic dissimilarity and plausible deniability.
talks.summary:
Sensitive location trajectories are hard for researchers to obtain, yet synthetic releases could preserve format and statistics while easing access. The work targets location traces specifically, including scenarios where users mix plausible fake trajectories with real queries to location-based services without degrading recommendations.

Prior anonymization and most differential-privacy mechanisms struggle with full-trajectory plausibility and scale. The approach uses a two-stage framework: a utility-preserving generative model built from seed traces, then a privacy gate that discards failing samples. Human mobility is split into geographic features (sensitive) and semantic features (useful, e.g., home, work, shopping). Seeds map to semantic “color” traces, then a hidden Markov model decodes new geographic paths that match semantics but differ geographically. Privacy relies on geographic dissimilarity from the seed and plausible deniability via alternative non-seed traces that could have produced the same synthetic output.

Evaluations report preserved semantic-similarity distributions and top-location visit proportions; against a state-of-the-art inference attack, the method yields higher adversary location error than competing fake-location techniques. The generator is released as open source. Practitioners gain a concrete pattern—semantic preservation with geographic replacement and post-generation privacy tests—for sharing mobility data more safely.

talks.title: Keeping Authorities "Honest or Bust" with Decentralized Witness Cosigning
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Keeping Authorities "Honest or Bust" with Decentralized Witness Cosigning.

talks.title: Downgrade Resilience in Key-Exchange Protocols
talks.teaser: Modular proofs and downgrade definitions show how TLS 1.3 transcript signing limits weaker modes under active attackers.
talks.summary:
The presentation frames downgrade attacks as an attacker-driven fallback to weaker versions or algorithms during protocol negotiation, with TLS as the central example because ClientHello negotiation spans many versions and cipher suites. It argues that classical authentication-style security models often fail to guarantee that the negotiated mode is as strong as both parties would prefer without an active adversary.

The speaker organizes real attacks into three roles. POODLE-style record-layer issues fit models where the full handshake is assumed strong. LOGJAM-like attacks show gaps when only part of the transcript is authenticated, allowing a weak group choice to break key confirmation. Attacks on obsolete hashes or signature schemes illustrate limits where no downgrade definition can rescue a broken primitive. The paper’s contributions are precise downgrade-security definitions using a downgrade predicate and ideal negotiation, plus a modular proof method that relates a simplified TLS 1.3 subprotocol to the full standard via simulators.

For TLS 1.3, signing the negotiated handshake transcript yields positive downgrade-security results under sound assumptions on nonces and signatures. Pure version downgrade to TLS 1.2 remains possible because the version is not signed; embedding the server version in the server nonce is offered as a backward-compatible patch with a proof sketch. Practitioners should treat downgrade resilience as configuration plus a few critical algorithms—especially signatures—and recognize that some legacy interoperability modes still lack full protection.

talks.title: Multiple Handshakes Security of TLS 1.3 Candidates
talks.teaser: Formalizes chained TLS 1.3 handshakes and proves key secrecy and authentication for draft 10 across resumption and 0-RTT modes.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how TLS 1.3, still a draft at the time, holds up when several handshake modes are chained together. The speaker explains that earlier TLS versions were patched one attack at a time, and that interactions among full handshakes, zero round-trip time, PSK-based resumption and resumption combined with DHE have enabled known attacks such as renegotiation and triple handshake. Earlier formal proofs covered only single runs, which leaves those dependencies unexamined.

To close that gap, the authors model a sequence of handshakes as a tree, where each node is one session and deeper levels can reuse keys from their ancestors. They extend the multi-stage key exchange security model to a multi-level version, with rules linking sessions across levels, a notion of level-key dependence, and semi-static server keys that are reused for about a week. Under standard assumptions on signatures, Diffie-Hellman and hash or pseudorandom functions, they prove by induction on the number of handshakes that the draft 10 protocol achieves key secrecy and matching security across modes and levels.

The model is also applied to TLS 1.2 patched with RFC 7627, where it captures the triple handshake attack through its matching conditions, which the speaker presented as evidence that the model is sound. In the question period, the speaker clarified that compromise of the semi-static key after a handshake is treated as revealing early traffic keys in the model. The practical takeaway is that secure individual handshakes do not guarantee security when they are composed, so protocol analysis should cover chained runs.

talks.title: Automated Analysis and Verification of TLS 1.3: 0-RTT, Resumption and Delayed Authentication
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Automated Analysis and Verification of TLS 1.3: 0-RTT, Resumption and Delayed Authentication.

talks.title: Key Confirmation in Key Exchange: A Formal Treatment and Implications for TLS 1.3
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Key Confirmation in Key Exchange: A Formal Treatment and Implications for TLS 1.3.

talks.title: No Pardon for the Interruption: New Inference Attacks on Android Through Interrupt Timing Analysis
talks.teaser: Shows how public Android interrupt counters leak lock patterns and foreground apps, enabling inference attacks from timing alone.
talks.summary:
Android phones carry sensors and peripherals such as touchscreens, cameras and GPS, and each hardware event raises an interrupt that the Linux kernel counts. Those counters are published in /proc/interrupts, which any process can read. The speaker argues that how these counts change over time can leak private information, extending earlier work that mostly focused on reading data directly from sensors.

The first attack targets Android lock patterns. Each swipe across the 3x3 grid produces a characteristic number of interrupts, so the observed counts can be split into strokes and matched to the lines drawn. Because the same swipe varies from one attempt to the next, the team built a general model of the relationship from a user study. A hidden Markov model then used the fact that patterns follow predictable sequences to recover the most likely pattern. Against a case where the attacker could make 40 attempts, the attack reached a 90 percent success rate, and knowing only the number of swipe lines still shrank the search space substantially. The second attack identifies the foreground application by recording interrupt patterns during UI refresh and launch animations. Different apps, including banking and security apps, produced distinguishable patterns. The speaker skipped that evaluation because of time.

The main takeaway is that a publicly readable interrupt counter is a new attack surface, one that could support phishing overlays that appear over a banking login. The speaker suggested access control on the interrupt file as a mitigation, noting that the data is mainly meant for debugging and that most current users are system-level tools.

talks.title: Inferring User Routes and Locations using Zero-Permission Mobile Sensors
talks.teaser: Researchers demonstrate that zero-permission smartphone sensors can infer user driving routes with high probability across multiple cities.
talks.summary:
Mobile platforms try to limit location leakage through permissions, yet gyroscope, accelerometer, and magnetometer readings need no consent and can be harvested by benign-looking apps. The presentation frames route recovery as matching a drive-specific subgraph against a prebuilt road graph built from OpenStreetMap and supplemented with speed limits from Nokia HERE.

The graph treats atomic road sections between intersections as vertices and models longer straight or curving segments, using gyroscope data for turns and curvature, accelerometer traces mainly for idle timing, and magnetometer readings for heading despite car interference and sensor drift. A search process related to trellis decoding scores candidate paths by turn angles, curvature, and travel time while filtering impossible connections; evaluations use individual and cluster rank metrics.

Simulations across eleven cities with injected noise levels and roughly two thousand routes per city show strong results for eight cities, with many true paths in the top ten under typical noise. Real collections of seventy routes each in Boston and Waltham place 30% and nearly 50% of drives in the top five, with grid layouts like Manhattan performing worse and winding networks like London and Rome performing better. The closing argument is that permissionless sensor channels pose a practical location-privacy risk warranting mitigation.

talks.title: TriggerScope: Towards Detecting Logic Bombs in Android Applications
talks.teaser: Shows how trigger analysis finds date, location and SMS conditions that hide logic bombs in Android apps.
talks.summary:
The talk addresses logic bombs in Android apps: hidden functionality that alters an app's output or actions and activates only under narrow conditions, such as a specific date or place. Since the malicious behavior is hard to specify, the approach focuses on the triggering conditions instead. The presented method, trigger analysis, is a static technique run on Dalvik bytecode. It uses forward symbolic execution to track time, location and SMS values.

Next, it reconstructs the full path predicate for each block by traversing the control-flow graph backward and simplifying the boolean formulas to remove false dependencies. Predicates comparing time, bounding locations or matching SMS content are flagged as suspicious, and are then followed across procedures to see whether they guard sensitive operations. Post-filters discard benign patterns such as null checks and sentinel timestamp comparisons. On a large set of benign Play Store apps, filtering narrowed the candidates to 35 flagged apps, which were treated as false positives. The analysis flagged a trigger in all 11 synthetic malware samples tested.

Examples included license-expiry dates, a location check that displayed a welcome message, a remote phone locator that returned GPS coordinates to an unauthenticated SMS, and a remote-lock app that unlocked on a specific SMS. The HackingTeam RCSAndroid sample aborted SMS propagation when messages matched a list of command strings. Limitations include support for only time, location and SMS sources, and no coverage of native code, reflection or dynamic loading. The main takeaway is that examining trigger conditions can surface hidden logic with few false positives.

talks.title: Following Devil's Footprints: Cross-Platform Analysis of Potentially Harmful Libraries ...
talks.teaser: A cross-platform study finds harmful libraries on Android and iOS via clustering, sandbox screening, and string anchoring.
talks.summary:
Mobile risk often rides in third-party libraries rather than whole apps, yet public catalogs skew toward clean releases and iOS makes library recovery far harder than Android. The presenters argue that cross-platform vendors motivate mapping Android library variants onto iOS binaries, because most popular iOS kits also ship on Android.

Their pipeline crawls about 1.3 million Android apps and 140,000 iOS titles, clusters packages into libraries with package-similarity scores, then flags harmful kits by embedding each candidate alone in a dummy app screened like a production binary. Shared command strings, metadata, developer identifiers, and related artifacts anchor class-level matches across Java and Objective-C implementations, with graph-style extension to rebuild iOS library boundaries. Detected Android behaviors are translated into iOS categories and checked with paired components submitted for the same class of automated review.

The measurement pass finds 763 libraries with thousands of variants, 117 marked potentially harmful on Android, and 23 on iOS after mapping. Roughly 2.94% of studied App Store apps and higher shares on alternate markets carry such libraries, including long-listed titles and very large download counts. Harmful capabilities include surveillance, unauthorized installs via private APIs, and evasion that skips permission prompts while still exfiltrating data. Contamination spreads through repackaged open releases and developers unknowingly embedding tainted SDKs.

talks.title: Unambiguous Encapsulation
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Unambiguous Encapsulation.

talks.title: Verification State-space Reduction through Restricted Parsing Environments
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Verification State-space Reduction through Restricted Parsing Environments.

talks.title: On the Generality and Convenience of Etypes
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for On the Generality and Convenience of Etypes.

talks.title: Grammatical Inference and Language Frameworks for LANGSEC
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Grammatical Inference and Language Frameworks for LANGSEC.

talks.title: The Correctness-Security Gap in Compiler Optimization
talks.teaser: Shows how formally proven compiler optimizations can still break security guarantees that programmers encode in source code.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at a gap between what a correctly designed and correctly implemented compiler optimization preserves and the security guarantees a programmer writes into source code. The speaker argues that optimizations with formal correctness proofs can still remove security intent. An early example comes from a GCC mailing list report, from around 2002, about scrubbing a password hash from memory: the compiler sees that the write is never read and removes it to save work.

The speaker then walks through other cases. Code that relies on a function boundary to separate a trusted region can be merged by inlining. Side-channel-resistant code that keeps timing uniform can lose that property when the compiler factors out a common expression. A Linux kernel null-pointer check was removed by GCC because the pointer had already been dereferenced, which treats the dereference as undefined behavior. Combined with other effects, that case became a privilege escalation bug. The speaker notes that each example is small on its own, but a few additional steps can make it exploitable.

The explanation offered is that correctness proofs compare behavior on an abstract machine defined by the language, while an attacker reasons about a concrete machine with memory persistence and timing. Rebuilding one example with a stack-pointer model shows that the same proof technique fails to close, so the speaker suggests the machine models need refinement rather than the proof techniques. The proposed research program covers testing, program analysis, theorem proving and more accurate machine models, with the question of whether an optimization is oblivious to an attacker who observes only part of the machine state. For practitioners, the takeaway is that a compiler's correctness result does not establish that security properties survive optimization.

talks.title: Geppetto: Versatile Verifiable Computation
talks.teaser: Presents a verifiable computation system that cuts proof generation cost for stateful, recursive and branching programs.
talks.summary:
Verifiable computation lets a client outsource a function to an untrusted cloud and check the returned result with a proof that is cheaper to verify than to compute. The talk frames this with a scientist who cannot afford a cluster and a provider that wants to show its outputs are correct. It recaps the Pinocchio line of work, which made verification cheaper than local computation, while proof generation on the worker side still lags the original computation by several orders of magnitude.

Geppetto targets that prover cost and the flexibility of the prover. For stateful work such as loops and MapReduce jobs, a multi-QAP encoding lets the worker commit to intermediate state as constant-size values and prove many computations against them, so the client does not receive all the state back. For proofs about proofs, the system uses elliptic curves that require the recursion depth to be fixed ahead of time and compiles keys for the specific verifier, gaining up to five orders of magnitude over the unbounded approach. For branches, the multiplexer moves to the inputs so an untaken branch drives its values to zero, tying proof work to the path actually executed. A streaming compiler built on clang and LLVM handles programs about 40 times larger than Pinocchio.

The speaker reports one to three orders of magnitude improvement for shared-state computations and up to five for bootstrapped proofs. In the Q&A, key generation was described as costing roughly one execution of the program, and the optimizations were said to combine independently. Certification of the compiler's output is flagged as a growing need as the compiler becomes more complex.

talks.title: The State of Hammer
talks.teaser: The session outlines five parsing backends, new combinators, tutorials, and attack-surface research on Hammer.
talks.summary:
Hammer is an open-source parser combinator library, and the speaker frames the past year as overwhelmingly driven by community contributions. The overview walks through what shipped, what people built on top of it, and what maintainers expect to tackle next.

Technically, all five advertised parsing backends are now in place: packrat parsing for context-sensitive grammars, GLR, LR and LL(k) for context-free cases, and a regex virtual machine. New combinators reflect awkward real protocols—endianness that flips mid-stream as in TIFF, alignment checks, DNP3 nesting that required scoped symbol tables, PNG-style permutations, and monadic bind for sequencing parsers. Contributors added language bindings and combinators; tutorial videos walk from environment setup through Base64 and JSON-RPC composition. Side projects include generating functions for grammars, tie-knot enumeration that raised viable knot counts toward roughly 266,000, in-progress link-layer grammars from pcap toward Ethernet, IP, and TCP, and substantial DNP3 work called out as especially painful to model.

Roadmap items include an All-Star backend matching ANTLR’s approach, moving away from packrat defaults that expose ordered-choice pitfalls, more bindings such as Lua, Rust, and Haskell, profiling to cut allocation churn on large buffers, and a general test framework before wider protocol grammar releases. Generating functions may help describe subsets of strings that trigger interesting parser behavior when studying attack surfaces, with related publication noted for Pure and Applied Computer Science.

talks.title: Connection-Oriented DNS to Improve Privacy and Security
talks.teaser: Shows how DNS can move from UDP to TCP with TLS, measuring the performance cost and the resistance to flooding attacks.
talks.summary:
The talk examines moving DNS away from plain UDP toward TCP, with TLS added so queries are private. The speaker explains that UDP-based DNS is open to amplification and spoofed flooding, and that queries and responses cross the wide-area network in clear text. The proposed change keeps protocol edits minimal: a client sends a special dummy query to signal support, after which both sides move to an encrypted TCP session on the same port.

The main concern is the extra round trips that connections add. The design addresses this with connection reuse, a fallback that stores small state on the client so a connection can restart in two round trips instead of four, query pipelining, and out-of-order processing on the server so slow answers do not hold up others. Trace-driven measurements showed reuse rates around 90% or higher at the suggested timeout, and server memory of roughly 4 to 8 GB, which the speaker considered manageable on current hardware. Modeled end-to-end results put the recommended mix, TLS between client and recursive resolver and TCP between recursive resolver and authoritative servers, about 20 to 30% slower than an all-UDP baseline.

On security, controlled experiments compared attack scenarios. Two attackers sending spoofed UDP queries were enough to drive the server to full CPU use and take it down, while TCP with SYN cookies handled the equivalent flood far better, and a single server tolerated thousands of non-spoofed TCP attackers. In the Q&A, the speaker said DNSSEC handles authentication while TLS provides opportunistic encryption, and that certificate validation can rely on DNS-based records or ordinary certificates. The takeaway is that TCP and TLS are long-established tools, but careful implementation makes them workable for DNS, and the speaker invited feedback through the IETF.

talks.title: Towards more Security in Data Exchange
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Towards more Security in Data Exchange.

talks.title: Error-Correcting Codes as Source for Decoding Ambiguity
talks.teaser: Shows how nested barcodes and error-correcting codes let one payload be read differently by barcode decoders.
talks.summary:
The talk treats file formats, network protocols and data streams as languages, and looks at how a chain of parsers reading the same bytes can disagree about what they mean. A typical pipeline has a synchronizer, then error correction or decompression, then a final parser, and sometimes a format classifier that picks one interpretation. Polyglot files are a familiar example, where one byte sequence is valid for several formats at once.

The speaker focuses on error-correcting codes, which are used in radio, storage and barcodes. Because the correction layer hides changes from the layers above it, a foreign packet can be placed inside a valid one, and both the outer and inner data remain standard compliant. The experiments embedded one 2D barcode inside another using QR, Data Matrix and Aztec codes, and tested 13 decoders, including multi-standard readers on iPhone and Android and a professional point-of-sale scanner. Results varied: some readers consistently chose the inner code, others the outer one, and some returned nothing or picked by chance, showing the behaviour depends on each implementation.

The practical concern is that an attacker who knows which reader prefers which code could target specific platforms, for example with QR payloads that trigger USSD codes, premium-rate SMS or browser exploits. Possible countermeasures include decoding every code found and letting the user choose, or preferring the stream with the highest data density, but these remain guesses. The speaker concludes that a rule set for dissecting multiple formats is unlikely to solve the problem in general, since the embedded data is valid under its specifications.

talks.title: Protocol State Machines and Session Languages
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Protocol State Machines and Session Languages.
talks.summary: A formal-methods researcher argues message grammars are insufficient for protocol security: session languages need state machines capturing SSH rekey cycles and happy-path MSC limitations. The talk bridges ad hoc bug hunting with verifiable models of multi-step authentication flows.

talks.title: Keynote: Dan Geer, "Dark Matter: Driven By Data"
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning Dan Geer, "Dark Matter: Driven By Data".

talks.title: The Miner's Dilemma
talks.teaser: Shows how open mining pools can attack one another with a withholding strategy and why that drives pools toward smaller, closed sizes.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at why cryptocurrency mining tends toward centralization. Because solo miners rarely find a full block, they join pools to share rewards, and the largest pools are open, so anyone can join. The speaker introduces a new attack called pool block withholding. An attacker registers with a victim pool and places a mole miner that submits only partial solutions, so the victim pays out rewards for work that never reaches the blockchain.

Using a game-theoretic model that works for pools of any size, the analysis shows that honest pool mining is not an equilibrium. Even when one pool gains revenue by attacking, two minority pools that attack each other both end up worse off than if neither had attacked, a tragedy-of-the-commons outcome similar to a prisoner's dilemma. The talk also covers how the blockchain's difficulty adjustment affects the timing of an attack, and how a pool can learn its rival's revenue rate by sending a small amount of mining power.

The practical takeaway is that open pools are vulnerable. Defenses such as bonuses for full solutions, seniority rewards, honeypot puzzles, or trust-based enforcement reduce the appeal of large open pools. The speaker argues this pressure should keep pools smaller and the system more distributed, though large open pools persist today partly for social reasons. The Q&A covered how a pool might detect moles and whether an attacker that also mines honestly can stay hidden.

talks.title: Forward Secure Asynchronous Messaging from Puncturable Encryption
talks.teaser: Explains how asynchronous messaging can get fine-grained forward secrecy without a server, using puncturable encryption.
talks.summary:
Asynchronous messaging such as email or SMS delivers messages to recipients who may be offline, which breaks the synchronous key exchanges behind protocols like OTR and the Signal-style ratchet. The talk presents a way to get forward secrecy for this setting without a trusted server holding prekeys, so that a later key compromise cannot expose stored old messages.

The speaker first walks through time-interval keys, then identity-based encryption and a hierarchical key tree that keeps the number of secret keys logarithmic. That structure fails when messages arrive late or out of order, since keys that could derive earlier message keys cannot be removed. The proposed puncturable encryption assigns each message a random tag and revokes decryption for that tag alone. A naive negation-based version grows with every message, so it is combined with the interval tree so that punctures reset each interval.

The authors built the scheme as about 4,000 lines of C++ on the Relic library and simulated message arrivals with a Poisson model. Choosing intervals that expect roughly one message each kept costs low, with decryption around 20 ms on a computer and about 55 ms on a phone. The scheme is best suited to bootstrapping a first exchange with a new contact, after which a ratchet provides per-message keys. The takeaway is that latency tolerance matters for forward secrecy in asynchronous channels.

talks.title: A fuzzing and protocol analysis case-study of DNP3
talks.teaser: Walks through a fuzzing campaign against DNP3 implementations and the protocol design flaws behind the bugs it found.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at DNP3, a standard used in electric power and other SCADA systems that grew from a serial protocol into a sprawling specification with loose message grammar. Adam Crane explains the core structure: function codes paired with object headers, with almost no rules on which combinations are allowed. That flexibility makes validation hard, and the protocol places little constraint on message content.

Crane describes a 2013 fuzzing campaign he built with a generational smart fuzzer, run against devices and software without source code or instrumentation. It used a simple metric: send a known valid packet, then attack packets in a tight loop until the device stops answering. The work produced around 30 CVEs. Recurring faults included infinite loops that exhausted memory, read errors, and buffer overruns, often caused by integer overflows in start-stop object headers. One reply from a field device carried a control object that should never travel in that direction, and a buffer overrun appeared only for particular trailing byte values. He also argues that a remote field site reached over serial radio or modem, which falls outside certain NERC CIP requirements, can be a path to the control center.

On the security side, he criticises DNP3's added authentication: field responses are optional to authenticate, aggressive mode requires speculative parsing just to be identified, and some objects declare lengths that disagree with their framing. His takeaways are to treat all incoming data as dangerous regardless of function, build parser tooling that works on embedded systems, and have standards bodies test designs with reference implementations.

talks.title: Nom, a Byte-oriented, Streaming, Zero-copy Parser Combinators Library in Rust
talks.teaser: Explores how Rust enables safe, zero-copy streaming parser combinators for tricky binary formats such as MP4.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens from a security angle on media and container parsing: hand-written C parsers for stacks like VLC face a steady stream of vulnerabilities, while ambiguous specs such as MP4 make correct parsing unusually hard. Some large formats see far fewer public bugs, yet simple fuzzing still turns up crashes, which motivates a safer, practical alternative.

The speaker introduces nom, a byte-oriented parser combinator library in Rust chosen for direct memory management without a garbage collector, slice-based zero-copy output tied to input lifetimes, and macros that chain combinators for readability. The middle covers streaming needs—incomplete input, producers that buffer and retry, consumers as seekable state machines—and developer tooling such as in-memory hex dumps, rich error chains that resist unhelpful backtracking, and pattern-based error management inspired by management of known bad inputs.

Benchmarking is framed as a usability tradeoff rather than a race to be fastest; parity with familiar Rust parsers matters. Adoption spans GIF, MP4, QUIC, Thrift, Cap'n Proto, and third-party streaming HTTP parsing. The close emphasizes embeddability alongside C, interactive debugging, and readiness for grad-level use despite Rust's steep learning curve, with TLS called out as still intimidating.

talks.title: CHERI: A Hybrid Capability-System Architecture for Scalable Software Compartmentalization
talks.teaser: Shows CHERI hybrid capabilities cutting compartment-switch cost toward plain calls for scalable in-process compartmentalization.
talks.summary:
The presentation opens by framing software compartmentalization as least-privilege isolation and noting that real designs trade security granularity against performance and complexity. Process-based sandboxes inflate TLB pressure, complicate multi-address-space programming, and push components toward awkward IPC; browsers may merge sandboxes when overhead grows. Prior CHERI work combined in-address-space capabilities, tagged memory, and MMU virtualization, plus compiler support so C code can use capability instructions instead of ordinary pointers.

The talk’s newer thrust applies that hybrid model to scalable compartmentalization inside one virtual address space. Virtual memory still suits coarse process boundaries; capabilities protect references with finer bounds and permissions. The design adds sealed capabilities, typed objects bundling code and data, and hardware-assisted call and return with software completion. Each thread carries a capability register file so mutually distrusting domains can switch without full scheduling, using an object-capability style runtime.

A Bluespec MIPS prototype on FPGA, CheriBSD changes, and LLVM-generated capability code support libraries that compartmentalize internally, legacy binaries in sandboxes, or fuller capability-system layouts. Benchmarks normalize against plain function calls: CHERI object invocation stays within roughly an order of magnitude of that baseline while Unix IPC paths sit far higher, especially without shared memory. Practitioners gain a path to granular isolation with familiar single-address-space debugging, while still owing careful reasoning about shared memory, pointer overhead, and side channels. Reference implementations are published openly.

talks.title: ADSNARK: Nearly Practical and Privacy-Preserving Proofs on Authenticated Data
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in ADSNARK: Nearly Practical and Privacy-Preserving Proofs on Authenticated Data.
talks.summary:
### Overview
This talk introduces ADSNARK (Succinct Non-Interactive Arguments of Knowledge on Authenticated Data), a cryptographic system enabling privacy-preserving proofs over authenticated data. The work is presented by Dario (joint work with Michael Backes, Manuel Barbosa, and Rafael Dowsley / Rafael Ryu). The core problem centers on a three-party application model: a trusted source (e.g., a biosensor or smart meter) authenticates raw data; a data owner (e.g., a patient or household) seeks privacy over that raw data while proving legitimate aggregation; and a service provider (e.g., an insurance company or utility provider) requires integrity guarantees without being able to see private inputs.

### Key Topics
- **Motivating Scenarios**: Real-world use cases include health insurance models (such as Generali in Germany using biosensor data for premium discounts) and smart metering for utility billing, as well as pay-as-you-drive insurance and loyalty programs.
- **Limitations of Prior Approaches**: Standard zero-knowledge SNARKs do not natively verify data authenticity from third parties. A generic combination involves embedding digital signature verification algorithms directly into an arithmetic circuit ($C'$ instead of $C$), but this incurs an estimated overhead of at least 1,000 multiplication gates per authenticated input, severely harming scalability.
- **ADSNARK Core Concept**: Instead of augmenting the SNARK circuit with expensive in-circuit signature checks, ADSNARK leverages state-of-the-art zk-SNARKs based on quadratic arithmetic programs (Pinocchio) and delegates the verification of authenticated inputs using a randomized homomorphic message authentication code (MAC) technique.

### Technical Details
- **Verification Outsourcing**: In standard Pinocchio-style zk-SNARK verification, a linear combination over inputs $vk_x$ is computed by the verifier. Since input $x$ is private to the prover in this setting, ADSNARK shifts the computation of $vk_x$ to the prover.
- **Homomorphic MACs over Group Elements**: To ensure the prover does not cheat and to authenticate the input, ADSNARK uses homomorphic message authenticators where coefficients are group elements rather than simple integers.
- **Input Randomization**: Releasing $vk_x$ directly would reveal private data. ADSNARK resolves this by randomizing $vk_x$ and employing homomorphic authenticators tailored for randomized computations.
- **Implementation & Performance**: ADSNARK was implemented as an extension of the `libsnark` library, reusing existing compiler toolchains, with additional cryptographic primitives sourced from the `SUPERCOP` framework. Benchmarks evaluated on constraint systems of 50,000 constraints with 100 to 1,000 inputs demonstrated that key generation and prover runtimes match plain zk-SNARK performance without signature verification overhead.
- **Verification Modes**: ADSNARK supports secret-key verification (comparable speed to plain SNARKs) and public-key verification. In public-key mode, verification time and proof size scale with the number of inputs (~100 bytes per input overhead), remaining below one second in practice.

### Takeaways
ADSNARK bridges zero-knowledge proofs and data authentication, allowing resource-constrained trusted devices (like sensors) to merely stream and authenticate data without performing heavy onboard computations or remaining online. Key open directions highlighted include achieving constant-size proofs in the public-key setting and extending these techniques to the RAM model of computation.

talks.title: A Messy State of the Union: Taming the Composite State Machines of TLS
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of A Messy State of the Union: Taming the Composite State Machines of TLS.

talks.title: Towards Making Systems Forget with Machine Unlearning
talks.teaser: Explains machine unlearning as a way to make trained systems forget deleted data, poisoned samples and private inferences.
talks.summary:
Deleting a record from an online service often leaves traces in the data derived from it, such as recommendations and trained models. The talk gives an example where a user removed a search from their history but still received related recommendations on another device. It also argues that a recommender can reveal private facts, such as a health condition inferred from item-to-item recommendations, and that a spam filter can be polluted by a malicious labeler. Retraining a model from scratch removes these effects exactly, but it can take days on large datasets.

The speaker's approach rewrites learning algorithms into a summation form, where per-record functions are added into a limited set of statistics. To unlearn a record, its contributions are subtracted from those statistics and the model is recomputed, which matches the retrained result while scaling with the number of statistics rather than the number of records. An adaptive variant covers algorithms whose statistics must be found iteratively, restarting from the previously converged point. Case studies covered an item-item recommender, a JavaScript malware detector, a PDF malware detector and an open-source spam filter built on decision trees, which could not be converted to this form. Changes to the recommender amounted to a very small fraction of its code.

The results show unlearning is much faster than retraining while producing the same outcome for systems that fit the summation form. The limits are that the approach covers only the learning algorithm's own lineage, not copies of models passed to other parties, and that identifying which data is poisoned remains an open problem.

talks.title: Protecting Private Keys against Memory Disclosure Attacks Using Hardware Transactional Memory
talks.teaser: Shows how private keys can stay inside CPU transactional memory, so an intruder's memory read wipes them.
talks.summary:
Private cryptographic keys kept in ordinary RAM can be exposed by memory disclosure attacks, such as over-reads in servers, even when the code itself is never tampered with. The speakers argue that existing defences are inefficient against this threat. They propose a system called Mimosa, which keeps the key out of RAM: it is stored encrypted, generated or decrypted on the fly, and used only inside a hardware transactional memory transaction. If another thread or an attacker tries to read that protected data during the transaction, the conflict aborts it, and the hardware automatically erases the intermediate sensitive values.

To make this practical, the authors reduced performance problems. They replaced instructions that cannot run inside a transaction, avoided true and false sharing of memory, temporarily disabled interrupts during the cryptographic operation, and added a short delay between transactions. With these changes the overhead was reported as low as 5%. In an Apache web server evaluation against OpenSSL and a variant without transactional memory, the three performed closely at low and medium loads, while the gap widened at high concurrency.

In the question session, the speakers acknowledged that disabling interrupts can affect other system activity and that tuning parameters may vary across platforms. They concluded that the approach protects keys against software memory disclosure and, because the key never reaches RAM, against cold boot and similar physical RAM attacks. They recommended the design for low or medium workloads.

talks.title: Security of the J-PAKE Password-Authenticated Key Exchange Protocol
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Security of the J-PAKE Password-Authenticated Key Exchange Protocol.

talks.title: Vetting SSL Usage in Applications with SSLINT
talks.teaser: Explains how misused SSL APIs in Linux applications break certificate checks, and how static analysis uncovered 27 unknown flaws.
talks.summary:
The talk examines how client-side applications use SSL/TLS libraries and why small API mistakes can quietly disable server certificate validation. The presenter notes that OpenSSL's interface is hard to use correctly, so developers often check results at the wrong point, leaving apps open to man-in-the-middle attacks. A real example was shown: an app that checks the peer certificate after the handshake, while a connection with no certificate still succeeds.

To find these mistakes at scale, the team built SSLINT, a static analysis framework. Correct library usage is modeled as signatures over program dependence graphs, covering both the data flow between SSL calls and the control-flow checks that must happen before reads or writes. A warning is raised when a signature fails to match. The tool, written in C++ on top of an existing static analyzer, was used on applications chosen from Linux distribution package dependencies that link against SSL libraries.

Across 485 Ubuntu applications totalling more than 22 million lines of code, the researchers reported 27 previously unknown vulnerabilities. Developers confirmed 14 of them, and four had been fixed by the time of the talk. Affected software included email clients, web applications, database tools and administration and performance testing tools. Some flaws persisted in current distributions even after upstream projects had fixed them. The presenter suggested moving toward alternative forks such as LibreSSL, and noted false positives from custom callbacks.

talks.title: SurroundWeb: Mitigating Privacy Concerns in a 3D Web Browser
talks.teaser: Presents a privacy-preserving 3D web browser that lets pages place content in a room without seeing sensor data.
talks.summary:
The talk presents SurroundWeb, a 3D web browser for immersive experiences in a room fitted with projectors, displays and sensors. Giving a web page raw sensor access could expose sensitive details such as object labels or a person's height and position, so the speaker frames the problem as a tension between functionality and privacy.

An online survey of 50 people asked what information they would share with a dance game, a 911 assistance app and a media player. Answers differed by application, and surface layouts seemed less sensitive than raw data. From this, the researchers defined three properties: detection privacy, rendering privacy and interaction privacy. SurroundWeb meets them with two abstractions added to HTML and CSS. The room skeleton exposes detected screens by position, size, resolution and supported events, but not the room itself. The detection sandbox lets pages place content relative to named objects without revealing whether they are present. A karaoke demo shows lyrics on a wall, a gesture playlist on a table and calorie facts under a coke can.

Sandbox content is non-interactive, the page gets no callback when it appears, and content is rendered eagerly to block side channels. In questions, the speaker said the sandbox cannot yet support interactive content, which might need a trusted intermediary later. The takeaway is that high-level room abstractions, rather than raw sensor streams, can balance immersive functionality with privacy.

talks.title: Heap Models for Exploit Systems
talks.teaser: Formalizes heap allocator behavior as a model that predicts chunk adjacency to help build reliable exploits.
talks.summary:
Julien Vanegue frames heap exploitation as a mostly manual craft and treats heap layout prediction as one of the hard sub-problems in automating exploit generation. Exploit writers often need to know which data sits next to a corrupted chunk, and allocators such as dlmalloc, ptmalloc and the Windows Heap differ widely, so generic techniques are rare. He reviews common heap bug classes, including heap overflows, invalid free, use-after-free and information disclosure like Heartbleed, to show why chunk location matters.

The core of the talk is a formal model of the heap as a transition system. Each primitive, such as malloc, free, realloc, coalesce, split and extend, moves the heap from one configuration to another. The model separates physical adjacency of chunks from logical free-list state, and argues that only extend and split change adjacency while the other operations reshuffle free lists. A fitness function such as best fit decides which chunk satisfies a request, and a worked test case shows how reusing a freed chunk of the same size could lead to a winning state.

Vanegue argues that metadata corruption is becoming less useful as allocators add consistency checks, so the practical focus should shift to which user data lies adjacent to other user data. He notes that multi-heap designs, the Windows low fragmentation heap and randomized allocators such as DieHard add complications the current model does not fully cover. The tool is still in development, so the talk presents research insights rather than evaluation results.

talks.title: Temporal Lensing and Its Application in Pulsing Denial-of-Service Attacks
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Temporal Lensing and Its Application in Pulsing Denial-of-Service Attacks.

talks.title: Post-Quantum Key Exchange for the TLS Protocol from the Ring Learning with Errors Problem
talks.teaser: Explains how a ring learning-with-errors key exchange can be built into TLS and how it performs against ECDH.
talks.summary:
The talk asks how post-quantum cryptography could be deployed in internet protocols now, given that quantum computers capable of breaking RSA and elliptic curve key exchange do not yet exist. It argues that authentication can keep classical signatures for now, while session keys need quantum resistance. The speaker introduces ring learning-with-errors, a polynomial variant that shrinks key sizes compared with plain matrix versions and whose hardness ties to lattice problems.

From this, the work builds a Diffie-Hellman-style key agreement. Because the shared values are only approximately equal, rounding with extra hint bits from the sender makes exact agreement almost always succeed, and revealing those hints does not weaken security. It was analyzed in a model for authenticated and confidential channels. One adjustment was needed: the server signature moves later in the message flow, since the usual signed Diffie-Hellman proof technique does not carry over to lattice assumptions.

The team built cipher suites with RSA or ECDSA authentication and AES, implemented the scheme in constant-time and variable-time C versions, and integrated it into OpenSSL and Apache. Raw operations ran about 1.75 times slower than OpenSSL's P-256 ECDH, but the server throughput gap in full TLS was around 25% and narrowed for larger transfers, with an extra 8 kilobytes per handshake. A hybrid suite pairing elliptic curve with the lattice scheme hedges against cryptanalysis. The speaker closes by cautioning that lattice assumptions are less studied, so parameters may shift, and calls for work on cryptanalysis and efficient constructions.

talks.title: Malicious-Client Security in Blind Seer: A Scalable Private DBMS
