talks.title: SoK: Secure Messaging
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding SoK: Secure Messaging.

talks.title: Ad Injection at Scale: Assessing Deceptive Advertisement Modifications
talks.teaser: Measures how browser ad injectors tamper with Google and other pages, and maps the affiliate networks and advertisers behind them.
talks.summary:
Kurt Thomas presents a measurement study of ad injection, where browser extensions, binaries and network intermediaries alter web pages to show deceptive ads without user consent. Complaints about injected ads often blame the visited site, so the study maps who is affected, how the software arrives and who profits.

Researchers embedded an integrity script in a sample of Google pages that recorded the expected content, then checked the rendered page shortly afterward. Across about 102 million page views, around 5 percent of clients had an injector, implying tens of millions of users. Most tampered pages contained injected JavaScript, and 65 of the top hundred scripts were tied to ad injection. Injectors run affiliate programs in which affiliates distribute software through bundling, social engineering or malware, and are paid per click or commission. Roughly a thousand affiliates were identified, and many extensions carried several injection libraries at once. Tracing injected ads on popular sites showed three ad networks supplying most of them, fanning out to about 3,000 advertisers, including well-known brands.

The researchers had 192 active Chrome Web Store extensions affecting 14 million users pulled, and they contacted affected advertisers and networks. The takeaway is that blocking individual extensions is whack-a-mole; lasting progress requires ad networks to stop syndicating traffic from injectors.

talks.title: Virtual Proofs of Reality and their Physical Implementation
talks.teaser: Explores virtual proofs that let a prover attest physical claims over a digital channel without classical secret keys.
talks.summary:
The presentation introduces virtual proofs of reality, a cryptographic primitive in which a prover substantiates physical statements about a local environment to a remote verifier over a digital link. The deliberate constraint is to avoid classical secret keys, conventional trusted sensors, and standard tamper-proof enclosures, motivated by treating shared secrets as high-value targets and by extending interactive proof ideas into the physical realm.

Three constructions illustrate what remains feasible under that model. A virtual proof of distance couples discretized separation between two speckle-forming optical platelets with a private setup phase where the verifier records laser position, angle, and interference patterns per distance level, then challenges the prover with random incidence parameters at proof time. A virtual proof of temperature fingerprints a deliberately temperature-sensitive integrated-circuit PUF during setup and later ties claimed temperature to matching challenge responses, including an FPGA proof of concept built from XOR bistable ring oscillators. Virtual proofs of destruction address irreversible change—such as shattered or burned objects—via an optical PUF nested inside an outer PUF whose removal is required to read the inner response, and via a quantum approach where measuring an unknown superposition destroys the state.

The talk closes by noting hardware proofs of concept for all three variants and a longer-term goal: encoding physical objects or processes into data that can later be shown to reflect real-world states. Audience questions probe exhaustive pre-distance enumeration—ruled out by standard strong-PUF un-simulability assumptions—and whether intermediate optics could fake separation without preserving the recorded wavefront phases.

talks.title: Cracking-Resistant Password Vaults Using Natural Language Encoders
talks.teaser: Shows how a password vault can resist offline cracking by using honey encryption with a natural language encoder.
talks.summary:
The talk covers password vaults, which keep a user's account passwords encrypted under one master password. It models an attacker who obtains the vault ciphertext from a server or the user's machine and runs an offline brute-force attack, guessing master passwords until a readable vault appears. The speaker argues that many human-chosen master passwords fall to such guessing quickly.

The talk first reviews camouflage, an earlier design that stores decoy vaults beside the real one, each under its own decoy master password, so wrong guesses still produce plausible output. The speaker shows a weakness: decoy master passwords share the real one's template, so an attacker who sees a plausible vault learns that structure and prunes guesses. In simulations using leaked real passwords, this cut the attacker's offline effort to about half of what standard password-based encryption requires.

The proposed fix is a natural language encoder, which maps passwords to bit strings using the kinds of models password crackers learn, so decoding random bits yields plausible passwords. Combined with honey encryption, it powers a prototype vault called NoCrack. Against simulated Yahoo leaks, the reported attacks needed far more online queries than a website would allow, such as 800,000 to recover nearly 87 percent of passwords in 2.5 million guesses. The takeaway is that decoy schemes must be checked against attackers who learn from the outputs they see.

talks.title: How Secure and Quick is QUIC? Provable Security and Performance Analyses
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in How Secure and Quick is QUIC? Provable Security and Performance Analyses.

talks.title: Riposte: An Anonymous Messaging System Handling Millions of Users
talks.teaser: Describes Riposte, a messaging system that hides which user wrote which message across millions of users.
talks.summary:
Encryption hides what people say, but the metadata of their communications still reveals who they contact, how much they send and when. The talk presents Riposte, an anonymous messaging design in which a large anonymity set of users each writes a message to a shared bulletin board. The servers learn the set of messages that were posted, but not which user wrote which one, and the design aims to resist an adversary who can see the whole network and control some servers and clients.

The talk builds up from a two-server straw man in which the bulletin board is held as secret shares. Each user sends blinding vectors so the servers can add their shares and recover the plaintexts without learning where each write landed. The main obstacle is bandwidth, because full database-sized vectors become gigabytes at scale. The fix borrows distributed point functions from private information retrieval, so clients send short keys that servers expand locally. A two-server version needs only AES, while a version tolerating more colluding servers uses public-key operations, which is slower. Defences against malicious clients are covered in the paper rather than the talk.

The speaker reported benchmarks for a database of about 65,000 rows, where a single server handles roughly 30 writes per second, or about a million writes in eight hours. The work parallelizes across cores and servers. The takeaway is that hiding metadata matters as much as hiding content, and that combining cryptographic tools with careful systems design can support anonymity sets about two orders of magnitude larger than prior work with similar guarantees. In questions, the speaker explained why ORAM was not used and why users' activity timing must be kept uniform to avoid biasing the anonymity set.

talks.title: Using Hardware Features for Increased Debugging Transparency
talks.teaser: Presents a malware debugger hosted in x86 System Management Mode, hidden from analysed code, and its stepping overhead.
talks.summary:
Malware increasingly detects virtualization-based analysis through anti-VM and anti-debugging checks, and hypervisor-based analysis tools carry a large trusted code base of their own. The presenter proposes a debugger that runs inside x86 System Management Mode, a firmware-level CPU mode whose memory is hidden from the operating system. Entry into this mode happens through system management interrupts (SMIs), which software can trigger through an I/O port or hardware events from devices such as network cards, keyboards, or timers.

The debugging client runs on the analysed machine and sends commands, while the SMI handler executes them and returns the results. Single-stepping is built on performance counters: a counter is preset so that it overflows after a chosen event, such as a retired instruction, and each overflow raises an SMI. Other hardware events can be used to get different stepping modes, such as branches or calls and returns. In the measurements shown, one mode switch into and out of the mode took about eight microseconds in total, but per-instruction stepping slowed execution by roughly 970 times. The system emulates side effects such as CPU, cache, memory, and I/O artifacts. Internal timers can be altered to mask the mode switches, but external timing checks cannot be defended against.

The talk closes by acknowledging that heavy stepping remains costly and that the approach trades performance for transparency. Future work would connect the system to popular debuggers through a generic interface, so analysts could use familiar front ends.

talks.title: Secure Track Verification
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of Secure Track Verification.

talks.title: Privacy and Access Control for Outsourced Personal Records
talks.teaser: Shows how to extend oblivious RAM to many clients with per-record access control, integrity, and a small overhead.
talks.summary:
The talk asks how to turn oblivious RAM, a technique that hides access patterns from a storage provider, into a multi-client design. A database owner outsources records and shares selected parts with chosen clients, as in a personal health record where a patient controls who sees treatment plans, prescriptions and bills. The speaker sets goals of secrecy, integrity and obliviousness against the server, modeled as cryptographic games where clients may be malicious but the server does not collude with them.

The speaker recaps path ORAM, where records sit in a binary tree and every access remaps a block to a new leaf. Its single shared key makes access all-or-nothing. The first construction, GORAM, uses public-key and predicate encryption with integrity proofs on each written path. The second, accountable GORAM, replaces those proofs with chameleon signatures plus logging, so bad writes are detected and rolled back after the fact. The third, scalable GORAM, swaps predicate encryption for broadcast encryption to get per-record read and write rights.

Benchmarks show integrity proofs take 110 to 180 seconds on the client across one gigabyte to one terabyte of storage, and dropping them in accountable GORAM gains about two orders of magnitude. Communication overhead against path ORAM is around 1 percent, or 7 percent for reads and 8 percent for writes on a mobile link. The speaker concludes that relaxing integrity buys much of the efficiency, and that the scheme suits databases around 250 megabytes but not yet terabyte scale.

talks.title: GenoGuard: Protecting Genomic Data against Brute-Force Attacks
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in GenoGuard: Protecting Genomic Data against Brute-Force Attacks.

talks.title: S$A: A Shared Cache Attack That Works across Cores and Defies VM Sandboxing ...
talks.teaser: Analysts investigate attack surfaces and defenses concerning S$A: A Shared Cache Attack That Works across Cores and Defies VM Sandboxing ....

talks.title: Controlled-Channel Attacks: Deterministic Side Channels for Untrusted Operating Systems
talks.teaser: Shows how a malicious operating system can recover application secrets from shielded programs using only page-fault traces.
talks.summary:
Commodity operating systems have large code bases, and a compromised or malicious OS, including one run by a cloud provider, can read a user's data. Shielding systems such as Overshadow, InkTag and Haven aim to take the OS out of the trust boundary by using a hypervisor or Intel SGX to hide application memory, while still relying on the OS for resource management, including page tables. This talk argues that this reliance leaks information.

The authors introduce controlled-channel attacks. Because the OS manages page tables, it can make pages inaccessible and observe the resulting page faults without timing measurements, producing a noise-free trace. Page granularity still reveals a lot: branches placed on different pages and large arrays indexed by secret values produce distinguishable fault sequences. The main case study targets Hunspell, where the page-fault trace of hash table lookups is split per word and mapped back to the input, recovering about 96% of the words in an entire novel. Against FreeType, the full rendered message was reconstructed with perfect accuracy, and libjpeg output yielded recognisable image sketches. Runtime overhead was modest, with Hunspell checking the whole novel in under three seconds.

Traditional mitigations are weak here. Rewriting applications to hide page-level access patterns is costly for large legacy code, and restricting how the OS manages memory may break functionality. The talk closes by asking the community to rethink shielding designs so that legacy applications stay protected from an untrusted OS.

talks.title: ObliVM: A Programming Framework for Secure Computation
talks.teaser: Presents a compiler framework that turns high-level programs into secure computation protocols with oblivious memory access.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces ObliVM, a programming framework that lets developers write secure computation programs in a high-level language instead of hand-built circuits. The central obstacle is that dynamic memory accesses can leak secret inputs, so the framework translates programs written in a RAM model into oblivious versions whose memory accesses and instruction traces do not depend on private data. A generic oblivious RAM construction is easy to use but is usually less efficient than customized protocols, which in turn are costly to implement by hand.

To get customized performance without that effort, the framework provides programming abstractions such as oblivious data structures, including heaps and binary search trees, along with MapReduce-style constructs. A loop coalescing technique lets programmers supply one total bound for a nested loop, which the compiler converts into a state-machine form. Using these tools, the team implemented three sparse graph algorithms that were reported to have better asymptotic complexity than the prior state of the art.

For performance, the speaker attributed about 50 times gain to the circuit back end compared with a 2012 solution, roughly 2,000 to 2,500 times to the language and compiler, and seven times to packing optimizations, for about a million-fold total. A 2012 binary search over a 1 GB database took about 12 hours per query, while a single query now takes a few seconds. Slowdowns compared with a non-secure baseline were about 100 to 113 times for distributed GMW. In questions, the speaker noted that the compiler currently emits Java code and that future work includes homomorphic encryption.

talks.title: Bitcoin over Tor isn't a Good Idea
talks.teaser: Shows how attackers can isolate Bitcoin-over-Tor users, fingerprint them through peer address messages, and deanonymize them.
talks.summary:
The speaker, from the University of Luxembourg, argues that Bitcoin is not anonymous and that routing it over Tor does not fix this. Bitcoin does not encrypt its traffic, so anyone between the user and the network, such as an internet provider or a malicious peer, can learn the user's address.

The first attack isolates clients. Bitcoin nodes ban an address once its misbehaviour score reaches 100, so an adversary who bans good Tor exit relays and honest peers, then injects their own, leaves Tor users only attacker-controlled options. Because the protocol has no peer authentication, a malicious exit can impersonate any peer. The reported effects include delayed or dropped blocks and transactions, which aids double spending, traffic confirmation attacks that reveal guard nodes, and linking several pseudonyms of one user within a session.

The fingerprinting method abuses address gossip: a node stores every address it receives, including junk, and shares them back when asked. In experiments, about 36% of a fingerprint survived ten sessions and half survived roughly 24 hours, enough to uniquely deanonymize a user. Two further attacks push clients toward malicious peers: filling the default 117 connection slots, and advertising honest peers with wrong port numbers. Hidden service peers, about 30 by the speaker's count, were discussed as an alternative, though they remain open to denial-of-service and Sybil attacks. No settled fix emerged from the questions.

talks.title: SoK: Research Perspectives and Challenges for Bitcoin and Cryptocurrencies
talks.teaser: Surveys open research problems across Bitcoin's network, transaction and consensus layers for academics and developers.
talks.summary:
This talk presents a systemization-of-knowledge paper that surveys Bitcoin research, built from several years of work across multiple institutions. The speaker argues that Bitcoin knowledge is scattered across the original white paper, forum posts, mailing lists, IRC and source code, and the paper aims to gather it in one place. The speaker also explains why the topic matters to researchers: billions of dollars of value, a real economy beyond criminal use, and a design that changed how the field thinks about cryptocurrency.

To organize the material, the speaker splits Bitcoin into three layers: a peer-to-peer network protocol, a transaction protocol with scripts and transaction graphs, and a consensus protocol built on mining and the blockchain. Most of the innovation is placed in consensus, which departs sharply from earlier Byzantine agreement research because participation is open and voting power follows computational power. Open questions include how a block-size change would affect the network, how far new privacy and smart-contract features can be pushed, including Turing-complete scripts, and which assumptions are needed to prove consensus properties such as fairness.

The closing part argues that researchers still lack a clear basis for changing Bitcoin's original design, so theory is needed to justify any change. The speaker addresses energy use, arguing that the power spent on mining supports a currency used by many people, and notes that mining-free consensus designs are being explored but lack large-scale practical experience. For practitioners, the takeaway is that many open problems remain across security research, and teaching Bitcoin is a useful way to introduce cryptography and systems topics.

talks.title: GraphSC: Parallel Secure Computation Made Easy
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding GraphSC: Parallel Secure Computation Made Easy.

talks.title: TinyGarble: Highly Compressed and Scalable Sequential Garbled Circuits
talks.teaser: Security researchers examine technical aspects of TinyGarble: Highly Compressed and Scalable Sequential Garbled Circuits.

talks.title: VC3: Trustworthy Data Analytics in the Cloud Using SGX
talks.teaser: Shows how VC3 runs confidential MapReduce analytics on an untrusted cloud using SGX enclaves and verifies distributed results.
talks.summary:
Running data analytics in the cloud exposes confidential data to the provider, its operators, intruders and possibly governments. Fully homomorphic encryption is still too slow for general-purpose computation, and earlier trusted-hardware approaches either left code or data unprotected, or relied on a large trusted computing base. The talk presents VC3, which protects MapReduce jobs from an untrusted cloud by keeping data and user code encrypted except inside Intel SGX enclaves, while keeping the trusted software to a few thousand lines.

The design packages the user's C++ map and reduce functions with a small library and a public protocol layer into an encrypted DLL, then runs key exchange and remote attestation before the job starts. Intermediate key-value pairs are wrapped and encrypted with AES-GCM, and their keys are replaced with a pseudorandom function over the original key. Each mapper and reducer sends summaries to a verifier, which checks that all input was processed, and that no data was duplicated or dropped. Availability attacks are out of scope, but the scheduler cannot read or silently alter results. An optional compiler enforces region write integrity, so writes through pointers cannot reach data outside the enclave, and a stronger variant also stops reads from leaving it, using a bitmap for write checks and range checks for reads.

The prototype ran on Windows Server 2012 with seven applications on a Hadoop cluster of eight workstations. The base system showed overheads below 1%, about 4.5% with write integrity, and about 8% with read and write integrity. Running map and reduce tasks in isolation showed higher overheads of roughly 4%, 15% and 25%. The takeaway is that trusted hardware can protect distributed analytics with a small trusted base, and the cost depends mainly on which memory checks are enabled.

talks.title: S&P15 Short Talks: Siona Listokin, Industry Self-Regulation of Data Privacy and Security
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for S&P15 Short Talks: Siona Listokin, Industry Self-Regulation of Data Privacy and Security.

talks.title: Understanding and Monitoring Embedded Web Scripts
talks.teaser: Shows how a browser-based tool traces what third-party scripts access on a page and checks it against security policies.
talks.summary:
Third-party scripts for ads, analytics and social feeds run on pages that also display usernames, email addresses or financial details, so they can read that data and send it elsewhere. JavaScript features such as eval and document.write, combined with compression and obfuscation, make static inspection of these scripts hard. The talk presented Script Inspector, a set of tools built around a modified Firefox that instruments browser APIs for storage, cookies and network calls and records a trace that a visualizer extension displays.

In a shopping-cart demo, the visualizer highlighted the product ID, quantity, price and cart total that one third-party domain had accessed, and a separate traffic capture confirmed those values were sent to that domain. In monitoring mode, the tool takes simulated sessions or reverse-proxy traffic, compares each access against a policy and alarms administrators to violations. Policies list permissions for DOM reads and writes, navigator properties, cookies and allowed network domains, and site-specific rules handle ad layouts that differ between sites. In a 40-day study of 100 randomly chosen sites from the top 1000 that embed 25 widely used scripts, 72 sites needed at least one site-specific permission, with 436 permissions added in total, about six per site.

The speaker noted that the approach complements Content Security Policy, since its selectors can describe ad placeholders, and that dynamic analysis cannot guarantee that every user-triggered behavior is observed. Minor script updates were not seen to break policies during the study, while a major rewrite might require retraining. The practical takeaway is to treat policies as a baseline that converges as alarms are reviewed, and to use the tool alongside static analysis.

talks.title: On Subnormal Floating Point and Abnormal Timing
talks.teaser: Shows how subnormal floating-point operations leak data through timing, enabling a browser attack that reads cross-origin pixels.
talks.summary:
A tight loop multiplying by a very small floating-point value, called a subnormal, can run more than twenty times slower than the same loop with ordinary numbers. Subnormals are an optional part of the IEEE 754 standard, and most processors handle them on a slow path, so timing depends on the data being computed rather than the code. The authors measured cycle differences across Intel Core i7 and Atom chips using both SSE and x87 units, and amplified the small gaps by repeating operations many times.

To turn this into a practical attack, the authors target Firefox SVG filters, building on an earlier pixel-stealing attack that exploited a fast path in one filter. Their version runs a convolution filter with an attacker-chosen subnormal kernel over an expanded copy of a target pixel, then times the rendering from JavaScript. The gap is about 20 milliseconds on typical machines, enough to read pixels from cross-origin frames. The attack stopped working in Firefox 27 when rendering moved to the GPU, and it has not been adapted to newer Nvidia GPUs, which handle subnormals with some slowdown.

The takeaway is to avoid floating point in security-critical code and use fixed-point arithmetic where non-integer math is needed. The authors released LibFTFP, a 64-bit fixed-point library built without data-dependent branches, division instructions or lookup tables, while noting that future hardware and compilers could still break constant time. They also argue that browsers should require CORS or CSP before scripts compute over foreign pixel data.

talks.title: Micro-Policies: Formally Verified, Tag-Based Security Monitors
talks.teaser: Presenters detail vulnerability discovery and exploitation in Micro-Policies: Formally Verified, Tag-Based Security Monitors.

talks.title: Counterfeit Object-oriented Programming
talks.teaser: Presents a code-reuse attack that chains C++ virtual functions on injected counterfeit objects to evade existing control-flow defenses.
talks.summary:
Code-reuse attacks such as return-oriented programming chain existing code fragments after a control-flow hijack, and many defenses watch for the telltale behaviour this creates, such as returns to unexpected places and stack pivots. This talk presents counterfeit object-oriented programming (COOP), which instead hijacks C++ virtual table pointers. Fake objects point to existing virtual functions, and those functions are called only from legitimate virtual call sites, so none of the usual patterns appear.

A main loop gadget, a virtual function that iterates over a container of object pointers and invokes a virtual function on each one, drives the computation, while other virtual functions act as individual steps. An addition gadget writes a sum into a field, and a string-copy gadget writes data. Overlapping counterfeit objects let one gadget's output become the next gadget's destination pointer. Working exploits targeted 64-bit Internet Explorer and 64-bit Firefox on Linux; the Internet Explorer one used 21 counterfeit objects, eight of them overlapping. A constraint solver arranges objects in a buffer, and a gadget search tool locates usable virtual functions in binaries. Main loop gadgets were found in common Visual Studio runtime libraries.

COOP injects no arbitrary code pointers, relies on no return semantics, and does not pivot the stack, so it evades code-pointer protection, code shuffling, heuristic detection and shadow stacks. The argument is that strong defenses need source-level knowledge of C++ semantics, since the binary-only defenses reviewed were judged vulnerable. In questions, the discussion covered Objective-C, detecting cross-library control-flow transfers at runtime, and randomising object layouts as a possible defence.

talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for S&P15 Short Talks: David Schneider, Certifying the Security of Android Applications with Cassandra.

talks.title: What the App is That? Deception and Countermeasures in the Android User Interface
talks.teaser: Shows how Android apps can hide phishing overlays, and proposes a visible origin indicator and a secret-image defense.
talks.summary:
Browsers show a URL bar that tells users where content comes from, but Android apps have no comparable origin indicator. The talk argues that the graphical separation between apps is also weak, and that one app can learn which app the user is about to open. Combined, these let a malicious app place a fake login window over a legitimate one at the right moment, as a demo of a counterfeit Facebook login showed.

The speaker grouped the techniques that exploit this missing separation into three categories, some already known and some new. An automated tool exercised Android window-management calls with different parameters and found a flag combination that takes over the full screen with no way for the user to escape. A static analysis detector checks whether an app both identifies the foreground app and draws over other apps, and whether those code locations connect in the control flow graph. Run on malicious and benign collections, it flagged a payment lookalike that mimicked the Play Store purchase window, and also app lockers that behave like overlays by design.

As a defense, the team proposed a system-level indicator in the navigation bar that shows the developer's organization name from an EV SSL certificate, paired with a secret image chosen by the user and blocked from screenshots. In a study of 308 Mechanical Turk participants, two percent of the standard Android group classified all four interactions correctly, while more than half of the group with the indicator detected the attacks. The takeaway is that the fix requires a modified system image, either built in or obtained by rooting, and the work points back to older trusted-path research.

talks.title: S&P15 Short Talks: Anoop Singhal, A Logic Based Network Forensics Model for Evidence Analysis
talks.teaser: Presents a logic-based model that rebuilds attack scenarios from alerts and logs when some evidence is false or deleted.
talks.summary:
The talk introduces a formal model and software tool for analysing digital evidence in network forensics. The speaker, from NIST with co-authors at George Mason University, starts from the problem that intrusion detection alerts can be false positives and that an attacker may delete traces, so the record of an attack is often incomplete. The goal is to reconstruct the attack scenario anyway.

The architecture centres on a logic-programming engine that holds rules for different attack types. Scanned evidence is converted into a standardised vulnerability format and stored in an analysis database, while a second database describes techniques attackers use to remove traces. Interaction rules and security policy are also fed in. The implementation extends an existing Prolog-based attack graph tool. A small example network, where an attacker can reach a database server through SQL injection, cross-site scripting or a buffer overflow, shows how an initial attack graph is produced from the vulnerabilities and alerts present.

Because that initial graph may be wrong, the analyst can test what-if hypotheses. The speaker describes enhancing the graph with expert knowledge and with the anti-forensic technique database, which adds paths representing possibly deleted events, shown in red in the example. The talk closes by pointing to related papers. The practical takeaway is that reasoning explicitly over incomplete alerts, and validating hypotheses, helps investigators judge which attack paths remain plausible.

talks.title: A Generic Approach to Automatic Deobfuscation of Executable Code
talks.teaser: Shows a taint-driven method that recovers simpler control flow from virtualized and ROP-obfuscated binaries.
talks.summary:
Malware often hides its logic behind protections such as code virtualization, emulation-based obfuscators and return-oriented programming. This leaves a reverse engineer with a tangled control flow graph that is slow and error-prone to read by hand. Earlier recovery methods tend to assume a particular protection, which breaks down when the unpacking routine is itself simulated. This work avoids such assumptions by treating a program only as a mapping from its inputs to its outputs.

The pipeline records an execution trace with an emulator, marks the inputs and outputs, and propagates taint forward and backward to find every calculation that touches them. Control dependencies, including implicit ones that arise from data dependencies, are identified using post-dominator relationships. Semantics-preserving simplifications such as constant and copy propagation and dead code removal are then applied. Because one shared handler serves many branches of the original program, basic blocks are duplicated so each use context stays separate before the final graph is built. In the demonstrations, a binary search program protected by a commercial tool and a Fibonacci program built with ROP tools were both recovered from their opaque traces.

Across four commercial obfuscators, including Code Virtualizer, Executor and VMProtect, the recovered graphs were generally more than 80 percent similar to the originals. The speaker acknowledged that the simplified code has not yet been executed to confirm identical behavior, because of pointer and memory issues. Results also depend on how precisely taint analysis separates input-dependent branches from the obfuscator's own branches. The takeaway is that a generic, assumption-light simplification can recover readable logic across several obfuscation styles.

talks.title: Readactor: Practical Code Randomization Resilient to Memory Disclosure
talks.teaser: Explains hardware-enforced execute-only memory and code pointer hiding to defeat direct and indirect disclosure attacks on randomized code.
talks.summary:
Fine-grained code randomization still fails once attackers use memory disclosure to recover layout, especially in browsers where script can drive JIT-oriented reuse. The work targets comprehensive protection for ahead-of-time and just-in-time code, real browser stacks, and practical speed, assuming standard deployable baselines such as non-executable data and address-space randomization alongside a strong adversary who can read and write permitted memory and run arbitrary computation in-process.

Readactor combines compiler instrumentation with virtualization-backed execute-only mappings on Intel hardware extended page tables, enforced through a thin hypervisor and Linux integration so code may run but not be read. LLVM changes separate code from embedded data, apply function-level reordering and related fine-grained randomization, and rewrite code pointers to trampolines in execute-only storage so indirect leaks from data pointers obscure true targets. For V8 inside Chromium, the design alternates writable and execute-only views so JIT compilation can mutate buffers yet deployed code stays non-readable, yielding an end-to-end hardened browser build.

Evaluation reports about 6.4 percent geometric-mean overhead on SPEC CPU 2006, with code pointer hiding near four percent and execute-only enforcement near two percent, largely from extra indirection and instruction-cache effects. Direct code-page disclosure is curtailed by execute-only enforcement; indirect layout inference via pointers is mitigated by hiding. Side-channel leakage and whole-function reuse when a pointer is already known are acknowledged gaps rather than solved here.

talks.title: S&P15 Short Talks: Volodymyr Kuznetsov, re: Missing the Point(er)
talks.teaser: Explains code pointer integrity, runtime isolation of code pointers, and limits of attacks on probabilistic CPI builds.
talks.summary:
Code pointer integrity (CPI) is framed as a defense that blocks control-flow hijacking driven by memory corruption, with reported overhead near eight percent and prior formal treatment plus open implementations. The design keeps direct and indirect code pointers in a dedicated safe region, checks accesses at runtime, and uses instruction-level isolation so unrelated program code cannot be steered into that region.

The speaker walks through a software fault isolation variant that maps the safe area into the upper half of user address space and enforces separation with a single-bit mask, yielding strong isolation on x86 with modest cost. A paper scheduled for the next day is said to target that isolation layer and a probabilistic flavor of CPI, not the technique’s overall model or its proof of correctness.

The takeaway is categorical: bypassing one randomized or weaker build does not break CPI as a family. Implementations with stronger probabilistic guarantees and fully precise, non-randomized modes remain viable, while the critique still exposes pitfalls that motivated releasing an SFI-based CPI implementation and hardening others.

talks.title: Securing Multiparty Online Services Via Certification of Symbolic Transactions
talks.teaser: Engineers explore architecture and security mechanisms for Securing Multiparty Online Services Via Certification of Symbolic Transactions.
talks.summary:
### Overview
Multiparty online services—such as third-party payment, single sign-on (SSO), and multiparty authorization—frequently suffer from critical logic flaws. According to the Cloud Security Alliance, these vulnerabilities rank as the number four top threat in cloud computing, enabling attackers to check out without paying, hijack accounts, or gain unauthorized permissions. While formal program verification could theoretically prevent these issues, developers rarely adopt it due to substantial practical hurdles: translating ambiguous protocol specifications into per-party properties, accurately modeling complex platforms and arbitrary attacker behavior, and proving inductive safety invariants across infinite state spaces. To address these barriers, the authors present Certification of Symbolic Transactions (CST), a practical approach that significantly lowers the verification burden by verifying intuitive, system-wide multi-party properties at runtime.

### Key Topics
- **Barriers in Traditional Verification**: Standard verification requires manually deriving formal specifications from informal protocol documentation, creating platform and attacker models, and deriving complicated loop invariants across infinite execution spaces.
- **Ambient Predicates**: Global, intuitive safety specifications defined across all participating parties (for example, ensuring an order is checked out if and only if a corresponding valid payment was completed at the cashier).
- **Symbolic Transactions (`simT`)**: Appending execution traces—specifically SHA-1 hashes of executed method source code—to transaction messages as they pass between parties.
- **Protocol Independence**: The ability of CST to enforce end-to-end security properties even when system implementations deliberately deviate from or violate strict protocol specifications (such as OAuth 2.0).

### Technical Details
CST operates directly on top of the actual execution platform without requiring an abstract model of the attacker, as transactions take place concretely. During a transaction, parties collect code identities into a message field called `simT` (symbolic transaction). Each step records the participating domain and a SHA-1 hash of the executed source method (e.g., `tstore.com::hash_place_order`). At the end of the transaction flow, the complete `simT` trace is passed to a verifier called the **certifier**.

The certifier consists of three components:
1. A **cache** storing prior verification results.
2. A **program synthesizer** that filters out steps from untrusted parties, stitches together the code of trusted steps, and appends an assertion representing the ambient predicate.
3. An off-the-shelf **C# program verifier** that symbolically checks whether the synthesized sequence logically implies the ambient predicate.

If the symbolic check succeeds, the result is cached and the transaction is committed; if it fails (for instance, if an attacker attempts to substitute checkout parameters using an untrusted store), the transaction is rejected.

The system was evaluated on open-source ASP.NET solutions, including two third-party payment systems (e.g., nopCommerce with Amazon Payments), three single sign-on solutions, and a multiparty gambling scenario involving four distinct entities. Integrating CST required fewer than 200 lines of code modified or added per party. Due to caching, CST achieved near-zero amortized runtime overhead. In an evaluation against 14 known vulnerabilities, CST successfully prevented 12 logic flaws (the remaining two were an explicit signature validation flaw and a client-side same-origin access violation).

### Takeaways
CST sits on the middle ground between static verification and runtime checking by executing symbolic verification on concrete transactions at runtime. Instead of requiring developers to understand complex protocol flows and design intricate per-party local checks, CST enables them to enforce straightforward, system-wide safety properties. Furthermore, because proof obligations apply only to the specific transaction executing at that moment rather than all possible transactions across an infinite state space, verification becomes practical and deployable in real-world systems.

talks.title: Missing the Point(er): On the Effectiveness of Code Pointer Integrity
talks.teaser: Research demonstrates that hiding CPI's safe region fails against side-channel and scan attacks that bypass the defense in seconds.
talks.summary:
Memory corruption remains endemic in unmanaged languages, and complete memory safety is often deemed too costly. Code Pointer Integrity (CPI) trades full safety for lower overhead by replacing code pointers with indices into a protected safe region. On architectures without segmentation, that protection depends on hiding the safe region's location with ASLR-style randomization.

The presentation argues that two core assumptions behind this design do not hold. Sensitive layout can leak without direct pointers, including through remote timing side channels that infer memory contents while corrupting dangling data pointers. Attackers can then locate the safe region with a slow non-crashing scan or a much faster crashing strategy that binary-searches memory; the latter is shown against nginx, yielding shell access after a modest number of worker crashes and byte scans.

Mitigations such as expanding randomization across the mmap space or shrinking the safe region alter the tradeoff but do not eliminate the crashing attack path. The speaker concludes that information hiding is a weak barrier, that CPI still raises effort for attackers, and that stronger approaches may depend on hardware-backed complete safety. A brief exchange with CPI authors clarifies that the study targets specific implementations rather than claiming the entire technique is theoretically broken.

talks.title: The Attack of the Clones: A Study of the Impact of Shared Code on Vulnerability Patching
talks.teaser: Measures how Windows users patch ten popular client applications, and how shared code and public exploits change patching speed.
talks.summary:
The talk looks at how client applications on Windows get patched after vulnerabilities are disclosed. Unlike server software, client programs cannot be scanned from the internet, so the researchers used a binary reputation dataset of roughly eight million Windows hosts to see which applications were installed. They tracked ten popular applications, including browsers, multimedia players, document software, an email client and a networking tool, across about 1,600 vulnerabilities over five years.

Installed files were mapped to vulnerable and fixed versions using the National Vulnerability Database and an open source vulnerability database, and the speaker noted that advertised program versions often did not match executable file versions. Survival analysis then showed how the vulnerable host population shrank over time. Chrome, which updates automatically, reached 50 percent patched within 15 days, while an application with fully manual updates never reached a milestone. Vulnerabilities in applications that share code were patched a median of 11 days apart, with a maximum gap of 118 days. Only 14 percent of hosts were patched when public exploits appeared.

The results argue that the simple linear vulnerability lifecycle does not capture shared-code cases, and the researchers built two proof-of-concept attacks that exploit them. Practical suggestions include consolidating how shared components are updated, and having installers detect and remove older versions of the same library.

talks.title: Cross-Architecture Bug Search in Binary Executables
talks.teaser: Industry experts analyze emerging threats surrounding Cross-Architecture Bug Search in Binary Executables.
talks.summary:
### Overview
This talk presents a method for cross-architecture bug search in binary executables without requiring source code or symbols. Motivated by developers copying and pasting code across projects—and consequently replicating vulnerabilities across platforms—the approach enables an analyst to take a known bug signature from one architecture (such as x86) and search for identical or similar vulnerabilities in binaries compiled for another architecture (such as ARM or MIPS).

### Key Topics
- **Cross-Architecture Code Similarity:** Comparing binary code across disparate instruction set architectures (x86, ARM, and MIPS), compilers, and optimization levels.
- **Sub-Function Granularity:** Searching for localized bug patterns rather than full-function matches, allowing bugs to be detected across different function implementations.
- **Semantic and Structural Matching:** Abstracting architecture-specific idioms by analyzing basic block semantics through input/output sampling rather than relying on strict symbolic matching or ASTs.

### Technical Details
- **VEX IR & Formula Simplification:** The system takes unstripped binary code and translates it into VEX Intermediate Representation (IR), which was heavily modified to abstract away architecture-specific idioms. For each basic block, the cumulative effect on registers and memory is compiled into expressions and simplified using the Z3 SMT solver.
- **I/O Sampling & Locality-Sensitive Hashing (LSH):** Rather than evaluating formula equality, the system uses random input vectors (empirically sampled between -1000 and 1000) to execute each basic block, collecting input-output pairs that represent its pointwise semantics. To avoid expensive set comparisons (like Jaccard index calculations), these pairs are compressed into Locality-Sensitive Hashes (LSH), allowing basic block similarity to be determined via a single hash comparison.
- **Search Algorithm (Best-Match Broadening):** A bug signature is defined as a piece of code containing the bug and minimal discriminatory context. The engine finds starting points by matching single basic blocks between the signature and target binary, then performs "best-match broadening"—a greedy, locally optimal expansion that incrementally adds neighboring matched blocks until the full signature is matched.
- **Evaluation:** Evaluated on real-world cases, including the OpenSSL Heartbleed vulnerability (TLS and DTLS functions), BusyBox vulnerabilities, and the Sercomm backdoor in closed-source router firmware across x86, ARM, and MIPS binaries.

### Takeaways
- The approach successfully ranks known vulnerable functions at or near the top of candidate matches, even across different CPU architectures and compiler optimization settings.
- Because the tool measures localized code similarity, it produces similarity rankings rather than proof of exploitability; it cannot verify path constraints or preconditions.
- To differentiate between vulnerable code and patched code (which often wraps vulnerable logic in conditional guards), analysts can compare code against both patched and unpatched signatures to see which version it resembles more closely.

talks.title: SoK: Deep Packer Inspection: A Longitudinal Study of the Complexity of Run-Time Packers
talks.teaser: Measures runtime packer complexity across thousands of malware samples using a new taxonomy and emulation-based tracing.
talks.summary:
Runtime packers compress or encrypt a binary's code and imports, then restore them in memory while the program runs, which slows reverse engineering. Estimates of how many malware samples use them vary widely, and generic unpacking tools often rely on assumptions that not every packer satisfies. The speakers propose a taxonomy that combines layers and regions, execution transitions between unpacking and original code, and code visibility into six complexity types.

They built an analysis framework on fine-grained dynamic tracing and whole-system emulation with virtual machine introspection, recording executed blocks, memory writes, API calls and process or file events. It was applied to almost 800 samples from off-the-shelf packers under various options, and to almost 8,000 custom-packer samples gathered over seven years from the Anubis database. Most off-the-shelf samples were type one or type three, and 10% kept no protected code in the last layer. Custom packers were mostly type three, with 14% lacking code in the last layer and no clear trend over time.

The findings challenge simplified models: over half of the packers used more than two layers, and interlaced transitions can confuse tools that look for a single jump into original code. Simple packers are easy to bypass, while the most complex ones are hard for malware authors to build, so medium complexity is common. The authors suggest the approach could support binary labeling and malware analysis, and note that samples that failed to run in their sandbox were removed.

talks.title: Unleashing Mayhem on Binary Code
talks.teaser: Mayhem discovers exploitable flaws in stripped binaries and outputs verified shell-spawning exploits using hybrid symbolic execution.
talks.summary:
The automatic exploit generation challenge asks tooling to find vulnerabilities and produce inputs that hijack control on a given program. Mayhem takes stripped executables without debug symbols, treats user input symbolically during exploration, and flags bugs when input can influence the instruction pointer. After a violation, it adds exploit predicates so a solver can craft concrete payloads that redirect execution to attacker-chosen code.

Binary-only analysis faces path explosion and memory costs in symbolic execution. The talk contrasts offline concolic reruns with online forking, then describes hybrid execution: fork until a resource limit, then suspend using path predicates as lightweight track points instead of full snapshots, cutting checkpoint size on a Ghostscript case from megabytes to hundreds of kilobytes. A second blocker is symbolic memory indices, where loads depend on input and naïve concretization failed roughly forty percent of exploit attempts. Index-based memory modeling refines index bounds from path predicates, represents possible memory values with index search trees, and applies piecewise linear approximation to shrink formulas and speed solving.

A demonstration feeds a compiled Ghostscript binary to Mayhem and replays generated input to spawn a shell. The system produced twenty-nine working exploits on Linux and Windows programs, including two previously undocumented bugs reported upstream. Practitioners should treat results as strong but bounded: coverage is incomplete, exploits are not guaranteed for every finding, and operating-system mitigations are out of scope.

talks.title: Signing Me onto Your Accounts through Facebook and Google
talks.teaser: A field study of Facebook and Google single sign-on reveals eight logic flaws that let attackers hijack relying-party accounts.
talks.summary:
The work reviews how Facebook and Google single sign-on behaves in production sites where users log in through identity providers instead of local passwords. Because identity provider and relying party servers are opaque, the analysis relies on browser-visible HTTP flows—the same evidence an external adversary could gather without insider knowledge.

The researchers frame SSO as browser-mediated message relays and use a traffic analyzer to build attack traces for three adversary roles. They report eight deployment logic flaws, each enough to sign into a victim’s account on a relying party; several cut across many integrators. One Google case shows sites trusting a valid signature while binding the session to an email field the attacker controls. A Facebook Connect case abuses Adobe Flash unpredictable cross-domain communication to steal client-side secrets that same-origin policy was meant to protect.

Disclosures went to the affected companies and standards bodies; Facebook acknowledged and fixed an issue within a day, and advisories followed for other findings. The closing argument is that secure SSO integration demands concrete scrutiny of signature scope, account linking, and client runtime behavior, because cookbook APIs and abstract protocol rules leave integrators room for repeatable, high-impact mistakes.
